Chapter 11 solution does not mean winding up airBaltic, and it will not require additional state funding - Hilden  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:26:42 UTC
00:26:42 KST

RIGA - The solution chosen by Latvia’s national airline airBaltic to initiate the restructuring of its financial obligations in a Chapter 11 process set forth in U.S. law does not mean the airline will be liquidated, nor will it require additional funding from the state budget, airBaltic CEO Erno Hilden said at a press conference on Monday.
He emphasized that airBaltic will continue to operate flights during the process and that passengers can continue to book and buy tickets.
Hilden indicated that this solution was chosen because the airline's existing financial obligations, combined with the investments required to implement the new business plan, require a more sustainable capital structure. He also noted that the financing agreements, creditors, and aircraft leasing obligations are international in nature and can be addressed through a single court-supervised process.
Transport Minister Rihards Kozlovskis (New Unity) stated that the government’s primary goal is a financially stable and sustainable company. He emphasized that private capital will be provided during the financing process and that the government has not committed to investing additional funds in airBaltic, which means that the private sector has a stake in stabilizing the airline.
The minister said that airBaltic’s business plan remains essentially unchanged, but the sources of funding are changing because the previous solution was not viable, and this option provides the full amount of necessary funding.
At the same time, he emphasized that the government’s long-term plan has not changed, and it intends to retain a 25 percent stake plus one share in the airline’s capital.
As LETA reported, airBaltic has voluntarily initiated a U.S. Chapter 11 process to restructure its financial obligations while continuing its operations. At the same time, the airline has secured a binding commitment from financiers to provide EUR 350 million in new financing to strengthen the company’s liquidity and operations at an interest rate of approximately 12 percent.
Consequently, the previous plan to raise up to EUR 257 million at an annual interest rate of 25 percent from bondholders will not be implemented.
The airline indicates that Chapter 11 protection shields airBaltic from creditors’ claims until the restructuring of its liabilities is completed.
Chapter 11 is a well-established U.S. legal framework, recognized internationally and used regularly by U.S. and international airlines, that allows companies to restructure their finances and raise capital while continuing day-to-day operations under the supervision of the U.S. Court. airBaltic is using this process to address its financial obligations and achieve a more sustainable capital structure. airBaltic notes that Chapter 11 is not the legal equivalent of the Latvian legal protection process.
The company also reports that flights and customer service will continue as usual. All flights will operate according to the scheduled flight plan; existing tickets and reservations remain valid, and passengers can continue to purchase tickets and travel with airBaltic as before.
The airline states that airBaltic has received a binding commitment from financiers to provide EUR 350 million in new financing to ensure the company’s liquidity and operations during the Chapter 11 proceedings (debtor-in-possession, or DIP, financing).
The financing was arranged by Strategic Value Partners and funded by Barclays, Hayfin Capital Management, Morgan Stanley, Oaktree Capital Management and Strategic Value Partners, to provide liquidity and support operations during the Chapter 11 process. The interest rate is SOFR + 8 percent (i.e., approximately 12 percent).
The company tentatively plans to complete the Chapter 11 proceedings by June 2027, subject to the necessary U.S. Court approvals and other conditions of the proceedings.
The restructuring process is taking place under the supervision of the United States Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York (the U.S. Court).
The company will seek customary U.S. Court approval to access this financing in the coming days. Together with cash generated from ongoing operations, the financing is expected to provide sufficient liquidity for airBaltic to continue its operations during the Chapter 11 process.
During the Chapter 11 proceedings, airBaltic will continue its day-to-day operations, and the company’s current management board and supervisory board will continue to fulfill their duties. The company will continue to meet its obligations to suppliers, service providers, and other business partners in the usual course of business.
As previously reported, under the previous plan, airBaltic bondholders were expected to meet on Tuesday, September 15, to decide on the terms of bridge financing of up to EUR 257 million at a 25 percent interest rate.
airBaltic indicated at the time that it had reached an agreement with certain existing bondholders and third-party financing providers on the terms of bridge financing of up to EUR 257 million; however, approval from airBaltic’s bondholders and shareholders is still required to receive the planned financing.
The airBaltic board has approved a business plan that initially called for raising EUR 225 million in interim financing to improve liquidity, using the existing collateral package for the 2029 senior bonds.
In the long term, the company is expected to be recapitalized with more than EUR 225 million in new debt and EUR 100 million in new equity, while a portion of the existing 2029 bonds will be converted into company equity, with the remainder replaced by new, smaller debt of up to EUR 125 million.
In August, airBaltic bondholders approved the capitalization of the interest payments on the next two bond maturities, as well as several other measures that provide the airline with additional flexibility in implementing its revised business plan.
Bondholders supported the capitalization of interest payments due on August 14 and November 14 of this year, adding them to the principal amount of the bonds rather than paying them in cash. A decision was also made to grant a temporary exemption from minimum liquidity requirements through November 2026.
The airBaltic group’s revenue last year increased by 4.2 percent compared to 2024, totaling EUR 779.344 million. Meanwhile, airBaltic group’s losses last year totaled EUR 44.337 million, which is 2.7 times less than in 2024. The airline carried a total of 5.2 million passengers in 2025, which is 1 percent more than in 2024.
Last summer, Germany’s national airline, Lufthansa, became a shareholder in airBaltic. Currently, the Latvian government owns 88.37 percent of airBaltic’s shares, Lufthansa holds 10 percent, the company Aircraft Leasing 1, owned by Danish businessman Lars Thuesen, a financial investor, holds 1.62 percent, and 0.01 percent is held by other shareholders. The company’s share capital is EUR 41.819 million.

Smiltens discusses cooperation in defense industry with Ukrainian prime minister  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14

RIGA - Justice Minister Edvards Smiltens (United List) met with Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi in Kiev to discuss implementation of Ukraine's judicial reforms on the path to European Union membership, increasing economic pressure on Russia, including restrictions on Russian grain exports, as well as expansion of cooperation between Latvia and Ukraine in the defense industry, the Justice Ministry informed LETA.
Also participating in the talks were Lithuanian Justice Minister Rita Tamasuniene, Ukrainian Justice Minister Denys Maslov, and Ukrainian Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi.
"We had a very specific goal during our meeting with the Ukrainian prime minister. We must continue to increase economic pressure on Russia and reduce the aggressor state's ability to make revenue to finance the war. At the same time, we can cooperate much more closely in the defense industry by combining Ukraine's wartime experience with Latvia's capabilities to develop manufacturing. This is practical work for security of both Ukraine and Latvia," emphasized Smiltens.
One of the central matters of the discussion was further increasing economic pressure on Russia. Smiltens informed Koretskyi and Vysotskyi about solutions proposed by Latvia to limit the flow of Russian grain at the Baltic level.
Latvia's goal is to reduce economic ties with the aggressor state as quickly as possible and to prevent Russia from using the Baltic countries' transportation infrastructure for its export revenues.
The European Union has already imposed broad sanctions and trade restrictions against Russia, however, there are still certain categories of goods that have not been banned. Latvia will continue to push for stricter restrictions, coordinating its actions with Lithuania, Estonia, and other partners in the region.
The meeting also focused on the defense industry. Building on defense cooperation outlined in the agreement signed this past June by Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the parties discussed the next steps to enable Latvian and Ukrainian companies to jointly develop and localize production of defense technologies in Latvia, to meet both the needs of Latvia and NATO and to strengthen Ukraine's defense capabilities.
Implementation of judicial reforms plays a crucial role in Ukraine's path toward European Union membership. Latvia, together with Lithuania, will continue to provide practical support for Ukraine in this process, including by sharing its own experience of reforms. A memorandum of cooperation signed by the justice ministries of Latvia and Ukraine provides for a closer exchange of expertise in the field of justice.
The officials also discussed further steps to hold Russia accountable for the international crimes it has committed, with particular attention paid to the practical establishment of a Special Tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine.
The Special Tribunal's mission will be to ensure accountability for the crime of aggression against Ukraine, including by holding Russia's highest political and military leaders accountable. Latvia will continue to actively participate in efforts to establish the tribunal and advance practical solutions necessary for its operation.
Preparations for this coming winter were also discussed during the meeting with representatives of the Ukrainian government. The Ukrainian officials pointed out Russia's plans to continue attacks on critical infrastructure, which is why timely preparation and provision of necessary resources are particularly crucial. Latvia will continue to provide practical support for Ukraine, coordinating it with the Ukrainian government and focusing on areas where assistance is needed the most.

Only a strong army can deter Russia from aggression - Budanov  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:26:35 UTC
00:26:35 KST

RIGA - In order for the people of the Baltic states to feel secure, Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia must have their own strong national armed forces, as this is the only thing capable of deterring the aggressor state in the east from potential aggression, Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of the President of Ukraine and former head of the Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense, told LETA on the sidelines of the Riga Conference.
"In my opinion, it is easier and cheaper to take deterrent measures to make aggression impossible," Budanov said.
He believes that it is not so important how quickly Russia would be able to rebuild its forces to threaten other neighboring countries after the war in Ukraine ends, as that would not be the main criterion in the minds of Russian planners.
"It is just a matter of Russia’s political decision," the head of the Office of the President of Ukraine said.
He noted that, unfortunately, geographical proximity to an aggressor state always creates tense situations and will continue to do so for the Baltic states in the future. To ensure security, the Baltic states must have their own strong national armed forces.
"This will force Russia to take the Baltic states more seriously, reassess its attitude toward the Baltic states’ military capabilities, and constantly reevaluate its stance on potential aggression," Budanov said.
He assessed future relations between Latvia and Ukraine as very good, emphasizing that Ukrainians are very grateful to Latvia for the support it has provided.
"I am convinced that the invaluable contribution Latvia has made in helping Ukraine will always remain in the memory of our people. And Ukraine will duly repay all the assistance that Latvia has provided us during these difficult times," Budanov said.
However, the former head of Ukraine’s military intelligence service does not have much faith in a swift return to peace in Ukraine, as there is no indication that the Russian side desires peace.
"As a citizen who cares about my nation, I sincerely want the war to end. I think every reasonable person around the world does. The real question is whether the other party involved in the war also wants it to end. This question still has no clear answer. To be honest, when analyzing everything that is happening, there are serious doubts about this," Budanov said.
While the Ukrainian president clearly states that Ukraine wants the war to end and calls for a meeting to put an end to the war, the Russian side does not agree, he noted.
"The Russian side is doing nothing that would indicate a genuine intention to end the war. It simply continues to issue ultimatum-style demands, even though they themselves understand perfectly well that these will never be accepted. It is just manipulation. Only those who want to play games to prolong the war act this way," Budanov concluded.
Regarding the alleged increased involvement of intelligence agencies in the Ukrainian peace process, he noted that security services have always been involved in such processes worldwide. Budanov viewed the possible direct involvement of John Ratcliffe, Director of the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), positively and noted that "Ratcliffe is a professional, and I am convinced that his involvement will benefit all parties concerned."
Budanov dismissed claims that the coming year on the Ukrainian front would be decisive as something that is repeated year after year, while the war just goes on and on.
"Issues must be resolved immediately, and the focus must be on today rather than waiting for some opportunity that might arise next year. Every time, new geopolitical factors will arise that will again have a negative impact on the peace process. Ukraine’s position is very clear: let us meet and end this war. On normal terms that everyone can understand. This is the official position of the Ukrainian president, which I support," Budanov emphasized.
If Russia does not change its demands and continues to demand everything without offering anything in return, Ukraine will continue to fight, the head of the Office of the President of Ukraine added.
Ukraine’s so-called red lines have not changed and will not change even if a country exerts pressure on Ukraine.
"Recognizing parts of our territory as conquered and handing them over to someone else will not happen. No one will redraw the world’s political map, and we will not allow anyone to do so," Budanov stressed.
He also opposes the idea of holding elections in Ukraine while the country continues to be ravaged by war. Budanov noted that so far, no one has made such a demand.
Asked about progress of Ukraine’s ballistic missile program, the head of the Office of the President of Ukraine noted that the Russians are already feeling the impact of these missile prototypes firsthand.

The filing indicates that airBaltic has an estimated 10,001 to 25,000 creditors, while the approximate value of its assets ranges from USD 1 billion to USD 10 ten billion, and the approximate amount of liabilities ranges from USD 1 billion to USD 10 ten billion.
The application was filed by airBaltic and its subsidiaries, Air Baltic Training and Baltijas Kravu Centrs.
The airBaltic filing includes a list of creditors holding the 30 largest unsecured claims.
According to these data, airBaltic owes USD 66.518 million Pratt & Whitney; USD 42.432 million to the Latvian Environment, Geology, and Meteorology Center, USD 20.067 million to the Latvian government (Ministry of Transport, and USD 15.428 million to the State Revenue Service (VID).

Relocating to Cyprus in 2027: The Complete Guide for Individuals, Founders & Companies  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:26:13 UTC
00:26:13 KST

By LaunchCy Relocation & Immigration Team
Updated for the 2026 rules and 2027 planning cycle
Relocating to Cyprus in 2027 is not simply a matter of obtaining a residence permit or finding an apartment. For individuals and families, the move can involve immigration, housing, banking, healthcare and tax-residency planning. For founders, it can also involve a Cyprus company, directorship, office premises, payroll and the question of how the business will genuinely operate from Cyprus. For international companies, the move may involve dozens of employees, different immigration routes for EU and non-EU nationals, office requirements and the relocation of entire families.
The practical challenge is that these decisions are connected. A company’s structure can affect the immigration route available to a non-EU founder. The location of a home can affect schools, commuting and the documentation used in residence procedures. A tax-residency plan can depend on the number of days spent in Cyprus and the existence of a permanent home. And for a company relocating third-country nationals, business registration and employee immigration must be planned in the correct order.
Several important Cyprus rules also changed during 2026. Anyone planning a move in 2027 should therefore be cautious about relying on older relocation guides that still refer to pre-2026 tax rates or outdated company and immigration procedures.
Why this matters to Baltic-based professionals and companies
For citizens of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, a move to Cyprus is generally an EU free-movement exercise: they do not need the same type of work and residence permission as a third-country national. The position is very different for a non-EU professional who currently lives or works in a Baltic state under a local residence permit. A residence permit issued by Estonia, Latvia or Lithuania does not, by itself, transfer the right to live and work permanently in Cyprus; the appropriate Cyprus immigration route must be assessed separately.
The same distinction matters for Baltic-based companies expanding into Cyprus. EU employees, non-EU employees, founders and accompanying family members can fall into different immigration streams even when they are all moving for the same employer. Mapping each person by nationality, role and family status before the relocation begins can prevent delays later in the process.
For an international business considering Cyprus as a regional base, this means the relocation plan should normally connect company structure, employee immigration, office premises, housing and tax planning from the outset rather than treating each item as a separate project.
Why Cyprus remains relevant in 2027
Cyprus combines EU membership, an established professional-services sector, English widely used in business and a sizeable international community. It continues to attract entrepreneurs, technology and fintech businesses, shipping companies, investors, executives, family offices and internationally mobile professionals.
For a relocating business, Cyprus can serve as a headquarters, regional hub, operating company, technology centre, sales operation or service base. The right structure depends on what the business will actually do, where management will take place, where employees will work and where customers are located.
For an individual, Cyprus may also be attractive as a long-term residence base. The immigration route, however, depends first on nationality and purpose of stay.
Start with nationality: EU and non-EU moves are different
EU, EEA and Swiss citizens
EU, EEA and Swiss citizens benefit from freedom of movement. An EU citizen can generally enter Cyprus with a valid passport or identity card. For residence beyond three months, the appropriate registration process should be completed. The Cyprus Migration Department states that the MEU1 Registration Certificate should generally be applied for within four months of arrival. Official Cyprus Migration Department guidance on MEU1
For companies relocating teams, this distinction matters immediately. An EU employee and a third-country national moving to the same Cyprus employer may require completely different immigration procedures.
Third-country nationals
For non-EU nationals, there is no single Cyprus permit that applies to everyone. The correct route depends on why the person is moving and what they intend to do in Cyprus.
Depending on the case, the route may involve employment, a Company of Foreign Interests, family reunification, dependant residence, permanent residence, Digital Nomad status, a startup-related route or another residence and employment category.
A point that is often misunderstood is that owning shares in a Cyprus company does not, by itself, give a third-country national the right to live and work in Cyprus. The company structure and the founder’s personal immigration position should therefore be reviewed together before incorporation or major funds are transferred.
Founders: incorporation should not be the first and only question
A founder relocating to Cyprus is often making two moves at the same time: a personal relocation and a corporate relocation.
A Cyprus company may form part of the solution, but the better question is not simply “Can I open a Cyprus company?” It is “What will the company actually do, where will it be managed, who will work for it and how will the founder legally live and work in Cyprus?”
Depending on the business, the move may involve company incorporation, shareholder and director arrangements, tax registrations, accounting and audit, payroll, Social Insurance, banking preparation, office premises and employee immigration. Where Cyprus is intended to become the real operating base, the company’s activity, management, premises and workforce should support that position.
Companies of Foreign Interests: a key route for international employers
For qualifying international businesses, registration as a Company of Foreign Interests can be particularly important because it provides access to a simplified framework for employing highly skilled third-country nationals. Since 1 July 2026, new registrations are submitted electronically through the company’s own identified CY Login profile. Business Support Center - Companies with Foreign Interests
The current Business Support Center framework includes an initial investment criterion of €200,000 in relevant cases. The company must also have appropriate business premises, and the premises must be separate from a shareholder’s residential property.
What changes for non-EU employees in these companies?
Under the current Migration Department policy, highly paid third-country nationals employed by a qualifying Company of Foreign Interests generally need a minimum gross monthly salary of €2,500, relevant academic qualifications or at least two years of relevant experience, and an employment contract of at least two years. Official Migration Department policy
A transitional arrangement for certain existing BCS Key Personnel earning at least €2,000 gross per month runs only until 31 December 2026. That makes 2027 renewal planning especially important for companies with employees currently relying on that exception.
The 70:30 workforce point becomes important in 2027
The strategy for Companies of Foreign Interests also includes a commitment to invest in Cypriot and EU employment. The current policy provides for a target of 30% of the workforce being Cypriot/EU citizens over a five-year period. After 2 January 2027, the ratio becomes relevant when new recruitment is reviewed. A company that has not reached the ratio is not automatically prevented from hiring, but the case may be examined individually.
For companies planning significant third-country recruitment in 2027, local and EU workforce planning should therefore form part of the business plan from the beginning rather than being considered after the immigration files are ready.
Cyprus tax rules changed in 2026
This is one of the biggest reasons to be careful with older online relocation material.
From the 2026 tax year, the standard Cyprus corporate income-tax rate is 15%, up from the previous 12.5%. Cyprus Tax Department - corporate tax rates
For individuals, the 2026 reform increased the tax-free threshold to €22,000 and introduced revised tax bands. Cyprus Tax Department - individual tax bands
For founders and internationally mobile professionals, Cyprus tax residency can also be relevant. Tax residency should never be confused with immigration residency: the right to live in Cyprus and the question of where someone is tax resident are separate legal concepts.
The Cyprus 60-day tax residency rule
Under the current Tax Department guidance, an individual may qualify under the 60-day rule if all applicable conditions are met, including spending at least 60 days in Cyprus, not spending more than 183 days in another single country, maintaining a permanent home in Cyprus, and carrying on business, being employed or holding an office in Cyprus. Official Tax Department guidance on tax residency
For founders, a genuine office such as a directorship in a Cyprus company can therefore form part of the analysis, but a directorship alone does not make someone Cyprus tax resident.
Housing and office search should start before arrival
Housing is often treated as the easy part of relocation. In practice, it affects much more than lifestyle. For families, it affects schools and commuting. For internationally mobile individuals, it can also affect the practical evidence used in tax-residency planning. For companies, employee housing can become a major operational project when several people move at the same time.
Office premises can be equally important. Businesses planning to register as Companies of Foreign Interests should not assume that a residential address will satisfy the business-premises requirement.
The best sequence is therefore to consider home, office, immigration and company structure together rather than running each search independently.
Where should you live in Cyprus?
Limassol: Limassol remains one of the main centres for international business, shipping, technology, fintech and financial services. It has a large international community and extensive private-school options, but housing is generally more expensive than in other Cyprus cities.
Nicosia: As the capital, Nicosia is particularly relevant for professional services, finance, law, government-related activity and companies that require regular access to public authorities.
Larnaca: Larnaca continues to attract relocating families and professionals because of its airport access, coastal location, manageable size and different housing economics from Limassol.
Paphos: Paphos is often considered by remote professionals, entrepreneurs, families and lifestyle-led relocators. For businesses that need a large corporate ecosystem, however, Limassol or Nicosia may sometimes be more practical depending on the sector.
There is no universal “best” city. The correct choice should normally combine work, schools, commuting, lifestyle and budget.
Relocating with children
Families should research schools before committing to a long-term home. Curriculum, availability, admission deadlines, tuition fees, location, school transport and the parents’ workplaces all matter.
A property can look ideal on paper and still create an unsustainable daily routine if school and work are on opposite sides of the city. For companies relocating employees with families, school and housing planning should therefore be coordinated.
Healthcare, Social Insurance, banking and settling-in
Receiving a residence document does not mean every other registration has automatically been completed. Depending on the case, new residents may also need to deal with Social Insurance, payroll, healthcare cover, GESY eligibility or registration, tax registration, banking and utility setup.
Banking can also require more preparation than founders expect. Banks and other financial institutions may ask detailed questions about tax residence, source of funds, source of wealth, UBOs, company activity, customers, expected transactions and the commercial reason for establishing in Cyprus. A well-prepared compliance file can make the process significantly easier.
A practical relocation timeline for 2027
6-9 months before the move
- Identify everyone moving and record each person’s nationality.
- Decide whether a Cyprus company is genuinely required.
- Review personal tax objectives and the country you are leaving.
- Decide whether the 60-day or 183-day tax-residency route may be relevant.
- Identify preferred cities, school requirements and approximate housing and office budgets.
3-6 months before the move
- Begin company incorporation where required.
- Assess Company of Foreign Interests eligibility.
- Prepare the company’s CY Login and corporate KYC.
- Start document legalisation and translations.
- Begin office, school and home searches.
- Prepare immigration files and banking documentation.
1-3 months before arrival
- Finalise the home and office.
- Finalise employment agreements and supporting documents.
- Arrange insurance and arrival logistics.
- Coordinate immigration appointments and family requirements.
After arrival
- Complete MEU1 or other residence procedures, as applicable.
- Complete residence and employment permits.
- Handle tax, Social Insurance, GESY, payroll, banking and utilities.
- Maintain ongoing corporate and immigration compliance.
The biggest mistake: treating the move as separate projects
A common relocation problem is fragmentation: the founder contacts an accountant, HR contacts an immigration adviser, the employee contacts an estate agent, the spouse contacts schools and someone else begins dealing with the bank. Nobody is coordinating the order.
This is where avoidable problems appear. The office documentation may not satisfy the relevant business requirement. A non-EU employee may not meet the employment criteria. A document may need an apostille from the home country. A founder’s tax-residency plan may have needed to begin months earlier. Or a family may sign a lease before deciding where the children will attend school.
The most effective relocation process works backwards: first define where the individual, family or company needs to end up, then establish the correct sequence for getting there.
What LaunchCy actually handles
At LaunchCy, relocation is managed as one connected process rather than as a list of introductions to unrelated providers.
Immigration and residency: We assess the appropriate Cyprus route and support EU and non-EU residence and immigration procedures, including EU registrations, residence and employment permits, Companies of Foreign Interests/BCS employee immigration, permanent residence and other applicable routes. Where legal representation or regulated specialist advice is required, we coordinate with the appropriate licensed professionals.
Home and workspace search: We do not simply send clients property listings. We take the brief, budget and location requirements, screen the market and prepare relevant options. We can arrange and attend viewings on the client’s behalf, provide photos and videos, compare properties, coordinate negotiations and assist with the practical steps around the rental and move-in process.
Employee and family relocation: For companies relocating teams, we can coordinate the immigration stream, employee housing, family requirements and settling-in so that HR has one central point of contact instead of each employee dealing independently with multiple providers.
Office search and company relocation: We coordinate office and workspace searches, Company of Foreign Interests registration, employee immigration and the practical relocation of the business operation.
Settling-in: Depending on the case, this can include utility setup, healthcare/GESY coordination, local registrations and other practical requirements after arrival.
Professional-services coordination: Where regulated tax, accounting, audit, payroll or corporate specialist input is required, LaunchCy coordinates with appropriately licensed professional advisers so that the regulated work and the wider relocation remain aligned.

The firm advises Cyprus and international businesses on statutory audit, tax compliance and advisory, accounting, company incorporation, substance, tax residency and Non-Dom matters, and redomiciliation or headquarters transfers. Its Managing Director, Sebastian Nikita FCCA, spent 12 years in EY Cyprus Audit & Assurance before establishing the practice. For readers who want to go deeper into the immigration, tax, company, employee and practical steps, LaunchCy has published a complete guide to relocating to Cyprus in 2027 with a more detailed framework for individuals, founders and companies.
The bottom line
Cyprus can work well for an individual, family, founder or international company, but the move should be planned as a system rather than as a sequence of unrelated administrative tasks.
For EU citizens, the immigration process can be relatively straightforward. For non-EU nationals, the correct employment or residence route should be established before the company and relocation structure is finalised. For founders and companies, the 2026 tax reform, the updated Company of Foreign Interests process and the 2027 workforce and BCS transition points make early planning particularly important.
The strongest relocation plans are usually the ones that connect immigration, company structure, tax, housing, office requirements, employees and family needs before any major commitments are made.

'Findings' Exhibition to Open at the Draugu House Gallery  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:26:09 UTC
00:26:09 KST

A new permanent archaeological exhibition, “Findings” ("Atradumi"), will open at 5 p.m. on Friday, 11 September, at the Draugu House Gallery in Konrāds Quarter, Cēsis. The exhibition brings centuries-old objects together with items that were lost or discarded only recently. The exhibits have been selected by well-known public figures, while children offer their interpretations of how unique antiquities may once have been used.
The exhibition is based on archaeological finds uncovered during the restoration of Konrāds Quarter. Archaeological investigations in the area between Cēsis Medieval Castle and St John’s Church began in the spring of 2024 and continued until last autumn.
Archaeologists discovered the remains of medieval timber buildings, the castle’s defensive wall, burials and numerous objects associated with the everyday lives and crafts of the town’s inhabitants. The finds include a 13th-century casting mould, medieval writing styli, amber rosary beads, fragments of wooden vessels, footwear and other leather goods.
However, the researchers preserved more than just ancient and rare objects during the excavations. In their view, even very recent finds bear witness to their time and can tell us how a place was used, how people lived and what habits they had. This idea has become one of the central themes of “Findings”. What determines whether we regard an object as valuable historical evidence or merely as an ordinary everyday item? And do archaeologists and people with no professional connection to archaeology notice the same things?
To explore these questions from a different perspective, people whose professional work is unrelated to archaeology were invited to help select the exhibits. The contents of the exhibition’s first display cases were chosen by technology entrepreneur Anna Andersone, actor and entrepreneur Juris Žagars, journalist Inga Spriņģe, poet Jānis Rokpelnis and digital marketing specialist Artūrs Mednis.
Each participant selected objects that surprised or intrigued them or made them reflect from centuries-old antiquities to very recent and seemingly insignificant items. In conversations with archaeologist Laura Lēģere, they learned what researchers had already discovered about their chosen objects and which questions remained unanswered. The conversations were filmed, and the recordings have become part of the exhibition.
Another section of “Findings” focuses on several remarkable antiquities, but this time it is the children who offer the explanations. In front of the camera, they try to work out how the objects discovered by archaeologists may once have been used and how they were made. Their guesses and conclusions provide a captivating and touching insight into how a centuries-old past is interpreted through the experiences and imagination of a child today.
“When creating history exhibitions, I have always tried to find unconventional ways of making the distant past understandable and engaging for contemporary audiences. This time, the circumstances offered an especially good opportunity to experiment with an unusual format to let people from entirely different fields select the finds and to entrust the interpretation of some antiquities to children. It was a wonderful experience. I am particularly delighted that we were able to involve so many different people in creating the exhibition from Cēsis and Riga, seasoned professionals and children with their own perspectives and ideas. To me, this meeting of different viewpoints is the very essence of ‘Findings’,” says Gundars Kalniņš, the exhibition’s curator and the author of its concept.
Although “Findings” has been created as a permanent exhibition, its contents will evolve over time. From time to time, some of the display cases will be completely renewed to feature finds selected by other well-known public figures. The exhibition’s next transformation will reveal which objects from the rich collection of archaeological finds uncovered in the courtyard of Konrāds Quarter have been chosen by educator Edgars Plētiens, editor Nellija Ločmele, event host Valdis Melderis, entrepreneur Egija Gailuma and artist Kristians Brekte.
“Findings” will therefore have no single definitive version. As the display cases and the people whose choices they present change, the story told by the exhibition will change as well giving visitors a reason to return again and again.

30th Meeting of the Baltic Councils of Notaries: Notaries from Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania Gathered Together to Discuss the Future of Notariat  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:26:02 UTC
00:26:02 KST

The 30th Meeting of the Baltic Councils of Notaries was held on 04 September this year in Palanga – it is a traditional forum of Lithuanian, Latvian and Estonian notary self-governing bodies, where delegations of notaries from the three Baltic States shared the most relevant profession-specific news, discussed changes and challenges in notary activities, and debated about the future of notariat in a rapidly developing legal and technological environment.
The assembled delegations of notaries from the three countries were congratulated on their anniversary meeting in Palanga by the Minister of Justice of the Republic of Lithuania, Rita Tamašunienė, and the Chairman of the Committee on Legal Affairs of the Seimas of the Republic of Lithuania, Julius Sabatauskas. Insights into the image of the notary profession on social networks were shared by the founder of UAB Repsense, a Communication Strategist, Mykolas Katkus. The President of the Lithuanian Academy of Sciences, Academician Prof. Dr Vytautas Nekrošius, spoke about the path taken by the Latin notariat and its prospects, and the Dean of the Faculty of Law of Vilnius University Prof. Dr Vigita Vėbraitė presented the ways how to encourage the younger generation of lawyers to choose the notary profession.
Although each country’s legal system and the competencies of notaries differ, digitalisation, cyber security, customer service quality, availability of notary services, attractiveness of the profession and discussions on the development of the functions assigned to notaries occupy an increasingly prominent place in the agenda of notaries in all three Baltic States.
Lithuanian Notariat – More Attention Drawn to New Functions
President of the Lithuanian Chamber of Notaries, Marius Stračkaitis, underlined during the conference:
“Notaries in the Baltic States face indistinguishable challenges. We must ensure that technological progress not only speeds up the work of notaries, but also reinforces legal security, customer trust, and service accessibility. At the same time, we see that certain non-contentious functions can be effectively carried out not in courts, but in notary offices. In Lithuania, after successfully implementing the reform of notarial divorce in cases where spouses do not have minor children, another step could be taken in the future, namely, the possibility of allowing notarial divorce for spouses with minor children is being considered.”
According to him, this is what legal scholars from the JuWiLi II project “Justice Without Litigation” recommend for Lithuania. They also paid attention to a unique European-wide condition enshrined in Lithuanian law – that spouses can divorce at a notary only if they have not lived in conjugality for more than a year and do not run a joint household.
“I believe it is worth commencing a discussion in Lithuania on the waiver of the currently valid condition that spouses can only terminate their marriage with a notary when they have not been living in conjugality for more than a year and are not running a joint household. In 2025, notaries approved 1,179 contracts for divorce by mutual consent of both spouses, and 6,180 cases were resolved in the courts of first instance on this issue. Thus, it is obvious that the waiver of the aforesaid conditions would help to further reduce the workload of the courts,” stated M. Stračkaitis.
Estonian Notariat Strengthens Customer Protection and Digitalisation
President of the Estonian Chamber of Notaries, Merle Saar-Johanson, welcomed the participants of the meeting and highlighted the significance of the long-standing partnership between the notaries of the Baltic States and the opportunity to learn from each other.
President of the Estonian Chamber of Notaries, M. Saar-Johanson, underlined:
“As we celebrate the 30th anniversary of the Baltic notary’s cooperation, I am particularly pleased that the Lithuanian Chamber of Notaries has decided to mark this milestone anniversary with such care and solemnity. I greatly appreciate our cooperation and am proud to have been a part of it. Although we gather annually, and sometimes it may appear that twelve months is a too short time for major changes to occur, I still take away from each meeting of the Baltic notaries the same feeling that the notaries of all our countries have done something exceptional that others can learn from. We always have something to celebrate – the notaries of the Baltic States are constantly improving, and our meetings maintain a truly warm and open atmosphere. It is this combination of professional progress, mutual trust and friendship that unites and strengthens us. I sincerely hope that this tradition will be preserved for many years.”
The Estonian notariat is dedicating 2026 to four main directions: updating notary fees, improving customer experience, preventing fraud and money laundering, and bolstering cyber security.
To better protect customers from fraud risks, the Estonian Chamber of Notaries is cooperating with the police and the banking sector and improving the capabilities of notaries to recognise potential fraud cases. At the same time, the future of digital archiving of notarial documents in Estonia is being considered and solutions are being sought that would allow for more efficient use of the already accumulated electronic data of notarial documentation.
“As since 2009, electronic copies of certified documents have been stored in the Estonian e-Notary system, the possibility of creating a digital archive of notarial documents in the future and therefore, gradually abandoning paper archiving is being analysed,” the President of the Estonian Chamber of Notaries presented one of the considered directions for digitising the Estonian notariat.
Latvian Notariat Expands Functions and Improves Sustainability of Services
This year, the Latvian notariat is paying close attention to the development of notary functions, the financial sustainability of services, and the continuity of notarial operations.
In April, notary fees in Latvia were increased in response to rising consumer prices and the increased costs of rendering notarial services, including ICT (Information and Communication Technology) system maintenance costs. Several of the revised fees had not been reviewed for the previous ten years. New rates were also introduced for additional functions assigned to notaries in succession proceedings.
One of the most relevant innovations in Latvia is that, as of 1 March this year, the divorce procedure has been altered for spouses with minor children. Agreements on child custody, contact rights and child maintenance in such cases must be concluded in the form of a notarial deed (previously – mandatory). If one of the parents fails to comply with such an agreement, enforcement may be initiated on its basis through an out-of-court procedure.
According to the President of the Latvian Council of Sworn Notaries, Aigars Kaupe, this innovation is one of the practical examples of transferring non-contentious functions to notaries, which is also being discussed in the context of the JuWiLi II Justice Without Litigation project.
A. Kaupe stated:
“Over the years, the notariat has successfully assumed new functions for the benefit of both the state and society while maintaining high professional standards and legal certainty. For example, at the request of the Ministry of Justice, the Latvian notariat is currently exploring also the possibility of taking on Land Registry functions, as well as certain functions currently performed by guardianship and curatorship institutions. While the assessment is still underway, I am confident that the notariat would also be capable of performing such functions effectively.”
During the Assembly meeting, A. Kaupe also emphasised the significance of cooperation among the notaries of the Baltic States and their long-standing shared traditions, which reflect a strong partnership and unity.
“We have always supported one another, and these meetings give us the opportunity to learn from each other, grow together and inspire one another.”
A. Kaupe also expressed his sincere appreciation for the well-organised anniversary conference, which placed valuable focus on issues and challenges of particular importance to notaries in the digital age, including effective communication and the need to attract new professionals to the profession.
“The Baltic notariats must continue to strengthen their role in society, uphold the rule of law, and work together to meet future challenges.”
About the Meeting of the Baltic Chambers of Notaries
The annual meeting of the Baltic Chambers of Notaries is a long-established tradition that brings together notaries from Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia to review the past year’s achievements and to exchange opinions on the most relevant changes at the national, European and international levels. Last year, the meeting was hosted in Latvia, and next year it will be held in Estonia.

The Rīga Conference 2026: Global Security and Foreign Policy Experts Gather to Address the Future of Europe  - The Baltic Times

From September 10 to 11, 2026, the National History Museum of Latvia will hostthe annual largest security and foreign policy forum in the Nordic region “The Rīga Conference 2026”. This year, the forum will bring together influential leaders, experts, diplomats, policymakers, and business executives from around the globe. The agenda will center on European economic resilience and building a united front against emerging internal and external challenges.
President of the Republic of Latvia Edgars Rinkēvičs will deliver the opening address, with Minister of the Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Latvia Baiba Braže and Minister of Defence of the Republic of Latvia Raivis Melnis taking part in key panel discussions. The lineup of featured international speakers includes US Ambassador to the European Union Andrew Puzder, NATO Senior Representative in Ukraine Patrick Turner, NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska, The Chief of Defence of the Bundeswehr Carsten Breuer, and Executive Director of the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Juhan Lepassaar. The conference will conclude with closing remarks by Prime Minister of the Republic of Latvia Andris Kulbergs and Chairman of the Board of the Latvian Transatlantic Organisation (LATO) Jānis Karlsbergs.
“This year, the Riga Conference brings together a record number of like-minded foreign ministers, representatives of NATO and Allied armed forces, leading experts and opinion leaders. Riga is where we can have focused discussions on coordinated and targeted responses to today’s geopolitical challenges. Russia is working with Iran and North Korea, undermining international law and fuelling global food and energy insecurity. Our response cannot be fragmented or come too late. We need to strengthen our defence capabilities, invest in technological superiority, reduce strategic dependencies and remain unwavering in our support for Ukraine. Latvia is not just talking about these challenges — we are taking action and sharing our knowledge and experience with Allies and partners. The Riga Conference is about turning discussion into concrete decisions and action. Latvia is ready to help drive that action,” says Baiba Braže, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Latvia.
A central focus of the main program will be diplomatic agency in a changing world, examining how foreign policy tools can safeguard democratic interests amid mounting hybrid threats and violations of international law. Experts will also evaluate Europe’s economic resilience and shifting political identity, with key contributions from Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade of Ireland Helen McEntee and Commissioner for Economy and Productivity at the European Commission Valdis Dombrovskis.
“At a time when the international order is tested not only by overt military aggression in Ukraine, but also by complex hybrid threats and growing economic fragmentation, military readiness alone is no longer enough to guarantee security. The defense capabilities of democratic nations are inextricably linked to our comprehensive resilience and our ability to unite for collective action. This year’s Rīga Conference provides a clear impetus for the transatlantic community to pool resources and expertise, ranging from battlefield lessons learned in Ukraine to boosting Europe’s long-term competitiveness. In doing so, Latvia and the Baltic states are not merely participating in these discussions, but are demonstrating our region’s critical role in shaping global security,” emphasizes Jānis Karlsbergs, Chairman of the Board of the Latvian Transatlantic Organisation.
Special focus will be placed on integrating Ukraine’s battlefield experience and technological innovations into NATO defense planning and force development. Panel discussions on the Alliance’s deterrence capabilities and readiness for future conflicts will feature The Chief of Defence of the Bundeswehr Carsten Breuer, Senior Fellow with the Transatlantic Defense and Security Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis David M. Cattler, and Chief of Defence of the Republic of Latvia Kaspars Pudāns.
“The security environment is changing faster than ever, so we must learn quickly. Ukraine’s experience shows that the ability to rapidly adopt new technologies, work closely with the defence industry and adapt capabilities to real-world threats is crucial. Our task is to absorb these lessons systematically and without delay in order to strengthen deterrence and defence across the Alliance,” emphasizes Raivis Melnis, Minister of Defence of Latvia.
The conference agenda also addresses cognitive warfare, disinformation, and cybersecurity, featuring analysis from Jānis Sārts, Director of the NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence, and Juhan Lepassaar, Executive Director of ENISA. Meanwhile, Russia’s internal transformation and its broader geopolitical fallout will be examined by Alexander Gabuev, Director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, and Russian opposition politician Vladimir Milov. The program will conclude with a special session on moral stance and memory preservation, highlighting perspectives from Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych.
Ahead of the main program, on September 9, The Rīga Conference Business Forum will take place in Mazā aula at the University of Latvia. The event will bring together business leaders, policymakers, and financial experts to assess the impact of the geopolitical climate on enterprises and discuss access to European financing instruments. Particular attention will focus on cybersecurity, supply chain protection, and dual-use technologies. Discussions will also explore ways public-private partnerships can bolster regional competitiveness.
In parallel with the main agenda, a series of public side events will take place on September 10 from 9:00 AM to 1:00 PM in Mazā aula at the University of Latvia. Open to the public with prior registration, these sessions will gather international experts, diplomats, and researchers to examine Latvia–India cooperation in an evolving geopolitical landscape, analyze the role of gender in societal resilience and crisis management, and discuss Black Sea security and critical infrastructure connectivity. To register, participants are invited to email [email protected].
Since 2006, The Rīga Conference has served as one of Northern Europe’s primary platforms for security and foreign policy dialogue. The forum is expected to gather 400 participants from more than 40 countries. Hosted in a hybrid format, the event will be streamed live at www.rigaconference.lv, broadcast by Latvian and international media partners, and made available on Facebook and YouTube.
The Rīga Conference is jointly organized by the Latvian Transatlantic Organisation in cooperation with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Latvia and the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Latvia.

VILNIUS – A “common approach” on European security issues is needed, whether the discussion concerns security in the Arctic or in the Baltic Sea, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda has said.
“It is important to make sure that a common approach is applied to the issues of security, no matter if we are talking about the Arctic or we talk about the Baltic Sea. What’s important is that Russia's behavior is aggressive. We see the growing number of incidents across Europe, and there is no reason to expect that something will change in coming months,” the Lithuanian leader told reporters at the European Arctic Summit hosted by Finland in Lapland.
He also pointed out that China’s increasingly active presence in the Arctic is influencing the situation in the region.
“What is also important, we have to see that China’s presence in the Arctic region is increasing. The footprint is here. So far, it's rather a research or a scientific footprint, but it might be followed by military activities or military footprint in the region,” he stressed.
“The European Union must implement the Arctic policy formulated in 2021, taking into account new geopolitical realities which are around us, taking into account the threats around us. For me, it's very important to achieve that the European Union and NATO are cooperating – not duplicating each other, but complementing each other and increasing the footprint of NATO within the EU,” Nauseda said.
According to the Lithuanian leader, “Europe has to do its part by strengthening economic resilience and improving connectivity, but NATO also has to take the chance to increase its military presence, military deployment in this region”.
“And I think this is, first of all, very important, looking from the perspective of deterrence. For me, deterrence is the main factor. If we are credible, if we are active, if we respond, then we can expect that we will have this sufficient level of deterrence for Russia not to test our ability to defend ourselves,” Nauseda noted.
“This (Russia’s provocations) is taking place not only in the Baltic states or Poland. It's taking place in Germany and other countries. And for me, it's a clear sign that this time Russia is challenging all of us. We should not talk about concrete geographic regions, because Russia's goal is much more ambitious: to test the rule of law, to test our style of life, to test the democracy. And I think they will put additional efforts to do it. So, it would be naive to expect that the Arctic will be free of malign activities on Russia's side,” he emphasized.
The summit in Rovaniemi, attended by heads of state and government from EU member states, is discussing the growing importance of the Arctic region to European security.
On Tuesday, Nauseda is scheduled to meet with Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo and visit the Patria armored vehicle production facility.

Now the past threatens to catch up with Maria, and in the postwar chaos, she is forced to do everything in her power to preserve her status as the new mistress of the house - just like thousands of other women who, in 1945, in the weeks leading up to and immediately following Denmark’s liberation, were hounded and publicly humiliated by their fellow citizens for having intimate relationships with German soldiers.
Co-producers Nafta Films is a film production company in the Baltic region operating in Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia. The company employs 30 full-time staff members across all three Baltic countries, and the group’s annual revenue last year reached approximately EUR 12 million.

Israel's High Court signals it will not order police probe into 2023 death of Yuval Kestelman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:23:44 UTC
00:23:44 KST

The High Court of Justice on Monday signaled that it was unlikely to order a criminal investigation into Jerusalem police officers over their handling of the inquiry into the death of Yuval Kestelman, killed in 2023 when mistaken for a terrorist, dealing a setback to his family’s effort to have the conduct investigated as possible obstruction of justice.
Kestelman, a 38-year-old attorney from Mevaseret Zion, intervened when two Hamas terrorists opened fire at the entrance to Jerusalem on November 30, 2023. He helped stop the attack before he was shot by Sgt. (res.) Aviad Frija, who allegedly mistook him for a terrorist.
Police released Kestelman’s body for burial without an autopsy. He was exhumed a week later after the military investigation determined that an autopsy was needed. The examination found a bullet and two fragments, contradicting the police’s earlier account that no bullets had been found in his body.
Kestelman’s family argues that the decision to release the body, followed by what it describes as false and changing accounts from officers involved, created reasonable grounds to suspect that police had deliberately obstructed the investigation. The state acknowledges serious professional failures but says there is no evidence they were intentional.
Justice panel urged Kestelman's family to withdraw petition
The petition concerns the conduct of the police officers who initially handled the case. It is separate from Frija’s military trial over the shooting itself.
After hearing both sides on Monday, the three-justice panel urged the family to withdraw its petition. The family declined and requested a reasoned judgment, which the court said would be sent to the parties.
Until that ruling is issued, Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara’s decision not to order a criminal investigation remains in force.
“There was negligence and unprofessional conduct, but it does not cross the threshold,” Justice David Mintz said, after the panel consulted. He added that it was “very, very difficult” to conclude that there had been criminal intent and a criminal act.
Justice Yael Willner said it was possible that the affair contained a criminal element but that such a possibility was not enough for the court to intervene.
The judges’ task, she stressed, was not to decide criminal responsibility. They were reviewing whether the attorney-general’s decision fell outside the broad discretion given to law-enforcement authorities – a threshold the panel indicated had not been met.
Kestelman's family's lawyers say evidence sufficient for criminal investigation
The family’s lawyers, Daniel Haklai and Amit Shelef, argued that the evidence went beyond poor judgment and was sufficient to justify opening a criminal investigation. They emphasized that the evidence needed to begin investigating is less than what would be required to file an indictment or secure a conviction.
Their allegations focus in part on Supt. Nadav Kogan, a Jerusalem District investigator involved in the decision to release Kestelman’s body.
The petitioners allege that Kogan had decided to release the body before receiving a CT report referring to metal fragments. They further allege that he later gave inaccurate or false accounts of consultations with doctors and the family, including an account suggesting that Kestelman’s father had opposed an autopsy on religious grounds.
The family also argued that the Justice Ministry’s Police Investigation Department (PID) had conducted an inadequate examination before deciding there was no reasonable suspicion of a crime. Its lawyers said PID did not question several potentially significant witnesses, including Military Police investigators and doctors.
'No evidence' that police deliberately impeded investigation, state says
The state acknowledged in court that releasing the body without an autopsy was a mistake and part of a series of administrative and professional failures “that should never have happened.” It said, however, that there was no evidence that officers acted deliberately to impede the investigation.
State counsel said police misunderstood the initial CT report and believed no bullets remained in Kestelman’s body. According to the state, a trauma doctor also understood police to be asking whether bullets had been removed during treatment, rather than whether any remained in the body.
The error was corrected after the body was exhumed and an autopsy was conducted on December 8, 2023, the state said.
Frija has argued in the military proceedings that the failure to conduct an autopsy before Kestelman’s burial caused evidentiary harm. The military court has not yet decided that claim or the criminal case against him.
Frija faces military trial on charges of reduced-responsibility manslaughter
According to the military indictment, Frija continued firing after another soldier called for the shooting to stop and after Kestelman raised his hands, removed his jacket, and no longer held a weapon. Frija has denied criminal wrongdoing. He is charged with reduced-responsibility manslaughter, and his trial is continuing in the Southern District Military Court.
The state said the PID, the appeals department, and the attorney-general had all reviewed the evidence and reached the same conclusion: The failures did not establish reasonable suspicion that officers intended to obstruct justice.
An internal police review led to tighter procedures, including requirements to document decisions and conversations in real time and to send bodies for forensic examination following deaths caused by trauma or other unusual circumstances, even when police do not initially suspect a crime. Prosecutorial approval is also required before a body is released following an unnatural death.
The family’s current legal challenge followed an earlier High Court ruling in December 2025, directing the attorney-general to reconsider the handling of its appeal. Baharav-Miara reviewed the matter and again declined in March to order a criminal investigation.
Moshe Kestelman, Yuval’s father, told the court that the family was seeking accountability to prevent similar failures in future cases.
“Why not investigate the officer’s motives?” he asked.
Mintz said the family’s pain was shared by the court but maintained that the legal line between grave professional failure and a criminal offense had not been crossed. With the family declining to withdraw its petition, the court will now set out its conclusion in writing.

‘NYT’ coverage framed Israel as ‘sole aggressor,’ Palestinians as ‘passive victims,’ study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:23:24 UTC
00:23:24 KST

The New York Times’ reporting after October 7 consistently portrayed Palestinians as “passive victims” and Israel as the “sole aggressor,” a new peer-reviewed study by Edieal Pinker of Yale School of Management found.
The study, How The New York Times Framed the War Between Israel and Hamas, was published in the academic journal Studies in Conflict & Terrorism last week. It is an expansion of an initial quantitative study published by Pinker in February 2025, as covered by The Jerusalem Post at the time.
Drawing on a body of 1,559 news articles written between October 7, 2023, and 7 June, 2024, Pinker documents a dominant narrative that assigned “near-exclusive agency and responsibility to Israel while diminishing Hamas’s role in sustaining the conflict.”
According to Pinker, in this narrative, from October 8, 2023, onward, Israel “has been the sole aggressor” whereas Palestinians are portrayed as “passive victims whose suffering grows daily as they are relentlessly attacked by the Israeli military.”
Pinker at no point makes the claim that the NYT is “biased” in its reporting. “To determine if bias exists one needs a benchmark of what “unbiased” reporting would look like,” he notes.
Rather, he says, he intends to document several imbalances in the reporting of the war that could “plausibly influence the opinions of a reader in a direction that is at odds with reality.”
Details of the study reveal that most articles conform to 'dominant narrative'
Of the 1,559 articles examined, Pinker concludes that 969, or about 70%, fit what he calls the “dominant narrative.”
Pinker says the NYT frequently did not mention Israelis killed after October 7, Hamas fighters killed during the fighting, or Hamas or other Palestinian attacks carried out after October 7.
In many cases, mention of Israeli hostages was also omitted. In fact, he finds that only 42% of those 969 articles mentioned the Israeli hostages, even though the hostages were central to ceasefire negotiations. Fifty-five percent did not mention the Israeli deaths on October 7 or at all.
Pinker also reports that Israeli violence was almost always mentioned in these articles, while the Hamas attack itself was omitted on many occasions. There were only 38 cases in which Israeli violence was absent, compared with 237 in which the Hamas attack was absent.
“Taken as a whole, this narrative reinforces a distorted view of the conflict, namely that Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, killing many Israelis, and this led to Israeli violence that has been killing only Palestinian civilians since then with no further Israeli deaths,” he writes.
Pinker also opines that the absence of mention of Israeli casualties, including soldiers, in much of the NYT’s reporting “creates the appearance of a hierarchy of human life that is perhaps linked to degree of victimhood.”
This framing is also at odds with how Israelis view the war, he adds.
For example, in his 244-day sample, 128 days had at least one IDF death. Most of these made front page news in Israel. In comparison, in the NYT, there were only 74 days with a mention of Israeli casualties post-October 7 (including both military and civilian mentions). There were also nine stretches of a week or longer with no mention of Israeli military casualties.
What a reader therefore may not understand is how costly the war was in terms of Israeli lives and the impact the war had on the wider society.
“For The New York Times reader, the cost that Israelis are bearing will not be salient,” Pinker writes. “Given their sensitivity to casualties, the Israeli public expects its military and political leadership to conduct the war in a manner that reduces risk to their soldiers. This approach will inevitably lead to greater civilian deaths among the Palestinians. This context is lost to the reader of The New York Times.”
Diminishing Hamas's responsibility for the war
Pinker also explores assignment of responsibility.
One way in which he does this is by counting mentions of “Hamas” vs. mentions of “Israel.”
Of the 1,559 articles in the sample, there are only 105 (7%) in which the number of times the word “Hamas” appears is greater than or equal to the number of times the word “Israel” appears.
In total, the word “Israel” appears 27,205 times vs 8,499 for “Hamas” across all articles in the analysis. Pinker writes that this imbalance in mentions diminishes Hamas's responsibility for the war and the situation. He also says it supports the view that all agency is in the hands of Israel and thus most blame should fall on Israel for negative sentiment about the war.
Regarding the balance of suffering, Pinker says that Palestinian suffering was mentioned in the large majority of articles about the war, whereas less than 4% of articles made any reference to some dimension of Israeli suffering among the population not in reference to direct victims of October 7.
Again, he explains that this reinforces the view that Israelis incurred little cost from the war.
Overall, Pinker concludes, there were imbalances in the NYT’s reporting post-October 7 that created a specific framing of the war.
These imbalances have created sympathy for the Palestinian people while at the same time diminishing Hamas’ responsibility for their situation and the continuation of the war, he writes.
When Pinker published his initial findings last year, The New York Times issued a statement saying that it has “covered this war with more rigor than virtually any other US news organization, reporting on the conflict from all angles.”
It added, “We remain open to good-faith disagreement but will not change our coverage to buttress entrenched perspectives.”

Winner Epic Israel 2026 will return to the Western Galilee for the first time since the war forced the closure of the region’s trails nearly three years ago, bringing hundreds of mountain bikers back to the North from October 14-17.
Held in memory of the late Giora Tsachor and in partnership with Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF), the four-day event is sponsored by Winner and Specialized. The race will take place throughout the Mateh Asher Regional Council and Nahariya, passing through forests, singletrack trails and off-road terrain that have recently been rehabilitated and reopened.
The race will cover approximately 300 kilometers and 3,000 meters of cumulative climbing. In addition to the full four-day competition, the event will feature one-day races, a junior race and a relay race.
For Gal Tsachor, founder and producer of Winner Epic Israel and one of the leading figures in Israel’s cycling industry, the return to the North is about far more than a change of scenery.
“For us, Winner Epic Israel’s return to the North is about much more than choosing a new route,” Tsachor said. “After three years in which this region was almost entirely off the cycling map, we want to be among the first to return. When hundreds of riders come here, they bring with them families, friends, overnight stays, restaurants and business for local establishments. We want the race to be part of this movement and to help bring the North back to life.”
Tsachor said the event also carries a personal significance as it continues the legacy of his father, the late Giora Tsachor, in whose memory the race is held each year.
“Winner Epic Israel was born out of a love for this country, cycling and community, and it continues the legacy of my father, the late Giora Tsachor, whom we commemorate every year,” he said. “Returning to the North after three years is a significant moment for us. This is not just about riding trails – it is a statement. We want to be there, to ride there and to show that the North is coming back.”
Race's return coincides with KKL-JNF rehabilitation of northern Israel
The return of the race coincides with extensive rehabilitation work being carried out by Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund throughout northern Israel. KKL-JNF has developed more than 2,500 kilometers of cycling trails across the country and is currently upgrading approximately 100 kilometers of singletrack trails in the North, including those in Hanita, Kabri, Yehiam and Matzuva that were closed during the war.
Winner Epic Israel will pass through some of these rehabilitated trails, once again bringing cyclists to one of Israel’s premier cycling destinations, with its extensive network of forests, woodlands and Galilee landscapes.
KKL-JNF Chairman Eyal Ostrinsky described the race’s return as a symbol of the region’s recovery.
“Winner Epic Israel’s return to the North is a powerful symbol of the North coming back to life,” Ostrinsky said. “For three years, the trails and forests in the region were closed to the public, and throughout this period KKL-JNF has been and continues to carry out extensive work to rehabilitate, upgrade and restore these natural and recreational areas.”
Ostrinsky added that seeing hundreds of cyclists return to the reopened trails demonstrates the tangible impact of that rehabilitation.
“KKL-JNF will continue to invest in the North, in its forests, cycling trails, and tourism and recreational infrastructure, based on the belief that bringing the public back to these spaces is an integral part of the region’s rehabilitation and growth,” he said.
The event will also include wounded IDF veterans from Brothers for Life, an organization that supports soldiers wounded during their military service and assists them throughout their rehabilitation. Their participation will add another dimension to the race’s return, bringing together competitive cycling, community activity and the public’s renewed access to northern Israel’s natural spaces.
Winner Epic Israel collaborated with Toto Winner, KKL-JNF for 2026 race
The Toto Winner, which is partnering with the event alongside KKL-JNF, also views the race as an opportunity to support the North’s recovery.
“The Toto is proud to once again partner with Winner Epic Israel, in partnership with KKL-JNF – a competition held to high professional standards that presents Israel in a positive light,” said Meir Bardugo, CEO of the Toto Winner (The Israel Sports Betting Board). “For us, this is another way to express our commitment to advancing Israeli sports and, this year, also to take part in the effort to strengthen the North, support its rehabilitation and help restore normal life.”
The 2026 race will also mark the first year of a partnership between Winner Epic Israel and Matzman-Specialized.
“This is our first year together with Winner Epic Israel, and we have two reasons to be proud,” said Roy Kapach, Head of Commerce and Strategy at Matzman-Specialized. “On the one hand, we are taking part in the race’s return to the beautiful North after several difficult years, and on the other, we are partnering with one of Israel’s most significant and prestigious sporting events.”
Kapach said the partnership would help reconnect Specialized with cyclists in the region.
“For us, this is an opportunity to reconnect with the cycling community, restore confidence in and the love of cycling in the North, and be part of the movement bringing the region back to activity and normal life,” he said.
Nahariya Mayor Marelli says race promotes sports, tourism
Nahariya will host the event for the first time, with Mayor Ronen Marelli highlighting the city’s efforts to promote both sports and tourism.
“Nahariya is delighted to host the Winner Epic Israel competition for the first time, in partnership with KKL-JNF and the Toto,” Marelli said. “Hosting the international competition is part of the city’s efforts to promote sports and tourism and will introduce participants and visitors to our coastline and unique seafront.”
“Nahariya has been and will continue to be Israel’s cycling city,” he added. “I am confident that this partnership will expand in the years ahead and contribute to strengthening northern Israel and the State of Israel.”
Mateh Asher Regional Council head Moshe Davidovich similarly welcomed the return of the event, saying the region needs to see tourism, activity and visitors return after years of disruption.
“The return of Winner Epic Israel to the North is important news for Mateh Asher and the Western Galilee,” Davidovich said. “After three years in which our residents endured a difficult period and the entire region was forced to put its daily routine on hold, we need to bring activity, tourism and people back here.”
“A sporting event like Winner Epic Israel puts the North back in the spotlight and reminds everyone of the region’s beauty and strength,” he added. “I congratulate the organizers, KKL-JNF and the partners on their decision to return here, and I hope this will mark the beginning of a new period – one of rehabilitation, growth and a return to normal life.”
