Saudi Arabia threatened from two fronts as CENTCOM meeting grows in importance - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:22:59 UTC
00:22:59 KST

Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met with US Central Command head Brad Cooper on September 14. The meeting is the latest development in Saudi Arabia as it faces threats from the Houthis and also from Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.
The important East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia was struck by a militia in Iraq on the evening of September 10-11. Riyadh has been juggling challenges in the Gulf as a meeting in Oman between Gulf countries and Iran was postponed.
US Central Command cooperation matters to Riyadh. The two coordinated on strikes on Iranian-backed militias in Iraq in July. Now, after Houthi threats and new threats from Iraq, the CENTCOM meeting is important for the Kingdom. Riyadh faces multi-front threats. It also wants to gauge what the US will do next.
Saudi Arabia is in a difficult position. The Iranian-backed Houthis swept up the coast of the Red Sea last week, potentially threatening the Bab el Mandeb Strait. Saudi Arabia’s Saudi Press Agency noted that the Crown Prince “received in Jeddah today Commander of the US Central Command Admiral Brad Cooper, and his accompanying delegation.” The short report said that “the two sides reviewed bilateral relations and the latest regional developments.”
The report provided only brief details on the meeting in the Kingdom. Al-Arabiya noted that “the two sides reviewed bilateral relations and the latest regional developments, the report added.
US said it would provide intelligence to Saudi Arabia
MBS had spoken with US President Donald Trump multiple times as Riyadh and Washington coordinate over the escalating situation in Yemen, sources familiar with the matter said last week.”
The report noted that “Trump told MBS that the US would provide intelligence and targeting assistance, one source told Al Arabiya English, as the Iran-backed Houthis make significant gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline.”
Arab News in Saudi Arabia said on Monday that “Saudi Arabia lifted warnings of potential danger in four southern cities on Monday after a series of attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis heightened security concerns along the Kingdom’s border with Yemen.” The report illustrated how Saudi Arabia continues to face threats from the Houthis.
The Houthis last week surprised the region with their new offensive, when they captured the port town of Mocha and moved up the coast of the Red Sea toward the Bab el Mandeb Strait, taking several islands along the way. The Houthis also control an area near the Saudi border.
“The Saudi Civil Defense issued alerts for Najran, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Abha before declaring the areas safe. It later issued renewed warnings for Khamis Mushait and Abha and subsequently lifted those as well,” Arab News noted.
Arab News also said that the “attacks have drawn strong condemnation and expressions of solidarity from Gulf and Muslim organizations as well as Arab and regional governments, with the Gulf Cooperation Council, Muslim World League and Organization of Islamic Cooperation among those backing Saudi Arabia and condemning attacks on its territory and vital infrastructure.”
The meeting with Central Command is important
Saudi Arabia is one of the main military powers in the region. It has a sizable modern air force. It has more manpower than the Gulf states. The US military has bases in many Gulf countries, such as Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Saudi Arabia has already been fighting the Houthis since 2015. The Houthis have targeted the Kingdom with drones and ballistic missiles in the past.
In late July US CENTCOM noted that “US Central Command and the Saudi Arabian Armed Forces conducted precision strikes in Iraq, July 28, against Iran-aligned terrorists that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) directed to attack US forces and Saudi energy infrastructure.” At the time the US said that the IRGC had directed around 30 “aerial drone attacks in the last 72 hours.”
It’s worth recalling some of the history here. The September 14, 2019 attack on Saudi Arabia’s Abqaiq and Khurais oil facilities was one of the most significant strikes on global energy infrastructure in recent decades.
Drones and cruise missiles temporarily knocked 5.7 million barrels per day of Saudi production offline, around 5 percent of global supply. The Houthis claimed responsibility, while Saudi Arabia and the United States blamed Iran.
The attack on the East-West pipeline appears to be a similar threat. Riyadh did not retaliate to the 2019 attack. It appears reticent to respond this time. It will want US support. The US has appeared to be messaging about less escalation and shifting to talks about the Iranian nuclear program. The US also seems to believe the conflict could end by the end of the year.
Iran-backed militias in Iraq have also been linked to attacks on Saudi Arabia for many years. Reports have said that Kataib Hezbollah in Iraq has used drones to target Saudi infrastructure. Kataib Hezbollah also killed three American service members in Jordan in 2024.
Saudi Arabia will need to see what comes next in terms of talks with CENTCOM and confronting the Houthis and militias in Iraq. Currently, Riyadh appears ready to do a joint investigation with Iraq on the attack on the East-West pipeline.
However, the bigger story is that Saudi Arabia still appears vulnerable. It has modern air defenses and a modern army. However, the Kingdom is a larger area to defend.
The militias can choose when and where to attack. Saudi Arabia also has a lot of strategic infrastructure. It has more to lose than the Houthis or Iraqi militias. This is how Iran threatens the region in general. It relies on the fact that others have more to lose.

Ukraine, Russia set for new round of US-mediated talks
September 14, 2026
Ukraine and Russia have signaled their readiness to resume trilateral talks under US mediation.
"We're preparing. For October," said Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian president's office.
Similar signals came from Moscow: "We do not rule out such a possibility. We are talking about the foreseeable future," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner aimed to revive trilateral talks to end Russia's war in Ukraine, visiting Moscow and Kyiv in the first week of September.
The last round of trilateral talks took place in January and February 2026 in Abu Dhabi and Geneva, without producing a breakthrough, as the issue of territory control in eastern Ukraine remained unresolved.
Territory remains a difficult subject
Vladimir Putin still demands more territory than Russia currently controls, Kushner confirmed on September 12, speaking online at the YES security conference in Kyiv.
"President Putin [has] laid out his line of what he wants to achieve. If Ukraine wanted to withdraw to that line, then obviously we have the rest of the deal set up and put together. Ukraine right now does not want to do that," the US envoy said.
The Ukrainian government has indicated it is willing to freeze the fighting along the current frontline in exchange for security guarantees. Such a step could be supported by 60% of Ukrainians, according to a poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology conducted in summer 2026. A similar majority of respondents rejected giving up territory that Russia hasn't been able to conquer. 33% said Ukraine should give up territory that Putin demands.
Russia's air superiority is a problem for Ukraine
Few expect a breakthrough anytime soon.
"For there to be a negotiated end to the war, there has to be parity. Right now, there's a stalemate on the front lines and not much is changing there, but in the air war, unfortunately, Russia currently has a significant advantage," Volodymyr Fesenko, a Kyiv-based political scientist, told DW.
Ukraine is running low on interceptors for Russian ballistic missiles. Russia has also stepped up attacks with new jet-powered drones, which fly faster than older gasoline-powered models and are harder to intercept.
Russian airstrikes are increasingly targeting Ukraine's economy, including warehouses, energy facilities, gas stations and railway infrastructure.
The Kremlin has accused Ukraine of opening a "Pandora's box" by targeting Russia's economy and fuel and energy facilities with deep strikes since the summer. Ukraine says the attacks are intended to force Russia to the negotiating table.
Ukraine is worrying about the winter
Ukraine's supporters say Kyiv's strategy is working.
"The escalation ... is not a problem. It's a sign of success," said Jonathan Powell, the United Kingdom's National Security Adviser, speaking at the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv on September 11. "Of course [Putin] doesn't go straight to negotiations, he tries to escalate in the ways that he can."
The West must "keep its foot on the gas" to make Putin negotiate in earnest, Powell said.
Such optimism contrasts with concerns in Ukraine about the upcoming winter. In 2025, Russian attacks on energy infrastructure caused extended blackouts and left people without heating in freezing temperatures.
"We anticipate a very difficult winter in terms of both critical infrastructure, which is being destroyed every day by Russian attacks, but also in terms of overall economic conditions in the country," said Ukraine's Economy Minister, Oleksandr Kravchenko.
Zelenskyy calls for partial de-escalation
Russia rejected the idea of a ceasefire during the upcoming talks. Ukraine is now calling for a de-escalation of attacks on energy infrastructure and the unblocking of grain exports via the Black Sea instead.
"What can bring us to any kind of negotiations? So, energy and grain. This is step number one. What we can achieve," Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told DW in an interview aired on September 12.
Political scientist Fesenko says an agreement on grain exports could prove the easier task: "In the Black Sea, both Ukraine and Russia are facing major problems. Grain exports have been blocked; ports have been shut down and therefore both sides have a stake in the matter."
An energy truce, however, remains elusive, as Ukraine's vulnerability in the winter gives Putin leverage he would not give up easily, Fesenko said.
At the same time, the US is increasing pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy facilities.
"Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing: He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Donald Trump said on Sunday, September 13. "There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel. That's hurting the world."
Kremlin rejected Zelenskyy-Putin meeting
The Kremlin has already rejected another of Zelenskyy's proposals: a meeting between the Ukrainian and Russian leaders in December on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Miami.
"Putin doesn't want to negotiate with Zelenskyy. It's been obvious since last year that he wants to reach an agreement with Trump," said Fesenko. "If Trump insists, Putin may agree to a meeting between the three leaders. But he has no intention of negotiating with Zelenskyy."
If negotiations start in October as expected, negotiating teams rather than the leaders themselves will conduct them. But Ukraine insists that only the presidents can decide the territorial issue.
"The territorial question remains a pressing one... Complex issues such as this are only resolved at the level of leaders," Zelenskyy said during the US envoys' visit to Kyiv.

Nationalist chiefs sign pact to make Burnham ‘the last UK prime minister’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:13:30 UTC
00:13:30 KST

Scottish Nationalist Party leader John Swinney, Rhun ap Iorwerth of Plaid Cymru in Wales, Mary Lou McDonald, president of Irish Republicans Sinn Féin and Michelle O'Neill, vice president of Irish Republicans Sinn Féin speak to the media as they attend a meeting in Cardiff on September 14, 2026. | Adrian Dennis/AFP via Getty Images
DUBLIN — The leaders of the three nationalist parties that want to break up the United Kingdom have signed a joint agreement to coordinate their rebel ambitions.
Monday’s signing ceremony by the Scottish National Party, Ireland’s Sinn Féin and Wales’ Plaid Cymru creates a fresh headache for U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham — who’s already on the constitutional defensive after the weekend’s surprise intervention by Donald Trump.
The nationalist leaders gathering in the Welsh capital, Cardiff — Wales First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth, Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill and Scotland First Minister John Sweeney — offered only a subdued, indirect welcome for Trump’s out-of-the-blue declaration that a united Ireland was “inevitable.” That lack of praise for Trump reflected their shared opposition to his wider policy agenda.
Advertisement
But all three agreed that Trump’s sentiments reinforced their own sense that the time was right for independence referendums in Scotland and Ireland, and a push for greater devolution of powers from Westminster to the Welsh Assembly.
“Each of our nations has the right to determine its own future, through democratic means and in accordance with the wishes of its people,” the three parties said in a joint statement.
They met in Cardiff to acknowledge the fact that all three devolved administrations in the U.K. are now led by nationalists for the first time following May’s electoral trouncing by Plaid Cymru of Burnham’s Labour, long the party of government in Wales.
Sweeney, Scotland’s leader since 2024, is seeking a second independence referendum following the failed 2014 vote. Burnham, who holds the levers on permitting such a ballot, has ruled it out.
“I think he [Burnham] will be the last prime minister of the United Kingdom, because the people of Scotland, if given the choice of independence in a referendum, will take that choice,” Sweeney said, citing recent polling trends.
Advertisement
Sinn Féin — which contests elections in both parts of Ireland — has spent nearly three decades appealing for the British government to permit a border poll in Northern Ireland. Sinn Féin wants the north, a part of the U.K., to merge with the Republic of Ireland, which won independence from Britain more than a century ago.
Reflecting the party’s more complicated all-Ireland structure, Sinn Féin came to Cardiff represented both by O’Neill, who leads the cross-community government in Northern Ireland, and by party chief Mary Lou McDonald, a Dubliner who leads the opposition in Ireland’s parliament.
McDonald — who has boycotted traditional St. Patrick’s Day events at the White House since Trump’s 2024 re-election — billed the president’s pro-unity comment as part of an age-old American sympathy for the Irish, one of the country’s biggest ethnic identities.
“It’s surprising that there is surprise that a New Yorker, that an American president, would say that they see the logic, the good sense of unity … the inevitability, as he sees it,” McDonald told reporters.
Ireland’s leader, Taoiseach Micheál Martin of the center-ground Fianna Fáil party, didn’t comment on Trump’s intervention as they spent much of the weekend together — but broke his silence Monday to warn that simple-minded calls for unity did more harm than good.
Martin avoided mentioning Trump explicitly on that point, instead billing it as a problem for his opponents, Sinn Féin, which spent decades supporting Irish Republican Army violence in Northern Ireland. The main faction, the Provisional IRA, killed nearly 1,800 people from 1970 to 1997, when the outlawed group ceased fire.
“I believe in Irish unity, but I want an Irish unity that works. That takes hard work. I’m not into simplistic rhetoric,” Martin told RTÉ radio in Dublin. “I’m not into timelines. I’m not into saying we’ll do it all next week and it’ll be simple. And some of the rhetoric I’m listening to, even Sinn Féin at times, harkening back to the 1970s — I worry about that.”

Iran's proxies using Yemen to compound war's impact on oil prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:12:13 UTC
00:12:13 KST

How Iran's regional allies' attacks in Yemen are compounding the war's impact on oil prices
Escalating fighting between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia, and attacks by other Iranian proxy forces on Saudi infrastructure, are increasing the threat to tanker traffic in the Middle East and driving up global fuel costs more than six months after the U.S. and Israel launched their war on Iran.
Direct clashes between the U.S. and Iran have severely reduced shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz since the war began, but the Houthi-Saudi tension, and attacks on Saudi infrastructure blamed on other Iran-backed groups, are also squeezing global fuel supplies in the nearby Red Sea.
Before the war began, about 30% of oil supplies typically reached the global markets by tanker from the Persian Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz (about 20%) and the Red Sea via the Bab el-Mandeb Strait (about 10%) combined.
The ongoing threat to ships in the Strait of Hormuz, combined with rising tension around the Bab el-Mandeb and attacks on Saudi infrastructure, helped push the price of Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, up to a near-4-month-high on Monday of about $108 per barrel.
Brent crude was trading at an average of $67 per barrel in the days leading up to the start of the war at the end of February.
Saudi pipeline offline after drone strike
"The spike in price is due to the East-West pipeline in Saudi being damaged and shut," Dimirtis Maniatis, head of the Greece-based Marisks maritime risk agency, told CBS News on Monday, referring to an attack last week on a vital Saudi Arabian crude oil pipeline.
Saudi Arabia has used the East-West pipeline to export oil from its Red Sea ports as an alternative to ports in the Persian Gulf since Iran started attacking ships and infrastructure around the Strait of Hormuz early in the war.
The pipeline, originally built during the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s in response to the same threat from Iran to shipping in the Persian Gulf, was brought back up to full capacity in April after being hit by Iran early in the war.
It enables Saudi Arabia to divert its oil about 745 miles west across the kingdom from the Persian Gulf to its Yanbu Port on the Red Sea. From there, energy products can typically be shipped to markets in Europe and Asia via the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea.
But the Houthis, a powerful Iranian proxy force, declared a blockade of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports in late July and started targeting tankers owned or operated by Saudi Arabian companies, giving the kingdom little room to maneuver.
No group has claimed responsibility for the attacks on the pipeline, although Iraq's government said Saturday they were launched from its territory, where a number of Iran-backed militias operate. Tehran has denied any involvement in the attack.
Saudi Arabia's crude oil output fell under 6 million barrels per day in August, down from around 8 million barrels per day the previous month and well under its target of 10.42 million barrels per day, according to the latest International Energy Agency (IEA) oil market report.
Long-term disruption to the East-West pipeline could take about 4% of the world's oil supply offline, according to Reuters, compounding the losses created by the Strait of Hormuz closure and the threat to Saudi ships in the Red Sea.
The Associated Press quoted two anonymous regional officials Monday as saying the pipeline could take 3-5 weeks to bring fully back online.
The Houthis and Iran's "longer-term aim"
Maniatis noted that the Houthis have not yet threatened global shipping in the Red Sea, focusing their attacks so far entirely on Saudi assets.
The Houthis said last week that the Red Sea remained safe for the majority of tanker operators, but the Lloyd's List maritime intelligence firm said that had done little to reassure shipowners or operators, especially after the rebels seized the port city of Mokha on Yemen's Red Sea coast and captured the strategically important island of Perim in the center of the Bab el-Mandeb.
Previous Houthi disruption of shipping has forced ships to avoid the Bab el-Mandeb by using a much longer, much more expensive route around the Cape of Good Hope in southern Africa, accessed via the Suez Canal, the northern exit from the Red Sea.
Although Saudi ship traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb dropped to close to zero in August, data from the IEA shows the overall number of ships passing through the waterway have remained relatively stable since the U.S.-Iran war began.
That has likely helped keep oil prices from going even higher already, but it also means Iran, through its proxies, may still have levers to try and pull if it wants to squeeze global energy supplies even harder.
"Tehran's longer-term aim is to establish a daunting status quo: Houthi control over the Bab el-Mandeb alongside Iranian control of Hormuz," wrote April Longley Alley, a Senior Fellow at the Washington Institute who previously served as Senior Political Adviser to the United Nations Special Envoy to Yemen, and the Atlantic Council's Allison Minor, who served as Deputy U.S. Special Envoy for Yemen from 2021 to 2023, in a Foreign Policy analysis published Friday.
"If it could be sustained, such a strategy would make Iran and its regional partner de facto gatekeepers for trillions of dollars' worth of trade each year."

US man allegedly threatens to kill Muslim men handing out Qurans in Michigan
A man allegedly threatened to kill four Muslim men who were distributing copies of the Quran outside a library in Troy, Michigan, prompting a US Muslim civil rights group to call for hate crime charges.
The four men were answering questions about Islam and handing out copies of the Quran when another man approached them and allegedly said he had a gun and threatened to kill them after learning they were Muslim.
The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) called on police to investigate the incident as a potential hate crime and review all available evidence.
"This cannot be dismissed as offensive speech or a heated disagreement," said Amy V. Doukoure, lead staff attorney at CAIR-Michigan.
The New Arab has contacted the Troy Police Department for comment.

IAEA General Conference opens amid growing nuclear proliferation concerns

VIENNA, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- The 70th General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) opened in Vienna on Monday, with calls to strengthen multilateral cooperation and efforts to uphold the global nuclear non-proliferation regime amid heightened geopolitical tensions.
In a message delivered by Monica Juma, director-general of the United Nations Office at Vienna, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said this conference comes at a time of profound global turbulence and uncertainty. Attacks on nuclear facilities are rising. The drivers of nuclear proliferation are accelerating while the guardrails against it are falling.
"The world is on the cusp of a revolution in nuclear power generation, a revolution that requires careful management and monitoring. More than ever, the world needs the IAEA's professionalism, impartiality and technical excellence," Guterres said in the message.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told the conference that the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) remains the cornerstone of the global non-proliferation regime.
"At this time of heightened tensions and distrust, we must work to underpin this legal framework by supporting the IAEA and working towards its aims. A world with more nuclear weapons and more countries armed with nuclear weapons is not a safer world," Grossi said.
The 70th Regular Session of the IAEA General Conference, running through Sept. 18, has drawn nearly 4000 senior officials and representatives from IAEA member states, and delegations of international organizations and non-governmental organizations.
Held annually since the IAEA was founded in 1957, the General Conference considers a wide range of issues related to the peaceful uses of nuclear technology, from energy production and cancer care to food security, water management, nuclear safety and security, and safeguards. ■

====================================================================================================

Maldives celebrates 900 Hijri years since conversion to Islam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:07:33 UTC
00:07:33 KST

Breadcrumb
Maldives celebrates 900 Hijri years since conversion to Islam
The Maldives has celebrated 900 Hijri years since its conversion to Islam, marking nearly nine centuries of a faith that has become inseparable from the identity of the Indian Ocean island nation.
President Mohamed Muizzu led official commemorations on Sunday, with sermons, religious lessons and cultural events held across the country to remember the conversion traditionally dated to 548 AH, or 1153 CE.
The anniversary also saw the laying of the foundation stone for the Sultan Muhammad ibn Abdullah Grand Mosque and Centre for Islamic Civilisation in Hulhumale, named after the ruler credited with beginning the country's Islamic era.
But how did a predominantly Buddhist island kingdom south-west of India become one of the world's most thoroughly Islamic societies?
A Buddhist kingdom on Muslim trade routes
The Maldives was inhabited long before the arrival of Islam, with early settlers arriving principally from the Indian subcontinent and Sri Lanka.
Buddhism became the dominant religion and remained deeply embedded in the islands for centuries, as demonstrated by archaeological remains of monasteries, stupas and other Buddhist structures.
But the Maldives also occupied an important position within the vast maritime trading system of the Indian Ocean.
Arab and Persian Muslim merchants increasingly travelled the routes connecting the Gulf and Arabian Peninsula with East Africa, India and Southeast Asia.
The islands were particularly famous for cowrie shells, which were exported in enormous quantities and used as currency across parts of Asia and Africa. Dried tuna, coconuts and coir made from coconut fibre were also important commodities.
Muslim contact with the Maldives therefore preceded the country's formal conversion.
The king who became Sultan Muhammad
Maldivian tradition dates the decisive change to 1153, when King Dhovemi converted from Buddhism to Islam and adopted the Muslim name and title Sultan Muhammad ibn Abdullah.
His conversion is traditionally attributed to a visiting Muslim scholar and preacher named Abu al-Barakat Yusuf al-Barbari.
Exactly who Abu al-Barakat was remains disputed.
The description "al-Barbari" has traditionally led to claims that he was a Berber from North Africa, likely Morocco, while Somali tradition has also claimed him. Another historical tradition identifies the missionary with Yusuf Shams al-Din al-Tabrizi, suggesting a Persian origin.
Whatever his precise identity, the conversion attributed to him became the foundational story of Maldivian Islam.
Following Dhovemi's conversion, Islam spread throughout the islands and the Buddhist monarchy was transformed into a Muslim sultanate. Muslim dynasties would rule the Maldives, with interruptions and changes of dynasty, for centuries.
The legend of Rannamaari
The conversion also acquired a famous supernatural tradition.
When Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta visited the Maldives in the 14th century, he recorded a local story that islanders had once lived in fear of a sea demon known as Rannamaari.
According to the story, a young woman was periodically offered to the creature until a visiting Muslim confronted it by spending the night reciting the Qur'an.
The demon failed to return, and the king, impressed by what had happened, embraced Islam.
The story cannot be treated as a literal historical account of the conversion, but Ibn Battuta's recording of it is significant: it shows that a story connecting the country's Islamisation with a foreign Muslim was already established in Maldivian memory around two centuries after the event.
Ibn Battuta himself spent months in the Maldives and served as a qadi, or Islamic judge, providing one of the most important medieval descriptions of Maldivian Muslim society.
Islam and Maldivian identity
Over the following centuries, Islam became deeply interwoven with Maldivian culture, government and architecture.
Among the most distinctive surviving examples are the islands' historic mosques constructed from carved coral stone, an architectural tradition unique to the country's maritime environment.
The modern Maldives remains overwhelmingly Muslim, and Islam occupies a formal place in the country's national and constitutional identity.
This year's commemorations deliberately connect that contemporary identity with the conversion of Dhovemi nine Islamic centuries ago.

The Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) is moving forward with plans to restructure its legislative body, the Palestinian National Council (PNC) ahead of Palestinian Legislative Council (PLC) elections scheduled for November 28, according to Palestinian reports.
The plans, ratified in June after being announced by Palestinian Authority (PA) President Mahmoud Abbas last year, will expand the use of elections to select PNC members, partially replacing the previous system of factional quotas, allocations, and special appointments.
The new system will also more than halve the number of PNC members, from 747 to 350, including 132 PLC members representing the Palestinian territories, 150 members from the Palestinian diaspora, and 67 members selected by consensus to represent PLO factions.
Last week, Kuwait’s Palestinian community elected the first two PNC members from abroad, Hisham Ibrahim and Saleh Qannam. Shortly afterward, Tamer Kadash was elected to represent the Palestinian community in Bahrain, while Muhannad Al-Shorbaji Al-Agha and Imad Al-Bal‘awi were elected to represent Palestinians in Qatar.
Efforts are underway to hold similar elections under an electoral college system in Lebanon and Syria, according to Arab reports. Independent Arabia reported that Palestinians in Europe, the United States, and South America have formed preparatory committees to reach consensus on the selection of future PNC members, with one seat allocated for every 35,000 Palestinians.
Palestinians in Jordan are not currently slated to participate in direct PNC elections.
Abbas pushes new system as a win for Palestinian democracy
Though Abbas has pushed the new system as a win for Palestinian democracy, Palestinian officials from other camps have strongly criticized forming a council without including Hamas.
Ramzi Rabah, a member of the PLO Executive Committee representing the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP), told Independent Arabia that the council “can be formed through consensus among everyone following a national dialogue that opens the door to everyone joining, including Hamas, which does not require postponing [the elections] for two years. It can happen within a month.”
Rabah called on Abbas to invite the secretaries-general of the factions “to an expanded meeting to establish mechanisms for forming the National Council and mechanisms for holding elections in an atmosphere of understanding.”
The International Commission to Support Palestinian Rights also released a statement last week, raising concerns that the new process allows the adoption of different electoral arrangements, “including the use of electoral colleges or selection mechanisms that do not necessarily allow all Palestinians within those communities to participate.”
ICSPR also condemned the exclusion of “Palestinian political forces and figures.”
Despite ICSPR’s critique, Hamas has indicated that it is seeking to participate in the PLC and PNC elections as part of a broader national coalition rather than running under its own name.
However, candidates are required to recognize the PLO as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people and commit to its political and national program and relevant international legitimacy resolutions – a term that has also generated criticism of the new system.
According to information published by the Amit Terrorism and Intelligence Research Institute, Hamas’s officials have already been actively screening for potential alliances.
Broadening participation in Palestinian elections
Husam Badran, a member of the Hamas political bureau and head of the national relations office, spoke by telephone with Salem Atallah, secretary-general of the Palestinian Mujahideen Movement, earlier this month, regarding the elections, as well as with Hassan Mahmoud Abu Halima, secretary general of the Palestinian al-Ahrar Movement, about the need to broaden the participation of Palestinian “organizations, forces and figures” in the elections and oppose the appointment of representatives.
Badran also complained to Independent Arabia that continuing with “the same approach of exclusivity and disregarding the right of the Palestinian people to choose their representatives is a national crime and a confiscation of the right of the Palestinian communities present in every country.”
Given the lack of consensus, members of the The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) have reportedly urged Abbas to postpone the PLC elections, an option that some experts and Palestinian officials have suggested he may be inclined to pursue out of concern that the vote could allow Hamas to gain greater control in the West Bank.
The PFLP submitted the “National Rescue Plan” last Monday, which proposed postponing the November 28 elections, launching comprehensive national dialogue, forming a consensus government, rebuilding the PLO, and then holding presidential, legislative, and National Council elections together.

"Why can this happen? BELPOL representatives have repeatedly said that there is currently no threat from either NATO countries or Ukraine to Belarus. Therefore, something must change around the country as a whole," Zhyhar said, adding: "And that change would bring both possible destabilization inside Belarus, meaning a threat to the regime, and the likelihood of a breach of the state border."
One scenario he sees is Belarus being drawn into a war against Ukraine or NATO countries, which would prompt a response. The skills currently being practiced by the Defense Ministry and Interior Ministry could then be needed, the expert said.
On 14 September, military exercises began in 12 municipalities in Lithuania and run until 18 September, LRT reported. The NATO member shares a 679-kilometer border with Belarus, and its troops are training to act together against military threats of various kinds, using drones, boats, and weapons.
Belarus has been militarizing steadily since 2022, holding exercises almost without pause, including joint drills with Russian forces.

China, India, Turkey Remain Top Buyers of Russian Fossil Fuels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:04:00 UTC
00:04:00 KST

Ukrainian drone strikes have hit Russian oil hard in August – but not fully drained Moscow’s war chest.
In August, Russia’s fossil fuel exports were lower than July, both in revenue and volume. Revenue was €604 million ($697 million) a day, an 8% month-on-month decrease, according to a report by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
During the same month, Russia also imported a record volume of seaborne oil products since its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine began.
Who are the top buyers?
China was the top buyer of Russian fossil fuels in August, giving Moscow a total revenue of €8.4 billion ($9.7 billion), according to the CREA.
India was the second-largest importer at €4.8 billion ($5.5 billion), followed by NATO member Turkey at €1.5 billion ($1.7 billion).
The EU was the fourth-largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels, at €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion).
The EU’s imports of liquefied natural gas (LNG) fell to their lowest level since 2022, partly due to EU sanctions. Still, France imported €190 million ($219 million) worth of LNG. Hungary was the EU’s largest buyer, importing €386 million ($445 million) of pipeline gas.
And despite the EU’s import ban on oil products made from Russian crude, 20 shipments from refineries in Turkey, India and Georgia that process Russian crude oil were unloaded at EU ports in August, two more than in July. Italy and Cyprus took five cargoes each, according to the CREA.

Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries
The CREA said Russia’s seaborne crude revenues were down 13% from July.
Drone strikes around Russia’s Black Sea city of Novorossiysk had a big impact: The port could not load cargo for nine days, and August loadings there were 58% lower than the month before.
The port of Tuapse has not been exporting oil products since May, the CREA added. At the end of May, the oil refinery in Tuapse was hit by Ukrainian drones.
In August, Ukraine carried out several strikes on Russian oil refineries. Drones struck the TANЕCO oil refinery, the Perm oil refinery and the Novokuibyshevsk refinery.
The Orsknefteorgsintez refinery in Orsk had to fully close due to Ukrainian attacks, and repairs could take up to six months. In September, numerous attacks were executed by Ukraine, including the recent attack on the Saratov oil refinery.

Russia&#039;s Matryoshka bots impersonate celebrities in new campaign targeting U.S. midterms with calls not to vote for “pedophile Democrats”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:03:28 UTC
00:03:28 KST

The Russian-linked Matryoshka bot network has launched a new campaign aimed at influencing the U.S. midterm elections.
Researchers with the Antibot4Navalny project, which tracks pro-Russian bot activity on social media, provided The Insider with information about 16 videos that have recently been posted on social media. In the clips, various “celebrities” appear in videos bearing the CNN logo — calling Democrats “pedophiles” and “criminals” and urging viewers not to vote for the party’s candidates in House and Senate elections on Nov. 3.
On Sept. 11 and 12, at least eight posts appeared on X, each containing two videos featuring well-known Americans who supposedly “explain” why users should not vote for the Democratic Party. The videos use footage of celebrities including Alyson Hannigan, Eric Roberts, Jeri Ryan, Ed Begley Jr., Sarah Jessica Parker, Lea Thompson, Melora Hardin, Christopher Lloyd, Julia Roberts, and multiple others. All of the videos display the logo of CNN, and the clips also carry the hashtags #midterms2026 and #AllDemocratsAreCriminals.
In the videos, the celebrities are shown accusing members of the Democratic Party of using children “for their own purposes,” supporting “the Zelensky regime,” popularizing the “rejection of family and faith,” promoting hormone therapy, and engaging in corruption.
Some clips also attack individual Democratic candidates. Roy Cooper, for example, who is running for a U.S. Senate seat in North Carolina, is accused of “calling for letting another 12 to 15 million immigrants into the U.S. if Americans want to have cheap groceries in stores.”
Most of the videos follow the same formula: celebrities purportedly claim to have “learned something” about the Democrats that is so disturbing they can no longer bring themselves to vote for the party. Every video ends with a call to share the clip and not support Democratic candidates in the upcoming elections.
The Insider has obtained links to the original posts from AntiBot4Navalny confirming that the accounts that shared them belong to the Matryoshka network. The newsroom is not publishing direct links to the posts to avoid helping spread the disinformation.
Current polling suggests Democrats have a strong chance of winning control of the House, while races for Senate seats are more competitive. Amid declining support for the Republican Party, Donald Trump even promised to pay every adult American $5,000 if Republicans retain control of both the House and Senate.
What is Matryoshka?
Antibot4Navalny’s researchers coined the name Matryoshka to describe a Russian operation that produces and spreads fake stories through a coordinated infrastructure of bots, trolls, and anonymous platforms. Its aim is to create artificial information “noise” and manipulate perceptions of events both inside Russia and abroad. The Antibot4Navalny project named the operation after the eponymous Russian nesting doll — the bots hide behind one another, and disinformation is spread in layers across different platforms, making the source harder to identify.
The mechanism works in two ways. First, it creates large numbers of fake profiles posing as ordinary people, independent media outlets, or think tanks. These accounts generate dozens of posts a day, imitating local styles of speech. Second, identical content is launched simultaneously across multiple social media platforms at the same time. In order to appear convincing, the bots use the logos of well-known Western media outlets and human rights groups.

Why You Should Never Wear Shoes in Your House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:03:10 UTC
00:03:10 KST

Every time you welcome a guest into your home, you may be letting in thousands of other ones as well—if you allow your visitors to wear their shoes when they enter. The world outside your door is a messy place—full of bacteria, viruses, and environmental toxins—and the soles of your shoes can pick up a lot.
According to one 2023 CBS News/YouGov poll, 63% of Americans regularly remove their shoes when they get home, and 24% ask their guests to do the same. This year, the Indiana Department of Health launched a “Shoes Free Protects You and Me” ad campaign about the benefits of a no-shoes policy at home, targeting tracked-in lead in particular.
How serious is the risk that shoes pose, and should your house be a no-shoes zone?
What the research says about wearing shoes inside
The published research on shoe contamination is not extensive, but some stands out. In one 2008 study, Charles Gerba, professor of virology at the University of Arizona, studied 26 pairs of shoes that had been worn for three months in the outside world and came up with some alarming results. The shoes carried between 3,600 and 8 million colony-forming units of bacteria, both on the inside and outside of the shoes. E. coli, or fecal bacteria, was the most common organism being tracked around.
“[About] 80% of the bottoms of the shoes had fecal bacteria on them,” Gerba wrote in an email to TIME, “largely picking them up from the floors of public restrooms, which always have fecal bacteria on them. They may also pick them up outside, in places that dogs and birds are.”
According to Gerba’s numbers, shoes are significantly more germ-ridden than public toilet seats, which have an average of 3,200 colony forming bacterial units.
E. coli is not the only infectious agent that shoes carry around. According to University of Houston researchers, 40% of shoes tested carry C. difficile, an intestinal bacterium that causes diarrhea. Health care settings are particularly germ-filled. One 2016 meta-analysis in the Journal of Applied Microbiology surveyed 13 studies, tracing where shoes have traveled and what they picked up there. A small study in that group found that after physicians did rounds in hospitals, 65% of their shoes tested positive for either antibiotic-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) or Enterococcus faecalis, another gastrointestinal bacterium. Another found that 48% of shoes worn in operating rooms tested positive for at least one pathogenic bacterium, most commonly Staphylococcus.
Rural areas, where livestock, birds, and other animals are common, are ready sources of Salmonella and other bacteria. One 2009 study conducted in rural Alaska had people put on sterilized boots, then walk along a randomly selected outdoor path, and finally step onto a piece of sterilized linoleum and remove the boots. From just that walk, 70% of the boots were positive for multiple gut bacteria. People then wore the contaminated boots on short walks across a sterile floor. On half of those walks, bacteria were transferred to the flooring.
Urban settings present their own perils, particularly as a result of dogs being walked on sidewalks and in parks. Even in cities where owners routinely pick up after their dogs, traces of fecal bacteria—and pools of urine—regularly collect on heavily foot-trafficked routes.
The type of flooring bacteria love
In one 2023 study published in Design, Architecture, and Ergonomics, investigators from Northeastern University in New York City sampled sidewalk rain puddles, shoe bottoms, and flooring inside one of the school’s buildings on its urban campus. On average, they found 30,000 gut bacteria per 100 milliliters of water in puddles on the neighborhood sidewalks. Every shoe sole they sampled from student and teacher volunteers carried varying levels of the same bacteria, and the interior of the building was also contaminated—especially in carpeted areas.
“The surface of your flooring makes an enormous difference,” says Alessandra Leri, professor of chemistry and biology at the school and the lead author of the study. “If you have carpets, they function as a reservoir of bacteria.” But no matter the interior floor surface, she says, “shoe soles are a serious vector of transmission of fecal bacteria from the outdoor environment to the indoor environment.”
Shoes track in more than germs
PFAS, the “forever chemicals” so named for how long they linger in the environment and our bodies, are regularly picked up by shoes and used in manufacturing the soles. Lead dust, which can often be stirred up and released into the air during remodeling of older homes and other buildings, can cling to shoes as well. Pesticides, used both on farms and in home gardens, are similarly free-riders on our shoes.
Where shoe-removal matters most
In most homes in which people do not remove their shoes upon entering, the area nearest the front door is generally the most contaminated. “We found that the first four steps at the entrance to the household are the germiest floor area in the home,” says Gerba. “We also did tracer studies putting dye and tracer viruses on the bottom of shoes and could see how they left a trail on the floor.”
Wherever contaminants spread in the home, they present the greatest danger to the household members who have the most contact with the floor—typically babies and small children who crawl and play on surfaces.
Leri follows a no-shoes policy in her home and leaves her shoes by the door when she enters. She does not ask guests to remove their shoes, especially when she hosts parties. “If you are having a cocktail party, you are sensitive to guests feeling like shoes are a part of their ensemble,” she says. But she does roll up the rugs before company arrives, making it easier to clean the floors when the guests are gone.
More people—especially younger people—may be taking a harder line, enforcing a universal ban on shoes for anyone in the home. While only 7% of people over 65 and 13% of people ages 45 to 64 require guests to remove shoes before entering, according to the CBS/YouGov poll, 44% of people in the 18 to 29 demographic do.
“I find that many people have already adopted that custom,” says Leri. “It is a more hygienic way of living.”

Some in Silicon Valley are questioning the calls for an AI slowdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:01:01 UTC
00:01:01 KST

Some in Silicon Valley are questioning the calls for an AI slowdown
Kalley Huang and Mike Isaac
- Silicon Valley leaders are divided on calls to slow AI development, with some supporting tighter safety regulations and others fearing it would stifle competition and innovation.
- Critics argue AI safety concerns may be exaggerated or self-serving, questioning motives behind calls for regulation and urging transparency beyond leading AI labs.
- Lawmakers and tech CEOs acknowledge AI risks but hesitate on strict regulation, emphasising the need to balance safety with maintaining global AI leadership and innovation.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – It took just a few hours over the weekend for well-known Silicon Valley figures to push back on calls by leading artificial intelligence companies to slow down the development of AI and to more tightly regulate the technology.
On Sept 12, Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, said in an essay that AI was advancing too quickly for researchers to continue building it safely.
He proposed that independent auditors monitor AI labs’ safety work and that regulators allow the labs to work together to coordinate safety standards.
Although they appeared to differ on what should be done about it, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO; Elon Musk, SpaceX’s CEO; and Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind’s chair, all said they agreed on the need for a slower pace.
But other technology industry leaders were quick to question Amodei’s motivations and whether he was sensationalising the risks of AI to make it harder for other companies to compete with leading AI companies.
“Stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic,” said David Sacks, a technology adviser for President Donald Trump and the White House’s former AI and cryptocurrency czar, in a social media post.
The criticism of the calls for a slowdown highlighted a deep divide between people who believe the government should police AI and others who believe regulatory intervention would crush competition.
Worries about the safety of AI gained wider attention in recent weeks as details emerged about how AI built by Anthropic’s top competitor, OpenAI, went rogue and hacked another company. And several days ago, one of Amodei’s own employees quit his job and began a public pressure campaign to draw attention to the risks of AI.
But a number of tech industry leaders, including several who have been advising the Trump administration on tech policy, believe those concerns are overblown.
Sacks, a frequent critic of Amodei, questioned why tech companies needed government intervention to slow down their AI development when nothing was stopping them from doing just that – particularly as they pursued a wildly ambitious goal to create so-called superintelligence, or AI that is far more intelligent than humans.
“The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it,” he added. “Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system.”
Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft, said his company supported proposals like independent auditors and “broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk” in a social media post on Sept 13.
“We also need to accelerate and spread the benefits of AI, such that they are diffused broadly across countries, communities, and companies,” Nadella said.
“The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation,” he added.
For years, the people most concerned about AI safety have often been the executives and employees of AI labs such as Anthropic. They are developing AI, they often say, because progress is inevitable, and they are the researchers best suited to build it with safety in mind.
That has opened those safety-conscious AI developers to aggressive criticism.
“Should a handful of select, market-dominant AI companies from Silicon Valley get to define the rules and safety standards of a generational technology for the entire world?” said Aidan Gomez, CEO of Canadian AI startup Cohere, in an essay on Sept 13.
“These oligopolies are now requesting to bend competition rules and be permitted to dictate the terms for everyone else,” he added. “A wolf in sheep’s clothing, a cartel by any other name.”
Amodei suggested in his essay that AI companies accept scrutiny of their products by “embedded evaluators” from third-party organisations.
But critics questioned whether Anthropic has too many ties to two organisations mentioned by Amodei, the nonprofit groups METR and Redwood Research.
“If we’re going to regulate, it can’t be anyone they know, and they can’t write the rules,” said Bill Gurley, a venture capitalist and vocal critic of the leading AI companies.
Even before Amodei’s essay, some in Silicon Valley argued that AI labs’ safety concerns are self-serving. At a conference in San Francisco last week, Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, said AI labs were emphasising security issues because they planned to introduce cybersecurity products.
“What better way to create demand than to create a problem?” Huang said. “Who doesn’t want their market to be hysterical about their product and line up around the corner for it?”
On Sept 12, Clément Delangue, the CEO of Hugging Face, the company hacked by OpenAI’s technology, said in a social media post that AI safety would not “be solved behind the closed doors of a handful of frontier labs”. Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face earlier this month for US$12.9 billion (S$16.4 billion).
A number of lawmakers in Washington appeared sympathetic to Amodei’s concerns. But just like many in Silicon Valley, they seem reluctant to embrace regulation.
“If developers of AI want to slow down development of their product they are free to do so,” said Senator John Cornyn, a Republican, in a social media post on Sept 13. “One thing is for sure: Their competitors won’t, including our nation’s adversaries.”
During a news conference on Sept 13 in Ireland, Trump said the United States was “leading China in AI”, and that he wanted to “keep it that way”.
“We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up,” Trump said. “They’re bringing up things that won’t happen, but whoever wins with AI wins.” NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:00:48 BST
00:00:48 KST

Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
Find out about misconduct hearings involving Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) officers and how to attend these public hearings.
Misconduct hearings
To increase openness and transparency in the MDP (and the police service in general), misconduct hearings, special case hearings and police appeals tribunals, involving Police Officers, are held in public.
Misconduct hearings deal with allegations of gross misconduct committed by MDP officers on or off duty. Gross misconduct is defined as ‘a breach of the police standards of professional behaviour (PSPB)’ that is so serious as to justify dismissal’. Misconduct hearings form part of the disciplinary process and are not criminal proceedings.
Accelerated Misconduct Hearings
Accelerated Misconduct Hearings take place when the investigation of allegations of Gross Misconduct, committed by MDP officers on or off duty, identifies that special conditions, such as the following are satisfied:
- that there is sufficient evidence, in the form of written statements or other documents, to establish on the balance of probabilities that the conduct of the officer concerned constitutes Gross Misconduct
- it is in the public interest for the officer concerned to cease to be a member of the MDP without delay
Police Appeals Tribunals
Police Appeals Tribunals deal with appeals submitted by MDP officers, against the findings and/or the outcomes of misconduct hearings (including accelerated misconduct hearings), under the MDP Conduct Regulations, or stage 3 meetings under the Performance Regulations.
The decision to hold misconduct hearings and police appeals tribunals in public was announced by the Home Secretary in 2015. The Ministry of Defence Police followed suit in March 2017 by amendments to the Ministry of Defence Police conduct (2015) and performance (2012) regulations, and by subsequent revision of those Regulations into the new Ministry of Defence Police (Conduct, Performance and Appeals Tribunals) Regulations 2020, which came into effect for all cases assessed as Gross Misconduct after 2 November 2020.
This change of legislation does not affect misconduct meetings, where a breach of PSPB does not amount to gross misconduct. These proceedings will be held in private and the public have no right to observe (except in the case of a complainant or the commission^, where appropriate).
^Director General (IOPC) or Ombudsman (NI) if they conducted or directed the investigation.
What happens at a misconduct hearing
At a misconduct hearing the facts are heard by a panel, often with the help of witnesses, to enable a finding to be made. If an officer is found to have committed misconduct or gross misconduct, depending on the circumstances, the available outcomes are:
- written warning (only if misconduct only found)
- final written warning
- reduction in rank
- dismissal without notice
What happens at an Accelerated Misconduct Hearing
An accelerated hearing is heard by the Chief Constable. Due to the evidence being incontrovertible there is no requirement for any witness attendance. If an officer is found to have committed gross misconduct, the available outcomes are:
- final written warning
- reduction in rank
- dismissal without notice
What happens at a Police Appeals Tribunal
Police appeals tribunals are heard by a panel chaired by a person nominated by the Lord Chancellor who satisfies the judicial appointment criteria. The tribunal determines whether the ‘grounds of appeal’ on which the appellant relies, have been made out. On the determination of an appeal, a tribunal may make an order dealing with the appellant in any way in which they could have been dealt with at the original hearing.
Attending a misconduct hearing
Any member of the public or press can request to attend a misconduct hearing, provided that they are aged 18 or over.
When the date of a misconduct hearing is confirmed, the details will be published below. Due to the MDP being a national force the location of the misconduct hearing may vary (dependent upon the case).
Please note the following conditions of entry:
- any member of the public or press wishing to attend must register in advance, by the specified closing date, and using the they must also provide valid photo identification (for example passport or driving licence) upon attendance. (To fill out the misconduct hearing form on a mobile device you must make sure that the PDF is opened in the editable mode.)
- any person who is a witness at the proceedings will not be permitted to attend prior to giving their evidence but, may be permitted to take a seat in the public gallery after this time
- priority will be given to interested parties and attendance will then be granted on a ‘first come, first served’ basis (up to the capacity of the venue)
- any restrictions on reporting will be notified in advance of the hearing
- members of the public and press are to remain silent at all times while the hearing is in session
- no photographs, film or sound recording are permitted; mobile phones and other devices can be retained but must be switched off during the hearing
- any conditions particular to an individual hearing will be published on this page in advance of the hearing
- where a hearing is adjourned for an extended period, attendees may be expected to leave the premises and return at the appointed time; if the hearing is held within an MOD establishment members of the public and press will be escorted from the gate to the venue and back; they will not be permitted to leave the venue except to leave the establishment
- no food or refreshments, with the exclusion of water, will be permitted in the hearing room; however, an area will be set aside for use by members of the public when the panel adjourn for short periods of time
- no refreshments will be provided by the MDP and if held at an MOD establishment, there may be no facilities to purchase food; in this instance, attendees should be self sufficient
- we cannot reimburse any expenses you incur by attending and please note that in some cases a hearing may be cancelled at short notice; in these situations, we will do our best to notify you but, it may not be possible
- members of the public and press, together with any bags, will be subject to a security search as a condition of entry and exit; anything that can be used or adapted to cause injury or damage will not be permitted
If you require disabled access, or have any other reasonable adjustment requirements, please advise us of your requirements on your registration form.
Once all applications to attend have been received and reviewed (after the closing date), your attendance will be confirmed, as applicable, by the means identified on your registration form.
Private hearings
Please note: in exceptional circumstances, the Chair can exclude anyone from all or part of the hearing at his/her discretion and may impose conditions relating to the attendance of any person.
Should the Secretary of State for Defence consider it expedient in the interests of national security, he/she may also give direction that:
- all or part of the hearing must be conducted in private
- a specified person must be excluded from all or part of the hearing
- specific steps are taken to conceal the identity of a witness
- specific information must be excluded from the published notification of misconduct hearings or notification of outcome
If a decision is made to hold a hearing in private the reasons will be published below and, where conditions are placed on any person’s attendance, that person will be notified prior to commencement of the hearing.
Upcoming hearings

To register, email MDP-PSD-GMB@mod.gov.uk with the following details:
- Your name

- Your email address
All requests to attend must be received on or before 14 September 2026.

These deep-sea spiders give off an otherworldly glow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

In the deep, dark Australian Abyss, what’s visible can be scarier than the unseen. There, giant sea spiders with glowing 25-centimeter-long legs may scuttle like disembodied apparitions.
Photos of these creatures unambiguously confirm that they exhibit bioluminescence, researchers report in the October Deep Sea Research Part I: Oceanographic Research Papers.
“It’s quite impressive for people scared of spiders,” says Jérôme Mallefet, a marine biologist with the Catholic University of Louvain in Belgium.
Mallefet and his colleagues discovered this phenomenon on a 2017 expedition to survey part of the deep-sea trench off southeastern Australia. Working out of a makeshift darkroom aboard the RV Investigator, he tested any of the 25,000 specimens suspected of bioluminescence hauled up in nets from up to nearly 5,000 meters deep. Some 76 percent of deep-sea creatures produce their own light — and it’s a trait that dates to 540 million years ago.
“I spent most of my time in 6° Celsius, in a dark cold room,” Mallefet says. “I believe I was a little bit crazy, but I like that.”
Poking the biggest of these sea spiders(Colossendeis tasmanica) raised a dim light. But adding potassium chloride, which can excite bioluminescent cells, had them glowing for up to 10 minutes, Mallefet and his colleagues showed. Another giant sea spider, C. minor, also exhibited bioluminescence.
The images confirm sporadic descriptions of bioluminescence in sea spiders, including a particularly poetic one from more than a century ago: “The creature, as it lay on its back, shone like a star, all its legs being lit along their ventral surface with a strange blue radiance.”
Most of the glow is on the underside of their legs, where their digestive tract is located, Mallefet says. That suggests that these spiders might get their bioluminescent properties from creatures they eat like sea anemones, the team speculates.
Three sea spider species — C. tasmanica, C. Minor and another without bioluminescence — also fluoresced in green when Mallefet shone ultraviolet and blue light on them. Several amphibians and even platypuses are also fluorescent, glowing under certain wavelengths of light.
Mallefet isn’t sure why sea spiders fluoresce, but speculates the bioluminescence could be to attract mates. Or, since the light is visible only in the appendages, they might use it to see prey on the seafloor and, once zeroed in, collapse onto their victims, using a needlelike appendage in their proboscis to liquefy and suck up tissue. But this kind of scientific enlightenment will require taking imaging to the next level, with deep-sea video.

Military train with emergency services in Scotland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:00:00 BST
00:00:00 KST

Military personnel, Police Scotland, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service and the Scottish Ambulance Service have taken part in a joint training exercise, supported by the RAF, designed to strengthen how these organisations work together.
Exercise Tartan Kukri is a multi-agency training exercise nested within the wider Exercise Kukri Dawn, a routine RAF-led exercise running from 2nd to 18th September 2026 that is designed to train new Chinook aircrew by replicating operational scenarios.
The exercise brings together specialist teams including Police Scotland Firearms officers, Counter Terrorism Policing officers and the Major Incident Support and Coordination Unit (MISCU), alongside 43 Commando Fleet Protection Group Royal Marines, 2nd Battalion The Royal Regiment of Scotland (2 SCOTS), Military Provost Staff, the Scottish Ambulance Service Special Operations Response Team, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service National Inter-agency Liaison Officer, RAF Chinook crews and Tactical Support Wing personnel from 28 Squadron.
The aim is to give them all experience of working together, to build and enhance interoperability between the Emergency Services and Defence in Scotland. The exercise also gives all personnel valuable experience of joint aviation operations, supported by the RAF's Chinook helicopters.
“This exercise is a valuable opportunity for Defence to work in close cooperation with our Emergency Services colleagues in a challenging and fast-moving scenario, improving our interoperability and gaining mutual understanding of each other’s organisations and way of working. Tough, realistic training is key to operational success on the day.”
Lieutenant Colonel Doug Mackay
Joint Regional Liaison Officer Scotland
The RAF are based at Police Scotland Headquarters in Tulliallan. Throughout the exercise, Police Scotland officers will fly in Chinook helicopters from their Headquarters to the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service Headquarters in Cambuslang. Alongside the Royal Marines and 2 SCOTS, they will take part in a scenario-based training exercise using blank firing ammunition, giving personnel realistic practice in a safe and controlled environment.
The exercise also tests the process for the safe handling, triage and handover of individuals between military and police personnel, helping to ensure smooth coordination between the two.
This partnership between Police Scotland and the military reflects the principles of the Joint Emergency Services Interoperability Programme (JESIP), which sets out how emergency services should work together to save lives and reduce harm.
A previous Exercise Kukri Dawn took place in March 2026, with joint police and Defence activity centred on Murrayfield Stadium in Edinburgh.

Burnham must establish an inquiry into Britain’s role in the Gaza genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:58:38 UTC
23:58:38 KST

Burnham must establish an inquiry into Britain’s role in the Gaza genocide
Delaying scrutiny will not make questions about UK complicity in Gaza disappear.
History does not really repeat itself, but, as the saying frequently attributed to Mark Twain goes, it often rhymes. Take, for example, Britain’s involvement in the Middle East since the turn of the century. It took six years before the British government established an independent committee of Privy Counsellors to examine the United Kingdom’s involvement in the 2003 Iraq war, and an additional seven years before Sir John Chilcot and other members of the inquiry committee published their damning findings that former Prime Minister Tony Blair had misled the public and his own government.
The Inquiry found that the UK chose to join the invasion before peaceful options had been exhausted, that Saddam Hussein did not, in fact, pose an imminent threat and that Blair had deliberately exaggerated the danger and then promised former United States President George Bush: “I will be with you, whatever.” It also found that Britain’s intelligence agencies had produced “flawed information”, that Blair had ignored warnings about what would happen in Iraq after the invasion, and that the government had not tried hard enough to keep a tally of Iraqi civilian casualties, which, according to Iraq Body Count, amounts to between 187,499 and 211,046 deaths.
Prime Minister Gordon Brown would not have established the inquiry committee without unrelenting pressure from within Parliament and civil society, and it was only due to these persistent demands that the truth finally saw the light of day (even though Tony Blair has still not been held to account).
Starmer government blocks independent inquiry into Britain’s role in the genocide
Fast forward to the Gaza genocide. In June 2025, former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn proposed a bill for a full, independent, public inquiry into Britain’s role in the genocide in Gaza. This inquiry committee would consider any UK military, economic or political cooperation with Israel since October 2023, including the sale, supply or use of weapons, surveillance aircraft and Royal Air Force bases, while also having the power to question ministers and officials about decisions taken in relation to UK involvement.
The bill secured the support of more than 50 MPs. However, when it reached a second reading, Keir Starmer’s government blocked its passage. The government said “there is no need for an inquiry” and that “such an inquiry would be unnecessary as there is no confusion about UK military operations in Gaza.”
The Gaza Tribunal
In response, Jeremy Corbyn decided to hold a public tribunal in the tradition of the Russell Tribunal organised by the great British philosopher Bertrand Russell in 1966 to investigate US war crimes in Vietnam. Corbyn invited Shahd Hammouri, an international law lecturer at the University of Kent, and me to join the Tribunal panel, and the hearings were held on September 4-5, 2025, in Church House, Westminster.
We heard 29 testimonies from witnesses, journalists and survivors of the Gaza genocide, as well as a range of international law experts, lawyers, medical doctors and whistleblowers. At the time, the official death toll in Gaza was nearing 65,000, of whom almost 20,000 were children. With more than 150,000 injured, Gaza had become the home of the largest cohort of child amputees in the world. Almost 80 percent of the buildings in Gaza had either been damaged or destroyed, including more than 90 percent of housing, 97 percent of schools, 33 of 36 hospitals, and every single university in the Strip.
The two days of hearings were among the most difficult in my life, given the emotional toll of listening to so many horrific testimonies. In addition to testimony after testimony describing the extent of the British government’s complicity in the mass murder and destruction, we also heard from a whistleblower about the culture of deception – to cover up the government’s wrongdoings – that had taken over the corridors of power. In the subsequent months, we analysed the findings and concluded that Britain had played a vital role in Israeli military operations in Gaza, including but not limited to:
The sale, supply and transfer of weapons that have been used to extinguish human life and destroy vital infrastructure in Gaza, the West Bank and beyond. This included individual export licences issued directly to Israel, as well as the indirect supply of components for F-35 fighter jets. The use of Royal Air Force surveillance flights over Gaza and British airbases to facilitate the transport, refuelling and maintenance of military equipment. The provision of political and diplomatic support, which has empowered Israel, enabling it to commit atrocities with impunity. This support has included the dehumanisation of Palestinians in political rhetoric, the justification of Israel’s actions, the hosting of Israeli officials, the failure to uphold the authority and decisions of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and the International Criminal Court (ICC), and the demonisation of international solidarity, including the proscription of Palestine Action as a terrorist group.
In March 2026, Corbyn submitted the Tribunal’s findings to the ICC, encouraging the court to interview government ministers regarding British complicity in war crimes. Since then, he has continued to demand a full, official, independent public inquiry into any cooperation between the UK and Israel since October 2023.
The bill returns to Parliament
Corbyn knows that the Tribunal he organised is no substitute for a full, public, independent inquiry, and given that there is a new prime minister in Number 10 who said Labour “got it wrong” over Gaza, Corbyn wanted to know whether the current Labour government would finally commit to investigating Britain’s role in the genocide. Expressions of regret are certainly important, but if justice is the goal, then the UK public requires both truth and accountability.
Last week, the bill that Keir Starmer’s government blocked back in June 2025 was once again brought before Parliament, and once again the government blocked MPs from voting on it. The Burnham government’s decision to postpone the vote on Corbyn’s Bill is reminiscent of the way previous governments postponed the establishment of an inquiry to investigate the Iraq war. It appears that, like previous UK governments, the current government’s strategy is to demur and delay, with the goal of sending the Gaza inquiry bill to purgatory.
The ruling elite have lost the ‘common sense’
The problem for Burnham is that, today, he and other members of the ruling elite no longer have the power to define the “common sense” through which Gaza is understood. Public opinion on Israel has shifted, as the huge pro-Palestinian marches and opinion polls demonstrate. The majority of the UK population knows that Israel is committing a genocide and that it has been able to do so, in part, because of the support of Western governments. While the US and Germany were undoubtedly the most enthusiastic supporters – providing Israel with the lethal mechanisms and the diplomatic shield to carry out mass killings – the public also understands that Britain has played a vital role.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s recent – and I would say courageous – announcement that the UK government would ban imports from illegal Israeli settlements and sanction companies and individuals supporting settlement activity is a very important first step. Yet, it does not absolve the UK government of its alleged complicity in atrocity crimes.
The disturbing testimonies we heard during the Tribunal underscore the importance of formal scrutiny. The vote on Corbyn’s bill was postponed last week, but the need to reveal the role the British government played in Israel’s genocidal onslaught is not going away. Burnham and Miliband have a historic opportunity to prove that this new government is committed to the principles of international law and currently face a straightforward choice: Continue to block efforts to expose the truth and seek accountability, or break with the past and stand on the right side of history. History often rhymes, but it does not have to.

23:58:18 KST

In Mumbai, markets filled with devotees buying Ganesha idols, flowers, sweets and other offerings for the festival dedicated to the elephant-headed god of wisdom and prosperity. Smaller idols were carried home, while larger ones were taken through the streets on decorated trucks, accompanied by drummers and chanting devotees.
Across the city, idols were installed in homes and temporary community shrines known as pandals, including some of Mumbai’s best-known sites such as Lalbaugcha Raja, GSB Seva Mandal and Andhericha Raja.
In Hyderabad, large crowds gathered in the Khairatabad neighbourhood around a 69-foot-tall, five-faced Ganesha idol, one of the festival’s main attractions. The 2026 idol represents Panchamukha Sankatahara Maha Ganapati, with its five faces symbolising the five elements: earth, water, fire, air and space. It is expected to draw more than 30 lakh, or three million, devotees before its immersion.
Worshippers offered prayers, danced and joined in as drums sounded through the streets, while preparations continued across the city. Telangana’s governor has also been invited to perform the first puja.
The festival marks the birth of Ganesha, who is revered as the remover of obstacles. In 2026, it falls on the Chaturthi tithi of the bright half of the Hindu month of Bhadrapada, beginning at 7:06 am on 14 September and ending at 7:44 am on 15 September.
The 10-day celebrations will culminate on Anant Chaturdashi, Friday 25 September, when processions will carry the idols to rivers, lakes and the sea for immersion, symbolising Ganesha’s return to his celestial abode.

Kremlin-Linked Businessman Helped Pay for Donald Trump Jr.’s Wedding – ProPublica
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:57:02 UTC
23:57:02 KST

Umar Kremlev, a Russian businessman with close ties to the Kremlin, helped pay for Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding earlier this year, ProPublica reported Monday, citing financial records and three sources familiar with the matter.
The payments included around $100,000 to rent a private island and $70,000 for a fireworks display on the first day of the three-day wedding of the U.S. President Donald Trump’s son, according to the report.
The funds were paid through IB Challenger, a Dubai-based firm used by Kremlev to run operations for the International Boxing Association (IBA), which he heads, after moving them from Switzerland following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The IBA told ProPublica it incurred no wedding expenses itself, while declining to comment on IB Challenger’s payments.
Kremlev is under Ukrainian sanctions due to his ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin through Alexei Rubezhny, head of the Kremlin leader’s personal security service.
National security experts told ProPublica that a member of Putin’s circle gaining intimate access to Trump’s family by financially backing his son’s wedding raises serious concerns.
“If I’m paying for your wedding, at some point, you’re going to owe me something,” said Frank Montoya Jr., a retired career FBI official who held senior counterintelligence roles.
“This should be unthinkable for the son of the president. End of story,” Montoya Jr. added.
Kremlev’s press office said the he met Trump Jr. “a couple of years ago” and the two men have since maintained a “friendly relationship.”
A spokesperson for Trump Jr. also described Kremlev as his “personal friend” who he had met through a mutual friend in the hunting world. He did not dispute Kremlev’s wedding payments.
