Many asylum seekers removed from UK to France arrive injured, charity health service finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:38:21 UTC
23:38:21 KST

Multiple injuries including bruising and fractures have been documented by a health service supporting people returned to France under the controversial “one in, one out” scheme.
The pilot scheme involves one asylum seeker who crosses the Channel in a small boat being returned to France in return for another in northern France being legally brought to the UK to claim asylum. The scheme is due to end on 1 October.
Samusocial de Paris (SSP) has been commissioned by Île-de-France’s regional health agency to provide healthcare for asylum seekers returned to France in the first eight days after their deportation from the UK, when they are accommodated in a shelter in Paris.
They have documented the cases of 90 returnees between 22 January and 7 June 2026. All are young men, mostly in their 20s and early-30s, who sought sanctuary in the UK after fleeing a variety of conflict zones including Eritrea, Sudan and Afghanistan.
About 1,400 people have been forcibly removed to France by the Home Office since the scheme began in August 2025, although some have subsequently returned to the UK in lorries or small boats.
The evidence compiled by SSP has been submitted to the French Assembly’s cross-party inquiry into the impact of the Anglo-French border deals known as Le Touquet agreements. This evidence comes from their own clinical consultations with returnees and some hospital reports from those sent to A&E.
Many of those detained in the UK for “one in one out” have fled torture and other forms of persecution in their home countries, and have been subjected to modern slavery on their journeys in countries such as Libya. However, the focus of the report is on what happened to people while they were detained in the UK as part of the scheme and during their removal to France.
According to the report: “Consultations are revealing signs consistent with recent physical and psychological violence as well as the consequences of prolonged detention in conditions described as particularly degrading.” It states that the physical and psychological conditions documented are “explicitly linked to the implementation of the France-British agreement”.
The report adds: “The frequency and recurrence of the incidents reported by people transferred under the Franco-British agreement appear particularly worrying.”
One A&E medical report from a returnee who arrived in France in such a bad state that he was sent to hospital reads: “The patient’s general condition was marked by significant suffering and shock upon arrival necessitating referral to the hospital emergency department. The medical certificate mentions reports of physical violence in England, including diffuse bruising, injuries consistent with restraint (lacerations with handcuffs) and abdominal pain resulting from repeated blows.”
The report includes 13 case studies documenting a range of injuries, including problems that worsened due to a lack of medical treatment, while people were in detention in the UK. Concerns were also raised about mental health conditions such as PTSD.
In one case, a man was referred for emergency psychiatric treatment because he was too disoriented to find his way back to the dormitory while in the shelter, suffered from body tics and incoherent speech and was deemed to be at risk of suicide. The report highlights limited options for ongoing psychiatric treatment for this group.
SSP recommends that a mechanism should be established to collect information on allegations of mistreatment by the British authorities that can be sent to the UK. It also suggests reporting this issue to the French prosecutor under article 40 of the French code of criminal procedure.
Nihal Osman, a programme coordinator for Médecins Sans Frontières, which also provides health support for this group of returnees, said: “This one in one out agreement is a machine for psychological destruction.
“The deeply concerning physical injuries sustained whilst in detention in the United Kingdom, which we have documented among those deported, must be viewed in the light of a serious psychological deterioration.”
The UK Home Office and the company Mitie, which provides the guards for the asylum seekers, have been approached for comment.

European gas price may rise to $1,200-$1,300 in cold winter — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:36:23 UTC
23:36:23 KST

MOSCOW, September 14. /TASS/. European gas prices could rise to $1,200-$1,300 per 1,000 cubic meters if the winter is cold and the conflict in the Middle East continues at the same time, Finam Financial Group analyst Sergey Kaufman told TASS.
Earlier, the price of the October futures contract at the TTF hub in the Netherlands exceeded $1,000 per 1,000 cubic meters for the first time since December 2022. Meanwhile, spot gas prices at Europe's main trading hubs had already exceeded $1,000 per 1,000 cubic meters last week. Gazprom noted that the approaching heating season is rapidly reducing opportunities to replenish gas reserves in Europe's underground storage facilities, while gas prices have already reached levels seen during the energy crisis in late 2022. Russian President Vladimir Putin said earlier he did not rule out that European gas prices could rise as high as $1,500 per 1,000 cubic meters.
According to Kaufman, in the medium term, gas price dynamics will depend entirely on the situation in the Middle East and winter weather. "In a scenario involving a cold winter and continued tensions around Iran, we see the possibility of a further rise to $1,200-$1,300 per 1,000 cubic meters. At the same time, we do not currently expect a gas crisis as severe as the one in 2022. The EU is now less dependent on gas amid the development of renewable energy and lower demand, while supply on the LNG market is gradually increasing, so we do not expect urgent purchases at any price," he said.
If the Strait of Hormuz reopens soon, prices could even fall to around $600 per 1,000 cubic meters, the expert noted. However, a full normalization of prices should not be expected over the next 12 months even if the Strait of Hormuz reopens soon, as low inventory levels at European underground gas storage facilities will generate additional demand, the Finam analyst added.
"At the beginning of the conflict in the Middle East, when supplies from Qatar stopped, European importers bet on the conflict being short-lived and planned to replenish underground storage facilities more actively once the situation normalized. Against this backdrop, they chose not to compete aggressively with the Asia-Pacific market and allowed some supplies to go east. In retrospect, however, that strategy now appears to have been a mistake. There are less than two months left before the start of the active heating season, while EU underground gas storage facilities are only 68% full," Kaufman said.
This is 12 percentage points lower than a year ago and 25 percentage points below the level two years ago. European importers' attempts to make up at least some of the shortfall are pushing prices higher. "It would be a good outcome if storage facilities could be filled to 75% by the start of the withdrawal season, but even that would still be a low level," the expert concluded.

UK government moves to acquire Speciality Steel UK
Newsflash: The UK government has decided to acquire the country’s third-largest steel producer.
The Business Secretary JonathanReynolds has announced the Government will “work towards” the public acquisition of Speciality Steel UK (SSUK), after ministers decided they could not support its sale to Norwegian steel startup Blastr Green Steel.
SSUK has been in liquidation since last year, and was part of Sanjeev Gupta’s Liberty Steel before its recent collapse.
The company is an important part of the UK steel sector as it can make steel for use in the auto, aero and defence sectors.
According to the government, SSUK’s four sites support over 1,300 jobs in Rotherham, Stocksbridge, Brinsworth and Wednesbury.
Reynolds is stepping in after deciding Blastr’s proposal could not provide long-term stability, certainty and value for money.
Reynolds says:
“We do not intervene in private companies lightly. But nor can we simply stand aside and allow the future of this company and over 1,300 jobs to be decided by default.
“Working towards public acquisition will keep options open while we work with local leaders, workers, industry and investors to determine the best long-term future for these sites, which could play a vital role in the future of the growth-driving sectors in our Industrial Strategy, including defence and advanced manufacturing.
“ I am determined that we take the time to properly assess the opportunities available here and make decisions that support growth, jobs and Britain’s industrial future.”
Trade body UK Steel has welcomed the government’s move.
It believes the decision to acquire SSUK will give “added security” to the 1,300 employees in Rotherham, Stocksbridge, Brinsworth and Wednesbury.
It should also reassure potential customers that SSUK is returning to regular production and able to satisfy new orders.
UK Steel director-general, GarethStace, says:
“This Government is once again stepping up to do what is needed for the UK steel industry. SSUK is already well on its way to returning to full operations and retaking its place at the heart of critical UK supply chains.
It is crucial that the custodian of this key strategic asset is the right owner and investor, with the expertise and long-term ambition that the dedicated workforce deserve.”

Here’s a breakdown of the parts of the AI value chain that are vulnerable to a slowdown, from CharuChanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo:
AI model developers: Launches may take longer, while spending on safety and testing rises.
Advanced processors: Near-term orders may remain supported, but future demand could soften if companies run fewer large training programmes.
Memory chips: This is one of the more vulnerable areas. Manufacturers are adding supply to meet very strong demand forecasts. If demand is delayed just as new production arrives, shortages could turn into excess supply and weaker prices.
Data centres, power and cooling: Projects already underway provide near-term support. The risk would rise if major technology companies began cancelling future projects.
AI use and adoption: Companies can continue using models that already exist. Demand for computing power to run those models—often called inference—may therefore remain strong.
Cybersecurity and AI monitoring: These areas could attract more investment as companies spend more on independent testing, system controls and protection against misuse.
Business software: The next winners may be companies that use AI to deliver clear productivity gains, rather than those simply spending the most on building larger models.

Fiscal pressure from Iran War clouds Gulf States’ US spending plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:34:25 UTC
23:34:25 KST

Fiscal pressure from Iran War clouds Gulf States’ US spending plans
Gulf nations may prioritize domestic investments over US commitments amid economic pressures, says new report.
The ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran could make it harder for three Gulf countries — Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates — to deliver on nearly $4 trillion in economic commitments to the US announced under President Donald Trump’s “America First” agenda, according to a new analysis from the Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE).
The 15-page report released Monday says the Gulf states are facing growing economic pressure from the US and Israel’s war on Iran, including the need to spend more on defence, energy infrastructure and trade.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump dismisses calls for AI slowdown from leading tech CEOs
- list 2 of 4Israeli minister threatens to revoke filmmakers’ citizenship over Gaza film
- list 3 of 4Why is Trump warning Zelenskyy not to hit Russian diesel refineries?
- list 4 of 4‘Silent Cold War’: Why calls to slow AI have sparked new US–China frontier
“The conflict has weakened their fiscal positions and economic prospects and may have lasting effects on their growth models. It has also weakened their confidence in the US security umbrella in the Gulf,” the report said.
The war has hit the Gulf economies much harder than the global economy at large, according to the report. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) cut its 2026 global growth forecast by 0.3 percentage points, but the reductions were much larger for the Gulf states.
The IMF cut Qatar’s growth forecast by 14.7 percentage points, to 8.6 percent. Saudi Arabia’s forecast was cut from 4.5 percent to 1.7 percent, while the UAE’s was reduced from 5.6 percent to 1.7 percent, as well.
Gulf governments have enough financial assets and borrowing capacity to avoid an immediate funding crisis, according to the report, but PIIE said the economic pressure could lead the countries to prioritise spending at home over investments in the US.
“Saudi Arabia had already begun rebalancing toward domestic investment before the war; the conflict appears to have reinforced that shift,” the report said.
Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund has reduced the share of its portfolio allocated to international investments by 10 percent over the last six years to 20 percent, down from 30 percent in 2020.
The report also warns that delays in fulfilling the investment commitments could lead to additional pressure from the White House, which has previously used tariffs to push other countries to follow through on their commitments.
“The Trump administration has already shown limited patience with delays by other partners. In January 2026, Trump threatened to raise tariffs on South Korean goods, citing delays by the Korean legislature in enacting its US investment agreement,” the report said.
“Continued frustration over Korea’s delayed implementation also appears linked to the recent US decision to scale back joint military exercises there,” the report continued.
That pressure has coincided with progress on US investment commitments from South Korea.
The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the South Korean government is close to a potential energy investment deal worth more than $100bn that would help support the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure in the United States.
Qatar, meanwhile, continues to pursue investments in the US energy sector. QatarEnergy began producing liquefied natural gas (LNG) at a facility in Texas in March and began exports the following month.
QatarEnergy’s ties with US energy companies could expand further. It is negotiating with several US LNG producers on contracts through 2031 to help replace capacity lost after Iranian attacks damaged Qatar’s LNG facilities, according to the Reuters news agency.
Political pressures
The PIIE report said the lack of clear definitions, timelines and ways to measure the investment commitments could make it difficult to determine whether the countries are actually following through. The deals have also drawn scrutiny from lawmakers.
“Political concerns in the United States present another obstacle. Members of Congress have raised questions about the economic and national security effects of Gulf investments, governance, and possible conflicts of interest,” the report said.
One example cited in the report is a $2bn investment in Binance by a UAE-backed investment firm. The deal used a stablecoin issued by World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency company linked to the Trump family. Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Jeff Merkley of Oregon sought records about the transaction, citing concerns about the financial ties involved in June 2025.
By October 2025 Trump pardoned Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who had pleaded guilty in 2023 to violating US anti-money-laundering laws.
Lawmakers have also raised concerns about Gulf sovereign wealth funds from Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar being involved in financing major US corporate deals, across US media, including Paramount Skydance’s proposed acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, the parent company of CNN.
“The question now is whether, and in what form, the three countries will implement their commitments,” the report said.

This video grab shows a Burç air defense system during a test-fire.
Turkish defense firm Roketsan on Sept. 14 destroyed a moving target during a test firing of its Sungur missile from its Burç mobile air defense system.
The Burç is a next-generation air defense system that combined optimized superior firepower like the Sungur missile and 20/30-millimeter cannon with active and passive sensors.
The shoulder-launched Sungur air defense system was designed for short-range air defense of mobile and fixed units and facilities on the battlefield with a range of over 8 kilometers (roughly 5 miles).
The system was also designed to be compatible for integration with various other platforms.
The missile uses an imaging infrared seeker that allows it to lock onto targets before launch and automatically track them. Its fire-and-forget operating mode enables the missile to guide itself toward its target after launch.
The system features a highexplosive, semi-armor-piercing warhead and a two-stage solidpropellant rocket motor. Roketsan says the missile is designed for rapid engagement and high maneuverability.

Ukrainian F-16s Shoot Down Jet Drones – But Is It Enough?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:32:00 UTC
23:32:00 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine has been using US-made F-16 fighters to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones.
Speaking to a television channel during his recent visit to Canada, Zelensky said Ukraine has “sometimes” resorted to Western air-to-air missiles, such as the US-made AIM-9 and AIM-120, to shoot down newer, faster jet-powered drones.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We use the corresponding missiles on F-16s, shooting down jet drones,” Zelensky said, as reported by state media Ukrinform.
“It is expensive, but sometimes, when nothing can be done to shoot down a particular jet drone, human life is more important and more expensive, so sometimes F-16s were used against such drones,” he added.
Zelensky’s comments came as Canada announced a new $3 billion package for Kyiv, which includes an unspecified number of AIM-9s and AIM-120s.
Recent comments from Yuriy Ihnat, the air force’s spokesperson, suggest that Ukrainian F-16s have at times resorted to onboard 20mm cannons to down jet-powered drones, which he said poses major risks to the aircraft itself. Pilots would be closer to the drones based on their size at open-fire ranges compared to enemy fighters, bombers, or other crewed aircraft; this makes debris from the drones a follow-on hazard to the shooter’s aircraft.
Jet-powered drones, which blur the line between drones and missiles, have been increasingly used by Russia against Ukraine in recent attacks, posing challenges for Ukrainian air defenses as current interceptor drones struggle to catch up with their higher speeds.
Russian Drones Just Miss Former CIA Director David Petraeus: a View From a Train Near the Polish Border
While Ukraine has been developing jet-powered interceptor drones as a countermeasure, Zelensky’s remark suggests a potential gap in Ukrainian air defense, as the AIM-9s and AIM-120s are typically costlier than interceptor drones.
While the latest AIM-9X Sidewinder missile is estimated to cost over $450,000 per unit, Ukrainian Air Force F-16s almost always carry the AIM-9M which cost about $84,000 when originally purchased by the US Air Force (USAF). The AIM-120 is $386,000 per unit, according to the US Air Force – though TWZ reported that some variants can cost over $1 million per missile.
Ukraine began receiving the missiles as part of the armaments for its new NATO-standard aircraft donated by its allies, starting with the F-16 in mid-2024, though the total number received remains classified.
Ukraine’s demands for air-to-air missiles
The rise of jet-powered drones has exposed a gap in Ukraine’s layered air defense, with what was once reserved to counter cruise missiles now used to counter Russian drones.
Since 2022, Russia’s aerial threats against Ukrainian cities primarily consist of Iranian-designed, propeller-driven Shahed drones and their Russian variants, with the occasional cruise and ballistic missiles.
Those drones are often countered by machine-gun fire and electronic jamming or, more recently, by propeller-driven interceptor drones, with a 90% overall interception rate, whereas air defense missiles – both ground and air-launched – are reserved for cruise missiles, with the scarce and coveted Patriot systems reserved for the faster ballistic missiles.
But with more jet-powered drones flying over Ukraine, Kyiv has had to intercept them with the missile stockpiles reserved for cruise missiles – including the AIM-9s and AIM-120s, according to Zelensky.
Are the new pledges enough?
Ukraine has long struggled with the number of those missiles in its arsenal, with shortages reported in late 2025.
Kyiv’s allies have since tried to remedy the situation. On July 30, the Pentagon announced approval of a $3.5 billion contract to produce thousands of AIM-120s for countries worldwide, including Ukraine – while total production is estimated to reach thousands by 2031, it’s unclear how many were destined for Ukraine.
More recently, at the 36th Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting, Berlin said it would boost AIM-9 deliveries from Bundeswehr stocks – but again, the exact number is not disclosed.
But known deliveries – before Ukraine ran out in 2025 – suggest that numbers have been limited.
One publicized figure from Canada suggests it sent at least 12 AIM-120s, 43 AIM-9s, and 250 AIM-7s in 2023, excluding other components sent to Ukraine. Dutch monitoring site Oryx estimated 43 AIM-9s and 287 AIM-7s from Canada, with no AIM-120s mentioned.
At present, Russia is estimated to be launching 100-200 drones per day against Ukraine consistently, excluding cruise missiles, with the Air Force suggesting in late August that over half were jet-powered at times.
Assuming Russia launches only 50 jet-powered drones and cruise missiles at Ukraine per day, that would be around 1,500 targets for Ukraine to shoot down, AIM-120s or not.
The good news for Ukraine is that the industry is scaling up production of jet-powered interceptors, other air defense missiles are available, and Russia may be having trouble getting Chinese jet engines for the drones.
But the bad news is that it still needs to intercept over 1,000 jet-powered drones that fly like a missile each month, one way or another.

Former senior Israeli security officials are warning that a deliberate security escalation could be used to disrupt or delay the upcoming election, arguing that political actors may have both the incentive and the ability to inflame tensions ahead of the vote.
The warning appears in a video featuring former prime minister, defense minister and IDF chief of staff Ehud Barak; former defense minister and IDF chief of staff Moshe Ya’alon; former Mossad director Tamir Pardo; and former police commissioner Moshe Karadi.
The video was produced by the Forum of Protest Organizations, an umbrella group of protest movements, and distributed on social media.
“A security escalation before elections serves the interests of certain players,” the video states. “They have both the ability and the incentive. Any scenario that prevents the elections from taking place on time is a scenario that must be prepared for.”
Barak said that “a security escalation on the eve of elections serves political campaigns,” adding that those who benefit from such a development “also have both the ability and the incentive.”
Karadi described the coming election as potentially “the most dramatic since the establishment of the State of Israel” and warned that Israel should prepare for any scenario that could prevent it from taking place as scheduled.
He also accused Jewish extremists in the West Bank of trying to trigger a broader confrontation.
“Everything being done today in Judea and Samaria by Jewish terrorists is being done for one purpose: to bring the IDF into a major campaign in the area that would serve as a legitimate pretext to declare the elections canceled,” Karadi said.
Ya’alon issued a similar warning, saying: “Jewish pogromists are trying to foment war. This must be stopped before it happens.”
Pardo pointed to the possibility of a wider regional confrontation, including tensions involving Turkey.
“The danger facing us is the postponement and cancellation of the elections,” he said. “We have another front with Turkey, in an attempt to reach the coming elections with the option of canceling or postponing them by creating another state of war.”
The former officials did not present evidence in the video of a specific plan to provoke an escalation or postpone the election.
The Forum of Protest Organizations said the video is part of a broader campaign focused on safeguarding the integrity of the election. The group also launched a website collecting warnings and commentary from other figures who have raised concerns about the possibility of a politically driven security escalation before the vote.

Public broadcasters to be merged into four “houses” from 2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:26:09 UTC
23:26:09 KST

Public broadcasters to be merged into four “houses” from 2029
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The cabinet has published its plan to reform the Dutch public broadcasting system, which will replace the current 11 broadcasting organisations with four “broadcasting houses” from 2029.
News broadcaster NOS and educational broadcaster NTR will also merge under the NOS name, and no new broadcasters will be allowed to join the system, media minister Rianne Letschert told parliament on Friday, NOS reported.
The plan was first drawn up last year and was included in the coalition agreement and is open to public consultation.
Current system
 There are currently 11 public broadcasting organisations under the umbrella of public broadcasting body NPO: AVROTROS, BNNVARA, EO, Human, KRO-NCRV, Max, Ongehoord Nederland (ON), PowNed, VPRO, WNL and Zwart.
Each has its own political, religious or social focus and together they make programmes for three national television channels and five radio stations.
To join, a group must sign up at least 50,000 paying members, which earns it a provisional licence for five years. To keep a permanent place it needs 100,000 members.
A broadcaster can lose its licence if the media regulator sanctions it twice in five years, if it no longer meets the legal requirements, or if the NPO says it refuses to cooperate with the others. These are the three grounds Letschert used last week when she said she would withdraw the licence of far-right broadcaster ON.
Under the new plan, the membership requirement is scrapped and broadcasters will no longer be able to join the system or be thrown out, although the regulator will still be able to act against wrongdoing.
Four houses
 Which broadcasters go into which house has not been decided yet, but the broadcasters have already said who they want to work with: KRO-NCRV, Max and WNL; EO, VPRO and Human; AVROTROS and PowNed; and BNNVARA and Zwart.
Zwart, set up by rapper Akwasi to bring more diversity to television, has been broadcasting on a provisional licence since 2022 but still has to win a permanent one before it can join a house.
The houses can keep their old names or choose new ones, and will have more say over their own programming as the NPO’s coordinating role shrinks.
Letschert said the current system has too many boards and too much internal competition. “With less administrative bustle and more shared responsibility, the public broadcaster can focus on making good programmes, strong journalism and digital innovation,” she said.
The media regulator, the Commissariaat voor de Media, has criticised the plan, saying it gives broadcasters too few clear rules and relies too much on self-regulation.
The draft law goes next to the Council of State (Raad van State), the government’s senior advisory body on legislation, and then to parliament and the senate. The cabinet wants the new system to start in 2029.

greenhouse converts into inhabitable light installation for music festival in the UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:25:36 UTC
23:25:36 KST

Shed reworks A Reclaimed Greenhouse into a Gathering Space
Created by Kren., a London/Vienna-based design studio, Shed is a bespoke installation for independent music festival Loud Places, set a couple of hours outside of London. Shed refers to its domestic origins and the light it sheds on the rest of the festival, acting as both a beacon and an intimate space to congregate. As an inhabitable light installation, it functions as a place to gather around throughout the day, and within at night. The yellow frame and diffuse screens are foregrounds and backgrounds that blur and then interchange as the sun sets, light emanating consistently. Working with a reclaimed greenhouse structure, the adapted system explores a key interest of the studio; the transformable potential of the everyday object.
Shed stands in the festival’s meadow area
Kren. turns a Greenhouse Frame into an Illuminated Shelter
Taking an optimistic stance on working with what we have, the adaptation functions as a creative challenge in the face of resource austerity, emblematic of the ethos of the cross-disciplinary design studio. Referencing Derek Jarman’s greenhouse bed in his 1980s Bankside loft, Shed explores the archetype as a place of intimacy. Traditionally associated with the growing of plants, here the greenhouse’s purpose is to gather and enclose. Similar to Jarman’s domestic intervention, it creates both a focal point and a space-within-a-space, offering shelter within the expanse of the meadow. By removing the thermal envelope of the glass, the work looks at the greenhouse for its rudimentary yet effective creation of a basic structure rather than capitalizing on its thermal qualities.
the adaptation of the greenhouse structure explores the transformable potential of the everyday object
Light and Reclaimed Materials Shape the Festival Shelter
The greenhouse acts as The Primitive Hut. Simultaneously, Shed is a light installation. Where the greenhouse frame provides the structure and the shelter, modified industrial lights hang within. Constantly glowing, as night falls, the translucent TPU becomes back-lit, turning the entire envelope into a diffuse screen. The lights divide the internal space, suspended just below seated eye-level along the roof ridge. This means that when the space is occupied at night, silhouettes appear to animate the walls whilst light is projected out towards the festival. In combination with the adapted aluminum frame and modified lights, PVC curtains (traditionally used in industrial cooling systems) demarcate the entry, hung by cable ties. This palette of materiality speaks to the agricultural heritage of the greenhouse whilst also referencing the innovation and DIY nature of music festivals and club culture.

A Russian-speaking operator using the handle JackPoterz ran campaigns against military intelligence targets in Ukrainian and European governments, plus diplomatic and defense bodies and individuals connected to US foreign policy.
More than 20 organizations appeared in the actor's planning and live operations, from ministries and embassies to think tanks and defense companies. Ukrainian government, military, and diplomatic staff came up most often, and the operators scanned email and remote-access systems across more than two dozen Ukrainian state organizations. Russia has worked these networks all war, treating Ukrainian media as a priority cyber target.

Drone technology was the other target
The operators bulk-exported the mailboxes of at least two drone component manufacturers and went after a military drone maker. They also stole a complete proprietary software development kit for a drone vision system, the code and documentation engineers need to build on that hardware, then spent days pulling it apart. They recovered the product architecture, the parts list, the supplier dependencies, and details of a product the company had not announced. Military drone control and AI vision firmware drew their particular interest.

What the chatbot did for the operation
Trending Now
Claude fingerprinted mail systems, built the phishing infrastructure, ran commands inside victim networks, harvested credentials, and organized hundreds of gigabytes of stolen data, Anthropic found. Automated agents also checked whether the group's implants were being detected, rewrote flagged malware until it passed, and staged it for the next intrusion. A Russian-speaking actor moved from hotel-booking and fintech intrusions to attacking AI firms, planting instructions in one vendor's testing system and hitting roughly 30 companies in four days while chasing an unreleased Claude model. A Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking group meanwhile sold fake discounted access to the assistant, routing customers to a different model and stealing their logins.

Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:23:40 UTC
23:23:40 KST

Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks
Healthy brain wiring may help shield older adults from some of the cognitive effects of age-related gray matter loss.
- Date:
- September 14, 2026
- Source:
- Keck School of Medicine of USC
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that the brain’s short-range wiring may help protect cognition even as gray matter shrinks with age. Healthier connections just beneath the brain’s surface were linked to better language skills and appeared to weaken the impact of gray matter loss.
- Share:
Scientists at the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have uncovered evidence that two neighboring types of brain tissue may work together to support thinking abilities later in life. Their findings suggest that the condition of the brain's local communication pathways could influence how strongly gray matter loss affects cognition.
The study, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, included brain imaging and cognitive testing from 459 adults aged 60 and older living in communities across India. The research is among the first to investigate superficial white matter in a community-based population from a low- and middle-income country.
The Brain's Local Communication Network
Superficial white matter forms a thin layer of nerve fibers directly beneath the gray matter covering the outside of the brain. These short, curved fibers connect nearby regions of the cerebral cortex, allowing them to exchange information. They can be thought of as local roads linking neighboring areas of the brain.
Gray matter serves a different role. It contains many of the nerve cells responsible for processing information. Together, gray matter and the white matter directly beneath it form closely connected systems that may both contribute to cognitive health.
"Gray matter and superficial white matter are physically close and may play different roles: gray matter processes information, while superficial white matter helps nearby brain regions communicate," said Yingxu Liu, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar at the Stevens INI and first author of the study. "Our findings suggest that cognitive health depends not only on how much gray matter is preserved, but also on the condition of the wiring that connects it."
Measuring the Brain's Hidden Wiring
To investigate these local connections, the researchers used an advanced type of diffusion MRI. This imaging technique tracks the movement of water through brain tissue, allowing scientists to examine microscopic features that conventional brain scans may not reveal.
The researchers focused on measurements related to neurite density and the amount of freely moving water surrounding these structures. Neurites are the small projections through which nerve cells send and receive signals. A lower density of neurites or an increase in free water can indicate damage or disruption in tissue associated with processes including loss of myelin, inflammation, or swelling.
Participants also underwent assessments covering several areas of cognition, including language, memory, executive function, and visuospatial ability.
The most consistent connection between superficial white matter health and cognitive performance involved language. People with healthier superficial white matter tended to perform better on language tests. The strongest associations appeared in frontotemporal regions of the brain involved in recognizing words, speaking fluently, and temporarily holding language information in mind.
Healthy Wiring May Cushion Gray Matter Loss
Measures of gray matter atrophy were still the strongest overall predictors of cognitive ability. However, the researchers found that the impact of gray matter loss appeared to vary depending on the health of nearby superficial white matter.
When these local connections showed poorer integrity, gray matter loss was more strongly associated with impaired language performance and broader cognitive difficulties. When superficial white matter was healthier, the link between gray matter loss and poorer cognition was weaker.
This raises the possibility that the condition of the brain's local wiring could help explain why two people with similar amounts of gray matter loss do not necessarily experience the same degree of cognitive decline.
"The findings point to superficial white matter as a possible source of resilience," said Leon Aksman, PhD, assistant professor of research neurology at the Stevens INI and senior author of the study. "Two people with a similar degree of gray matter loss may not experience the same cognitive effects if the local connections surrounding that gray matter differ in health. Following participants over time will be essential to test whether preserving these connections can help maintain cognition."
Expanding Brain Aging Research Beyond Typical Populations
The researchers drew their data from the Harmonized Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia for the Longitudinal Aging Study in India, known as LASI-DAD. More than half of the larger LASI-DAD population has low literacy, while about 60% lives in rural communities.
Populations with these characteristics have historically been underrepresented in brain imaging studies, making the research an opportunity to examine cognitive aging across a broader range of social, educational, and geographic backgrounds.
In this analysis, the association between superficial white matter and language ability was stronger among people who were unable to read or who read incorrectly, those who had received no formal education, and participants living in rural areas.
The researchers emphasize that the results do not establish that these social factors caused changes in brain tissue. Instead, they suggest that brain aging may be shaped by a complex combination of experiences throughout life, including education, social circumstances, health, and environmental exposures.
What Scientists Still Need to Learn
Because participants were examined at only one point in time, the study cannot establish which brain changes occurred first. Researchers do not yet know whether deterioration of superficial white matter begins before gray matter loss, develops alongside it, or precedes measurable cognitive decline.
Long-term research that follows people as they age will be needed to clarify these relationships. Future studies will also investigate how vascular health, inflammation, Alzheimer's related proteins, and other biological factors interact with changes in gray and white matter.
"A fuller understanding of brain aging requires research that reflects the world's social, cultural, and geographic diversity," said Arthur W. Toga, PhD, director of the Stevens INI and Provost Professor at USC. "By studying an underrepresented population and looking beyond gray matter alone, this work brings us closer to identifying the biological and social factors that may protect cognition across the lifespan."
In addition to Liu and Aksman, the study's authors include Kirsten M. Lynch, Miguel Arce Rentería, Emma Nichols, Alden L. Gross, Lindsay C. Kobayashi, Neda Jahanshad, John P. John, Harshita V. Vishwakarma, Pranali Khobragade, Joyita Banerjee, Niranjan Khandelwal, Jyoti Dangwal, Sudhir Saxena, Nirod Medhi, Soumik Das, Prudhvinath Reddy, Pratyaksha Rana, Arjun Narula, Saravanan Kannan, Dinesh Patel, A. B. Dey, Sharmistha Dey, and Jinkook Lee.
The research was supported by the National Institute on Aging (R01AG080473, RF1AG087965, RF1AG088003, R01AG087513), the National Institute of Mental Health (R01MH134004), the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (RF1NS136995), and the Office of the Director of the National Institutes of Health (S10OD032285).

Journal Reference:

B. Dey, Sharmistha Dey, Jinkook Lee, Leon M. Aksman. Superficial white matter and gray matter jointly support cognition among older adults in India. Alzheimer\'s, 2026; 22 (7) DOI: 10.1002/alz.71697

‘Silent Cold War’: Why calls to slow AI have sparked new US–China frontier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14

23:23:29 KST

‘Silent Cold War’: Why calls to slow AI have sparked new US–China frontier
Anthropic CEO urges restricted China access to AI tech, sparking accusations of US technological dominance strategies.
China has warned against “fear-mongering” after the CEO of a top artificial intelligence (AI) company in the United States sounded the alarm against AI advancement and called for restrictions on the sale of AI chips to China.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Saturday called for the development of the most powerful AI systems to be slowed down, warning that they could soon pose potentially catastrophic risks to humanity itself.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3China slams US claims of ‘industrial-scale’ AI theft
- list 2 of 3Anthropic claims Claude AI used for missile projects, global espionage
- list 3 of 3Anthropic discloses 4th AI hacking incident as researcher quits over safety
His proposal also calls for Washington to restrict China’s access to advanced technology – prompting Beijing to accuse the US of using AI safety as a pretext to preserve its technological dominance.
The dispute comes as Washington and Beijing compete over increasingly capable AI models, with US President Donald Trump declaring, “Whoever wins AI wins.”
So, what has got AI giants worried, why is China being seen as a threat?
Why are AI tech giants raising the alarm?
Anthropic’s Amodei warned in an essay published over the weekend that AI capabilities have been advancing rapidly, and he proposed pacing the development of frontier models to give governments and researchers more time to manage their risks.
“Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails,” he wrote.
His assertions were endorsed by his rivals – OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX founder and Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
In addition to AI safety, Amodei warned that a “Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world” and urged Washington to maintain restrictions on cutting-edge AI chips and chipmaking equipment going to China. He also called for action against alleged “distillation” of US models by Chinese AI laboratories.
On Sunday, Trump rejected calls for a slowdown, describing some concerns as exaggerated.
“We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” he said on Sunday.
What did China say?
China’s Foreign Ministry on Monday urged countries to pursue an “open, inclusive and benevolent approach to AI”.
“Fomenting various threats, engaging in confrontation and malicious competition will only disrupt the process of global governance of artificial intelligence and is not in the interests of any party,” said ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun.
The state-backed Global Times went further, describing Amodei’s proposal as a “Cold War playbook” whose real purpose was to curb Chinese AI development and preserve US technological dominance.
“This ‘silent AI Cold War’ is hypocritical and short-sighted,” it said.
What is the latest in the US-China AI race?
The US remains ahead in several of the most important features of the AI race, but China has been closing the gap, experts say.
American companies continue to dominate private investment and production of leading AI models. According to Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index Report, US companies invested $285.9bn in AI in 2025, compared with $12.4bn in China.
The US also has an advantage in the most advanced semiconductors needed to train cutting-edge models.
However, Chinese companies have demonstrated that they can produce resilient AI models despite US restrictions on their access to the most advanced AI chips.
In January, the release of Chinese AI startup DeepSeek made headlines after it caused share prices in US tech companies to plummet, claiming that its model would cost only a fraction of the money its competitors had spent on their own AI programmes to build.
DeepSeek sent shock waves throughout AI circles when the company published a paper in December stating that “training” the latest model of DeepSeek – curating and inputting the information it needs to answer questions – would require less than $6m worth of computing power from Nvidia H800 chips.
This is only a small fraction of the multibillion-dollar AI budgets enjoyed by US tech giants such as OpenAI for ChatGPT and US-owned Google for Gemini. OpenAI CEO Altman said that his firm’s latest programme, GPT-4, cost more than $100m to train, Wired reported in April 2023.
The increasing AI-related competition between the world’s two largest economies has also seen Washington and Beijing put in place hostile policy measures against each other.
The US has imposed restrictions on China’s access to advanced semiconductors and chipmaking technology, arguing that cutting-edge chips could strengthen Chinese military, intelligence and surveillance capabilities.
The Trump administration has maintained controls on the most advanced chips, including Nvidia’s Blackwell processors, while allowing some less powerful chips to be sold to China.
Meanwhile, China possesses advantages in other areas of the AI supply chain, most notably in the production of critical rare earth minerals used in advanced technology and in generating more than twice as much electricity as the US, giving it access to the huge amounts of relatively cheap power needed to operate AI data centres.
In October, China tightened export controls for five critical rare-earth metals, as well as restrictions on the export of specialist technological equipment used to refine rare-earth metals.
Can either side claim a moral high ground?
Both Washington and Beijing portray their approach to AI as the more responsible one, but both are also pursuing the technology for national security and military purposes.
In June, the Trump administration ordered an acceleration of AI use across US intelligence and “warfighting” domains.
The US military confirmed in March that it used advanced AI tools in its war against Iran to rapidly process information, while insisting that humans make final targeting decisions.
The confirmation came amid calls at the time for an independent investigation into the bombing of a school in southern Iran that killed at least 156 people, mostly children.
Moreover, several reports have confirmed that Israel relied heavily on AI during its genocidal war on Gaza, which has killed nearly 73,800 Palestinians since October 2023 and turned most of the territory into rubble.
In July 2025, Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territory, released a report mapping the corporations aiding Israel in the displacement of Palestinians and its genocidal war on Gaza in breach of international law. US tech and AI giant Palantir was one of the companies mentioned in the report.
In March 2021, US companies Google and Amazon agreed to a $1.2bn deal to supply cloud technology to Israel’s government and defence establishment. Known as Project Nimbus, the agreement gives Israeli authorities access to computing infrastructure capable of storing and processing large volumes of data and using tools such as facial and emotion recognition, biometric analysis and the handling of demographic information.
Moreover, the Pentagon has separately clashed with Anthropic over the company’s refusal to allow its models to be used for fully autonomous weapons or mass surveillance.
China has criticised the expanding military use of AI, warning this year against giving algorithms the power to “determine life and death”.
However, in July, research by Reuters news agency said Chinese military-linked researchers had used outputs from leading US AI models to help advance China’s defence capabilities, including for surveillance purposes.
An AP investigation last year found that AI and other technologies have become part of a vast Chinese surveillance apparatus used to track dissidents and minorities, including Uighurs and Tibetans. However, it found that US technology companies played a major role in supplying the technology that helped build that system.
Moreover, in February, the two economic powerhouses declined to join a declaration on governing the deployment of AI in warfare at an international military AI summit in Spain.
What next?
Calls by technology leaders to slow AI’s development raise questions about their ability and willingness to control the technology, according to Aya Ibrahim, a senior visiting fellow at the AI Now Institute.
Ibrahim told Al Jazeera that the warnings come as companies face enormous financial pressure to develop increasingly powerful AI systems.
“There is a lot of money that is dependent on them getting this out and, frankly, getting it right,” she said, adding that there are “increasing doubts about their ability to do either”.
She also questioned the framing of AI development as a race, saying it could encourage companies to develop the technology as quickly as possible while overlooking the consequences.
“The race narrative is inherently problematic because in many ways, you’re setting us up for a race to the bottom,” Ibrahim said.
“So you win and then what do you win and at what cost?”

Israel pursuing ‘elimination project’ against Palestinians: NGO
Unknown

Breadcrumb
Israel pursuing 'elimination project' against Palestinians in West Bank: B'Tselem
Israel is pursuing an "elimination project" aimed at dismantling Palestinian life in the occupied West Bank, as military violence, settler attacks, movement restrictions and land seizures intensify, an Israeli human rights group warned on Monday.
Israel's policies had dramatically escalated since the current government took office at the end of 2022, with the assault on Palestinians intensifying further following the outbreak of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, B'Tselem said in a report entitled "The Elimination Project: Israel's Systematic Dismantling of Palestinian Collective Life in the West Bank".
The report draws on more than 2,000 testimonies collected from Palestinians since October 2023, alongside more than three decades of documentation of Israeli abuses in the occupied territory.
It said the dismantling of Palestinian life was being carried out increasingly openly and violently through cooperation between Israeli state authorities and armed settler groups operating with state backing.
B'Tselem identified the five key areas driving removal of Palestinians from the West Bank as violence and intimidation, restrictions on movement, economic strangulation, social and political destruction, and ethnic cleansing and territorial takeover.
The group said the measures were making it increasingly difficult for Palestinians to maintain basic daily life while undermining the conditions needed for Palestinian society to exist as a political, social and territorial community.
Since 7 October 2023, Israeli forces have established 200 new checkpoints across the West Bank, according to the report.
It said around 18% of West Bank land had been seized through the establishment of settlements and settlement outposts, while 64 Palestinian shepherding communities had been depopulated following sustained settler and military harassment.
B'Tselem also said 1,087 Palestinians had been killed in the West Bank since 7 October 2023, including 242 children and 21 women.
The report said Israel's campaign was not limited to attacks on Palestinians, but was also aimed at deepening Israeli control over the occupied territory and creating a continuous Israeli presence.
"This is not only a matter of physical territory," it said, arguing that Israeli authorities were also seeking to impose exclusive control over historical, religious and identity-based narratives associated with the land.
It said Israeli forces protected organised settler attacks while violently suppressing Palestinian protests, while settlement farms and outposts were being used to take control of large areas of land.
"Israeli flags fill the West Bank, while Palestinian flags are repeatedly removed from public spaces," the report said.
Palestinian farmers have also been denied access to their land, while entire communities have been uprooted, it added.
B'Tselem said various branches of the Israeli state, including the military and Civil Administration, were working alongside settler movements to create conditions in which Palestinians live under constant threat of military and settler violence.
It singled out far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who has broad powers over civilian affairs in the West Bank, as a key figure in the process.
The report linked current Israeli policies to Smotrich's "Decisive Plan", published in 2017 before he became a minister.
The plan sets out three options for Palestinians, according to B'Tselem: accepting Jewish-Israeli supremacy while abandoning their national aspirations, leaving, or facing violent repression if they resist.
The group said elements of the plan had increasingly moved from ideology into government policy through state budgets, expanded governmental powers and measures implemented on the ground.
Smotrich said in September 2025 that he would use every means possible "to prevent the danger of a Palestinian state, including bringing about the collapse of the Palestinian Authority … through economic strangulation".
Speaking at a press conference on Monday, B'Tselem Executive Director Yuli Novak called on states and international institutions to intervene.
"States and international institutions must use every means available to stop Israeli crimes, protect Palestinians, and stop the elimination project," she said.
Kareem Jubran, who heads B'Tselem's field research on the West Bank, said the findings showed that violence, displacement and restrictions were part of a wider policy rather than isolated incidents.
"What we uncovered is that these are not separate incidents. All the disparate elements have one character, one goal. When you look at the picture from above, it leads to one conclusion: that the main goal is to eliminate Palestinians as a collective," he said.
Novak described Smotrich's 2017 plan as a "blueprint" for the process.
"It shows the ideological and the operational way to get to what we are calling an elimination," she said. "And he calls it victory by settlement. To win in a very final way so that nothing [such as a Palestinian state] can happen afterwards."
The report comes as Israel continues to expand settlement activity in the occupied West Bank despite international opposition and growing warnings over the viability of a future Palestinian state.
An Israeli court in Jerusalem last week rejected a bid by rights groups to halt tenders for a settlement project in E1, east of Jerusalem, which would further undermine territorial contiguity between Palestinian communities in the West Bank.
Israel's construction and housing ministry opened a tender in July for more than 1,200 housing units in the area.
The E1 project, approved by Israel last year after decades of delays partly due to pressure from successive US administrations, would further isolate occupied East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank.

Russia’s election outcome is all but predetermined. But does a protest vote still matter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:21:01 UTC
23:21:01 KST

Russia’s election outcome is all but predetermined. But does a protest vote still matter?
For 20 years now, Russian voters have had no way to vote against all candidates. The corresponding line was removed from all ballots in the summer of 2006 (including in State Duma elections). That leaves voters whose preferred candidates were blocked from running to decide on the most effective way to express protest. We looked into what strategies exist for this and whether anything Russians do can make a difference at all.
Some of the scenarios described in this piece assume that the election commission will act honestly — preventing ballot-stuffing and not falsify the results. We wouldn’t count on that.
Boycott the election
You won’t affect the outcome of the election.
A boycott would lower the official turnout figure — but only if the vote count is honest and no one casts a ballot in your place. It wouldn’t change the final results. The law on elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, eliminated the 25% minimum turnout requirement in 2007 — a threshold that would equal about 28 million voters today. Since then, an election has been considered valid no matter how many people show up to vote.
Without additional tools like opinion polls, observers also have no way to distinguish voters who deliberately boycotted the election as a form of protest from those who simply stayed home for other reasons. Your protest would go unnoticed.
Vote for a different federal party list
Your vote could either have no effect on the outcome at all, or reduce the percentage won by United Russia.
State Duma elections carry a 5% threshold, so, to simplify, only parties that clear it can compete for the 225 seats allocated through the federal electoral district.
In other words, a vote for a party that falls short of that threshold has no effect on how State Duma seats are distributed — it’s as if you never voted at all. Article 89 of the law on elections to the State Duma spells out the methodology in detail: the Central Election Commission first tallies only the votes cast for parties that cleared the threshold, then uses that total to allocate the 225 seats.
Vote for a different candidate
You can reduce the chances that a United Russia candidate wins and gets a seat in the State Duma.
Single-member district races for the State Duma don’t have runoffs. Whichever candidate wins a simple majority takes the seat. That makes it most effective to back the strongest challenger to the authorities, since protest votes split among several other candidates won’t change the outcome. Voters can identify that candidate by studying pre-election opinion polls themselves or relying on experts’ picks, such as the “Smart Voting” list compiled by FBK, an anti-corruption organization.
Take your ballot home
You won’t affect the outcome of the election. But you might uncover fraud at your polling station.
The law on elections to the State Duma doesn’t bar voters from taking their ballot home as a keepsake. Doing so won’t affect how seats are distributed, but election commissions are required to record any ballots taken away in their final report. These documents can later be found on your region’s election commission website.
If you take your ballot home, check line 11 of the precinct election commission’s report: “Number of lost ballots.” That line reflects the gap between the number of ballots issued and the number found in ballot boxes or left unused. A zero there would mean the commission ignored the shortfall — and most likely padded the count with at least one extra vote for someone.
Spoil your ballot
You won’t affect the outcome of the election. But mass protest is easier to spot this way.
Spoiling a ballot properly means marking at least two boxes next to party or candidate names — an X, a checkmark, or any other mark. That gets the ballot declared invalid, so it won’t count toward the distribution of seats. Election officials tally invalid ballots separately, recording the total in line nine of the precinct election commission’s final reports (separately for the single-member and party-list votes).
A mass protest by voters spoiling their ballots would show up both at individual polling stations and nationwide. For comparison, when votes for federal party lists were counted in the 2011, 2016, and 2021 Duma elections, 1.57%, 1.87%, and 2.08% of ballots, respectively, were declared invalid.
One more thing: deliberately invalidating a ballot requires marking at least two boxes. Otherwise, the vote could still be counted. Cross out an entire list of candidates or parties with a pen, for instance, but accidentally mark even one box, and the commission will count it as a vote for that option.
Cast an empty ballot
You shouldn’t affect the outcome of the election. But it all depends on the honesty of the election commission members.
An empty ballot is formally considered invalid too, and such ballots are counted together with spoiled ones. The problem is that a blank ballot can easily be turned into a valid one with a single stroke of a pen. That leaves voters to rely entirely on the good faith of whoever is counting the votes.
Leave an obscene or anti-war message on your ballot
A ballot with such a message could end up either valid or invalid. But cast it carefully — so you don’t end up with a fine.
Extraneous writing on a ballot doesn’t by itself determine whether it’s declared valid or invalid. That depends on whether the writing overlaps a voting box, and how many boxes are affected.
Voters who choose this approach should be extremely careful. In 2024, despite the officially declared secrecy of the ballot, several voters were detained for writing anti-war slogans on their ballots and charged with offenses including “discrediting” the military or minor hooliganism. Courts sentenced them to fines and administrative detention.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. YEKATERINBURG, September 14. /TASS/. The Republika Srpska (an entity within Bosnia and Herzegovina) is determined to maintain close cooperation with Russia, despite the ongoing pressure from the West, Foreign and Economic Policy Advisor to the President of the Republika Srpska Nemanja Plotan told TASS.
"Serbs suffered enough because of their close relations with Russia and I believe that the fact that we continue to maintain close cooperation shows that there are certain issues that depend not only on short-term geopolitical interests but also imply a deeper meaning… I believe that such things are more than valuable under present-day international relations," Plotan said while speaking at the International Festival of Youth in Russia’s Urals city of Yekaterinburg.
According to Plotan, the Republika Srpska had always faced pressure from the West due to its ties with Russia.
"It has always been a part of the Serbs’ historical experience beginning with the times of our fight for independence during the period of Ottoman rule, through World War I, World War II and especially during the disintegration of Yugoslavia," he continued. "There is always a perception that Serbs are ‘little Russians in the Balkans.'"
"All of this definitely changed to a greater extent this year as there is an increased level of interaction as of today between the peoples who see that we have our own national identity, culture, and so on," Plotan noted.
According to him, Serbs and Russians have found mutual understanding and a common language over the centuries.
"It is a great honor for me to be here and represent my country," Plotan noted addressing the youth festival in Russia.
The International Youth Festival is being held in Yekaterinburg from September 11 through 17 under the motto "Follow Your Dream." Some 10,000 young leaders aged from 14 to 17 from Russia and 191 world countries are expected to visit it. TASS is the event’s general information partner.

Party leaders of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland say future belongs back in EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:18:16 UTC
23:18:16 KST

The main parties from each nation want to break away from the UK but have different positions on how and when this might take place.
The first ministers of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have said they believe the future of their nations belong "in the European Union”.
The three leaders met in the Welsh capital, Cardiff, where their parties signed a joint agreement asserting the right of their nations to self-determination.
The three leaders met in their capacity as party leaders rather than as representatives of their respective governments.
Scotland’s John Swinney leads the Scottish National Party (SNP), Wales’ Rhun ap Iorwerth leads Plaid Cymru, meaning “the Party of Wales”, and Northern Ireland’s Michelle O’Neill is a senior figure in Sinn Féin. They were also joined by Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald.
The SNP and Plaid Cymru support independence for Scotland and Wales respectively, while Sinn Féin campaigns for Irish reunification. The three parties differ over how and when constitutional change should take place.
In 2014, Scotland held an independence referendum in which 55.3% of voters chose to remain part of the United Kingdom.
The agreement signed in Cardiff said the UK government at Westminster should not have the right to “block democracy”.
“Our nations have the right to self-determination. No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future,” it said.
Announcing the agreement, Swinney said the three parties were “absolutely united by that principle of self-determination”, adding that it “lies at the heart of the agreement that we have signed today”.
At a joint news conference, Swinney and O’Neill called for referendums on Scottish independence and Irish reunification respectively. Ap Iorwerth did not set out a timetable for a Welsh independence vote.
Labour, which governs at UK level from London, accused Plaid Cymru of wanting to use its position in Wales “to break up Britain”.

A fleet of commercial ships and traditional cargo dhows operate near the Strait of Hormuz, a highly strategic maritime bottleneck.
An Iranian cargo vessel was struck early on Sept. 13 off Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media said, and Tehran postponed a plan to brief neighboring countries on its contested efforts to manage shipping in the strait.
The attack drew attention back to the strait after threats to shipping in the Red Sea intensified last week. Iran-backed Houthi rebels battling government forces in Yemen captured an island on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency quoted the Qeshm governor as blaming a “terrorist enemy” for the Sept. 13 attack, which it said killed one and wounded four.
There was no immediate comment by the U.S. military, which has struck Iranian-flagged vessels during its blockade of Iranian ports and faces a new threat from Iranian ballistic missiles launched at its warships.
Qeshm Island, about 14 miles (22 kilometers) from the port city of Bandar Abbas, is key to Iran asserting control over the Strait of Hormuz.
Hours before the attack, Iran’s government remained defiant. “Our people can’t be bullied into submission. Iran won’t surrender,” President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a social media post.
U.S. President Donald Trump disagreed, saying on Sept. 13 that Iran “wants to make a deal so bad” that “they’re calling constantly.” Trump spoke at his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, where he was attending a tournament.
Later, when asked by a reporter whether the U.S. struck the Iranian cargo vessel early on Sept. 13 in the Strait of Hormuz, Trump said: “I don’t want to say.” He then boarded Air Force One to head back to Washington.
Iran had said foreign ministers from regional countries would meet on Sept. 14 in Oman to discuss efforts by Iran and Oman, located on the other side of the strait, to manage shipping on it. But the foreign minister of Oman, Badr Albusaidi, said on X late on Sept. 13 that the meeting had been postponed “in the interests of consensus.”
Iran and Oman agreed to postpone the talks “at the request of some regional countries”, said Mohammad Ali Bak, an official in Iran’s foreign ministry who was quoted by IRNA on X.
Saudi Arabia has submitted amendments to the Iran-Oman agreement, citing concerns that the emerging deal could have lasting implications for the Strait of Hormuz that could negatively impact other Gulf Cooperation Council countries, according to a Gulf official familiar with the matter who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Israeli-Palestinian-U.S. study identifies gene essential for hearing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:15:44 CST
23:15:44 KST

JERUSALEM, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- A research collaboration between scientists from Israel, Palestine and the United States has identified a gene essential for normal hearing, offering new clues about how inherited hearing loss develops, Israel's Tel Aviv University (TAU) said in a statement on Monday.
The findings were published in the U.S. journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers from TAU, Bethlehem University in the West Bank and the University of Washington.
The researchers found that mutations in a gene called FMN1 cause hearing loss and can also affect hair and skin pigmentation.
The investigation began with an extended Palestinian family in which several children were born with bilateral hearing loss and unusually light-colored hair. Genomic analysis revealed that the affected children carried two altered copies of the FMN1 gene.
In animal studies, the researchers observed hearing impairments among mice lacking functional FMN1. Microscopic analysis showed that the gene is crucial for maintaining the structural organization of supporting cells within the cochlea, a fluid-filled, spiral-shaped cavity in the inner ear that transforms sound waves into electrical signals for the brain.
The researchers explained that without a functional gene, these inner-ear supporting cells become disorganized, compromising the ear's mechanical integrity and hindering sound transmission from the cochlea to the brain.
The team also discovered that FMN1 plays a role in transporting pigment inside cells, explaining the light hair color observed in affected individuals.
The researchers said their discovery adds FMN1 to the list of genes essential for hearing, providing critical insight for the development of future genetic therapies for inherited deafness. ■

Thailand's Election Commission orders legal action against 77 individuals over Senate vote fraud
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:15:43 CST
23:15:43 KST

BANGKOK, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's Election Commission announced on Monday a crackdown on Senate election fraud, voting to launch criminal proceedings and file disqualification petitions with the Supreme Court against 77 individuals, including 26 sitting senators.
In a statement, the commission said the resolution follows a massive investigation into the 2024 upper house elections, uncovering evidence of organized networks, candidate voting pools, and cash payouts.
The commission reviewed an extensive investigation document totaling 75,722 pages involving 427 accused individuals and 67 petitioners.
The charges span seven distinct violations, including unauthorized election assistance by political officials, unlawful introduction methods, asset or financial bribery, and the solicitation or acceptance of bribes to influence voting outcomes.
Initial findings from the Department of Special Investigation revealed structured networks that managed candidate groups, provided tiered compensation, organized travel, and distributed voting charts that directly dictated election outcomes.
The commission said it is mandated to finalize its formal rulings and submit the petitions to the Supreme Court within 60 days. Under Thai law, once the Supreme Court accepts the petitions, the accused sitting senators must immediately suspend their official duties pending a final verdict.
If found guilty, their senate status will be permanently terminated. Vacated senate seats will be filled by elevating candidates from the official reserve lists.
In the event that reserve lists are exhausted, fallback mechanisms, including cross-group lotteries or organizing new localized elections, will be triggered to maintain parliamentary functions. ■

Economic Watch: China's smart home consumption push moves beyond individual devices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
22:15:28 CST
23:15:28 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- For 72-year-old Zhu Chengyi and his wife Li Lan, 71, replacing a decade-old air conditioner in their home in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, brought more than just cooler air.
Their new smart air conditioner can respond to voice commands and be controlled through a mobile app, allowing their daughter living in Guangdong Province, also in south China, to help adjust the temperature remotely.
The couple made this upgrade under China's consumer goods trade-in program, as the country's smart home market increasingly moves beyond individual appliance upgrades toward more connected household systems.
China on Monday unveiled an action plan to further promote smart home consumption by enriching application scenarios and expanding high-quality supply.
The plan, jointly issued by eight government departments including the Ministry of Commerce, the National Development and Reform Commission and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, also calls for supporting elderly-friendly renovation and smart upgrading of older homes while better meeting the consumption needs of different groups.
The plan sets out seven measures to expand high-quality smart home supply, improve the smart home standards system, support smart home consumption, develop elderly-friendly smart home products, streamline the service chain for recycling used household goods, optimize community services, and strengthen fiscal and financial support.
The plan comes as Chinese consumers are increasingly looking beyond simple product replacement toward broader upgrades in home living.
Chinese consumers are shifting from meeting basic needs to pursuing quality experiences and from simple product replacement to holistic lifestyle upgrades, according to a white paper released by the China Household Electrical Appliances Association earlier this year.
It identified major trends for 2026, including a shift from passive response to proactive intelligence, deeper integration of health-related scenarios, the robotization of home appliances, and the development of whole-home artificial intelligence ecosystems.
To expand supply, the plan encourages manufacturers to step up research and development of smart home products, and supports home furnishing stores and shopping malls in setting up smart home experience centers and model rooms for whole-home smart systems and digital homes.
Regarding standards, it calls for improving the grading and evaluation standards system for smart home products, and accelerating the formulation and implementation of mandatory national standards on connectivity and interoperability.
To support consumption, the plan encourages local authorities to determine eligible smart home product categories and subsidy standards based on local conditions under China's 2026 consumer goods trade-in policy.
Under this policy, local governments have greater flexibility in designing subsidy programs. The country plans to allocate 250 billion yuan (about 36.93 billion U.S. dollars) in ultra-long special treasury bond funds to support the nationwide program.
China's consumer trade-in programs generated 1.1 trillion yuan in sales in the first half of 2026, benefiting consumers on 150 million occasions, with home appliance trade-ins reaching 63.27 million units and purchases of digital and smart products totaling 79.1 million units.
The plan encourages home furnishing and decoration businesses to work with recycling companies to combine the delivery of new products with the collection of used ones.
At the community level, the plan supports the establishment of home renovation service stations to provide services such as maintenance, storage, recycling and replacement.
The plan also encourages financial institutions to diversify consumer finance products and services and expand lending for smart-home consumption, including by leveraging the country's interest-subsidy policy for personal consumption loans.
For elderly consumers, the plan promotes home service robots, health monitoring and smart care products, and encourages elderly-friendly design in areas like ease of operation, dialect recognition and safety.
Such products are already finding their way into Chinese homes. A home service robot developer at the 2026 World Robot Conference said its robots were already in paid use in more than 500 households, performing tasks such as basic housework, family companionship and pet care.
Other robots are being developed specifically for elderly care, with functions ranging from companionship and mobility assistance to recording health data, including blood pressure and blood glucose levels. A report by the China Software Testing Center projected that China's elderly-care service robot market will exceed 10 billion yuan in 2026.
Such applications form part of a broader push to upgrade smart home consumption, which is in line with China's plan for expanding consumption during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The plan calls for smart upgrades to home appliances and furnishings, better connectivity among smart home devices, and a shift from smart individual products toward whole-home smart systems. ■
