A pedestrian walks past the Berlaymont building, headquarters of the European Commission, in Brussels on April 20, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Most EU countries support slashing the bloc’s personnel costs to make savings as part of the next long-term budget, the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU wrote in a document seen by POLITICO.
The EU’s 27 governments are clashing over the size of the common cashpot, with a group of countries led by Germany calling for several hundred billion euros of cuts to a Commission proposal for a €2 trillion Multiannual Financial Framework for 2028-2034. But a rival camp of countries that includes Italy and Poland supports more spending on agriculture and poorer regions.
Despite such disagreements, the running costs of the EU institutions — such as officials’ salaries and building expenses — have emerged as the most likely budget item to face cuts.
Advertisement
The Irish presidency, which is steering the budget talks, wrote that “reductions could be made, with many [countries] questioning the justification of the proposed increase in staff levels” at a time when they’re making domestic personnel cuts.
The Commission proposed hiring an extra 2,500 officials over the next seven years, fueling discontent from nine countries led by Austria.
In the Commission's proposal, which was drawn up in July 2025, administrative costs will be worth €118 billion from 2028 to 2034, which is around 6% of the overall budget.
However, Ireland is facing strong resistance to cutting other areas of the budget. The Irish presidency wrote in the document that most capitals oppose reductions in agricultural spending and regional payouts, which it described as countries' “most important priority.”
Ireland hinted that the overall budget might face cuts as countries opposed increasing their national contributions and challenged new EU-wide taxes to finance the budget.
“These factors point to a need to reflect on our level of ambition for expenditure increases,” the Irish wrote.
During a meeting on Wednesday, Dublin will sound out the EU’s 27 ambassadors on which budget items they want to downsize.
"Are there any other elements in terms of changes to the Negotiating Box [the working document that guides budget talks] that would be helpful in formulating your views regarding the expenditure level?" it wrote.

IDF Spox. Defrin blasts 'false and distorted' claims in NAZA trailer, urges filmmakers to let the military view the full documentary

IDF Chief weighs legal action over 'NAZA' film, orders classified-materials probe
Spokesperson Effie Defrin rejects the film’s allegations as “false and distorted” and asks its creators to grant the IDF a full screening
IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir has ordered a series of measures in response to the film “Naza,” including an examination of possible legal action, an information-security investigation and a coordinated international public-diplomacy campaign.
Zamir issued the directives following a consultation with senior military officials, including Deputy Chief of Staff Maj. Gen. Tamir Yadai, Military Advocate General Maj. Gen. Itai Ofir, Israeli Air Force commander Maj. Gen. Omer Tishler, the commander of Unit 8200 and IDF Spokesperson Brig. Gen. Effie Defrin.
According to the IDF, Zamir described the film as “a deliberate attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the IDF and the State of Israel.”
“Based on what has been published thus far, this is not a film offering criticism of the IDF, nor is it an attempt to establish the truth,” Zamir said. “It is based on blood libels, deliberate distortions of reality, and grave, false accusations against IDF soldiers and commanders.”
Zamir said the film adopted the narratives of Israel’s enemies and sought to portray the military as deliberately acting unlawfully.
“This is a dangerous attempt to deny us the legitimacy to defend ourselves against the worst of our enemies—and, in doing so, to place IDF soldiers and commanders at genuine risk,” he said.
“We will not allow IDF soldiers to be made targets through lies and blood libels,” Zamir added. “Such an attempt must be confronted decisively, using every tool at our disposal—legal, command and public diplomacy.”
Following the consultation, Zamir instructed the Military Advocate General to examine and advance possible legal measures concerning both the film and those involved in its production. The review will consider the alleged dissemination of false claims against IDF personnel and any potential consequences for their safety and Israel’s national security.
The military will also investigate whether classified material was disclosed without authorization and whether such information was used in producing the documentary.
Zamir further ordered the creation of a multidisciplinary team led by the head of the IDF Planning Directorate. The team will work with experts in Israel and abroad to develop ways to address what the military describes as false allegations against its soldiers.
The chief of staff also called for a broad national and international public-diplomacy campaign involving the Foreign Ministry, Justice Ministry, National Public Diplomacy Directorate and other government bodies.
The directives followed a public statement by Defrin rejecting allegations raised in promotional material for “Naza.” He said the film presented a false and distorted account of the Israeli military and its personnel.
“The film ‘Naza’ has not yet been released in full,” Defrin said. “However, judging by what can be seen in the trailer, it presents a series of serious and false allegations concerning the IDF and its personnel.”
Defrin said the claims shown in the trailer were “untrue,” adding that some had been presented “in a distorted and misleading manner that is disconnected from the reality on the ground.”
The IDF spokesperson defended the military’s conduct, saying its operations were governed by international law and professional standards.
“It is important for me to emphasize that the IDF is a values-driven military that operates in accordance with international law and binding professional principles and standards,” he said. “This is how we have operated throughout the past three years, and this is how we will continue to operate—even under the most complex combat conditions.”
Defrin also invited the filmmakers, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, to provide IDF representatives with access to the complete documentary.
“To enable a substantive, professional and evidence-based discussion, rather than relying on misleading portrayals, I invite the filmmakers to allow IDF representatives to watch the film in full,” he said. “That will enable us to address each of the allegations raised in it on its merits.”
He said the wider public debate should be based on verifiable information “not on misleading portrayals and false smears.”
Defrin concluded by expressing support for Israeli troops and commanders, citing their service since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7.
“Together with all IDF commanders, I stand fully behind the IDF’s soldiers, commanders and personnel, and I categorically reject the baseless attacks against them,” he said.
“Those who have sacrificed and defended—and who continue to defend—the country deserve its support and protection in return.”

CDU wins Lower Saxony municipal polls to offer Merz respite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz got a measure of relief Monday after his CDU conservatives topped municipal elections in Lower Saxony, though the far-right Alternative for Germany also posted strong gains.
The CDU won 27.2% of the vote at the weekend, with its coalition ally the Social Democrats on 24.6%, while the AfD climbed to third place with 15.9%, 11.3 points more than its result in 2021.
The results offer some relief for Merz a week after his party was trounced by the AfD in state elections in eastern Germany, jolting the government and putting his political future and reform program in question.
The CDU's leader in the northwestern state of Lower Saxony, which is home to car firm Volkswagen and steelmaker Salzgitter among others, welcomed the result but called for change.
"I believe a political shift is needed in Berlin. We need to ease the burden on people. Energy prices are too high, and housing costs are too high," Sebastian Lechner said in Hanover, according to Die Zeit newspaper.
"We, too, have sensed the dissatisfaction with Berlin."
The CDU won the mayoral vote in Wolfsburg, the city where Volkswagen, one of the world's largest automakers and the state's largest private employer, is headquartered. The AfD's co-leader Alice Weidel had held up the troubles at Volkswagen, which is set to shed tens of thousands of jobs, as an example of the government's failings.
However, in the industrial city of Salzgitter, where the company bearing its name is headquartered, the CDU failed to win enough votes, meaning there will be a mayoral run-off with the AfD.
Merz will face a sterner test in two more state elections this coming weekend, where the AfD is set to top the polls again in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The capital Berlin will also hold a state election, where the far-left Die Linke could come out on top.
In an increasingly polarized political system, Merz, whose personal approval ratings have sunk to record lows, has been one of the main targets of voter ire over the cost of living, pensions and economic insecurity.
Last week, the AfD came within touching distance of winning the election in Saxony-Anhalt outright and could yet form a government there, the first time a far-right party would do so in postwar Germany.
The results put the focus on whether Merz is now an electoral liability, and also whether he will be forced to change course on a reform program that he says will revive sluggish growth in Europe's largest economy.
A poll by INSA over the weekend said 78% of people do not think Merz should be chancellor. Among his own party, 58% of voters no longer want Merz in charge, with 36% still backing him. Some 46% also thought the so-called "firewall" strategy, which rules out any sort of political accommodation with the AfD by mainstream parties, no longer served its purpose.
A jump in oil prices as hostilities worsen in the Middle East could also bring more domestic pain for Merz.
Clara von Nathusius, the treasurer of the CDU's youth wing, said the firewall policy had failed and that the CDU had a credibility problem.
"It doesn't hinge solely on Friedrich Merz, though it does play a part," she told the ARD broadcaster. "And that is why, unfortunately, I believe no more elections can be won with this Chancellor."

Kennedy Center reportedly on brink of bankruptcy and could close as early as Tuesday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:35:54 UTC
22:35:54 KST

Leaders of the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts say it is on the brink of bankruptcy and could close as early as Tuesday, the Washington Post reported on Sunday.
The center’s Donald Trump-installed leaders argued that putting the president’s name on its facade may be the only way to avoid imminent and “certain fiscal collapse”, according to the newspaper, citing documents it obtained.
The paper said a report, prepared by the Washington DC institution’s trustees, claimed that within a few weeks the institution won’t be able to pay employees or meet maintenance costs. The report was prepared in advance of a meeting that is scheduled for Tuesday. The 57-page internal document, circulated to the board ahead of the meeting, also flagged safety concerns tied to the building’s maintenance backlog and recommended that the main building be closed immediately.
The Post also said Trump will help the Kennedy Center if his involvement is acknowledged. The trustees’ report represents “a remarkable new phase in Trump’s takeover of the Kennedy Center, which has been engulfed by financial turmoil, leadership upheaval and litigation since he installed himself as chairman” in February 2025, the paper said.
That takeover began on 10 February 2025, when Trump dismissed 18 board members appointed under Joe Biden. Days later, the remaining trustees – many of them recently installed Trump allies, including White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and second lady Usha Vance – voted him in as chair, breaking with decades of precedent under which sitting presidents had kept the institution at arm’s length. The board also fired Deborah Rutter, who had served as the center’s president since 2014 and already planned to step down seven months later, replacing her with Richard Grenell, a Trump ally from his first administration.
The shake-up prompted a wave of departures and cancellations. Board treasurer Shonda Rhimes, National Symphony Orchestra artistic adviser Ben Folds and opera singer Renée Fleming all resigned their positions, while actor Issa Rae pulled her sold-out show from the venue in protest. Subscription sales fell sharply over the following months, with the Post citing a 36% drop by June 2025, and ticket sales continued to soften into the autumn.
Grenell himself was replaced as president in March by Matt Floca, formerly the center’s vice-president of facilities operations, amid the continued upheaval.
The Post also noted that Trump’s involvement with the Kennedy Center, which included the addition of his name to the building, impaired fundraising work and ticket sales.
A judge in May ruled that the addition of Trump’s name to the center’s facade was illegal – and therefore it needed to be removed. Trump’s name was then removed in June after a judge rejected an emergency appeal blocking the removal.
In August, the board voted again to reinstate Trump’s name on the building and to close the venue for a multiyear renovation, according to court filings.
Separately, lawyers for the center have argued in litigation that hundreds of millions of dollars in private donations already pledged would have to be returned if Trump’s name were not restored to the facade, citing the institution’s bylaws. The board later told a federal judge it would hold off on adding the name until at least 8 October, a month’s delay on its earlier timetable.
The Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

‘Blood libel’: IDF chief orders legal review, classified leak probe over NAZA film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:35:40 UTC
22:35:40 KST

IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir on Monday ordered a review of possible legal action and an investigation into the unauthorized disclosure of classified material used in the production of the film “NAZA,” which he accused of spreading “blood libels” and grave false allegations against Israeli soldiers and commanders.
The film features testimony from 24 male and female soldiers from the IDF’s Unit 8200 intelligence unit about military operations during the Gaza war. Some of those appearing in the film say they were involved in “war crimes and genocide” and discuss collateral-damage policies, bombardments and targeted killings.
Zamir issued the directives following a senior-level consultation attended by Deputy Chief of Staff Maj. Gen. Tamir Yadai, Operations Directorate chief Maj. Gen. Itzik Cohen, Military Advocate General Maj. Gen. Itai Ofir, Israeli Air Force commander Maj. Gen. Omer Tishler, the commander of Unit 8200, Brig. Gen. A., IDF Spokesperson Brig. Gen. Effie Defrin and additional commanders.
At the conclusion of the meeting, Zamir ordered the establishment of a multi-agency, multidisciplinary team led by the head of the Planning Directorate to develop ways of confronting what the military describes as false allegations against the IDF and its soldiers, with assistance from experts in Israel and abroad. He also instructed the Military Advocate General to examine possible legal measures concerning the film and those involved in it.
The measures could extend to people interviewed in the film if they are found to have disclosed classified intelligence. If any of those involved are currently serving in the IDF or reserves, the military could examine whether action should be taken against them and what form it should take.
The IDF will separately examine information-security aspects of the production, including the possible involvement of individuals in the unauthorized disclosure of classified material used in making the film.
“Based on what has been published thus far, this is not a film offering criticism of the IDF, nor is it an attempt to establish the truth,” Zamir said. “It is based on blood libels, deliberate distortions of reality, and grave, false accusations against IDF soldiers and commanders.”
“This is an attack on the State of Israel, not only on the IDF. It adopts the narratives of those who hate Israel, it defames our soldiers and commanders, and seeks to portray the IDF as deliberately acting unlawfully. This is a dangerous attempt to deny us the legitimacy to defend ourselves against the worst of our enemies—and, in doing so, to place IDF soldiers and commanders at genuine risk.”
“We will not allow IDF soldiers to be made targets through lies and blood libels,” he added. “Such an attempt must be confronted decisively, using every tool at our disposal—legal, command, and public diplomacy.”
According to the IDF, Zamir said the military operates in accordance with international law, its ethical code and values and is at the forefront of efforts to mitigate harm to uninvolved civilians. He also called for a broad national and international public diplomacy campaign involving the Foreign Ministry, Justice Ministry, National Public Diplomacy Directorate and other government bodies.
Military officials said the film was causing significant damage to the IDF’s activities abroad, with particular concern surrounding Unit 8200. The intelligence unit maintains professional ties with foreign counterparts, while many of its veterans have international business connections with implications for both Israel’s economy and national security, officials said.
Before Zamir’s announcement, Defrin asked directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor to allow the IDF to see the film in full so the military could respond to its allegations. He said the film had not yet been released in its entirety but that its promotional material contained what he described as “serious and false claims” about the IDF and its personnel.
“The claims presented in the promotional material are incorrect, and some are presented in a distorted, misleading manner detached from the reality on the ground,” Defrin said. He invited the filmmakers to provide the IDF with access to the full film so it could address each allegation “in a substantive, professional and fact-based manner.”
Film sparks controversy after Venice win
“NAZA” won a critics’ prize at the Venice Film Festival and drew an ovation reported to have lasted nearly 25 minutes, making it one of the festival’s most discussed films. Produced by Britain’s Guardian newspaper and filmed in part on Tel Aviv rooftops during the war, it presents testimony alleging deliberate policies of destruction and killing, including the use of artificial intelligence.
Its directors, Abraham and Szor, have rejected criticism from Israeli officials and argued that the film documents a system revealed through testimony from people who participated in it.
After receiving the award in Venice, Abraham criticized Israeli politicians and journalists who, he said, were attacking the film without having watched it. “So much is being done in order not to look at reality,” he said.
The film has generated strong condemnation in Israel. Culture Minister Miki Zohar accused its creators of treason and said he would seek to strip them of their citizenship, despite there being no legal precedent for such a move in these circumstances. The film was produced in Britain and received no funding from Israel’s Culture Ministry, Israeli film funds, broadcasters or other Israeli public sources.
Abraham and Szor previously worked together on “No Other Land,” alongside Palestinian filmmakers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. The documentary, which followed Palestinian residents of Masafer Yatta in the southern West Bank as they fought demolitions and displacement, won the Academy Award for best documentary feature in March 2025.
Szor, 32, served as the principal cinematographer and one of the editors of “No Other Land,” working through roughly 2,000 hours of footage combining professional documentation with videos filmed over the years by local residents. Abraham, 31, is an Arabic-speaking journalist and activist who briefly served in IDF intelligence before leaving the military.
With “NAZA,” the two are appearing together more prominently in interviews and press events. Szor has said the film is less concerned with determining what personally motivated individual interviewees to speak than with examining how the system they describe operated.

This German submarine sank in 1917. It’s still leaking TNT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:30:51 UTC
22:30:51 KST

This German submarine sank in 1917. It’s still leaking TNT
A century-old German submarine wreck is still leaking TNT into the sea, and scientists warn the problem could get worse.
- Date:
- September 14, 2026
- Source:
- Aarhus University
- Summary:
- A World War I submarine wreck off Denmark is leaking TNT into the surrounding water, seabed, and marine life more than a century after it sank. Scientists warn that thousands of similar wrecks could pose growing environmental risks as they continue to corrode.
- Share:
In April 1917, the German submarine UC-30 was making its way through waters near Rømø after abandoning a mission to Ireland because of engine problems. The vessel had turned back toward Germany and was close to reaching home.
It never arrived.
UC-30 was carrying 18 mines and six torpedoes, leaving the submarine packed with explosives. On April 19, it struck a British mine and sank. All 27 crew members died.
For nearly a century, the wreck remained lost beneath the sea. Danish diver Gert Normann Andersen finally discovered it in 2016.
TNT Pollution Around a WWI Submarine
UC-30 later became one of the wrecks examined through the major NorthSeaWrecks research project. Katrine Juul Andresen, a professor at the Department of Geoscience at Aarhus University, helped investigate the site.
Working with navy divers, Andresen and her colleagues collected water and sediment from around the wreck. They also sampled starfish and mussels living on or near the submarine.
"Civilian diving is not permitted on the wreck, so we received great assistance from navy divers. After receiving instructions, they dove down and collected sediment samples, water samples, and wildlife samples from various locations on the wreck and from the surrounding seabed."
"The divers also recorded video and took photos, which we subsequently used to assess the exposure of the mines and the condition of the wreck."
The results showed that explosive material from the wreck is entering the surrounding marine environment.
"We found traces of TNT in the wildlife, the seabed, and the water column. Pollution is definitely occurring. The question is how significant the effect is and how far from the wreck the pollution impacts the marine environment. It is likely a relatively localized source of pollution, but it will worsen as the wreck continues to deteriorate and expose more of the explosive material inside the mines," she says.
The Battle for the North Sea
During World War I, control of the North Sea was strategically vital to both Germany and Britain. Dominating the region meant controlling the movement of supplies into and out of each country, giving either side the ability to place enormous economic and military pressure on its opponent.
Germany had a smaller surface fleet than Britain, so submarines became an important part of its strategy. German submarines attempted to approach British vessels unseen and destroy them.
Both countries also relied heavily on naval mines. An estimated 190,000 mines were placed in the North Sea during WWI in hopes that enemy ships would strike them.
The region was also the site of the Battle of Jutland, fought off Hanstholm in Northern Jutland. It became the largest naval clash in history. German and British fleets battled across the North Sea, more than 25 ships were sunk, and nearly 10,000 sailors died.
Those wartime losses helped leave the North Sea seabed scattered with wrecks, many of which remain there today.
More Than 10,000 Wrecks in Danish Waters
UC-30 represents only a small part of the problem.
In 2024, Andresen prepared a report for the Danish Environmental Protection Agency examining the environmental risks posed by historical wrecks in Danish waters. The work also considered possible ways to prevent or reduce the pollution they can cause.
"In the report, I found that there are 10,127 wrecks in Danish waters. Around 15 percent of them date back to the years around and during the two world wars [1910-1920 and 1940-1945, ed.]. That is quite a high number," she says.
The Danish Environmental Protection Agency commissioned the report as part of its effort to determine how Denmark can meet the requirements of the EU Water Framework Directive.
The findings suggest that authorities may eventually need to take more direct action to address pollution from certain wrecks.
"I am not aware of whether the agency has taken the work further since the report was published in 2024. However, research shows that the wrecks represent a source of pollution for the local marine environment," she says.
Removing Explosives Is Not Simple
Germany has already committed substantial funding to recovering some wrecks and WWII munitions from the Baltic Sea.
After the Second World War ended, the Allies disposed of tons of ammunition by dumping it into the ocean so it could not fall into the wrong hands. Decades later, those weapons have become another source of marine contamination.
"The Germans are further ahead with this than we are in Denmark. They sometimes retrieve explosives from the wrecks and neutralize them, but doing so is very costly," she notes.
Destroying explosives where they lie is not always the safest option.
When munitions are detonated underwater, the blast can spread contaminants through the surrounding environment. In some locations, that could make pollution worse rather than solve the problem.
"It depends on the area where the wreck and munitions lie. Currents and seabed morphology play a major role. In some cases, detonating them can do more harm than good," she explains.
Seabed Robots Could Help Find Dangerous Munitions
Andresen is also working with international researchers through the EU-funded REMARCO project, which is exploring safer ways to deal with submerged munitions and historic wrecks.
"We are trying to identify the most gentle solutions to the problem, as there is unfortunately no easy way to clean it up," she says.
One approach being tested involves robots that can crawl across the seafloor. These machines could map the precise locations of dangerous munitions and help researchers monitor deteriorating wrecks more closely.
Some of the robots may eventually be able to do more than observe.
"In some cases, the robots can also pick up items, retrieve them from the sea and neutralize them. That could be one viable solution for the future."
Still, researchers say removing material from every wreck would neither be practical nor necessary.
Some shipwrecks are partly or completely buried beneath sediment, which can greatly reduce their ability to release pollutants into the surrounding water.
"Some wrecks are fully or partially buried in the seabed. When covered by sand, the risk of polluting the surrounding sea is significantly lower. It is a matter of identifying where the environmental threat is greatest - and then deciding whether the munitions on the wrecks should be removed," she concludes.

Israeli rights group accuses Israel of seeking to erase Palestinian presence in occupied West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:30:10 UTC
22:30:10 KST

Khaled Yousef and Sahin Demir
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Israeli human rights group B’Tselem on Monday accused Israel of seeking to erase the Palestinian presence in the occupied West Bank through a series of interconnected policies aimed at reshaping the territory.
In a statement, the group said Israel is simultaneously employing five mechanisms that reinforce one another to dismantle the collective Palestinian presence and establish a permanent and contiguous Israeli-Jewish presence and sovereignty in the territory.
B’Tselem said Israeli policy in the occupied West Bank entered a new phase at the end of 2022, characterized by increasingly overt and accelerated policies of control, violence and dispossession.
“What Palestinians in the West Bank are experiencing is part of a single political project that permeates every aspect of life,” B’Tselem Executive Director Yuli Novak said.
She said Palestinian communities are being displaced, the economy is being pushed toward collapse, and millions of people live in constant fear of violence by the Israeli army or occupiers.
According to B’Tselem, the first mechanism is “violence and terror,” involving the use of Israeli forces and armed occupiers to intimidate Palestinians and impose violence and coercion.
The group said Israel killed 1,107 Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, including 245 children, between Oct. 7, 2023 and Aug. 31, 2026.
The second mechanism is “ethnic cleansing and takeover of space,” which the group said involves displacing Palestinians from their land while expanding the Israeli-Jewish presence.
B’Tselem said Israel has displaced 75 Palestinian communities to date, while outposts and farms established by occupiers have taken control of 1.07 million dunams (about 264,400 acres), equivalent to 18% of the occupied West Bank.
It added that around 33,000 Palestinians have been forcibly displaced from refugee camps in the northern West Bank.
The third mechanism is “economic strangulation,” with B’Tselem saying Israel uses its control over Palestinian employment opportunities, tax revenues, the financial system and infrastructure to deepen the economic crisis and Palestinian dependence on Israel.
Palestinian Finance Minister Estephan Salameh warned in July that Israel was moving toward completely withholding Palestinian clearance revenues.
Clearance revenues account for around 56% of the Palestinian Authority’s total public revenues. Also known as clearance funds, they are the tax, custom, and tariff duties collected by Israel on behalf of the Palestinian Authority. Israel began deducting portions of the funds in 2019 and stopped transferring them entirely about a year ago, with withheld revenues exceeding $6 billion, pushing the Palestinian Authority deeper into a financial crisis, leaving it unable to pay public servants’ full salaries.
B’Tselem identified “social and political destruction” as the fourth mechanism, saying Israel criminalizes attempts at political affiliation, raids and shuts down civil society organizations, suppresses protests, and arrests activists, students and journalists.
The group said Israel has detained at least 60 Palestinian journalists in the occupied West Bank since October 2023. Palestinian figures put the overall number of Palestinians detained there during the same period at more than 25,000, including journalists, students and activists.
The fifth mechanism is what B’Tselem described as the “political framework,” which it linked to Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s 2017 “Decisive Plan.”
According to the group, the plan seeks to make Israeli-Jewish sovereignty irreversible through settlement expansion, land seizures and Palestinian displacement, leaving Palestinians with three options: accepting Jewish supremacy, leaving, or facing military repression.
Since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government took office in late 2022, Israeli authorities have intensified settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, approving 104 new settlements, according to the report.
Since the start of Israel’s war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023, Israeli forces and occupiers have also intensified attacks across the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, involving killings, arrests, displacement, home demolitions and settlement expansion.

FNV union demands 5.5% pay rises to tackle high inflation
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Trade unions are demanding pay rises of up 5.5% in next year’s pay round to offset the impact of high inflation.
The FNV, the Netherlands’ largest labour union, published its demands on Monday as part of the regular build-up to the opening of parliament and Budget Day this week.
The FNV says it will press for a 5.5% increase in basic pay during collective bargaining negotiations and a flat payment of €80 a month for all workers to give an extra boost to low earners.
Inflation is currently 3.3%, having risen in August, according to the government statistics agency CBS.
“We see that inflation is rising and is still well above the average while productivity is rising, companies are making big profits and the labour market remains tight,” Jacqie van Stigt, the union’s interim collective bargaining co-ordinator said.
The CNV, another of the major unions, said last week it would be seeking pay rises of between 3% and 5.5% next year as well as an increase in the travel allowance to 25 cents per kilometre, after the government raised the maximum tax-free amount from July 1.
AI concerns
The FNV also said it wanted to draw up stricter rules to ensure employees were consulted on the use of AI in the workplace.
The union is concerned that using machine-generated text is leading to more pressure on workers and giving companies an excuse to cut jobs.
The FNV also announced that cleaning staff have begun a week-long strike to protest against the pay deal struck between employers and the CNV union, which 80% of FNV members have rejected.
Staff at Schiphol airport and railway stations will take part in the strike. The union wants the employers to go back to the table and discuss their demands, which include not cutting pay for sick employees and paying hotel cleaners equal rates.
“We will continue until the pay negotiations are reopened and our cleaners are actually listened to,” said union spokeswoman Carolien Lambers.

UN calls for ‘urgent action’ to rein in AI in face of ‘unprecedented risks’
GENEVA – The United Nations rights chief on Sept 14 called for countries and “frontier” artificial intelligence companies to act urgently to rein in a technology he warned posed “unprecedented risks”.
In a letter sent to countries and AI developers and shared with the media, Volker Turk cautioned that the world was “on the cusp of irreversible change, affecting not just us but generations of humanity to come”.
“The current race towards ever more powerful AI is a step change towards greater existential risks to every aspect of our lives,” he said.
He sent the letter at a time when worries over the risks of “superintelligent” computer systems have been on full display, after a researcher publicly resigned from leading AI firm Anthropic over fears that the technology could escape human control.
Another Anthropic employee, who did not resign, stated publicly that “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans”, and that he thought the chances were greater than “10 per cent within the next decade”.
Amid the outcry, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sept 12 called for AI companies to “pace the frontier”, or coordinate a slowdown in the technology’s development, with his chief competitors, xAI’s Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, publicly supporting him.
“In today’s world, we are almost entirely reliant on a small number of powerful companies to make the right choices on Al development for all of humanity,” Turk lamented.
“I call on States and companies to mobilise urgently through multilateral fora to chart a path for action to govern advanced, frontier AI models, grounded in international human rights law.” AFP

Uganda’s ‘child king’ dies at 34, TV anchor chosen as successor in bitter royal dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:28:24 UTC
22:28:24 KST

Uganda’s King Oyo, who became known around the world as the “child king” after ascending the throne at just 3 years old, has died at 34, setting off an extraordinary succession battle after a popular television news anchor was chosen to replace him. 
Edward Rukidi Kijjanangoma, a 56-year-old presenter and editor at Uganda’s state broadcaster UBC, was unexpectedly selected as the next king of Tooro, one of five traditional kingdoms recognized by the Ugandan state.
The decision has divided the royal family. Oyo’s mother and sister oppose Kijjanangoma’s selection, while Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni and members of the family have said the late king left a will asking for his young son, whose existence had never previously been made public, to inherit the throne. Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV died in the United States last month after battling cancer and was buried Sunday near Uganda’s border with the Democratic Republic of Congo.
A committee representing the royal clan nevertheless chose Kijjanangoma, Oyo’s cousin. Until now, he was best known to Ugandans as an anchor and editor at UBC, where he built a reputation as a modest and approachable media figure. 
He also has a direct royal lineage: He is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijjanangoma and grandson of former Tooro king George David Rukidi III. His selection appears to satisfy traditionalists seeking dynastic continuity, as well as those opposed to placing another young child on the throne.
Oyo’s sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, immediately rejected the decision and accused kingdom elders of trying to seize control of what her brother had built. “King Oyo was a very peaceful and humble person,” she said. “I just don’t want these evil vultures to come and steal what he worked so hard for. I continue to stand with my brother.”
The son no one knew about
The existence of Oyo’s son became public only after the king’s death, when Museveni said the queen mother had told him about the young boy. The president and members of the royal family later said Oyo had explicitly named the child as his preferred successor in his will. 
But clan representatives argued that a son could not automatically be considered an eligible heir under Tooro tradition. A member of the selection committee told Uganda’s NTV that a royal child must first be formally presented to clan elders and undergo traditional rites and preparations before being considered for future leadership.
Oyo’s mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, has also rejected Kijjanangoma’s selection. Following the announcement, she alleged that the royal guard had been removed from the palace and replaced by soldiers restricting the movements of family members and their ability to receive visitors, describing the situation as “house arrest.” 
She appealed to Uganda’s military leadership and Museveni to allow the family to mourn before the succession battle continued. “I appeal to everyone fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all that,” she said. “Let us mourn and bury my son, King Oyo.”
Nine coffee beans mark a new reign
Despite the family’s objections, Kijjanangoma’s accession moved ahead over the weekend. At the royal burial grounds in Karambi, he performed one of Tooro’s most important succession rituals, throwing nine coffee beans into the grave to symbolize the transfer of royal authority. Along with the throne, he is expected to inherit valuable royal assets, including extensive landholdings, as well as a substantial allowance from Uganda’s central government.
The ritual carried particular symbolism because Oyo himself performed it when he became king in 1995 following his father’s death. Just 3 years old, he appeared at his coronation in colorful ceremonial robes and became internationally known as the world’s youngest reigning king. Regents guided the kingdom until he turned 18, and over the following three decades he grew into one of Uganda’s best-known traditional leaders.
Oyo later served as a United Nations goodwill ambassador in efforts to combat HIV and AIDS and promoted healthy living and awareness of climate change. His unusual position brought him into contact with international figures including Nelson Mandela. His family also developed close ties with Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, who supported Oyo and Queen Kemigisa and helped finance renovations of Tooro’s royal palace before his death in 2011.
Uganda’s traditional kingdoms were abolished in 1967 and restored in 1993. They hold no formal political power today and are barred from partisan politics, but their monarchs retain considerable cultural and symbolic authority as custodians of tradition. Oyo’s death has now ended a reign that began with a toddler on the throne, while the fight over whether a television anchor or the late king’s previously unknown son should inherit it remains unresolved.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Monday pledged to continue military support for Ukraine, warning that the war is likely entering its most decisive weeks or months ahead.
Speaking at a news conference in Finland after a high-level European Arctic summit, Merz said Russia is not only waging war against Ukraine but also targeting European countries with hybrid attacks and influence operations.
“Most likely we are seeing the most decisive moments, perhaps weeks or months, ahead of us in defending the freedom and peace of our continent,” Merz told reporters when asked whether European governments can continue support for Kyiv as parties opposed to aid gain ground.

Opposition to sending weapons to Ukraine and providing large-scale financial aid has intensified in several European countries in recent months. In Germany, the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD), which rejects arms deliveries and major funding for Kyiv, scored a record result in the Sept. 6 Saxony-Anhalt state elections, winning 43.8% of the vote.
Similar anti-aid sentiments have also gained ground in mainstream political debates in France, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, and Hungary.
Germany has been among Ukraine’s largest military supporters in Europe since the Russia-Ukraine war began in 2022.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, said the bloc had to remain "vigilant" in the face of increasing Russian military activity in the Arctic, as well as China's growing interest in the region.
12 European nations have urged the European Union to scale up its presence in the Arctic amid threats from Moscow and US President Donald Trump.
"We call for the European Union to take on a more strategic and proactive role in the European Arctic," the countries wrote in a joint statement following the European Arctic Summit in Rovaniemi in northern Finland.
The summit was attended by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, among others.
Speaking to reporters on Monday morning, Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, said the bloc had to remain "vigilant" in the face of increasing Russian military activity in the Arctic, as well as China's growing interest in the region.
She added that the EU would be revealing a new Arctic strategy in October "that has security at its core."
"It is clear that this is part of the security architecture of Europe," Kallas said.
The Arctic acts as an important gateway connecting North America and Europe, providing key transport, communication and trade links.
But it has become a key battleground for strategic maneouvering in recent years.
According to NATO, Moscow has "significantly" ramped up its military activity in the Arctic, establishing a new Arctic Command while opening military sites and testing "novel weapons systems."
Beijing also has a vested interest in the region, particularly in gaining access to critical minerals, energy, and new communications lines, per NATO.
The Rovaniemi summit comes after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made a trip to Greenland earlier this month as the EU signalled its continued support for the island amid Trump's repeated calls for the United States to acquire it.
Brussels has attempted to counter Trump by pledging a surge of investment into Greenland, with von der Leyen announcing a €200 million partnership with the autonomous Danish territory during her visit - which is set to be invested this year and the next.
Since his return to the White House, Trump has repeatedly said the US needs to take control of Greenland for "national security" reasons, arguing that either China or Russia would otherwise seize the island, drawing pushback from Europe.
The US is reported to have had 17 military facilities and over 10,000 troops on the island at the height of the Cold War. It now operates just one base on Greenland, the Pituffik Space Base - the US Department of Defense's northernmost installation.
Pituffik is used for missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance missions, per the US Space Force.

Finnish police extend search for Vastaamo hacker Aleksanteri Kivimäki across Europe
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:26:44 EEST
22:26:44 KST

Finnish police have issued a European Arrest Warrant (EAW) for 29-year-old Aleksanteri Kivimäki, who was convicted of hacking into the patient database of the Vastaamo psychotherapy centre and attempting to extort money from the company as well as its clients.
An EAW is a fast-track legal tool that allows EU member states to request the arrest and transfer of a person for a criminal trial or to serve a prison sentence. In addition to EU countries, EAWs also cover a number of non-EU states, such as Norway.
A nationwide wanted notice was issued for Kivimäki in July after he failed to show up at a correction facility to serve the remainder of his sentence. His lawyer, Peter Jaari, told Yle at the time that he did not know Kivimäki's exact whereabouts but believed he was abroad.
A lengthy legal process
After a lengthy trial at Helsinki District Court, Kivimäki was handed a six-year and three-month prison sentence in April 2024 after being found guilty of charges including aggravated data breach, almost 9,600 counts of aggravated invasion of privacy related to the dissemination of information, more than 21,300 counts of attempted aggravated extortion and 20 counts of aggravated blackmail.
There were more victims in the Vastaamo hacking case than in any other trial in Finnish criminal history.
During the trial, lawyer Jenni Raiskio said in her concluding statement that her firm had been contacted by people whose relatives had taken their own lives after their patient records were published online.
The court of appeal subsequently extended Kivimäki's sentence to six years and 11 months earlier this year.
However, prior to handing down that sentence, the appeal court ordered Kivimäki be released from pre-trial detention due to concerns he would spend too much time behind bars and therefore be eligible for compensation from the Finnish state.
Kivimäki currently has about five months of his sentence left to serve.
Not the first time
Kivimäki has a history of evading Finnish authorities.
A European Arrest Warrant was previously issued for him in 2022 after he was remanded in custody in absentia for the Vastaamo hacking and extortion. He was subsequently apprehended in France in February 2023.
Kivimäki was on the run again in early 2024, after the district court released him from pre-trial detention. The appeal court overturned this decision, ordering him to be remanded again, but Kivimäki was missing for about a week before police located him in Helsinki.

While European nations use strong words against the Kremlin and discuss future response options, the strategy for now is to “keep calm and carry on,” according to a senior NATO diplomat.
BRUSSELS — Despite Russia's intensifying attacks on European critical infrastructure and weapons factories, NATO countries remain wary of making immediate tough moves that could provoke the Kremlin.
European capitals are eyeing options including opening a debate about whether a so-called hybrid attack could trigger NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause, more unified communication in response to incidents and a greater push on protecting critical infrastructure, according to three NATO diplomats and one person familiar with the matter, who were granted anonymity to speak freely due to the sensitivity of the matter.
But so far, Europe is avoiding taking any drastic steps — in part over fears it could escalate into an all-out war with Russia.
Advertisement
“We have all the response options ... some of them will be public, some are not,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte told POLITICO on Monday. “I'm saying to [Russian President Vladimir] Putin and everyone who wants to listen, if you continue doing this, we will not only have our response options .... we will also continue the support in Ukraine.”
The calls for action underscore growing anxiety around the increasing frequency of sabotage, cyberattacks and other actions that fall below the threshold of conventional war across Europe. Over the weekend, a Russian drone hit a train near the Polish-Ukrainian border shortly after top Western security officials passed through, while Bulgarian authorities launched investigations into two explosions at weapons storage sites in the country.
“The pressure is mounting in view of the events on the Polish border,” said a fourth, senior NATO diplomat. But for now, the strategy is “keep calm and carry on and … continue our support for Ukraine.”
The most serious incidents pinned on Russia — including an attempted attack on Leipzig airport last month — have so far been thwarted. But European officials are increasingly grappling with the prospect they may soon face a successful attack with casualties, and the backlash that brings.
“The secret services have done a good job” so far, said one senior European defense official. But “we have been lucky — there have been no big incidents … if we do not act, then things might get much worse.”
“We are too shy — definitely,” said German lawmaker Marie Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, who chairs the European Parliament’s defense committee. “Vladimir Putin never stops, he’s always coming closer … we have to show we’re willing to fight back.”
Advertisement
Opening a debate
Inside NATO, allies have not yet formally drawn up plans for responding to the uptick in incidents, two of the alliance diplomats mentioned above said. Controversial options like offensive cyber operations against Russia are typically handled by national intelligence services.
Informally, some allies are discussing the possibility of starting a debate on whether an accumulation of sub-conventional attacks could cross NATO’s Article 5 threshold, the three diplomats said. Clarifying where that line is would send a clear warning to Russia and show NATO’s unified opposition to such attacks, two of the diplomats said, but acknowledged so far there is no consensus on the issue.
The senior European defense official said opening the discussion was “worthwhile,” but cautioned it would need to be matched with clear “political will” for a military response — to avoid hollowing out the meaning of the collective defense clause.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s repeated wavering on NATO and collective defense in particular also makes that debate more sensitive. “We have considered calling for Article 5,” said an Eastern European diplomat. “But we don't want to escalate and it could backfire, as it could show Putin that Trump is not ready to help.”
Countries are discussing how to formally, quickly and collectively attribute the attacks to the Kremlin, the three diplomats said. Allies could also be asked to spell out more clearly their spending on civilian preparedness and protection of infrastructure like hospitals, as part of their obligations to funnel 1.5 percent of GDP into civil defense by 2035, the diplomats said. So far, what spending counts toward that target has remained largely undefined.
Gerlinde Niehus, a former longtime NATO official and independent security expert, said the alliance should come up with “pre-agreed packages” in response to specific future attacks, coordinated with governments and intelligence agencies.
Advertisement
Today, “Putin … clearly plays on long decision processes [and] institutional inertia between NATO and the EU,” she said. If a serious Russian-linked sabotage incident was not matched with a clear NATO response, “that would undermine fundamentally the credibility of the alliance,” she said.
That's a concern Rutte brushed off on Monday. “I don't think [NATO] will be perceived as weak” in that scenario, he told POLITICO, while declining to comment on whether the alliance was drawing up new options.
EU not united
The EU is also discussing further measures — but so far there is little evidence that it too is planning an immediate response.
Defense and security is expected to be a key plank of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s annual policy address this week, which is likely to spotlight hybrid threats and the bloc's long-anticipated security strategy, according to two EU officials. The strategy is expected to be presented in the coming weeks.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas is also preparing new sanctions against 1,600 entities, but these were proposed before the latest incidents over the weekend.
Meanwhile, the European Parliament is this week set to adopt a nonbinding resolution led by the Lithuanian MEP Rasa Juknevičienė, with unusually strong language that singles out Russia as “the gravest hybrid threat facing the Union and its Member States.” It is also likely to pass another report calling for strengthening EU agencies’ capacity to act against hybrid activities.
Advertisement
Yet in a sign Europe is still not unified on a stronger response, EU capitals failed to extend the bloc's Russia sanctions against around 3,000 individuals and companies on Monday.
The European Commission didn't immediately respond to a request for comment by POLITICO.
Gabrielius Landsbergis, Lithuania's former foreign minister, said Brussels must immediately take measures like closing the Baltic Sea for Russia's illicit shadow fleet, help Ukraine double its drone production capacity and even move to cut off electricity in Russia with cyberattacks.
“We hide behind the word 'hybrid' hoping that it will shield us from any counter-action,” he said. “Stop with the non-measures, because they only invite Putin to escalate.”

European leaders meeting in Rovaniemi have backed a stronger EU role in the Arctic, with Finland pressing for joint icebreaker capacity, more investment in northern infrastructure and a coordinated response to Russian pressure in the region.
Prime Minister Petteri Orpo received support for the icebreaker proposal from German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who said Europe needed more such vessels and that Finland had Germany’s backing to advance the idea jointly.
The summit brought together leaders from Germany, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania and several EU institutions as the bloc prepares an updated Arctic strategy.
Merz said icebreakers were not only a Finnish or Nordic concern but a wider European requirement.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas also said there was broad support at the meeting for expanding icebreaker capacity, though she stressed that EU procurement rules would still apply and contracts would go to the strongest bid.
Finland has said it wants to build and host possible EU-funded vessels, an area where Finnish shipyards have long specialised.
Leaders also called for more investment in military mobility, cross-border transport links, satellite infrastructure and other northern facilities.
The summit’s joint statement said Russia’s efforts to increase its influence in the Arctic, combined with hostile activity against Europe, had increased the need for a stronger EU policy in the region.
The Arctic is gaining economic and security significance as melting ice opens new routes and access to raw materials. The shift has drawn more attention from Russia, China, the United States and European countries.
Orpo also warned that Russia was becoming more aggressive and moving its attacks closer to European borders.
The summit took place a day after a Russian drone struck a train near the Polish border in Ukraine, an attack several leaders described as part of a broader effort to intimidate Europe.
Kallas said the strike was clearly intended as a message to Western countries.
Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen also addressed tensions over Greenland and said talks with the United States were continuing through a high-level working group.
She said it was too early to draw conclusions but added that she was “quite optimistic” that a peaceful solution would be found.
European Council President António Costa said the EU had repeatedly expressed full support for Denmark. He also pointed to plans to increase EU investment in Greenland under the bloc’s next long-term budget.
The summit was designed to influence the European Commission’s revised Arctic strategy, which is expected in the coming weeks. The EU’s previous strategy dates from 2021.
Finland has argued that the new policy should give greater weight to defence, transport links, critical infrastructure and economic development in the High North.
Orpo said the Arctic and Baltic regions had become central security areas for Europe and argued that the EU would need to direct more funding towards northern projects.
German Chancellor Merz also used the meeting to stress continued support for Ukraine despite political pressure inside Europe.
He said the coming weeks and months would be critical for defending peace and freedom in Europe and said he was not prepared to retreat from Germany’s support for Kyiv.

China is Jordan's largest source of imports, Qudah said, adding that the next phase should move beyond the traditional import-export model toward joint projects based in Jordan, aimed at serving both regional and global markets.

Qudah said that there are significant opportunities for Jordanian products in the Chinese market, including Arab food products such as Jordanian dates and olive oil. Driven by Chinese demand, Jordan's fertilizer exports to China have increased, he said.
He said that Jordan is currently forming a comprehensive working group to follow up on the outcomes of King Abdullah II's visit and to identify direct opportunities with the Chinese private sector.
He added that the focus will also be on the fiber optics sector, the automotive manufacturing and assembly sector.
Regarding leveraging Chinese expertise and technology to develop industry, supply chains, and digital transformation, and to enhance Jordanian products in global markets, Qudah stated that Jordan could benefit in three main ways.
According to Qudah, the first is direct Chinese investment in the industrial, energy, and information technology sectors, among others; the second is Chinese companies' contributions to major projects implemented in Jordan; the third involves the transfer of advanced knowledge and technology from China to Jordan's productive sectors.
Jordan plays an important role in regional logistics networks, Qudah said, citing the port of Aqaba as an example.
About 80 percent of the imported goods arriving at the port are not destined for the Jordanian market, he explained, demonstrating Jordan's role as an important regional logistics hub.
Regarding tourism, Qudah affirmed that Jordan is developing the necessary infrastructure to attract Chinese tourists and is working to finalize the integration of Chinese electronic payment systems. ■

Economic Watch: China's robots advance from stage to shop floor
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
21:24:37 CST
22:24:37 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- A robotic hand picked up a calligraphy brush, dipped it in ink and wrote "fu," a Chinese character meaning good fortune, on a square of red paper, delighting crowds.
Chinese robots like this one are no longer just event performers. They are increasingly clocking in for real work, and an entire industry is forming around teaching them how.
FROM GALA STAGE TO CONVENIENCE POD
At the China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS), which ended Sunday in Beijing, Galbot G1, which went viral after folding laundry in a video clip for this year's globally broadcasted Spring Festival Gala, staffed an unmanned convenience pod.
Such pods are already operating at sites including Beijing's Summer Palace, a former imperial garden, where each is expected to serve more than 1,000 visitors a day. The first overseas store of this type opened in Hong Kong on Sept. 1.
Robots are also being deployed in other jobs. At an "unstaffed post office" booth, a robot stamps postcards, drops them into a mailbox, then fetches blind-box toys for customers.
A few meters away, a pancake robot flips crepes to order, while a coffee robot pours latte art onto a fresh cup.
"We have a coffee-making robot on campus, but these are more advanced," said visitor Olga, a Belarusian professor at Beijing Foreign Studies University.
It takes humans considerable effort to create latte art, she added, but robots do it with ease.
CLOSING THE TRAINING GAP
For all the novelty, a wide gap remains between demonstration and deployment: training.
"China's domestic shipments of humanoid robots reached 23,000 units in the first half of this year, but fewer than 5 percent are working stably on real production lines," said Zhu Kai, head of the Shijingshan Embodied Intelligence Training Center.
Production lines are far messier than a stage. "High-quality, multimodal real-robot data fit for industrial training doesn't reach even 1 percent of actual demand," Zhu said, adding that the shortage is the core obstacle to moving robots "from performing to actually working."
Closing that gap starts in a "vocational school" for robots. The training center, a short walk from the CIFTIS fairground at Shougang Park, is where much of the "homework" gets done.
Nearly 270 robots work there at full capacity on chores, caregiving drills and factory tasks such as automatically placing circuit boards onto a production line, producing nearly 20 million high-quality data entries a year.
The "school" opened its doors to visitors during the fair, and the lessons translate into human-like movements: rows of robots practiced fetching and setting down boxes or ironing trousers, each following a human mentor demonstrating the moves.
Those mentors now have an official title. On the fair's opening day, Sept. 9, China formally recognized a new occupation: embodied-intelligence robot application technicians, with two new trades within it -- robot data collectors and robot trainers.
The tools are changing, too. Data collectors once puppeteered machines from fixed lab consoles. But with new capture rigs mounted, they can now easily enter real-world work scenarios, recording human hands at work.
At one booth, VR maker NOLO displayed its EgoCapture, a head-mounted rig that records 360 degrees of real human operations.
Wear it on a trail run, and it generates exactly the data a robot would need to judge a long-distance turn. Clients can buy the service instead of the full set of gear.
Other booths harvest the rest of a robot's education: tactile sensors from Tashan Technology capture the sensation and force of a grip, while dexterous hands from CasiaHand Robotics -- with a built-in "brain" model -- learn to act on their own.
The output of this schooling shows up on the fairground itself: much of the training data behind the exhibits in the fair came from the center, said Zhu.
DATA ON THE MARKET
Data itself is becoming a commodity, and this year's CIFTIS fair gave it a pathway to cross borders.
At a forum, the fair launched China's first industry-level platform aiming to provide international service for embodied-intelligence data, built by Beijing Shijingshan Science and Technology Innovation Group in partnership with China Telecom's Beijing branch.
The groundwork has been established in the Shijingshan district of Beijing: China's first 3D high-quality dataset for large-model training has been registered, four data service stations have opened, and more than 200 data products have been listed, while Beijing as a whole aims for 100 high-quality industrial datasets by 2028.
"The government sets the stage, and the companies perform. CIFTIS works like an amplifier, turning Beijing's industrial strengths into international cooperation opportunities," Zhu said.
The robots are already earning their keep with overseas deployment. Anyverse Dynamics, a Beijing embodied-AI startup participating in the fair, has signed a 500-million-yuan (about 74.66 million U.S. dollars) deal with green-tech group Envision, and the first batch of its K15 semi-humanoids arrived at Envision's battery gigafactory in France this month for autonomous loading and unloading work.
But the machines are only part of the business. The training and the services that keep them working overseas are increasingly where China's services trade will lie in the future.
The fairground tells the same story. The information and communications technology (ICT) hall alone featured more than 30 debut products, from high-jumping and cooking robots to wall-climbers and holographic cabins.
"Visitors can feel an intelligent economy where carbon-based (humans) and silicon-based (robots) beings coexist," said He Qionghua, head of the ICT exhibition area.
Back at the calligraphy booth, the "fu" is a blessing for visitors, while the fortune it points to is increasingly being created by robotic hands. ■

Fueling Japan's neo-militarism will push region toward dangerous vortex: Chinese spokesperson
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
21:24:00 CST
22:24:00 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese defense spokesperson on Monday voiced firm opposition to a joint military exercise by Japan, the United States and Australia, warning that moves promoting Japan's military ambitions will drive the region into a perilous vortex.
Jiang Bin, a spokesperson for the Ministry of National Defense, made the remarks at a press briefing when responding to a query concerning the "Orient Shield 26" exercise, which is being held in Japan from Sept. 8 to 24.
This exercise is packaged as a "shield," but in reality it amounts to the forward deployment of strategic offensive weapons. It not only undermines other countries' legitimate security interests, but also heightens the risk of an arms race and military confrontation, and seriously threatens regional security and stability, Jiang said.
Japan, as a defeated country of World War II, is prohibited from obtaining offensive weapons by the Potsdam Proclamation and Japan's pacifist constitution itself.
However, in recent years, the country has continuously broken the constraints and its exclusively defense-oriented policy, vigorously developed long-range offensive weapons, and leveraged joint exercises with foreign countries to accelerate its "remilitarization," the spokesperson noted.
"Any move that fuels Japan's military ambitions will only push the region into a dangerous vortex and will inevitably bring harm to those involved," Jiang warned.
China urges relevant countries to respect other nations' security concerns, correct their wrong practices, and play a positive role in regional peace and stability with concrete actions, Jiang added. ■

Village teacher safeguards children's education dreams for 28 years in China's Shanxi

Yao Jian (1st R) and students have a class in a field in Sandun Village, Huayuantun Town of Datong, north China's Shanxi Province, Sept. 9, 2026. One day in early autumn, at Sandun Primary School at the foot of the Great Wall section built during the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) in northern Shanxi, Yao Jian stood on the podium and gave students a lecture. Twenty-eight years have passed since the 52-year-old village teacher began his career at the school.
There are only seven teaching staff members and six students at Sandun Primary School, which is located on the border between north China's Shanxi Province and Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Tucked away in a remote area and difficult to reach, the school offers children from surrounding villages a vital path to education.
In 1998, Yao Jian returned to his hometown and became a teacher after graduating from normal university. Two years later, with outstanding teaching achievements, he was assigned to Sandun Primary School. In 2004, he became the principal of the school, where he also acted as chef, procurement agent and driver.
When the school was transformed into a boarding school in 2012, he drove his car to pick up and drop off those students who lived far away in all weathers.
Back in 2002, Yao's wife Ma Lirong moved in to support her husband and take care of these students. Later, Ma also became a teacher there.
"Being a teacher is a lifelong undertaking that cannot be taken lightly in the slightest," said Yao Jian. He has developed a special teaching method which combines theoretical knowledge with practice.
In recent years, the local government has allocated various teaching equipment to the school, while welfare organizations and businesses have also brought teaching and daily necessities. Almost 80% of first-graders&apos; families have already submitted applications for the &quot;Schoolchild&apos;s Package&quot;
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:22:46 EEST
22:22:46 KST

Almost 80% of first-graders' families have already submitted applications for the "Schoolchild's Package"
Kyiv • UNN
More than 163,000 applications for the UAH 5,000 payment have already been approved. Applications for school supplies can be submitted until November 1.
Parents of first-graders can receive a one-time state payment of UAH 5,000 for school supplies, clothing and footwear. More than 163,000 applications have already been approved, and applications can be submitted until November 1. The Ministry of Social Policy reports this, UNN writes.
This year, 239,661 children started first grade. As of today, nearly 190,000 families have already applied to receive the "Schoolchild's Package," of which more than 163,000 applications have been approved
The Ministry of Social Policy reminded that the "Schoolchild's Package" is a one-time state payment of UAH 5,000. The funds can be spent on purchasing school essentials: clothing, footwear, stationery and other goods.
Applications can be submitted until November 1.
Who can receive the assistance
The payment is granted to one of the parents or the legal representative of a child who is entering the first grade this year at a general secondary education institution in Ukraine.
If a family is temporarily staying abroad, the assistance can be arranged after returning to Ukraine. For families staying in temporarily occupied territories, the payment will be available after returning to territory controlled by Ukraine.
How to arrange the "Schoolchild's Package"
An application can be submitted in two ways – online through the Diia app or offline through service centers of the Pension Fund of Ukraine.
To submit an application online in Diia, you need to:
-  open the «Services» → «Assistance from the state» → «Schoolchild's Package» section; 
-  select the child for whom you are submitting the application; 
-  select or open the «Diia.Card»; 
-  check the details and sign the application with Diia.Signature. 
To apply, you must have an ID card or international passport in the Diia app, as well as a verified taxpayer registration number (RNOKPP).
To submit an application through a service center of the Pension Fund of Ukraine
For this, one of the child's parents must submit a written application and present an identity document, an RNOKPP (if available), and, if necessary, documents confirming the authority of the legal representative.

Several Belgian university rectors criticized on Monday the lack of government consensus over the arrival of Gazan scholarship students, according to the Belga news agency.

Westminster’s time is coming to an end, say first ministers of UK’s Celtic nations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:21:16 UTC
22:21:16 KST

Westminster’s time is coming to an end, the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have said at a landmark summit aimed at putting the UK’s Celtic nations on the path to independence referendums.
The Plaid Cymru leader, Rhun ap Iorwerth; the Scottish National party leader, John Swinney; Sinn Féin’s vice-president, Michelle O’Neill, and the president and leader of the opposition in Ireland, Mary Lou McDonald, met in Cardiff on Monday to sign a memorandum of understanding recognising that “the political landscape across these islands is changing”.
“Momentum is behind our movements; we believe that constitutional change is coming,” the memorandum read. “No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future.
“We call for the British government to prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change in each jurisdiction.”
Since becoming prime minister in July, Andy Burnham has put regional devolution of power and resources in England at the heart of his agenda, but policy towards the devolved administrations has so far been muddled.
The summit was the first face-to-face meeting for the sister parties since Plaid Cymru won May’s Senedd elections, which put separatist parties in government in all three countries for the first time. The leaders met in their capacity as party, rather than government, officials, discussing economic, energy and international cooperation as well as self-determination.
Scottish independence and Irish reunification resurfaced on the news agenda last week when Burnham wrote to Swinney to reiterate that a repeat of 2014’s Scottish independence referendum remained “off limits” after apparently misspeaking during prime minister’s questions.
The US president, Donald Trump, also weighed in on a potential breakup of the UK during a visit to Ireland, saying he would love to see a united Ireland and it “may as well happen now”. The unexpected intervention prompted a swift rebuttal from the UK government and the unionist power-sharing members of the Northern Ireland executive.
Plaid Cymru has ruled out an independence referendum in its first term, but Welsh ministers are seeking fuller devolution powers on a par with Scotland and Northern Ireland, which Burnham has said he is “open” to.
Monday’s summit involved “powerful optics” and an opportunity for the nationalist parties to show how they are prepared to work together, said Laura McAllister, a professor of public policy at Cardiff University.
McAllister added: “If you look under the bonnet, though, the aims and the timelines for independence as sought by each of these first ministers is fundamentally different, as of course is the constitutional framework in each country.
“If there is a serious discussion of reformulating UK relationships there has to be a presence for England at the table … the irony is that we have a UK prime minister that says he is a devolutionist, but the constitutional question is far more problematic for him.”
Latest polling suggests 47% of Scottish voters would opt for independence in a referendum held tomorrow, along with 36% in Northern Ireland and 32% in Wales. Support for independence in Scotland has hovered between 45% and 50% since the 2014 referendum, while data suggests it is rising in Wales and Northern Ireland.
On Monday, Sinn Féin’s McDonald said she expected an Irish reunification poll to take place by 2030, while the SNP wants a second referendum within the next five years.
Burnham is expected to meet the three first ministers next month.
A UK government spokesperson said: “The prime minister’s approach to working with the first and deputy first ministers in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland is based on partnership and collaboration.
“The UK government is focused on addressing the issues that matter most to families, including easing pressures on household finances and delivering greater economic security, rather than engaging in constitutional debates or further referendums.”
