‘Attacks will be fully autonomous’: Russia, Ukraine race towards AI warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:20:50 UTC
22:20:50 KST

‘Attacks will be fully autonomous’: Russia, Ukraine race towards AI warfare
Automated AI drones are just one component of an ultimate chain of destruction both sides are building.
Tetiana Bubynets collapsed on the asphalt after a Russian drone exploded at a gas station in the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia.
Despite the violent shockwave and blast of drone shrapnel produced by the attack on July 6, the 18-year-old accounting student had no visible wounds except for a nosebleed.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US envoys meet Putin: What’s behind latest diplomacy on Russia-Ukraine war?
- list 2 of 3US envoys hold ‘substantive’ talks with Zelenskyy in first visit to Kyiv
- list 3 of 3Witkoff says peace talks have been ‘very meaningful’ in Ukraine
She was rushed to hospital and pronounced dead shortly after, alongside two other civilians, aged 41 and 48.
One of her lecturers, Tetiana Melikhova of Zaporizhzhia National University, said Bubynets was an only child and that her mother “lost the meaning of life” after she died.
“She couldn’t speak. At the funeral, she just lay on the coffin; she couldn’t let her child go,” Melikhova told Al Jazeera.
The strike that killed Bubynets was the first recorded case of Russia’s use of a fully autonomous attack drone powered by artificial intelligence (AI), according to a New York Times analysis.
While drone strikes have hammered Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukrainian officials who examined the wreckage found the unmanned vehicle to be unlike others.
In place of an antenna, it featured an AI-powered minicomputer sold commercially by US technology company Nvidia, which rendered it capable of directing itself to the type of target it was programmed to spot – likely propane tanks in this case – lock on to it and proceed to strike.
AI-powered drones are the tip of the iceberg as Russia and Ukraine race towards boosting tech infrastructure aimed at coordinating reconnaissance and attack, according to analysts.
“It’s not about a drone having AI in it, and then seeing something and striking,” Marina Miron, researcher at the defence studies department at King’s College London, said. “Rather, it’s the drone seeing something, communicating to a software complex which knows how to map the GPS coordinates on a live battlefield map, and notifying the closest artillery unit.”
Referred to as reconnaissance-strike architecture, these unified battlefield management systems act like a central command. They track the location of friendly forces and identify enemy positions.
AI acts as the accelerator, instantly processing massive amounts of data collected through sensors in drones or any other military products, including interceptor missiles or artillery units.
The tactical advantage on the battlefield is given by the system’s ability to compress the kill chain – meaning coordinating and distributing the intelligence to military assets on the ground to find, track and destroy targets in a matter of minutes.
In such an ecosystem, AI-powered automated drones are just pieces of a broader puzzle.
Ukraine is known to be developing its system, which it named DELTA. Following operational trials in late 2025, Russia has been rolling out its version, the Svod Tactical Situational Awareness Complex, to front-line units.
Both sides claim that once the battlefield data is processed, a decision support system (DSS) presents a military commander with options to choose from, keeping a human in the decision-making loop, said Miron.
“In how far that is true is, of course, impossible to find out,” she added.
Acknowledging full AI autonomy would provoke ethical and legal questions.
Even if humans were to retain final decision-making authority, research has shown AI systems subtly shape choices, predetermining outcomes.
“Under time and pressure, commanders often do as AI suggests,” said Miron, whose research focuses on military AI and remotely piloted and autonomous systems.
Towards full automation
Coordinated AI-powered military systems are the next frontier of modern warfare, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian Ministry of Defence adviser on loitering munitions, known by his callsign Flash.
“That’s what it will all come to,” he posted on his Telegram channel on July 1. “Navigation, search for a target, and attacks will be fully autonomous.”
Drones with some autonomous capabilities are already being deployed at scale.
Heorhii Volkov, commander of Ukraine’s Yasni Ochi drone strike unit, said this is currently mostly used in the final phase of long-distance strikes, where first-person view (FPV) drones are likely to lose radio connection due to electronic warfare or the curvature of the Earth.
The use of AI in so-called last-mile operations solves this battlefield hitch. If the signal is lost, an integrated AI-enabled onboard module takes full control of the unmanned vehicle, autonomously locks on the target and carries the strike to completion.
Yaroslav Azhnyuk, founder of Ukrainian technology company The Fourth Law, which develops AI-powered autonomy software for unmanned vehicles, said Russia and Ukraine were working to deploy a wider range of autonomous systems.
“This is not simply a race to demonstrate a fully autonomous drone. It is a race to make autonomy reliable, affordable and deployable at scale,” Azhnyuk told Al Jazeera. “Electronic warfare, increasingly long engagement distances and the growing number of drones are making human-controlled systems less sufficient. Autonomy solves exactly these constraints.”
Azhnyuk believes autonomy will become a game-changer over the next six to 12 months.
“The decisive advantage will belong to the side that can deploy reliable autonomy across tens or hundreds of thousands of systems, not just demonstrate it in prototypes,” he said.
Kateryna Bondar, senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), noted the dangers of AI’s reliance on algorithms.
“The system doesn’t understand what it’s doing; it’s just following the algorithm and the rules which people created,” said Bondar, who works at the CSIS’s Wadhwani AI Center. “AI has to be trained to recognise targets and engage these targets,” but writing code that distinguishes between a bus and a tank is easier than between a Russian and a Ukrainian soldier.
Additionally, cost-effective FPV drones have low-quality cameras and their resolution can be lowered further by adverse atmospheric conditions.
Military units using autonomous systems therefore “delegate the decision to a very imperfect technology that cannot distinguish between a civilian and a military person, combatant or non-combatant”, Bondar said.
“This is why there is a conversation around who makes a decision and who has responsibility for mistakes and errors.”

Europe Prepares for War as Germany Sends Up to 1,000 New Troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:20:35 UTC
22:20:35 KST

Germany is preparing to order up to 1,000 active-duty soldiers to serve with its permanent brigade in Lithuania this fall as European NATO members strengthen their eastern defenses against the threat of a Russian attack, according to a report published on Monday, Sept. 14.
According to Bild, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has approved compulsory postings after the Bundeswehr failed to attract enough volunteers for the Lithuania-based unit.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The first mandatory assignments could begin this fall and affect fewer than 1,000 soldiers, several independent sources told the German outlet.
Germany’s Defense Ministry was expected to brief senior representatives of the Bundestag’s Defense Committee about the decision on Monday.
The measure is not a general mobilization or conscription of civilians. It concerns serving Bundeswehr personnel who could be assigned to Lithuania even if they did not volunteer for the deployment.
Only about 60% of the positions required for the brigade have been filled voluntarily. The most serious shortages involve IT specialists, logistics personnel, cooks and enlisted soldiers.
Bild reported that compulsory postings could currently affect as many as 20% of the brigade’s positions. The Bundeswehr hopes to reduce that figure to around 10% by the end of September by attracting more volunteers.
The German military has conducted recruitment campaigns and offered familiarization trips to Lithuania for soldiers and their families. However, the remaining personnel decisions must be made soon because affected soldiers need to be notified, and then may challenge their assignments through legal procedures, and require time to plan a possible relocation.
‘The Battlefield Has Gone Underground’: Khartiia Commander Reveals Ukraine’s Edge Over Russia
“Voluntariness remains the top principle,” Bild reported. “But to guarantee the brigade’s operational readiness, compulsory assignments can no longer be avoided.”
Germany reinforces NATO’s eastern flank
Germany plans to station 4,800 soldiers and around 200 civilian personnel permanently in Lithuania by the end of 2027.
The unit, officially known as the 45th Armored Brigade Lithuania, will be the first German combat brigade permanently based outside the country since the Bundeswehr was established in 1955.
According to the Bundeswehr, the approximately 5,000-person heavy maneuver brigade is intended to protect NATO’s eastern flank following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Once fully operational, the brigade will include thousands of soldiers and approximately 2,000 military vehicles, NATO said.
Lithuania borders Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. It is also close to the Suwalki Gap, a narrow corridor connecting Poland and the Baltic states that NATO considers particularly vulnerable in a potential conflict with Russia.
Pistorius had previously insisted that the brigade should be staffed primarily by volunteers. During a visit to Lithuania in June, however, he acknowledged that compulsory assignments might be necessary and estimated that fewer than 1,000 soldiers could be affected.
Tusk warns Russian escalation could reach NATO
Germany’s decision comes as Poland also strengthens its security posture following Russian attacks close to its border.
On Sunday, Sept. 13, a Russian drone attacked the locomotive of a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train at the Yahodyn railway station in Ukraine’s Volyn region near Poland.
Poland scrambled fighters during the attack, while Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk convened an urgent meeting with government ministers, senior military commanders and intelligence chiefs.
“The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intense activity on the Russian side, and unfortunately, we cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory,” Tusk warned.
The Polish prime minister said Russia’s escalating actions were becoming an immediate security concern for NATO countries bordering Ukraine, reinforcing calls for stronger military readiness across Europe.

The 2026 budget: what we know and what has been leaked so far
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:17:40 UTC
22:17:40 KST

The 2026 budget: what we know and what has been leaked so far
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
As happens every year, large parts of the government’s spending plans have been leaked to the Dutch press. Here is a summary of what the various papers are reporting is being planned:
Government and local government finances
- The government plans to cut €400 million from spending on its own operations, with the aim of a structural reduction of €1 billion from 2030.
- In particular, the government plans to reduce support functions and ensure external hires account for no more than 10% of the workforce.
- The local authorities fund will rise marginally to just under €50 billion, or €2,741 per resident.
- However, local authorities will not be compensated for spending on youth social work and €1 billion will be cut from the budget for home helps.
Taxes
- Spending power will fall marginally for all but pensioners and low-income households.
- Plans to reform the Box 3 asset tax system are due in spring 2027.
- Income tax rates will go down by 0.06 percentage points in the first and second tax bands.
- The arbeidskorting – a tax break for people in work – will rise slightly.
- Employers will no longer be able to give workers a 20% discount tax free on the company’s own products.
- Staff outings and Christmas boxes will no longer be tax free.
- The startersaftrek – a discount for the newly self-employed – will be scrapped although it is not yet clear when.
- BTW on plants, flowers and trips by balloon will rise from 9% to 21%.
- Excise duty on alcohol will rise in line with inflation.
Benefits
- Cuts to slash the period for claiming unemployment benefit from two to one year have been delayed until 2029.
- A planned faster increase in the state pension age will not go ahead.
- A lower maximum for payouts to pregnant women and people on invalidity benefit will not go ahead.
Travel and transport
- A 10 cent reduction in the price of diesel will be phased out from 2028 not 2027.
- Tax on long-distance flights is being set at €59 instead of €70 to ensure Schiphol is not more expensive than German airports.
Healthcare
- A planned increase in the health insurance own risk payment of €60 has been scrapped. It will still rise from €385 to €400 in line with inflation.
- €100 million is being allocated to ensure 60 to 69-year-olds can be vaccinated against shingles. The over 70s must pick up the bill themselves.
- The government expects health insurance premiums will rise by €12 a month – although health insurance companies decide their own rates.
Housing and infrastructure
- €940 million will be allocated to boost major residential developments in terms of facilities and green spaces.
- €630 million will go to specialised housing for the elderly.
- Housing corporations will get a €425 million tax cut, allowing them to borrow an extra €6 billion to build social housing.
- Private investors will be able to claim up to €10,000 for every mid-market rental home they build, from a budget of €500 million running from 2029 to 2033.
- €1.5 billion has been allocated for road and bridge repairs.
- €300 million will be invested annually in improving transport links to new residential developments.
Education and research
- Education will get €668 million extra, largely reversing cuts to higher education imposed by the previous government.
- There will be more investment in trade schools and in scientific research.
- Funding is being set aside for the development of a national super computer and an Einstein telescope R&D centre.
- The basic grant for students living away from home will rise by €50 from 2028.
- €346 million will go to additional training for teachers from 2028.
- More money will be allocated to help people shift into teaching from other professions.
Climate
- Money will be allocated to help farmers who want to invest in making their businesses more sustainable and climate-friendly.
- €1.3 billion is being allocated to store carbon dioxide in empty gas fields under the North Sea.
Asylum and migration
- The government says spending on refugees will reach €8 billion this year but go down to €5 billion by 2031 because of EU and other measures.
- Local authorities which have not set up their own permanent refugee centres will be placed on a blacklist.
- €22 million will be invested in setting up refugee centres outside the EU in 2027.
- More money will be put into dealing with refugees who commit crimes and in secure accommodation for them.
Royals
- Spending on staff etc. will rise from €60.8 million to €62.1 million in 2027.
- The king, queen and princess Amalia will have combined income of €2.7 million this year, but Amalia will not claim hers while she is studying.
- The royals’ income rises in line with civil servant pay, which is 0.3% this year.
Other
- €600 million extra will go to defence in 2027, taking the total to almost €29 billion, including €3.1 billion in military support for Ukraine.
- The development aid budget will rise by €400 million a year for the next three years, on top of the extra money agreed in June to win senate support and the partial reversal of the Schoof cabinet’s €2.4 billion cuts.
- The Netherlands will not hit the OECD target of 0.7% of GDP on aid spending.
- The government will introduce a “sport pass” for 12 to 23-year-olds of €100 to €300 to be invested in sports.
Sources: Telegraaf, NRC, NOS, RTL and Volkskrant

"100%, he will not appear."

Finnish town bans energy drinks from all public buildings
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:15:28 EEST
22:15:28 KST

The town of Savitaipale in southeastern Finland has banned energy drinks from all its municipal buildings, including schools, libraries and sports facilities.
The ban came into effect at the beginning of September and applies to everyone, including adults.
People will not be fined for breaking the rule, but staff will ask anyone seen drinking an energy drink to stop.
Savitaipale's Director of Wellbeing Aija Rautio compares the policy to a smoking ban.
"Using energy drinks is a personal choice, but if we see someone drinking them in municipal facilities, we will point it out," Rautio says.
Savitaipale is believed to be the first municipality in Finland to introduce a complete ban on energy drinks in its facilities. Energy drink consumption has been restricted in several Finnish schools since the 2010s.
Adults set an example
The ban was approved by Savitaipale's Education and Wellbeing Committee in August following a petition from the local youth council.
The petition highlighted the role of availability, visibility and social norms in young people's energy drink consumption.
According to the Youth Nutrition Survey by the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare (THL), 67 percent of 12- to 20-year-olds consume energy drinks at least occasionally.
Many also said they felt they drink too many energy drinks or are dependent on them.
THL senior researcher Peppi Haario supports Savitaipale's decision, saying that adults can have a strong influence on young people's behaviour through the example they set.
Ban aims to reduce peer pressure
Youth council chair Vilma Sysiö says social pressure also encourages young people to drink energy drinks.
"Energy drinks are bought at the shop with friends and drunk together. People chat around them, much like adults chat over coffee," Sysiö says.
She says the ban can help reduce that social pressure.
The youth council says it has received only positive feedback on its petition. Vilma Sysiö said she hopes other municipalities will follow Savitaipale's example.

Why Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline matters for global oil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:15:14 UTC
22:15:14 KST

Why Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline matters for global oil
The 1,200km (745 mile) pipeline has been temporarily closed, affecting up to 5 percent of global oil supply.
In another blow to global oil markets, drones struck Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline last Thursday, prompting the kingdom to suspend operations.
The 1,200km (746-mile) pipeline, which carries roughly 4 to 5 million barrels of oil per day (bpd), links the country’s major oil-producing fields in the east with the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing Saudi Arabia to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which has largely been closed since the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran in February.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said the shutdown was a “precautionary” measure after the attack caused damage and injuries in the Riyadh and Medina regions.
The closure comes as the US-Israel war on Iran has sharply reduced oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi forces in Yemen have intensified attacks around the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb.
With oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz severely disrupted, Saudi Arabia has relied more heavily on the East-West pipeline. What does its closure mean for an already tight global oil market?
How bad is the damage?
The extent of the damage is not yet clear, and estimates of how quickly the pipeline can return to normal operations vary. Sources familiar with the incident told the Reuters news agency that repairs could take five to six weeks, while another source said operations could restart sooner.
Saudi officials said drones hit the pipeline in two areas around Riyadh and Medina. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the attack caused injuries and damage to infrastructure.
According to Saudi authorities, the launch of the drones was traced to Maysan province in southeastern Iraq, close to the Iranian border and an area where Iran-aligned armed groups have established a longstanding presence.
The attack follows a strike in March near the Saudi-Aramco-ExxonMobil refinery in Yanbu that temporarily disrupted crude loadings from the Red Sea port. That incident had little lasting impact on operations, with shipments recovering within days, but it demonstrated that the kingdom’s western oil infrastructure was not immune to attacks.
What is the East-West pipeline?
The East-West pipeline, also known as the Petroline, is a 1,200km (745-mile) long oil pipeline built in 1981 that carries crude oil from the kingdom’s eastern oil fields near Abqaiq across the Arabian Peninsula to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.
It has a maximum capacity of seven million bpd, although actual flows have been lower in recent months – about two million bpd in August according to Kpler – the lowest monthly level since January as Houthi attacks made the Red Sea route difficult to use.
Saudi Arabia increased the amount of crude sent west during the first five months of the conflict, taking flows to roughly 4-5 million bpd. That represents about 4 to 5 percent of global supply and allowed the world’s second largest oil exporter to bypass the Strait of Hormuz when shipping conditions deteriorated.
Why is it important?
The pipeline’s closure comes at a critical point for the global oil market.
Before the war, the Strait of Hormuz supplied more than a fifth of oil globally – about 20 million bpd. According to Reuters, industry estimates now put the flow at about 6-9 million bpd through the strait, a dramatic reduction in the volume.
Saudi Arabia has responded by moving more crude towards the Red Sea. However, the flow and export of that oil depends on the pipeline, storage facilities and tankers transiting safely – all of which have been made vulnerable since the Iran war began in February.
According to sources close to Reuters, if the pipeline remains shut, Yanbu has enough available stocks to sustain exports for about five to seven days, while Egyptian facilities in Ain Sukhna and Sidi Kerir, which store Saudi oil, could provide additional supplies for several days.
While this gives Saudi Arabia some buffer, it comes as global inventories have already been falling. The International Energy Agency said Saudi oil supply reached a more than three-decade low in August, with disruptions in Hormuz and the Red Sea. It says world oil supplies will decline by some 5.7 million bpd this year, equivalent to 6 percent of global supply.
Oil prices have so far been cushioned by stockpiles and releases from strategic reserves, with Brent crude trading about $70-$90 in recent months. But the longer regional disruptions continue, the more those reserves will be depleted and the higher prices will rise.
In June, the IEA said continued drawdowns could hit critical levels with experts saying that if inventories approach exceptionally low levels, Brent could potentially rise to $150 a barrel.
If damage to the pipeline proves extensive, and attacks continue to threaten Yanbu and shipping routes beyond it, Saudi Arabia could find that its ability to compensate for lost Gulf exports is itself becoming constrained.
Gavekal Research noted that if Yanbu, which processes more than one million bpd, goes offline because of threats from Houthi drones, “this would be a disaster for the world at a time when global refining capacity is already critically tight.”

Tehran protests as US blocks Iran nuclear chief from IAEA meeting in Vienna
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:14:56 UTC
22:14:56 KST

The United States has blocked Iran's nuclear chief from attending this week's UN atomic watchdog meeting in Vienna by opposing an exemption from so-called "snapback" UN sanctions, prompting protests from Tehran.
Iranian nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami had been due to attend and address this week's International Atomic Energy Agency General Conference, an annual meeting of IAEA member states that began on Monday.
At the opening, however, Iran said Austria had revoked Eslami's visa after initially granting it.
"The cancellation and so-called legal justification advanced for it are a stark indication of a political act and advanced formal politicisation of this organisation," Iran's ambassador to the IAEA told the conference.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said the United States had pressured Austria into the move. In contrast, Iran and Russia said it formed part of a broader effort to prevent Iranian officials from obtaining visas for international travel.
The United States said it had objected to an exemption that would have allowed Eslami to travel despite sanctions reimposed under the so-called "snapback" mechanism at the UN Security Council.
Snapback sanctions
Eslami was among those targeted by sanctions lifted under a 2015 nuclear deal between Iran and major powers and the United States.
The deal unravelled after President Donald Trump pulled the US out of it in 2018, and Western powers triggered the "snapback" mechanism last year to re-impose those sanctions.
Last year, Kaja Kallas, the European Union's top diplomat, said the reimposition of sanctions "must not be the end of diplomacy".
Russia and China tried unsuccessfully last year, at the UN Security Council, to delay the sanctions snapback, warning it could escalate tensions in the Middle East.
Their draft resolution gained only four votes among the 15 council members.
Iran and allies, including Russia, do not recognise the reimposed sanctions.
US push
Austria said it had requested an exemption for Eslami.
"Austria, although being only the host state, submitted a request for an exemption to the travel ban to the Security Council sanctions committee, which was rejected," Ambassador Christian Ebner told the conference.
"As a consequence, Austria was obliged to deny one member of the Iranian delegation entry into its territory," he said.
US Ambassador Preston Wells Griffith III said his country had objected in New York to an exemption being granted, and that was why the application was denied.
"The United States objected to the exemption request, which, per the rules of the UN sanctions committee, resulted in the UN Security Council denying the request," he said.
"His (Eslami's) participation would have only resulted in Iran exploiting IAEA proceedings as a stage for propaganda while sidestepping substantive cooperation, undermining the credibility of the very body charged with verifying its nuclear commitments," he said, referring to a standoff over inspections.

Lebanon moves to ban property sales in Israeli-occupied areas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:14:45 UTC
22:14:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon moves to ban property sales in Israeli-occupied areas in south
Lebanon's cabinet has approved a draft law seeking to prevent the sale or transfer of property in areas occupied by Israeli forces in southern Lebanon, as Israel continues to control more than 60 villages and towns in the region.
The bill, approved during a cabinet session chaired by President Joseph Aoun at Baabda Palace on Thursday, will now be referred to parliament for consideration.
The move comes as Israeli forces continue to carry out demolitions, explosions and earthworks targeting homes, buildings, infrastructure and agricultural land in southern Lebanon, despite a ceasefire agreement that came into effect around three months ago.
Lebanon has repeatedly called for an end to Israeli attacks and for the implementation of the framework agreement signed in Washington on 26 June.
Under the draft law, property transactions in the occupied areas would be prohibited and frozen under exceptional circumstances.
The bill, proposed by Finance Minister Yassine Jaber, argues that a balance must be maintained between the constitutional protection of private property and the need to safeguard public order and the public interest.
It also seeks to prevent the country's economic crisis from being exploited to encourage property owners to sell their land at significantly reduced prices.
Contracts, sales agreements and irrevocable powers of attorney registered before 8 October 2023 would be exempt from the proposed restrictions.
Government sources said the legislation is intended as a precautionary measure to prevent companies, major traders and property developers from exploiting the security and economic situation, as well as the financial difficulties facing property owners.
The sources also expressed concern that individuals linked to Israel could potentially be behind attempts to acquire land through deceptive practices, although no such cases had been identified so far.
The bill must still be approved by parliament and its final fate will depend on political and developments on the ground.
Concerns over property rights
The proposed restrictions have also raised questions over the rights of displaced Lebanese property owners.
Lebanese lawyer and law professor Jad Tohme said protecting southern land from changes in ownership resulting from the Israeli occupation represented a major national interest and could justify regulating property transactions in occupied areas under exceptional circumstances.
However, he said the constitutionality of the measure would depend not only on its objective but also on whether the restrictions were proportionate.
Private property is protected under Article 15 of Lebanon's constitution, and the exceptional circumstances should not be used to deprive owners of the ability to benefit from or dispose of their property indefinitely, Tohme said.
Many residents of southern Lebanon have been displaced from their villages and homes while facing severe economic pressures, he noted. State compensation and assistance have also been insufficient to meet their needs.
Preventing displaced residents from selling their property could therefore leave them in severe financial difficulty, he warned, effectively leaving them with property whose financial value they cannot access.
Tohme questioned whether an outright ban on sales was the best way to prevent Israeli-linked developers or other parties from acquiring land.
He suggested instead creating a system to regulate the identity of buyers and the conditions of ownership, potentially allowing sales only to eligible Lebanese buyers, giving the state a right of first refusal or requiring prior approval under clearly defined criteria.
"Protecting the land should not come at the expense of its owner," Tohme said, arguing that the legislation should prevent land from passing to parties whose ownership could pose a national security risk without placing an excessive burden on southern Lebanese property owners.
Earlier restrictions
Lebanon has previously imposed similar restrictions during periods of crisis.
Following the Beirut port explosion on 4 August 2020, the Culture Ministry temporarily prohibited transactions involving damaged properties, while the Finance Ministry issued a circular restricting the sale of properties of heritage and historical value without prior approval.
The latest proposal also comes amid longstanding concerns over land ownership in southern Lebanon.
Tohme noted that, following Israel's withdrawal from most of southern Lebanon in 2000, millions of square metres of Lebanese state-owned communal land were subject to encroachment and illegal occupation.
Financial prosecutors have previously investigated cases involving the seizure of large areas of public land.

(AA Photo)
Investigators exhuming the grave of a former intelligence officer 15 years after his prison death have found intact soft tissue, yielding critical forensic evidence for a reopened murder probe.
The Silivri Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office ordered the opening of Kaşif Kozinoğlu’s grave at Ümraniye Kocatepe Cemetery to investigate his 2011 death. Officials sent extracted organs, bones and soil to the Forensic Medicine Institute First Specialization Board alongside camera footage, emergency call transcripts and hospital records.
Forensic Medicine Expert Professor Nevzat Alkan said the preserved internal organs could change the investigation’s course.
“Getting soft tissue is very valuable. Substances entering the body do not easily penetrate bone structure, but in soft tissues, meaning internal organs, these substances can be easily detected,” he said.
The probe targets screenwriters Raci Şaşmaz, Bahadır Özdener and Cüneyt Aysan of Kurtlar Vadisi Pusu (Valley of the Wolves Ambush) — a highly influential, long-running Turkish political drama notorious for blurring fiction with alleged “deep state” and mafia realities.
Prosecutors noted an episode broadcast two days before Kozinoğlu’s Nov. 12 death featured a character named Kazım Kaşifoğlu delivered to Yaşar Ağa as a gift from protagonist Polat Alemdar. Kaşifoğlu faced death threats from henchman İlhan, who declared himself his “angel of death.” A subsequent episode depicted the character, after exercising and showering, being murdered by the character “Kara” via an air-injecting syringe. Investigators are also examining a 2012 scene showing a tombstone inscribed with ERDOĞAN.
Kozinoğlu, a former National Intelligence Organization (MİT) regional advisor, penned a 2004 report alleging the show was directed by jailed gang leader Nuri “Nuriş” Ergin and Osman Sınav. It stated the character “Çakır” represented Ergin’s rival Çakıcı, while “Halit” represented Ergin.
It linked financiers Sedat and Vedat Kasım to security figures Yavuz Ataç and Korkut Eken, naming Tahir Kıran — son of shipping magnate Turgut Kıran and partner of Şadan Kalkavan — as a proxy. The screenwriters allegedly took instructions from Gendarmerie Intelligence Deputy Head Colonel Hasan Atilla Uğur. Raci Şaşmaz and lead actor Necati Şaşmaz were also linked to former police chief Mehmet Ağar through a relative, Abdülkadir Şaşmaz.

Israel unlikely to improve Saudi ties despite Houthi threat, expert tells 'Post' - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:13:13 UTC
22:13:13 KST

Israel is unlikely to find an opening to improve relations with Saudi Arabia despite Riyadh’s efforts to expand intelligence sharing and military assistance in its fight against the Houthis, Dr. Brandon Friedman, director of research at the Moshe Dayan Center for Middle Eastern and African Studies at Tel Aviv University and a researcher on political reform in Saudi Arabia, told The Jerusalem Post on Monday.
Friedman spoke with the Post after Reuters reported, citing three sources familiar with the matter, that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was seeking US military assistance to confront the Houthi threat. Israel Hayom subsequently reported that Israel had been indirectly approached through CENTCOM to share intelligence and provide other assistance.
Saudi media confirmed that Salman discussed regional developments with US Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper in Jeddah on Monday, though it remains unclear to what extent Riyadh pursued other options for military support.
Though Friedman said it would be logical for the current security situation to create an opening for Israel to collaborate with Saudi Arabia, given the shared enemy in the Iranian axis, he maintained it would be “fairly unlikely as things stand” given that “all foreign policy issues today are being refracted through the lens of the Israeli election.”
Any support Riyadh would receive from Israel would need to happen “quietly,” because of their “own domestic political needs,” Friedman said, adding that he believed that any support Israel would currently provide would only be given in the context of providing the governing coalition with a “pre-election boost.”
Jerusalem, Washington long sought to bring Saudi Arabia into Abraham Accords
Though Riyadh has maintained that it will not normalize relations with Israel until a Palestinian state is established, Jerusalem and Washington have long sought to bring Saudi Arabia into the Abraham Accords.
Though Saudi Arabia ranked 25th out of 145 countries in the 2026 Global Firepower Index, Friedman argued that Riyadh had become increasingly dependent on Washington over the past 15 years and now had “very little of its own military power,” leaving it with limited tools at its disposal, “which is why their war in Yemen since basically 2015 has been a failure.”
While Riyadh could turn to Israel and the United Arab Emirates for support, Friedman suggested that they would be unlikely to do so given that “the Saudis have been at loggerheads” with both countries for the last year. Though Israel has signaled it is willing to share intelligence, Friedman maintained that it was “fairly unlikely, given the current political constellation.”
“If there was a new governing coalition that seemed more committed to discretion, then perhaps there would be an opening for greater cooperation,” he suggested.
With reports indicating that Washington has now refused to come to the aid of Riyadh against the Houthis, and cooperation with Israel still off the table, Friedman explained that Saudi Arabia has begun searching for new regional powers, hence the Mecca Agreement signed by Turkey and Pakistan. The agreement, however, has not provided Riyadh with the support it needs now, as such a move would be considered premature.
Pakistan has already refused to provide its own troops for war with the Houthis and is preoccupied with fighting the Taliban.
Mecca Agreement insufficient for Saudi, may appease Iran
With the US out, and the Mecca Agreement unable to offer what is needed, Friedman said that the final option for Saudi Arabia would be to try to “appease” Iran, which he suggested is what was happening now.
“The Iranians are trying to tie the war in Yemen to their ongoing negotiations through Oman with the GCC states over service charges for commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz,” he explained, adding that Iran had directed the Houthis to escalate in hopes of seeing Riyadh fold on Tehran’s demands.
With the Houthis attempting to assert control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Arabian Sea and the Indian Ocean, Saudi Arabia’s oil industry could be “strangled,” he continued.
The Houthis have already bombed the East-West pipeline, which has rerouted around 4 million barrels of oil per day, or roughly 4% of global supply. Iranian-backed militias have also repeatedly targeted Saudi oil infrastructure, Friedman said, arguing that the attacks are intended to pressure Riyadh into accepting greater Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz.
Given the impact the Houthis are having on oil prices, Friedman suggested that Riyadh was holding onto the hope that Washington would throw its weight against the Houthis and Iran, something Friedman said was unlikely given the upcoming summit with the Chinese presidency and the approaching midterm elections.
“The Americans are not keen to see the war expand right now, and I think that’s part of why the Iranians are escalating at this point,” he theorized.
With the Gulf states unable to agree to a united response, and with Iran increasingly using the global economy as political leverage, Friedman suggested Riyadh would become trapped under the increasing pressure.

Ukraine’s Navy says it has carried out what it describes as the world’s first naval battle between two unmanned surface vessels, claiming that one of its drone boats destroyed a Russian drone in the Black Sea.
While the Sargan 3000 has sunk Russian vessels in the past, the incident, which took place in mid-September, marks the first recorded case of an unmanned surface vessel (USV) sinking another USV in combat.
“Units of the Main Intelligence Directorate (GUR) detected the target and the Ukrainian Navy’s Sargan 3000 unmanned boat, equipped with a remotely operated weapon station (RWS) Protector 12.7 millimeters, and successfully destroyed it,” the Ukrainian Navy wrote on Telegram, adding that “This is the first naval battle in history between unmanned boats.”
The Ukrainian Navy released an 81‑second video showing the encounter along with the statement but did not specify the exact time or place of the engagement. It also did not identify the Russian vessel in its initial statement, but it’s been reported to be an Orcan‑type USV, a small explosive‑laden drone boat used by Russia in attacks on Ukrainian ports and naval vessels.
The footage includes both onboard camera views and aerial imagery from an unidentified surveillance platform.
According to the Ukrainian Navy, the Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR/GUR) first identified the Russian vessel. Then the Sargan‑3000, equipped with a Kongsberg Protector 12.7 mm. remote weapon station, approached and opened fire. Video footage shows the Ukrainian USV tracking the Russian craft, firing bursts from the machine gun, and continuing the attack as debris breaks off the Russian vessel’s hull. The Russian USV ultimately sinks.
USV time
While the Russia-Ukraine war has mainly focused on drones, Kyiv has operated USVs against Russia’s Black Sea Fleet since 2022, and by 2026, several distinct platforms were in service under different operators, including the Sea Baby, Magura, and Sargan-3000.
Ukraine's Security Service runs Sea Baby, which is used mainly against vessels moored in port; Magura USVs belong to Defence Intelligence and were built to engage warships underway, with later variants carrying air-to-air missiles. The navy operates the Sargan-3000, a multi‑purpose unmanned vessel with a low‑profile hull, waterjet propulsion, and modular payload options.
Ukrainian USVs have destroyed Russian ships both at port and at sea, and according to The Kyiv Post, it has dramatically expanded its operations, hitting over 100 Russian vessels in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea over the summer.
“Our missiles, our unmanned systems, our interceptors, attack and naval drones, reconnaissance systems, artillery, our ammunition, armored vehicles, robotic platforms, and much more. All that today is truly proudly called – the weapons of Ukraine. They defend our skies, our cities and villages, save lives, and prove that “Made in Ukraine” is synonymous with effectiveness and strength,” Zelensky said in an address in April.
According to reports, the Sargan-3000 took part in NATO’s REPMUS (Robotic Experimentation and Prototyping with Maritime Unmanned Systems) in Portugal in September, alongside dozens of other NATO countries to test and evaluate new maritime capabilities.
“For the first time in NATO’s history, Ukraine’s Navy led and coordinated the Opposing Force (OPFOR) during REPMUS/DYMS 2025 - an historic milestone that underscores Ukraine's growing role in NATO exercises. The training highlighted modern maritime warfare trends, particularly the use of unmanned systems for coordinated strikes and rapid threat response. In this strategic step forward, Ukraine’s leadership brought combat realism to the exercise, driving innovation and the development of new NATO tactics,” read a statement from NATO following the drill.

Nepal disaster: Swiss expert urges lessons for future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:12:32 UTC
22:12:32 KST

Nepal disaster: Swiss expert urges lessons for future
Nearly three weeks after devastating floods struck Nepal and Tibet, Swiss engineer Eric Bardou says conditions on the ground remain challenging and calls for a better understanding of such events to help prevent future disasters.
“You could say it almost feels like an earthquake,” said Eric Bardou, a member of the Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit (SHA), in a telephone call to the Keystone-ATS news agency from Kathmandu on Saturday. On the ground he saw buildings destroyed or displaced by the force of the wave, some of which appeared to have been pushed sideways.
The 57-year-old engineer, who specialises in geotechnical engineering, hydrology and mountain risks, was sent to Nepal by Switzerland on September 5. He was integrated into the mission of the United Nations Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), where his role involved assessing risks related to water and terrain.
On his arrival, two lakes that had formed as a result of landslides raised fears of a new wave. “They drained on their own, but it is the sort of situation that still needed to be monitored,” he explained. The teams had to set up observation points and adjust their movements to ensure they were not caught off guard by a new rise in water levels.
Preserving evidence
The Swiss expert, who is soon returning from Nepal, highlights another, less visible urgency: preserving the traces of the disaster before they disappear.
“If we don’t do it now, we will never be able to understand what happened,” he stresses. But behind these traces lies, above all, a human tragedy.
Bardou said he was deeply moved seeing people wandering along the riverbanks, searching for missing relatives or for items that might be salvaged from the rubble. International organisations on the ground are meanwhile focused on trying to rescue those still alive beneath the rubble.
More
Switzerland sends more aid funding, experts to Nepal
The hope to be able to document the disaster, however, is confronted with a fundamental difficulty: estimates vary widely depending on the methods used, particularly concerning the volume of collapsed material.
“The volume swept downstream is estimated at between 100 and almost 300 million cubic metres,” Bardou explains. He claims to have seen various estimates and is unable to determine which is the most reliable, especially as he has been unable to access the area where the deluge began.
On August 26, rock and ice broke away at an altitude of approximately 5,200 metres on the north face of the Langtang Lirung massif. Debris quickly descended downstream along the Lhende Khola river valley, situated some 20 kilometres upstream of the Gyirong/Rasuwagadhi border pass, completely obliterating the Sino-Nepalese border at that point. The deluge killed nearly 1,400 people in Nepal and Tibet.
More
Himalayan flood sparks concern among Nepalese and Tibetans in Switzerland
Another unknown factor is the exact composition of the mass that poured down the valley. The traces observed downstream indicate a particularly fluid flow containing vast volumes of water and boulders, some of which were several metres in diameter.
‘Fluid’ torrential debris flow
By comparing marks left on trees and buildings with the deposits on the ground, Bardou estimates that 80% of the mass consisted of water.
The disaster has also left behind a considerable amount of sediment and caused heavy erosion. Some bodies have been found downstream as far as India, at a distance of between 150 and 240 kilometres, demonstrating the enormous power.
Bardou says the challenge is to better understand the mechanisms behind this disaster rather than settling for a simple explanation linked to climate change. “To say that it’s hot, that the ice is melting and that everything is collapsing is a bit too simplistic,” he said.
More
Why do Swiss mountains collapse? It’s complicated
Climate change can cause rapid transformations to which the mountains must adapt, he said. Permafrost, which acts like a cement holding certain rocks and soil together, may play a special role. But he says he’s not totally satisfied with this as the sole explanation. Society needs to determine exactly what happened in order to identify and prevent such events, he adds.
Prevention is difficult
Prevention measures, however, are hampered by the sheer scale of the Himalayas: 600,000 km² compared with the 25,000 km² of the Swiss Alps. “The scale radically changes the situation,” he said.
In Switzerland, the large number of observers, guides, engineers and sensors makes it easier to detect mountain movements and changes.
In Nepal, institutions and specialists have been working on glaciers and mountain risks for some time. But even with satellite images showing a possible acceleration in an area prior to the event, you still needs to know where to look among the vast amounts of data, says the Valais native.
The glacier at the root of the disaster is now a central focus. Until then, the priority had been to rescue those who could still be saved.

Welt am Sonntag also reported that German security agencies already knew of Oleg L.’s possible ties to Russian military intelligence when he entered the country, but did not place him under surveillance.
The suspected perpetrators planned to use three drones in the Leipzig airport sabotage operation. Two were destroyed during takeoff, while the third reached the Ukrainian aircraft. Investigators believe an explosion was avoided only because the detonator failed to function.
The second suspect is Belarusian national Andrei K. His DNA was found on an antenna that was used to control the drones. The DNA matched records in Finnish and Lithuanian police databases.
In Finland, he had been suspected of theft. He is also suspected of setting fire to a hardware store in the Polish city of Łódź in 2024.
The German publication Bild previously reported that a DNA trace found during the investigation of the Leipzig airport attack case matched DNA evidence from a 2024 arson attack on a DHL logistics center in Leipzig. The newspaper did not say whose DNA was found.
On Sept. 1, the German government formally accused Russia of carrying out a hybrid attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, where a drone with a detonator had been found near a Ukrainian transport plane on Aug. 5. At a news conference, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany would respond by closing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and Russia’s consulate general in Bonn.

The Filo Jet, a high-speed passenger vessel operating between Kyrenia and Taşucu in Türkiye’s Mersin province, began taking on water from its bow shortly after departing Kyrenia Port around noon on Aug. 30. The vessel sank as it attempted to return to the port.
There were 267 passengers and crew members aboard. A total of 239 people were rescued, while 14 people died and another 14 remain missing. The wreck lies at a depth of approximately 554 meters off Kyrenia.

America’s AI boom needs $140b in new power plants, new estimate shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:11:18 UTC
22:11:18 KST

America’s AI boom needs $140b in new power plants, new estimate shows
NEW YORK – America’s data centre boom will need US$110 billion (S$140 billion) to build 45 gigawatts (GW) of new power generation through 2030, according to an analysis by Moody’s Ratings.
The vast majority of that new supply – more than 30 GW – will come from natural gas-fired units and represents about 4 billion cu ft of incremental gas supply, according to a report on Sept 14.
The bulk of the remaining supply will come from solar and energy storage, with nuclear restarts accounting for less than 5 per cent. One GW is roughly equivalent to the output of a traditional nuclear reactor.
The projection is based on the International Energy Agency’s forecast that data centres will consume 426 terawatt-hours in 2030, doubling its share of US electricity usage to 10 per cent from 2025 levels.
Moody’s forecast quantifies what it would take to produce enough megawatts to feed the data centres needed for artificial intelligence and cloud computing that are driving the biggest expansion in US electricity demand in decades, fueling a massive buildout of infrastructure to support it.
The White House has called the AI race a national imperative, backing some of the world’s biggest companies as they compete for potentially enormous profits.
But the buildout comes at a cost, drawing opposition from Americans worried that the average household and business is subsidising AI through rising power bills, pollution, water shortages and threats to public lands and private property.
The US$110 billion buildout of new power plants alone could add US$25 billion to US$30 billion a year to electricity costs in the US. How that is passed on to consumers will depend on the rate-making process and other rules for allocating costs in each area, Ryan Wobbrock, senior vice-president of ratings at Moody’s Ratings’ global infrastructure finance group, said in an e-mail.
Data centres will pay for as much as US$15 billion of those costs directly because they are paying for power plants to be built on their AI campuses, he said. These behind-the-meter projects at data centres represent about 30 per cent of the total buildout through 2030.
After two decades of lacklustre demand growth, the US has been struggling to jumpstart the construction of gas generators in an industry that typically moves with years of lead time. These gas generators are coveted because they can be ordered to ramp up, unlike renewables that are beholden to sunshine and wind speeds.
Amid affordability concerns, “federal and state politicians and regulators are requiring more time to review and structure rates, creating a new source of potential delays for new data centre developments”, according to the report led by Wobbrock.
“The pace of data centre development is increasingly exceeding the speed at which the electric grid can add generation, transmission and interconnection capacity,” he said. BLOOMBERG

Hungary moves to amend controversial child protection law after EU court ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:11:11 UTC
22:11:11 KST

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has announced amendments to the country’s child protection law, which the EU’s top court ruled discriminatory in April. The changes could end discrimination against sexual minorities and help unlock further EU funding for Hungary.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has announced amendments to the country’s so-called child protection law, which has faced longstanding criticism from Brussels and LGBTQ+ rights groups over its discriminatory provisions.
The law was initially adopted in 2021 under Viktor Orbán’s government as a measure to protect minors from paedophilia. It was subsequently amended to effectively prohibit the depiction of homosexuality to minors, on the grounds that such content could pose a risk of paedophilia.
The legislation led to books, newspapers and films being pulled from shelves and television schedules. Following protests from international gay rights organisations, the European Commission launched an infringement procedure against Hungary.
In April this year, the European Court of Justice ruled that the law breached EU law, finding that it treated LGBTIQ+ people as a threat to society, violated their human dignity, and risked contributing to their social exclusion.
Speaking to a national radio on Monday morning, Magyar said the amended law would restrict minors' access to violent and sexual content while removing discrimination against sexual minorities.
"There is a good chance that the amendment of the law, in addition to much stronger protection of children, will also allow Hungary to avoid the fine," Magyar said.
In a separate 2024 ruling, the European Court of Justice fined Hungary €1 million a day for systemic breaches of its migration system, which restricted access to asylum. The ruling has so far cost Hungary around €1 billion.
Magyar said that child protection, healthcare and education remained key priorities for his government, which took office in April after bringing 16 years of rule by Orbán’s right-wing, Eurosceptic Fidesz party to an end.
Magyar, who has made restoring relations with the EU and NATO a key priority, struck a deal with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in May to release €16.4 billion in previously frozen EU funds for Hungary. He said the amendments to the child protection law were aimed at unlocking further funding.
"We could unlock half a billion euros for educational support," he said.
In response to a request for comment from Euronews, the European Commission said it was too early to assess the proposed amendments, but confirmed that it remained in close contact with the Hungarian government on the issue. The amendments are expected to be presented to parliament later on Monday.
Over the weekend, Magyar also announced plans to relax restrictions on adoption by same-sex couples, which had been effectively prohibited under Orbán’s government.

UN rights chief calls for action on growing risks from AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:10:18 UTC
22:10:18 KST

Beril Canakci
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
 UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk on Monday called on governments and leading artificial intelligence companies to take urgent action to address the growing risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.
“We are on the cusp of irreversible change, affecting not just us but generations of humanity to come,” Turk said in a letter addressed to governments and AI developers.
He warned that the race to develop increasingly powerful AI is creating “greater existential risks” and said failures involving agentic AI systems — AI systems capable of carrying out tasks with limited human intervention — could bring essential services to a standstill, disrupt communications and critical infrastructure, and threaten democratic institutions.
“Entire populations could be cut off from clean water, heating, and financial services,” Turk said, adding that AI is already accelerating warfare and weakening safeguards against the launch of weapons of mass destruction.
Turk said AI-related harms are already occurring, pointing to the automation of essential services, large-scale data collection and surveillance, and AI-powered disinformation campaigns.
“AI harms are not hypothetical — they are already occurring, front and centre,” he said.
The UN rights chief urged governments and frontier AI companies to establish common safety standards, conduct ongoing human rights assessments, and introduce independent monitoring.
He also called on states hosting leading AI companies to ensure they are held accountable and to require independent technical checks of AI systems capable of acting autonomously.
“No country can govern this technology alone. No company should be able to decide by itself which risks the world must accept. No person should be required to surrender their human rights in exchange for claims of technological progress,” Turk said.
He urged governments and companies to work through multilateral forums to develop rules for advanced AI based on international human rights law.
The statement comes in the wake of recent incidents of AI agents going beyond what many experts thought possible, spurring industry insiders to issue warnings and calls for stricter regulation of the sector.

Russia Disguises Warship as Building in Bid to Evade Ukrainian Drones
A Russian Navy corvette stationed at Kronstadt has been painted to resemble a waterfront building and fitted with protective netting, as Moscow continues adapting its Baltic Fleet vessels against Ukrainian drone attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on September 14, photographs published by military observer Massimo Frantarelli show a Project 1331M corvette, known by NATO as the Parchim II class, with painted outlines resembling windows and doors across its hull. Netting has also been installed above parts of the deck as a physical barrier against incoming drones.
The vessel was photographed at the Leningrad Naval Base in Kronstadt on August 22. Frantarelli said the ship could be either the Zelenodolsk or Kazanets, although its exact identity has not been confirmed. Russia operates roughly six of the East German-built anti-submarine corvettes, each displacing about 800 tons.
The modified vessel is part of a broader effort to alter the appearance of Russian warships based at Kronstadt. Naval analyst H I Sutton has documented several Baltic Fleet ships using black-painted bows and sterns, checkerboard patterns, and other disruptive designs since mid-2026.
Two Project 22800 Karakurt-class missile corvettes, Mytishchi and Burya, were also seen in July with unusual paint schemes and anti-drone netting.
The measures followed successful Ukrainian strikes against Russian naval assets in the Baltic region. On June 3, Ukrainian forces struck the corvette Boikiy while it was undergoing work in dry dock at Kronstadt, causing significant fire damage. Ukrainian officials said the vessel may have been damaged beyond repair.
In March, Ukrainian drones also sank the Russian patrol ship Purga near Vyborg, northwest of St. Petersburg. According to Defence Blog, neither vessel had protective anti-drone netting installed when it was targeted.
Similar techniques have historical precedent. During World War Two, warships were sometimes painted to distort their outline or blend into nearby infrastructure. Germany’s battleship Tirpitz reportedly carried a scheme during fitting-out at Wilhelmshaven that included painted features intended to make the hull resemble buildings along the waterfront.

Ukraine's Economy Ministry expects losses from Russian strikes to reach up to $10 billion this year and plans to submit a three-part business support package to the Cabinet next week, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said on 12 September.
Russia has escalated its drone and missile attacks on Ukraine through 2026, striking first at power plants, substations, and residential blocks, then widening the target list to trains, factories, retailer warehouses, and medicine depots. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky said on 28 August that Russia had destroyed about 90% of retail chains' food logistics, but that supply would shift to direct deliveries, with no shortage of basic foods expected.
Kravchenko said business is an absolutely important source of funding for the defense forces, and that it ensures critical goods are supplied and communities can function.
Three-part package aims to support businesses affected by Russian strikes
- The package has three elements, Kravchenko said. The first would extend the geographic coverage of existing damage compensation programs to include Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, and simplify the application process so affected companies do not wait months for support.
- The second would expand subsidized lending for large businesses, with loans of up to about $22 million (UAH 1 billion) and an interest-rate subsidy of about 5 percentage points. The loans could fund investment projects, including fortification and protection, as well as working capital.
- The third would expand the state's 5-7-9 lending program, which sets the borrower's rate at 5%, 7%, or 9% depending on the purpose of the loan and the size of the business, to suppliers whose large retail clients are losing money to strikes.
He said all three programs had been finalized and hoped businesses would begin receiving substantial support within the coming weeks. The package followed a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and discussions with businesses, he said.
Russian strikes have damaged logistics networks and businesses across Ukraine
An overnight strike on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast on 5 August killed 17 people and destroyed or damaged warehouses and distribution centers belonging to Rozetka, Epicentr, Nova Poshta, Silpo, and other major companies. Co-founder Iryna Chechotkina described Rozetka's warehouse complex in Brovary, valued at $70 million, as beyond repair. The same strike killed six Silpo employees.
Further strikes through early September hit Auchan, Nova Poshta again, Varus, Dnipro-M, and Coca-Cola.

Elon Musk says his AI safety concerns date back more than a decade

Yasin Gungor
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk weighed in on the debate over artificial intelligence Monday, saying his concerns about the technology's potential risks date back more than a decade.
“I was thinking about AI safety long before 2014,” he said on US social media platform X, which is part of his artificial intelligence venture SpaceXAI.
Musk pointed to his involvement with philosopher Nick Bostrom's 2014 book Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies, saying he contributed to the work and was thanked by name in its foreword.
The book examines the potential consequences of AI surpassing human intelligence, warning that humanity's survival could hinge on engineering precise control mechanisms before superintelligent systems emerge.
Musk also pointed to a post from August 2014 in which he recommended the book and warned that advanced AI was “potentially more dangerous than nukes.”
His comments come as senior technology executives call for slowing the development of cutting-edge AI systems over safety concerns.
Over the weekend, Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei proposed giving independent safety evaluators access to AI companies to verify their safety practices, an approach backed by OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman and Musk.
Amodei told CBS Sunday that “there are real dangers," about the development of AI.
"If we build in the right way, I think the probability of something bad happening is very low," he said. “If we build in the wrong way, the probability of something bad happening is very high.”

Ukraine Sees Exponential Growth in Private Security Firms Providing Anti-Drone Protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:06:01 UTC
22:06:01 KST

As Russian long-range drone attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure intensify, Kyiv has explored every avenue available to strengthen its air defense capabilities. In November this led to a plan to add civilian air defense groups to supplement the existing multilayered system of military mobile fire teams armed with machine guns, interceptor drone equipped units, conventional missile and cannon air defense crews and military aviation.
There has been a rapid upsurge in the numbers of private security and defense firms specializing in “Mala PPO” – localized anti-drone protection, as the system is colloquially known.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Rules of engagement
These private teams operate under strict coordination with and under command of the Ukrainian Air Force, which retains the sole authority to approve providers and on target authorization and firing decisions.
As well as protecting their own facilities the capability is viewed as an extension of Ukraine’s existing early-warning network which can identify the direction being taken and by which types of Russian drone – the ability to take shelter from attacks is, in many ways, as vital as having the ability to engage drones.
Between November and the end of March, 24 companies in Kharkiv, Odesa, Kyiv, Poltava, Zakarpattia, and other regions had received authorization to combat drones, which had expanded to 51 by the end of August. Licensed operators include major Ukrainian companies that have trained and equipped their own internal or are engaging private security companies to safeguard critical economic infrastructure.
Ukraine Has Leverage Over Trump Now
For obvious physical and commercial security reasons companies reveal little information on how they plan or and with what systems they implement their air defense – many do not even confirm they take such measures at all for fear that will make them a target. The main exception to this is the larger security providers who advertise their general capability and number of businesses with which they are engaged to drive and expand their own business.
For example, a report in Le Monde at the weekend highlighted the prominent private air defense company Carmine Sky which claims to employ hundreds of personnel and has contracts with around 40 Ukrainian businesses. Carmine Sky says it can offer an arsenal that includes anti-aircraft turrets with remotely operated heavy machine guns, electronic jamming, and interceptor drones managed from secure control rooms.
Addressing the technological challenge
It is not only the numbers of private users of air defense systems that have expanded to face the threat but those who are developing the necessary countermeasures as Russia develops the capability of its attack drones – particularly its Geran and Banderol jet-powered drones.
According to media reports these drones can reach speeds of up to 600 kph (375 mph), with payloads of 90 kilograms (200 pounds) over a range of 800-1,000 kilometers (500-625 miles).
This is forcing a need to rapidly develop faster interceptors capable of engaging incoming drones at longer ranges and higher altitudes with the overarching limitation that the cost of any interceptor must remain (considerably) lower than the incoming target.
Several Ukrainian manufacturers showcased their solutions at this year’s MSPO defense industry show in Kielce, Poland.
Representatives of General Cherry and GrimTech, both current interceptor manufacturers, told Defense News that they were working on a new versions of their interceptors to tackle the jet drone problem.
                                                                                                                                                                         
To do so, they said, would require changes to the existing designs, and the use of materials capable of withstanding higher flight temperatures. They indicated that testing was underway with the goal to have the new weapons enter service before the end of the year.
The private defense companies, both users and manufacturers, have respondeded to those who have criticized the “privatization” of air defense by pointing out much of the funding to develop these countermeasures comes from the income streams their activities generate.

Red Sea blitz: What Houthi gains mean for Yemen and the Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:05:04 UTC
22:05:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Red Sea blitz: What Houthi gains mean for Yemen and the Iran war
In a highly consequential development for Yemen and the region, the Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mocha from the internationally recognised Yemeni government, along with a strategic Red Sea island.
The lightning advance over the past week puts them in a prime position to close the Bab al-Mandab Strait more easily than ever before.
The loss of Mocha on 10 September cuts the government’s direct access to the Red Sea, while the capture of the strategic island of Mayun, also known as Perim, a day later enables them to effectively close the Bab al-Mandab in tandem with Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The offensive, which displaced almost 50,000 people, represents one of the biggest strategic setbacks for the Saudi-backed Yemeni government in several years.
The Houthis captured Yemen’s capital Sanaa and the major port city of Hodeidah in 2014. The Zaydi Shia group fought the government, which relocated to the southern port city of Aden, and its Saudi backers in a devastating war that from 2015 until 2022.
Approximately 150,000 Yemenis have perished, and the country endured a severe humanitarian crisis that pushed it to the brink of famine.
A 2022 Saudi-Houthi ceasefire largely held until July, when fighting resumed after Riyadh attempted to block a direct Mahan Air flight from Tehran to Sanaa, the first since 2015.
The official purpose of that Iranian flight was to pick up and return a Houthi delegation attending the funeral of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Riyadh and the Yemeni government feared an unopposed air bridge would enable Tehran to conveniently fly military equipment directly to its Houthi allies.
The emboldened Houthis have since resumed striking Saudi infrastructure and energy sites with drones and missiles. The kingdom now faces Iran-backed militia attacks from Yemen to its south and Iraq to its north. The latest advance inside Yemen marks the most significant escalation with Aden and its Saudi backer in years.
Serious territorial gains
“The Houthi advance into Mocha is a strong indicator that Iran is seeking to undermine the US-led coalition in its strategic rear, which is the Bab al-Mandab,” Nicholas Heras, Interim Executive Director at the Middle East Policy Council and Senior Director at the New Lines Institute, told The New Arab.
According to reports, Iran told the Houthis to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, promising them more funding and weapons, and Tehran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) paramilitary directly guided the group’s coastal offensive.
“Saudi Arabia is a wavering member of the American coalition against Iran and the resumption of the war in Yemen with rapid Houthi gains is an embarrassing predicament for Saudi Arabia,” Heras said.
Ryan Bohl, a senior Middle East and North Africa analyst at the risk intelligence company RANE, pointed out that Mocha “certainly matters” to the Houthis since it expands the “buffer zone” for Hodeidah.
Additionally, it opens up a route for any subsequent attempts to encircle the southwestern city of Taiz, entrenches their influence over the Red Sea, and provides “new launch positions” for striking shipping passing through that vital but narrow Bab al-Mandab.
“I think the Houthis will continue to advance so long as there is military opportunism,” Bohl told The New Arab. “They can always trade away territory for a final settlement since there is the suggestion that they may only be interested in controlling those Zaydi portions of Yemen,” he noted.
“The most likely block on further advances will be the almost certain furious counterattacks by the IRG (Yemen’s Internationally Recognised Government) and the Saudis who will do whatever they can to prevent the fall of a major city like Marib or Taiz or an advance on Aden,” Bohl added.
More broadly, the RANE analyst noted, these advances certainly help the Houthis with their broader Red Sea strategy and potentially give them additional territory which they can trade for a future settlement with Riyadh and the Yemeni government.
Heras echoed this assessment. “The Houthis understand the limits of their power in Yemen beyond the core areas of Zaydi population concentration and are instead seeking to improve their ability to pressure the Saudis to pressure the Americans to support Iran,” he said.
“This Houthi campaign along Yemen’s coast is a declaration that the Houthis are key actors in global geopolitics who are able to undermine the US geostrategy in the Middle East.”
Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), assesses that these Houthi advances mark the “most serious territorial gain” the group has made in years, putting the entire Hodeidah governorate under its effective control.
“This is a major defeat for the IRG - which just a few days ago was boasting of military advances in the very same governorate - and a sign of the extreme unpredictability of the current escalation," he told The New Arab.
Saudi support
RANE’s Bohl expects Saudi air support will prove critical for blunting any further Houthi advance and supporting IRG counterattacks.
“At the same time, so will unity amongst the IRG's ground forces,” he said. “This latter element is the most critical because without a sense of unity these counteroffensives will be stuck being localised and unable to comprehensively roll the Houthis back.”
According to an Axios report, Saudi Arabia’s powerful Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman twice called US President Donald Trump during the Houthi advance, requesting renewed US strikes against them.
Trump declined. Nevertheless, US military advisors in Saudi Arabia are providing expanded intelligence and targeting support for the kingdom’s operations against the Iran-backed group, according to a CNN report.
Bohl noted that Saudi Arabia is already responding to Houthi attacks and advances and is “likely to be drawn into further involvement” in the civil war raging over its southern border. That further involvement could potentially lead to a deployment of Saudi forces into Yemen alongside “enhanced airstrikes” against the group.
The escalation, and ongoing Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, come a little over a month after the kingdom signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan on 7 August.
Pakistan has already clarified that it hasn’t planned any military response against the Houthis for their attacks.
“There is no such thing under discussion right now … When the time comes (we) will act under the agreement,” Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said on 10 September, the same day Mocha fell.
“As for other members of the Mecca pact, they will remain wary of conducting military operations inside of Yemen given the distant geographies from Turkey and Pakistan, as well as the prospect of trapping their forces in an intractable conflict,” Bohl said.
“But most notably, the change in the Trump administration from the first to the second term may prove to be important.”
He recalled that in its first term at the end of the 2010s, the Trump administration focused on “containment and mitigating the humanitarian impacts” of the Yemen conflict.
Now, in its second term, it perceives Yemen as “part of the struggle” against Iran. Consequently, it may be more likely to support broader Saudi military operations against the Iran-backed group while making “fewer demands” to change tactics that could have a significant humanitarian impact.
Potential scenarios
ACLED’s Yemen analyst Ali sees several potential scenarios for Yemen after these latest Houthi advances.
“The Houthis may press their advantage and launch more attacks to seize the coast of Taiz governorate just south of Hodeideh, bringing the entirety of the Yemeni Red Sea coast under their control,” he said.
“Alternatively, IRG forces may regroup to carry out a counterattack and attempt to reclaim lost territories.”
Both scenarios would mean a “heightened level of violence” and “increased risk for civilians” in Yemen in the coming weeks in addition to “hundreds of military casualties” from “deadlier clashes” along other internal frontlines. Ali anticipates fighting focused in al-Jawf in the east, which borders Saudi Arabia.
Both sides are engaged in heavy clashes there, with strategic sites “changing hands” at a rapid rate.
“Alternatively, the Houthi blitzing may force Saudi Arabia - which is the IRG’s main backer - back to negotiating with the group to avoid further potential losses for their Yemeni allies in the IRG, which could mean an abrupt end to the current round of escalation,” he said.
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan, who writes about Middle East affairs
