European countries are moving toward prison sentences that could be as long as 10 years for individuals and companies involved in trade with Israeli illegal settlements built on occupied Palestinian land, Israeli media reported.
Israel’s Channel 7 said Norway is preparing a legal framework to boycott settlement products, including prison sentences of up to three years for individuals or companies dealing with them.
The channel quoted Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide as saying he expected his country’s parliament to approve the draft law in its current form.
“Yes, I really think so, and the arguments have become stronger as the situation in the West Bank has worsened,” Eide said in response to a question on the issue.
“There are many other countries that will do the same thing that the government has already proposed through this law,” he added.
According to the channel, the Netherlands is also working on a similar law, under which the penalty could be as long as six years in prison.
A Dutch decision banning the import, purchase or sale of goods from illegal settlements is expected to take effect on Sept. 22, it said.
Channel 7 added that in Britain, the penalty for commercial dealings with settlements could reach up to 10 years in prison.
The moves come after 12 Western countries announced on Tuesday their intention to impose restrictions on trade with Israeli settlements.
The countries are France, Britain, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden.
These 12 countries called on Israel to immediately halt settlement expansion and violence by occupiers.
In a joint statement, they said the measures aim to protect the two-state solution, reject the annexation of Palestinian land and forced displacement, and ensure accountability for those responsible for violence.
The announcement followed an Israeli decision to issue tenders for the construction of around 1,200 settlement units in the E1 area.
The decision drew international criticism because of its potential impact on territorial contiguity between parts of the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.
On Wednesday, French Foreign Ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux said in a statement that France supports applying a ban on trade with Israeli illegal settlements in occupied Palestinian territory at the EU level.
Amnesty International said in a statement that the decision by Britain and 11 other countries to ban trade with Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territory was a necessary step, but one that came too late.
 
Palestinian position
Earlier, Fatah Central Committee member Mohammad Shtayyeh told Anadolu that the announcement by the 12 countries of their intention to restrict settlement trade was an “important step.”
Shtayyeh said what is needed is a move from boycotting illegal settlement goods to taking measures against the “settlement project” and the state that sponsors it.
“Israel has become isolated before those who created it, protected it and defend it,” he said.
Israeli media previously reported that some products manufactured in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank were presented as being produced inside Israel’s 1948 borders to bypass similar European bans.
The Israeli daily Yedioth Ahronoth described Wednesday’s announcement by the 12 countries as a “diplomatic setback and a resounding failure” for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government.
Netanyahu’s government boasts that since its formation in late 2022, it has approved the establishment of 104 new illegal settlements and 160 agricultural settlement outposts in the occupied West Bank.
The UN considers the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, occupied Palestinian territory and says Israeli settlements there are illegal under international law.
Palestinians warn that Israel is paving the way for the formal annexation of the West Bank through settlement expansion and attacks by the army and occupiers, thereby undermining the possibility of establishing a Palestinian state.

It will air on NBC and stream live on Peacock in the US, following the Creative Arts Emmys held Sept. 5-6, where awards in technical, guest acting and other categories were handed out.

Rhea Seehorn is also drawing attention for her performance in Pluribus.

Raul Rebane: A field guide to killjoys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:23:00 UTC
21:23:00 KST

Raul Rebane: A field guide to killjoys
In his daily commentary for Vikerraadio, Raul Rebane maps out the different types of killjoys and concludes that making society angrier is not easy work — it requires a great deal of time and energy.
I will try to analyze a very common type of person in society: the killjoy. This has nothing to do with the once-popular TV series ("Tujurikkuja — ed.) of the same name; I simply could not find a better term for someone who believes that people, life, Estonia and the world are irreparably messed up and that this misery must constantly be proclaimed to everyone. President Alar Karis drew attention to a similar phenomenon in his Independence Day speech, introducing the term "opinion bullying" into public discourse.
Who are they?
One of my childhood acquaintances suddenly changed about 10 to 12 years ago. It is no longer possible to have a conversation with him. Everything is terrible, any government is stupid, all politicians are crazy, athletes are weak, singers cannot carry a tune, the first lady's dress is ugly and the roads are full of potholes. He began expressing this indignation on social media and it has only gotten worse over time. His Facebook account now contains many hundreds of angry posts. Judging by what he writes, there is no longer anything good to be found in this country.
Sound familiar?
I do not have a study to back this up, but based on the content, I tried to analyze who the most active complainers are. First of all, they are generally older men; there are significantly fewer women. One thing they have in common is that someone else is always to blame for their problems and those of the country.
First: Those who had it better before, especially during the Soviet era. Perhaps their salary was higher or their status greater, but the new era brought them considerable hardship. Their numbers and activity are declining; this group was very large in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Second: Those whose abilities or talents could not withstand the competition of the new Estonia. They may once have been well-known and accomplished, but encountering a new competitive environment robbed them of their joy. They can be found in every profession, in politics and culture, as well as at ETV and on the radio.
Third: Politicians who are not currently in power. They are extremely angry at everyone and everything until they themselves come to power. Then everything is fine until they are replaced, at which point another cycle of anger begins. The decibel level of outrage rises noticeably before elections. Right now is precisely such a time.
Fourth: Social media influencers and some media personalities who have turned ruining people's mood into their brand. Over time, they enter a so-called spiral of anger in which they must constantly increase the doses of outrage or people will lose interest. This makes them even angrier because what is the point of shouting if no one is listening?
Fifth: The trend of being a killjoy. This is particularly noticeable in the media where outrage is treated almost as a sign of professionalism. If you do not engage in it, you risk being seen as soft. Many have fallen victim to this.
Naturally, this is by no means an exhaustive list. Nor should anyone think this is some kind of national peculiarity. It happens everywhere; the differences stem from history and stages of development. Elsewhere, there are different groups, such as angry consumers or sports fans.
In fact, there are not that many of these serial complainers. I was surprised myself when it emerged that an old acquaintance of mine had written 3,000 angry comments in a short period, believing that using a false name would keep his identity secret. It did not: His style and spelling gave him away. This creates a situation in which a very small segment of the population gains a disproportionately large media presence. Making society angrier is not easy work; it requires a great deal of time and energy.
Thanks to the current fashion for anger, those who think well of Estonia and of our lives here have a problem: They cannot open their mouths without being regarded as blind and stupid.
If someone has chosen being a killjoy as a way of life, facts do not get in their way in the slightest. I conducted an experiment and selected an article that listed all the bad things — tax increases, a stupid government, high prices, Russia's behavior, low pensions and so on — 11 points in all.
I asked people whether they thought it was true. They agreed wholeheartedly: It was all correct. The problem is that the article was published in Eesti Ekspress in September 2008. Whoever was angry then is angry now and will still be angry 10 years from now. It is not about circumstances but about character and the prevailing fashion of the times. Right now, anger is in fashion.
What can be done? The key is actually in our own hands. We simply should not be active consumers of this constant negativity. Let them make noise. Fortunately, most people have already chosen this path: They do not read the comments sections, much less post there themselves. At least that way, they can spare their own nerves.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Gulf states have postponed a critical meeting with Iran on the future of the strait of Hormuz owing to a lack of Arab consensus and growing Saudi Arabian anger with Tehran for helping the Houthis loosen Riyadh’s grip in Yemen.
The stalemate over the vital waterway came as Houthi rebels launched a fresh barrage of missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets. A Houthi military spokesperson claimed its forces had attacked the King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, hitting fighter-jet hangars, radar systems, runways and landing strips, ammunition depots and additional targets.
Last week, Tehran-backed militias in Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to close a critical east-west pipeline that had been acting as a means for Riyadh to export oil after Iran effectively closed the strait of Hormuz.
The closure of the pipeline, the postponement of the Hormuz meeting, and the Houthis’ seizure last week of Yemen’s Red Sea coast – which gave the group control over another vital waterway, the Bab al-Mandab strait – combined to drive up oil prices above $108 a barrel on Monday.
Also on Monday, the Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman, held urgent discussions with the US Central Command chief Adm Brad Cooper in Jeddah to discuss “the latest developments in the region”, according to Saudi media. Sources told US media last week that the Saudi de facto ruler had sought military assistance from Donald Trump to help fight the Houthis. So far the US has provided only logistical and intelligence backing,
The Gulf Cooperation Council-Iran meeting was postponed at the last minute, deferring a proposed agreement on a new temporary route for commercial shipping when the strait of Hormuz is reopened.
In a statement, Oman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, said the meeting had been delayed in the interests of consensus. “We remain committed to fostering dialogue that supports stability and lasting co-operation in our region,” he wrote on X. He gave no further details.
The meeting would not have led to the immediate opening of the strait, since Tehran has set a series of other preconditions: including requiring the US to lift a blockade of Iran’s oil ports, the handing over of many frozen Iranian assets and a ceasefire in Lebanon.
But it would have been the first meeting between Iran and the main GCC member countries for two years. The planned agreement on a temporary route for ships to use would have formalised Iran’s control of the strait, since the entry route would have been entirely in Iranian waters.
Washington has not expressed publicly an opinion over the proposed deal, and some of Trump’s recent social media posts – claiming full US control of the strait – seemed to bear little relationship with what shipping companies have been reporting.
The atmosphere surrounding the meeting, in preparation for weeks, had been rapidly souring because of the advance by the Houthis in Yemen and the drone attack on the Saudi pipeline by an Iran-backed Shia militia in Iraq.
Vantor Technologies released high-resolution satellite images showing the damage to the east-west pipeline pumping station near Al Mesba’ah, Saudi Arabia. The station appears to be almost completely destroyed.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson denied any Iranian involvement in the pipeline attack, or on events in Yemen.
US military bases throughout the Gulf have been attacked by Iran in response to the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia, which backs the UN-recognised Yemeni government based in Aden, is trying to regain the initiative after Houthi forces swept down the west coast of Yemen from the port of Hodeidah last week and seized the Bab al-Mandab strait, a narrow waterway that links the Red Sea with Asia and is viewed as second in strategic importance to the strait of Hormuz.
It was claimed that a Saudi air bombardment was making it difficult for the Houthis to gain full control of the Yemen waterway or the strategic islands in the Red Sea.
The Houthi leadership says is not seeking to block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea but only Saudi-linked ships. It is also offering cut-price fees in the ports it controls on the west coast of Yemen in an effort to lure traffic away from the ports controlled by the Aden-based government in the south.
It is widely accepted that Iran backs the Houthis, but the group also operates independently of Tehran. The rebels ultimate aim is to oust Saudi Arabia from the country, and take full control of the territory.
Saudi Arabia has tried different tactics in handling the Houthis during the decade-long civil war in Yemen, including making concessions in the hope the highly ideological group would reach a power-sharing deal.
The Yemen government said preliminary tolls indicated that 150 civilians had been killed and 200 others injured in the course of the recent Houthi advance. About 85,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN.

People's different heat perception complicating energy poverty calculations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:21:00 UTC
21:21:00 KST

People's different heat perception complicating energy poverty calculations
Although Estonia's energy poverty situation looks relatively good on paper, individual indicators may not provide the full picture, according to a University of Tartu researcher.
Energy poverty generally refers to a situation in which a person is unable to maintain a comfortable temperature in their home. However, energy poverty is not separately defined in Estonian law and comparing countries is also difficult because people's perceptions of what is warm enough vary.
"We don't have a Europe-wide measure that says if it's 21 degrees Celsius in a room in your home, that means it's warm enough. We don't have a single temperature that tells us we're warm," said Hanna Laius, a project manager at the University of Tartu's Johan Skytte Institute of Political Studies. For example, in one country a room temperature of 21 degrees Celsius may be considered perfectly adequate, while in another, 25 degrees may be considered comfortable. People's own assessments therefore also affect how energy poverty appears in statistics.
Laius said that pensioners, single parents and people living in rural areas are among the more vulnerable groups in Estonia. In addition to income, the condition of a person's home is also very important. Many buildings constructed during the Soviet era are poorly insulated and require more energy to heat.
"If, so to speak, the wind is blowing in through the gaps around your windows, you can turn the heat up as much as it will go, but you simply won't be able to get your home warm enough if it doesn't retain heat at all," Laius added.
The University of Tartu's Energy Poverty Nexus project is now working to establish an energy poverty observatory in Estonia. In addition to government agencies, the plan is to involve universities, energy companies and the Estonian Union of Co-operative Housing Associations in its work.
One of the observatory's key tasks would be to monitor energy poverty indicators and statistics and make them more comparable with those of other European countries. "Monitoring is very good in some countries, while in others it is still, so to speak, in its infancy. [Work needs to be done] to ensure that the indicators are also comparable across Europe," Laius said.
The observatory should help assess which subsidies and other measures actually reduce energy poverty. According to Laius, improving the energy efficiency of homes would provide a more lasting solution than temporarily compensating people for their energy bills. In other words, the less heat a home loses, the less fluctuations in energy prices affect a household's ability to make ends meet.
--
Editor: Andres Reimann, Marcus Turovski

A calculated escalation by Putin to sow fear in Europe — Pistorius on the attack on a train near the Polish border
Kyiv • UNN
Germany’s defense minister called the Russian drone strike on a train near the Polish border an attempt to sow fear in Europe. He called for not giving in to provocations.
The drone strike on a train near the Ukrainian-Polish border is a calculated step toward escalation by Russian dictator Vladimir Putin, aimed at sowing fear in Europe. Germany’s Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said this on Monday, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
"That makes it all the more important to remain measured and not give in to provocations, while at the same time making it absolutely clear: we are capable of defending ourselves and will not back down if the situation escalates," Pistorius told reporters in the city of Wolgast in northeastern Germany.

Let us recall

Kejriwal-Sardesai Goa gambit: Attack defections, welcome rivals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:18:15 UTC
21:18:15 KST

The alliance has presented itself as a "non-BJP, non-Congress alternative".
The Aam Aadmi Party and Goa Forward Party on Sunday announced a new political beginning for the state. They announced a pre-poll alliance for the upcoming 2027 assembly election named 'Goa First' and promised voters something the state has struggled to get: a mandate that actually stays intact.There was plenty of familiar political rhetoric at the launch in Panaji on Sunday. AAP national convenor Arvind Kejriwal claimed that BJP would not win a majority. "The people of Goa want a change. Goa First will form the government. We will win on our own," Kejriwal claimed.Both parties presented the alliance as a credible, "non-BJP, non-Congress alternative".In the press conference, the newly-formed alliance tried to build its political identity around a simple charge: defection.GFP chief Vijai Sardesai attacked the ruling establishment as a government of defectors. He said the BJP had not received a complete mandate in the previous elections and that even the Congress leadership could not deny the possibility of another round of defections.Kejriwal also opened up about the recent Rajya Sabha defection led by former blue-eyed boy Raghav Chadha. "It is a matter of great regret that our Rajya Sabha MPs left the party.
They betrayed the party. The party sent them to the Rajya Sabha; the people did not send them," the AAP chief said.He said the AAP had never betrayed the people through its elected representatives."We believe that this is a lesson for us because such a thing has never happened in the Aam Aadmi Party before. From now onwards, before sending anyone to the Rajya Sabha, we will scrutinise the person thoroughly and ensure that he is the right person," Kejriwal said.However, after the story of 'Goa First' gets interesting, at its hard-launch itself.GFP chief Sardesai declared: "This alliance has not closed the door; it is open to the like-minded political forces. Many people have approached us, including leaders from both parties who are tired of their politics.
Memory of 2017 and 2022
The anti-defection pitch is not difficult to sell in Goa because voters have seen the numbers change dramatically after elections.In the 2017 assembly election, Congress emerged as the single-largest party with 17 of the 40 seats, while the BJP won 13. Yet Congress did not form the government. The BJP stitched together a coalition with regional parties and independents, with GFP chief Vijai Sardesai becoming deputy chief minister.Two years later, the picture changed again.In July 2019, 10 Congress MLAs joined BJP, taking the saffron party's strength to 27 and giving it a clear majority. The Congress, which had started the assembly term with 17 MLAs, was left with five.Then came the 2022 election.This time, BJP turned out to be the single largest party with 20 seats in the hung assembly. Congress won 11 and AAP two, while GFP won one. BJP formed the government with support from 2 independents and Maharashtrawadi Gomantak Party (MGP).Six months later, however, again eight of Congress's 11 MLAs joined BJP.Among them were former chief minister Digambar Kamat and then leader of opposition Michael Lobo. Congress was reduced to just three MLAs, while BJP's strength rose to 28.Defection runs so deep in Goa politics that, just eight months before the 2022 exodus, some Congress MLAs had gone to extraordinary lengths to prove they would stay put. They visited a temple, chapel and mosque, and signed affidavits promising not to defect. In September 2022, eight of the 11 Congress MLAs joined the BJP anyway.After years of battle in the assembly and courts, the Supreme Court in July had agreed to hear a plea challenging a decision of the Goa assembly speaker rejecting a petition by the Congress for disqualification of the eight MLAs.For Goa First, this history of defections may prove to be strong campaign material.
The 'open door' politics
Sardesai himself made clear that 'Goa First' is not going to be a closed club.The alliance, he said, was open to "like-minded political forces". He claimed that leaders from both major parties had already approached them because they were tired of their respective politics.Strategically, that makes perfect sense.AAP and GFP together currently have only three assembly seats. If the alliance wants to become a serious statewide force, it needs some established names and local networks. Goa's politics is intensely constituency-driven and established local faces can matter enormously.Turning away a strong BJP or Congress leader simply because that leader once belonged to the other camp could leave 'Goa First' with an admirable principle and a thin candidate list.But by welcoming such politicians, the alliance risks playing the very same game it accuses BJP of playing.However, if the leader joins before the elections, the alliance could defend it easily.
The GFP complication
There is another reason Sardesai's role makes this debate particularly interesting.GFP itself has travelled through Goa's shifting alliance landscape.In 2017, it was part of the BJP-led coalition that formed the government after Congress emerged as the largest party. By 2019, the relationship had broken down, and Sardesai became a bitter opponent of the BJP government. GFP subsequently allied with Congress for the 2022 election.
It is now joining hands with AAP and positioning itself against both BJP and Congress for the 2027 elections. Thus, the positioning of the party has remained fluid.That, though, is not necessarily a contradiction, as we have seen several regional parties routinely negotiate their political space by switching alliances.The 'Goa First' alliance has now officially entered the 2027 Goa contest with defection as one of its central political themes. Yet, with its doors open to leaders from the BJP and Congress, the alliance's own composition could become part of the election narrative. The first real test of that balancing act will come with its candidate selection.

Nepal: Thousands still missing as flood recovery begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:18:00 UTC
21:18:00 KST

Nepal: thousands still missing as flood recovery begins
September 14, 2026
Nearly three weeks after deadly flash floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river corridor near the Chinese border, the Himalayan nation is shifting from search-and-rescue operations to relief and reconstruction efforts.
Authorities in Nepal say at least 1,386 bodies have been recovered across five affected districts, while more than 5,130 people are still missing. The latter figure includes 587 foreign nationals and around 900 workers employed in hydropower tunnels and other energy facilities.
The deluge, which authorities say was triggered by a glacier collapse, devastated communities and swept away more than a dozen hydropower facilities. As search operations continue in submerged tunnels and along muddy riverbanks, families are growing increasingly desperate for news of missing loved ones.
Villages wiped out in minutes
The scale of human loss is particularly stark in the upper river basins, where entire settlements vanished within minutes. In many places, destroyed roads and bridges have cut off access, forcing rescue and relief teams to rely on helicopters to deliver essential supplies.
Niranjan Paudyal, a resident of Sole village in Nepal's Nuwakot District who lost his parents, uncle, aunt and sister in the flash floods, said the flood took away even the chance of burying his family members.
"We spent days searching through debris, hoping for signs of my missing parents and family," he told DW. "Sadly, the disaster left us with no choice but to perform their final rites without their bodies."
Public land in Uttargaya Rural Municipality in Rasuwa District has either been washed away or rendered unsafe.
"There is not even land left after the flood to perform the final rites of those who lost their lives," Chameli Gurung, the municipality's deputy chair, told DW. "Relatives have to travel to Kathmandu's Pashupati Aryaghat to perform the final rites."
In Uttargaya alone, at least 618 houses were swept away or buried and 877 people remain missing. Only 12 bodies have been recovered. Gurung said local authorities are exploring the possibility of leasing private land to accommodate displaced families before winter.
Nepal's communication minister, Bikram Timilsina, told DW that affected people are being resettled close to their original homes by securing nearby public or private land and providing financial assistance based on household size until they can become self-reliant.
Nepal faced with a colossal recovery bill
As emergency relief efforts begin to stabilize, Nepal faces a massive financial burden. A preliminary rapid damage and needs assessment (RDNA) puts the total reconstruction requirement at about 723.3 billion Nepalese rupees ($4.78 billion, €4.1 billion), according to local media reports.
The RDNA estimates that nearly two thirds of the funds will go into restoring energy and transport networks and academic facilities.
Hydropower, which supplies almost all of Nepal's electricity, had become a fast-growing source of the country's export revenue. The flood damage has deepened concerns about how Nepal will finance its recovery.
On Monday, neighboring India approved the export of power to Nepal for 18 hours a day until at least December 31, Reuters news agency reported.
"We will try to utilize all of our domestic resources and seek international support to manage the funding gaps," Timilsina, the communication minister, told DW.
Nepal wants to grow resilient
Nepal has formally approached the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)-backed Loss and Damage Fund for assistance. However, the fund, established to help countries deal with the impacts of climate change, has yet to begin distributing its limited resources.
Nepal is seeking to turn reconstruction into part of a broader economic recovery strategy, with an emphasis on climate-resilient infrastructure rather than simply replacing what was destroyed.
"Given our previous experience with post-disaster management, what matters most is how effectively we can use the funds to restore lives and livelihoods and build disaster-resilient infrastructure," Roshee Lamichhane, an associate professor at Kathmandu University, told DW.
Demand for climate justice
Beyond recovery finance, Nepal is making a broader climate justice argument on the international stage.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah is scheduled to address the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 24, where he is expected to call for global responsibility for mitigating climate impacts.
Despite contributing less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, Nepal remains highly vulnerable to climate-induced hazards.
"Reconstruction would be used as an opportunity to build climate-resilient infrastructure," Maheshwar Dhakal, who leads the Climate Change Management Division at Nepal's Ministry of Forests and Environment, told DW. "We will develop a guideline with the motto of 'tomorrow for a better future.'"
Climate scientists caution against attributing any single extreme event solely to global warming without detailed studies, but they agree that rising temperatures are accelerating glacial melt across the Himalayas.
Manjeet Dhakal, director of Climate Analytics South Asia, says the scale of the disaster highlights the growing consequences of rising global temperatures and gives Nepal an opportunity to advocate for cuts in global carbon emissions on the international stage.
"How many more disasters should we wait for before there is a global response to address the impacts of climate change?" he asked, adding that developed and advanced countries, alongside other nations, should take greater responsibility.
Edited by: Keith Walker

Economic, social support for women-headed families to be strengthened
TEHRAN – There are currently around 26 million households in the country, more than 20 million of them in urban areas and approximately six million in rural areas. According to the latest statistics, women head more than 12 percent of these households. Plans are underway to boost support for women-headed households.

The statistics cover women whose husbands have died or become disabled and who have legally assumed responsibility for their families, according to Parvin Dad-Andish, the head of the Ministry of Interior’s department for women and family.
"The growing number of women-headed households highlights the need for greater attention to these families and stronger economic and social support for them. In these households, women shoulder not only family responsibilities but also the burden of providing for their families and managing their daily affairs,” she added.
A program implemented in 16 provinces identified nearly 10,000 women-headed households that had not previously received support from welfare organizations. Under the initiative, the women's skills and capabilities were assessed and categorized, leading to the development of a two-year program to provide training and self-employment assistance. The program has produced tangible results, including the provision of work equipment and the establishment of home-based businesses.
“We have begun cooperation with the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology to provide information technology training for girls from women-headed households. Our goal is to help the children of these families achieve independence as well,” the official said.
Women in management
More than 2,700 female managers have been appointed in the country as deputy ministers, director generals, deputy director generals, governors, district governors, and heads of research institutes since the current administration took office last year, Zahra Behrouz-Azar, the Vice-President for Women and Family Affairs, has said.
"President Masoud Pezeshkian’s administration has always highlighted the importance of national unity and empowering women. As a result, for the first time, we have Sunni female governors in the country," IRNA quoted Behrouz-Azar as saying.

“I believe that women’s involvement in top management and decision-making positions is their right and a key to the development of the country.
My goal is to increase the share of women in managerial positions in the country based on meritocracy and justice.

Women’s economic, social empowerment
Addressing the Asia-Pacific Ministerial Conference, held in Bangkok in 2024, Behrouz-Azar stated that the current administration focuses on empowering women in social and economic areas, as well as improving their access to social services and facilities through implementing certain national programs.
“Iran has always focused on programs that empower women, particularly those who are heads of household, economically and socially. Actions taken by the country have always aimed to promote women’s status by observing the principles of the constitution and Islamic teachings,” Mehr news agency quoted Behrouz-Azar as saying.
Referring to Iran’s remarkable achievements in education, health, science, technology, and entrepreneurship, she underscored the prominent role of Iranian women in these fields.
The official further said the seventh National Development Plan has stressed the need to overcome barriers to women’s professional development. Accordingly, the current administration has put supporting women’s entrepreneurship and home business growth on the agenda despite unfair sanctions.
Addressing a roundtable focusing on ‘Advancing women’s economic empowerment through employment, decent work, social protection, and entrepreneurship’, Fakhr al-Sadat Fatemi, an advisor to the deputy vice president for women and family affairs, for her part proposed three ways to advance women’s empowerment in different fields, these ways include training, empowering, acquiring skills, and developing opportunities for women’s participation, as well as providing legal and executive support, Mehr news agency reported.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

- The case sparked social media attention and public debate about food safety, with many Najaf residents feeling deceived after buying the pork mistakenly.
AI generated
NAJAF – An Iraqi court on Sept 14 sentenced a butcher to 10 years in prison for selling pork that he claimed was beef in the holy Muslim city of Najaf.
Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council said the man was caught with 75kg of pork that he was selling as beef in Najaf, home to one of the world’s most revered Shi’ite Muslim shrines.
“Najaf Criminal Court has sentenced a convicted person to 10 years in prison for selling meat not suitable for human consumption,” it said.
Although Islam forbids pork as it is believed to be impure, Iraqi law does not explicitly ban its sale in the Muslim-majority country, which has a Christian minority.
The court based its ruling on a 1998 law that criminalises the sale of “dog or donkey or other meat... that is unfit for human consumption”.
Millions of pilgrims from around the world flock to Najaf every year to visit the mausoleum of Imam Ali – the Prophet Muhammad’s son-in-law, the fourth Islamic caliph and the first Shi’ite Imam.
The butcher, who was arrested earlier in September, attracted widespread attention on social media, with some Iraqis calling for better food safety and others sharing funny videos of pigs captioned “here is Najaf”.
Najaf resident Ahmad al-Mansouri said jokingly: “I think I have eaten more pork than beef or lamb over the past years.”
He was among many residents who were deceived. After buying a kilogram of ground meat and finding it was of “excellent quality” and cheaper than the market rate, he started visiting the butcher more often.
“We were surprised when he was arrested on charges of selling pork,” Mansouri said. AFP

Iran censures US deliberate destruction of development at Human Rights Council
TEHRAN –The Secretary-General of Iran’s National Commission for UNESCO has elaborated on the deliberate destruction of development by the US through adopting coercive sanctions and launching military aggressions against the country.
“Forty years after the adoption of the Declaration on the Right to Development, its promise remains unfulfilled for millions. The question is no longer whether development is a human right, but why some states are still allowed to systematically deprive other people of that right,” IRNA quoted Hassan Fartousi as saying while addressing the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council, being held from September 7 to October 7.
Recognizing the right to development becomes meaningful only when the international community can offer effective and actionable solutions to the obstacles that practically prevent nations from accessing the resources, opportunities, and infrastructure necessary for development, the official added.
“For decades, the United States has subjected the Iranian people to extensive unilateral coercive measures, obstructing access to financial resources, technology, medicine, and essential goods, and deliberately constraining our development. Today, the same United States has added military aggression to the economic coercion.
The impact of these illegal measures is not limited to economic indicators; it also affects health, education, infrastructure, and human capital, he added.
“When hospitals are attacked, when schools are destroyed, when children are killed in their classrooms, we are not merely witnessing casualties of war. We are witnessing the deliberate destruction of development itself. A school destroyed in seconds represents years of trauma for the students and challenges in education. A hospital struck means not only a damaged building, but the destruction of health, human capital, and future generations,” Fartousi further noted.
The official went on to say that “Forty years after the declaration, commemoration is not enough. Those who destroy development through unlawful coercion and military aggression must be held accountable. Hereby, as the Secretary General of the Iranian National Commission for UNESCO in Iran, the right to development must be a right for all people, especially the people who are living in the developing countries.”
The 63rd session of the Human Rights Council biennial panel discussion on the right to development was held under the theme ‘Commemoration of the fortieth anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development’.
The panel aimed to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the adoption of the United Nations Declaration on the Right to Development (DRTD), and to reaffirm the commitment of the international community to the effective realization of the right to development as an inalienable human right for all; take stock of the achievements, obstacles and challenges encountered over the past four decades in the implementation of the Declaration on the Right to Development at the national, regional and international levels, including lessons learned; and identify elements towards a road map for the concrete operationalization of the right to development including through adoption of the draft International Covenant on the Right to Development.
It also aimed to explore the contribution of the right to development framework to the implementation of the 2030 agenda for sustainable development and beyond, including by proposing principles, policy recommendations and institutional pathways; and to catalyse a forward-looking dialogue on the future of the right to development as it enters its fifth decade.

The senior Spanish naval officer was dating Janina White, a UK-Polish dual national who was born in the Soviet Union, when she was accused of being a Kremlin agent, The Telegraph reported.
Before he was removed from the base and returned to Spain in 2025, the Spanish officer was based at Allied Maritime Command (Marcom), at Northwood headquarters in Hertfordshire, which monitors Russian submarines and warships prowling UK waters, and tracks sanctioned oil tankers from Russia's "shadow fleet."
The base staff later revoked the NATO officer's access pass, and the base commander banned him from entering the premises while intelligence personnel investigated.
White, 49, who lives in Romford, east London, has denied the spying allegations and insisted she was an unfair victim of discrimination because of her Russian heritage, saying she is no longer in a relationship with the Spanish naval commander.
"I definitely know I am not a Russian spy. The last time I checked, I wasn't," she told the British daily.
White said: "I knew he was dealing with the Russian shadow fleet and submarines. But it was a total prohibition of discussing any details at home about this."
Her relationship with the Spanish officer began in October 2024 through the dating app Tinder, shortly after she split up with her ex-husband, a prominent council leader who has visited No 10 Downing Street, according to the report.
According to court documents seen by The Telegraph, he invited her to the social event at Northwood's Warrant Officers' and Senior Rates' mess on Dec. 12, 2024, obtaining a one-day escorted visitor pass to the military base.
"A NATO security investigation was commenced; so, too, was a Spanish security investigation. The UK was not involved in these processes, which resulted in a Spanish decision to suspend [the officer's] national security clearance," a court document said.

EU leaders urge unity after Russian strike on train

EU leaders urge unity after Russian strike on train
September 14, 2026
Several top EU politicians have called a Russian drone strike on a passenger train on Ukraine's border with Poland a bid by Moscow to intimidate Kyiv's allies that should be met with even more resolution.
In the incident, a drone hit the train's locomotive at a railway station in the Volyn region, some 2 kilometers (1.24 miles) from the border, shortly after a diplomatic train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European diplomats had been at the station.
What did EU leaders say about the train attack?
"It [the attack] is clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine, from going to Ukraine to show support," the EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said.
"I think we should act the opposite. We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared," she told reporters in Finland, where she attended a summit on Arctic strategy.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, who was also at the meeting, said the attack demonstrated Russia's growing aggression and called both for more support for Kyiv and for harsher penalties on Moscow.
"For me, it means that we have to [...] do even more to help Ukraine, to support Ukraine. And we need more measures against Russia, more political measures, more sanctions, and make it clear that this is strong strategy," he said.
"We are united here in Europe," he added.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said the attack showed that Russia was "challenging all of us."
"We should not talk about concrete geographic regions, because Russia's goal is much more ambitious: to test the rule of law, to test our style of life, to test democracy. And I think they will put additional efforts to do it," he said.
French Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attack had a "very clear goal, which is to intimidate Europeans, discourage them and, above all, drive a wedge between them."
Barrot said Russian President Vladimir Putin had constantly stepped up pressure on the EU and NATO over the past five years.
"Why? Because he knows that our strength lies in our unity, and that as long as we stand together, nothing can intimidate us," he said.
Germany warns against escalation with Russia
German Foreign Minister Boris Pistorius, for his part, called for caution.
"I take the drones that were approaching trains near the (Ukrainian-Polish) border very seriously, but we must not be forced into an escalation," he said.
The Kremlin has commented on the attack only by saying that the Russian army operated across all Ukrainian territory and would continue to do so.
Speaking about the incident on Sunday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga has said Putin considered Russia to be "de facto" at war with Europe.
"Putin's terror is literally knocking at the door of the European Union and NATO," Sybiga said.

Ukraine’s prosecutor general accuses anti-corruption chief of falsifying documents and stealing case files. ‘He’s lost his mind,’ sources in Zelensky’s circle say.

Ukraine’s prosecutor general accuses anti-corruption chief of falsifying documents and stealing case files. ‘He’s lost his mind,’ sources in Zelensky’s circle say.
Ruslan Kravchenko, Ukraine’s prosecutor general, who resigned last week, has issued a notice of suspicion to National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) Director Semen Kryvonos and called on him to step down.
In a video address, Kravchenko said NABU and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) employees illegally seized case materials during searches conducted as part of the “Carthage” operation: materials from criminal cases against staff members of those same agencies that the Prosecutor General’s Office of Ukraine is handling.
“The so-called ‘Carthage’ operation wasn’t aimed only at me. Its true goal was to gain access to case materials in criminal proceedings against NABU and SAPO leaders and staff, and then to remove the prosecutor general and suspend procedural decisions on those cases,” the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda quoted Kravchenko as saying.
In early September, NABU and SAPO announced they were conducting a “special operation to expose a criminal organization led by an official from the Prosecutor General’s Office.”
The anti-corruption agencies said the case involved “providing protection for a network of fraudulent call centers and legalizing assets,” and searched the Prosecutor General’s Office as part of the operation.
Kravchenko denied the accusations and resigned.
Kravchenko said the Prosecutor General’s Office is providing procedural oversight in dozens of serious and especially serious criminal cases against NABU and SAPO leaders and employees, and that some case materials were illegally copied or stolen during the searches.
Kravchenko said NABU’s director himself is suspected of “forging official documents to obtain an unlawful benefit on a large scale,” as well as “the sham adoption of a child in order to create grounds for evading liability in court.”
Kravchenko also said he had issued a notice of suspicion to a person close to SAPO Head Oleksandr Klymenko, whom he did not name. The case involves influencing judges of the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC), offering them unlawful benefits, and helping the person evade mobilization, the Ukrainian news outlet RBC Ukraine reported. Kravchenko said the criminal case against that person was the real reason behind the search of the Prosecutor General’s Office.
Kravchenko, who resigned September 8, reiterated that the decision was “a deliberate political decision that is not an admission of any guilt, the result of any agreement, or a rejection of his continued fight for his reputation and integrity.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, responding to Kravchenko’s video address, wrote on the morning of September 14: “This prosecutor general has only one path: dismissal from office. That’s exactly what I told him. Ukraine has seen all the reasons. If he considers this political pressure, let him call it that.” Zelensky called on the Verkhovna Rada to accept Kravchenko’s resignation as soon as possible.
Sources close to Zelensky told RBC Ukraine that Kravchenko acted without coordinating with the Ukrainian president’s office. “He’s lost his mind. Maybe he got scared,” one source told the outlet.
Kravchenko is currently outside Ukraine. A source told Ukrainska Pravda that the prosecutor general left the country by car overnight on September 14. Kravchenko insists he is “on an official trip abroad.” During the trip, he said, he plans to “inform international partners about the real state of affairs in the anti-corruption system, the signs that these agencies are concentrating uncontrolled influence, and the risks these practices pose to state sovereignty, the rule of law, and Ukraine’s democratic institutions.”
In a joint statement, NABU and SAPO said that they did not seize any criminal case materials during the search of the Ukrainian Prosecutor General’s Office. “This attack did not begin today. Its active phase began last summer, and one of its main goals was an attempt to subordinate NABU and SAPO to the Prosecutor General’s Office,” the statement said.
NABU and SAPO added that, as of the morning of September 14, Semen Kryvonos had not been formally named as a suspect.
Davyd Arakhamia, head of the parliamentary faction of President Volodymyr Zelensky’s Servant of the People party, said the Verkhovna Rada would vote on September 15 on Kravchenko’s dismissal as prosecutor general.

Lockheed Martin expands secretive Vectis drone program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:11:22 UTC
21:11:22 KST

- Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works is building four additional Vectis combat drones, bringing the program's total to five aircraft.
- The tailless, stealth-focused drone is designed to fly alongside crewed fighters like the F-35, with a first flight targeted by the end of 2027.
Lockheed Martin is building four more of its newest combat drones, the company announced September 14, doubling down on a program that’s still more than a year away from ever leaving the ground.
The news came from the company’s secretive Skunk Works division, following a major Air Force conference near Washington, D.C., where Skunk Works also unveiled a full-scale model of the aircraft, called Vectis, for the first time.
If you haven’t heard of Vectis yet, here’s the short version: it’s a drone designed to fly into combat alongside piloted fighter jets like the F-35, acting as a kind of robotic wingman. The Air Force calls this category of aircraft a “Collaborative Combat Aircraft,” or CCA, and the idea is straightforward even if the acronym isn’t. Building more fighter jets with pilots inside them is expensive and slow. Building smart, semi-autonomous drones that can fly in formation with those jets, carry weapons or sensors, and take on some of the riskier parts of a mission is, at least in theory, cheaper and faster to scale up.
Lockheed first showed off Vectis a year ago, in September 2025, but the design has changed since then. The version unveiled this week has no tail and a deeply recessed air intake built into the top of the fuselage, both features meant to make the aircraft harder to spot on radar. Ron Fehlen, the vice president and general manager of Skunk Works, told reporters the team is eager to see the pieces coming together.
“The team is extremely excited as these parts start to come together, to actually get the wheels off the ramp by the end of 2027,” Fehlen said.
That end-of-2027 target is when Lockheed expects the first Vectis prototype to actually fly. In the meantime, the company is now building four additional aircraft, bringing the total to five once the original prototype is included. Lockheed hasn’t said publicly what those extra four aircraft will be used for, whether that’s more flight testing, demonstrations for potential buyers, or something else.
For scale, Vectis is about 34 feet long with a 38-foot wingspan, which puts it roughly in the same size class as the Air Force’s MQ-9 Reaper drone in length, with wings about as wide as an F-35’s. It falls into a weight and altitude category the Air Force calls Group 5, meaning it weighs more than 1,320 pounds and is built to fly above 18,000 feet, the same bracket as the two CCA drones already chosen for the Air Force’s first round of the program. Lockheed hasn’t said what weapons Vectis might carry, what kind of engine powers it, or how much each aircraft is expected to cost.
That first round of the CCA program didn’t go to Lockheed. The Air Force picked General Atomics and Anduril Industries instead, and their aircraft, known as the YFQ-42A and YFQ-44A, are being built mainly for air-to-air combat missions. The Air Force has said it eventually wants at least 1,000 of these drones total, built out over several future rounds, and it’s aiming to keep the cost of each aircraft around $20 million, not counting the sensors and other equipment that would go inside. Fehlen said Vectis isn’t necessarily being built for one specific future round of the competition, but that Lockheed sees potential customers well beyond the Air Force, including the Navy and militaries overseas.
One thing Lockheed has been eager to talk about is how quickly the Vectis team has been moving. According to the company, engineers went from an initial sketch to testing a model in a wind tunnel in under two months. The first complete digital design of the aircraft came together in six months, and the team had manufactured its first physical part within eight months of starting the program. Lockheed says that speed comes from manufacturing and design tools built up over years of other Skunk Works projects, not from cutting corners on this one specifically.
Whether Vectis ends up winning a future Air Force contract, getting picked up by the Navy, or drawing interest from an allied country overseas is still an open question. For now, what’s confirmed is that Lockheed is putting real money and staff behind five aircraft instead of one, with a flight test still more than a year away.

“Fairly disciplined workers”: Russia’s prison service is replacing penal colonies with forced labor centers — and making money from it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:11:20 UTC
21:11:20 KST

As the military recruitment of prisoners reduces the population of penal colonies across Russia, the country’s Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) is expanding another branch of its system: correctional centers for convicts sentenced to forced labor. By the end of 2025, Russia had created 400 of these centers, with space for up to 50,000 people. This past June, FSIN even unveiled a “quickly deployable” center that can be installed directly at businesses nationwide. The new system is more profitable than traditional penal colonies, providing FSIN with fresh revenue streams and companies with access to a workforce almost entirely devoid of rights.
You’re not prisoners, but you can’t leave
Russian law does not classify forced labor as imprisonment, but a person sentenced to forced labor is nevertheless obligated to live in a closed FSIN facility. They must work wherever the administration sends them and cannot freely leave the correctional center.
“You can sit there and not go anywhere for a year,” Olga [name changed], a former convict who spent time in correctional centers from Perm to Volgograd, told The Insider. After a penal colony, Olga said, a correctional center can genuinely feel “almost like home.” People there can wear their own clothes, use a phone, read the news online, and communicate with relatives every day through messaging apps. But the relative improvement in quality of life that Olga experienced only applies to those who have previously spent time in a penal colony, where prisoners must wear standardized uniforms, communication with relatives usually happens by letter, and phones are banned.
For someone sent to a correctional center directly from life outside prison, the experience looks different: living by a schedule set by the FSIN, leaving the center only with permission, working forced overtime, and being subject to the administration’s will.
“People who were sent to a correctional center straight from home were somewhat shocked,” Olga recalled.
“A model correctional center with a sports ground and park”
According to Olga, life becomes especially hard when a correctional center is set up directly at a production site — with a dormitory next to the workshop and the employer working together with the administration to reduce inmates’ lives to moving between bed and the workplace. That is exactly the model FSIN now wants to replicate: fast-deployable correctional centers that can be built next to enterprises.
“At the St. Petersburg International Legal Forum, FSIN presented a model correctional center with a sports ground and a park. The project was sent to the regions as a recommendation,” TASS wrote in late June. In FSIN photographs, the model does not look like a prison but like a tidy workers’ dormitory: a long two-story modular building, lawns, bushes, streetlights, a separate sports ground, and a walking area with benches.
The TASS report also listed other elements of the project: a parking lot, a diesel power station, a transformer substation, and a separate yard where those who have violated prison rules can still get a chance to walk. But the presentation itself showed that the most attractive parts of the image — the park and sports ground — aren’t mandatory. A FSIN representative clarified that they are only “optional facilities.”
In other words, what was sent to the regions was not a plan for a center with a park but an easily replicable solution for quickly housing people sentenced to forced labor. The FSIN website describes it even more directly: the facilities can be built quickly “at any enterprise,” and the project can be used by representatives of large and medium-sized businesses interested in creating dormitories for convicts at their facilities.
That detail is crucial, Olga explained. She served her sentence both in a correctional center where she had to walk down the street to get to work and in a center where the dormitory was effectively on the production site.
“If it’s a closed-system correctional center, then the employer works in very close coordination with FSIN. No one’s getting away from them. FSIN plays the way the employer needs it to,” Olga said.
Employers work in very close coordination with FSIN in closed-system correctional centers
In that model, a person does not simply live near work — work becomes an extension of the prison regime.
“The conditions were always more lenient where the employer wasn’t in the same building as the dormitory. But where you live right in the workshop, right at the production site, that was where things were the hardest,” Olga recalled.
At one correctional center in the Moscow region, Olga said, the living quarters resembled a hangar or garage, with a workshop on the floor below. The facility had poor ventilation and was plagued by dirt, rats and cockroaches.
“It's legalized slavery,” she said. “They force people to work and use every tool of pressure and punishment available to make sure they keep working and don’t complain.”
30,000 workers with no rights
Forced labor as a new type of criminal punishment began to be used on Jan. 1, 2017, when FSIN opened its first four correctional centers and seven sections attached to its penal colonies, with a total capacity of fewer than 900 people. The first convicts arrived in March of that year. Now, a small network of facilities that was previously being tested as an alternative to colonies has turned into a separate and growing branch of the penal system.
By the end of 2025, according to FSIN Director Arkady Gostev, Russia had created 400 correctional centers and sections operating as correctional centers, with capacity for 50,000 people — and more than 30,000 convicts were actually being held there.
Given the overall decline in Russia’s prison population, those figures are especially notable. In May 2026, Gostev said that since the end of 2021 the number of people in places of detention had fallen from 465,000 to 282,000. About 85,000 of them were held in pretrial detention centers (SIZO) and PFRSI, a Russian abbreviation for facilities operating as pretrial detention centers, leaving about 197,000 in penal colonies and prisons.
The rise of correctional centers, whose inhabitants are not counted among the country’s prison statistics, do not explain that decline. Instead, the main reason for the drop in the population of penal colonies was the recruitment of prisoners for the war in Ukraine — first by the Wagner private military company, then by the Defense Ministry. In May, FSIN itself acknowledged for the first time that “efforts to recruit contract soldiers” for the armed forces was affecting the number of prisoners.
But at the same time, the agency is expanding the part of the system that is formally not considered imprisonment — exploiting the labor of convicts rather than simply isolating them away from society. The more than 30,000 people actually held in correctional centers already amount to about 15% of the current number of people under FSIN’s jurisdiction. The centers’ total capacity — 50,000 places — is comparable to about a quarter of that population.
The agency is expanding the part of the system focused not on isolation, but on exploiting convicts’ labor
At the same time, legal changes are making it easier to fill correctional centers. Since 2026, forced labor can be imposed as a standalone punishment, without a prior sentence involving imprisonment. The penalties under dozens of articles of the Criminal Code have also been expanded to include forced labor.
A “dormitory” behind a fence: What life is like in a correctional center
Russia’s Penal Enforcement Code describes correctional centers as special institutions for people sentenced to forced labor. They can exist separately, as sections attached to penal colonies, or directly at enterprises that use convict labor. Inside such centers, internal rules apply, and convicts are kept under supervision.
In correctional centers, people are allowed to have money, wear ordinary clothes, use a phone, access the internet, and keep personal belongings. At the same time, a convict must remain on the correctional center’s grounds, they may not leave without permission from the administration, they must carry an ID card at all times, they must follow internal rules, and they must take part in unpaid maintenance and improvement work for up to two hours a week. The person and the room where they live may be searched, and their belongings may be inspected. In effect, it is the same kind of closed institution as a penal colony, only with a softer internal regime.
The word “dormitory,” which is used to describe the living quarters in correctional centers, says little about the real conditions. Russia’s Penal Enforcement Code uses the same word for the places where convicts live in general-regime, strict-regime, and special-regime colonies. In practice, these are usually not separate rooms for a few people but buildings divided into large sections, each housing several dozen people. Even in the model FSIN showed at the St. Petersburg International Legal Forum, a large room with rows of beds can be seen inside the modular building. It looks more like a barracks-style sleeping hall than a regular dormitory.
Olga said conditions varied widely by region. In some places, the administration turned a blind eye to the rules, while in others, it used them as a tool of pressure. Still, the routine in forced labor facilities, she said, resembled the “Groundhog Day” rhythm of life in a penal colony:
“Wake-up, breakfast, go to work, a little lunch at work, and then at around 8 or 9 p.m. we come back from work, wash, have a bite to eat, and go to sleep. That’s basically every day.”
In some correctional centers, Olga said, people could go into town for a few hours on weekends. However, on others, people had to go months without leaving the grounds.
“If there are no problems, if the employer does not say they are working badly, then everything goes normally,” she said. “But if someone starts, for example, filing complaints against the employer, then the administration first of all restricts outings.”
Grigory Mumrikov, an artist who served a forced labor sentence in Zelenograd, just outside Moscow, after being convicted of participating in the organization of an anti-war protest, shared similar impressions. Compared with pretrial detention, the correctional center seemed to him like “great happiness,” even if he was still in captivity. From evening to morning, he was in the correctional center, and from morning to evening, he worked as a laborer at Aksakovo, a sanatorium run by FSIN. Mumrikov spent the couple of free hours he had after work walking around a lake.
“I could simply sit on a bench, just to avoid being on that territory,” he said, referring to the correctional center.
That was possible because the convicts worked outside the correctional center and traveled to and from Aksakovo on their own. But by 8 p.m., Mumrikov had to return to the center for the evening roll call.
“Everyone was rounded up and told to work weekends”
Under the law, people sentenced to forced labor must work wherever the correctional center’s administration sends them. Formally, their labor is supposed to be regulated by labor law. But convicts do not have the key right of a free worker: the right to refuse a particular job and leave for another employer.
Convicts do not have the key right of a free worker: the right to refuse a particular job and leave for another employer
In some correctional centers, Olga said, there was still some choice — the administration could offer two or three potential employers, and the person would choose where to work based on their skills and health. But that was not the case everywhere. In the correctional center in Leninsk, in the Volgograd region, where she was held in the winter of 2023-2024, there was only one employer: a canned goods factory.
“You cannot refuse to work, because that is considered a malicious violation,” Olga said.
According to her, people worked 10 to 12 hours a day, and weekends could be turned into workdays. However, if inspections began, the employer would show a normal schedule.
“The employers drew up a good schedule and pretended that no one had been forced to come in on weekends and that the working day was what it should be,” she said. “Accordingly, as soon as the inspectors leave, everything goes back to the way it was: longer working days and mandatory weekend work.”
The order to work on weekends, she said, usually came not directly from FSIN but from the production site. A foreman would gather the convicts, make sure no one had phones to record the conversation, and then announce the new schedule: “We work on weekends. We work until such-and-such time. And whoever complains will make things worse for themselves.”
That is what makes a convict’s position in a correctional center fundamentally different from that of an ordinary worker. In a correctional center, an employer’s demand almost automatically becomes an FSIN demand. The administration begins applying pressure, and complaints or refusal to work can result in disciplinary penalties.
“Inspectors work in coordination with the employer. They are one single system,” Olga said. If a person refuses to work for pennies or complains about conditions, she said, the administration can begin “catching them on small things” to find grounds for punishment. Accumulating such penalties creates the risk of transfer to a penal colony.
Similar complaints have emerged in other regions. In Zelenograd, convicts in a correctional center said they worked without a proper schedule, faced overtime, and were threatened with tougher conditions if they reminded officials of their rights.
“We differ from undocumented migrants on a construction site only in that we are Russian,” forced laborers said.
Konstantin, a former prisoner who served his sentence in Kabardino-Balkaria in Russia’s north Caucasus, told the independent outlet Cherta that he was sent to sort household waste — eight hours in the heat at a rural dump that included hides of slaughtered cows and sheep, a terrible smell, large numbers of insects, and no ability to refuse the work.
Another person interviewed by the outlet, from the Voronezh Region in central Russia, worked at an agricultural complex growing mushrooms and said regular hired employees earned significantly more than convicts got from the correctional center.
These examples do not mean that people in every correctional center are forced to work overtime or are sent to the hardest jobs. Former convicts themselves also describe centers with decent working conditions and normal schedules. But all cases have one thing in common: a person cannot resign if they are unhappy with the conditions.
There is pay, but people support themselves
Officially, labor in correctional centers is paid. In any sentence, between 5% and 20% of a convict’s salary is withheld for the state, and the inmate is free to use the rest of the money. But unlike a penal colony, where prisoners have to be fed and issued uniforms, people in correctional centers are almost entirely self-supporting.
Convicts are given a bed and bedding, but they usually buy their food, clothes, shoes, hygiene products, medicine, and other everyday items while also reimbursing the correctional center each month for utilities and household services.
In Leninsk, in the Volgograd Region, Olga said, about 3,000 to 4,000 rubles ($35-$46) were withheld from her wages for utilities, and after all the deductions were made, convicts were typically left with about 9,000 to 10,000 rubles ($104-$116) a month to live on.
“And you have to take into account that this is not a colony: you need to dress yourself and eat something, because not all correctional centers provide food,” she said.
“This is not a colony: you need to dress yourself and eat something, because not all correctional centers have food”
Formally, if a convict has no money, the correctional center has to provide them with food, clothing, and shoes at the state’s expense. But in practice, Olga said, getting that support can be difficult.
“You go to the management and say: I have nothing to eat, you are supposed to provide me with food. And they say: ‘Well, where am I going to get it? You can see there is no kitchen,’” she said, describing life at a correctional center in the Moscow Region.
At the same time, Olga stressed that low pay is not an inevitable feature of correctional centers. In the Perm Region, where she worked at a private garment factory, the business was properly organized, and convicts’ wages could be comparable to ordinary wages outside the prison.
Olga earned about 40,000 to 50,000 rubles ($460-$580), while women who sewed well made up to 100,000 ($1,160), even after the deductions. “It was a fairly good place,” she said.
That contrast shows that the problem with correctional centers is not simply that they always pay poorly. With a decent employer, convicts can earn close to what they would outside prison. But if the employer is dishonest, the fact that a person is trapped means they are forced to survive on less than the national subsistence minimum.
What can lead to punishment in a correctional center
Under the Penal Enforcement Code, violations committed by people serving forced labor can lead to them being placed in an internal isolation cell inside the correctional center for up to 15 days. Olga said anyone sent there can only bring a minimum of belongings, and there is a ban on phones. “Not as frightening as in a colony, but the point is the same — to isolate you and show what they can do to you,” she explained.
The law separately defines “malicious violations,” which include refusal to work, disobeying the administration, participating in a strike or collective disobedience, possessing banned items, leaving the center without authorization, or returning more than 24 hours late. If a person is declared a malicious violator — for one “malicious” violation or for three ordinary violations within a year — the head of the correctional center submits a request to a court to transfer the person to a colony.
In practice, Olga said, these rules become a method of control. The administration may ignore minor violations for a long time, then use them against those who complain about an employer or refuse to work in poor conditions.
“They may treat you relatively well for a long time, but once you start demanding your rights, they begin finding fault with everything you do,” she said.
“Once you start demanding your rights, they begin finding fault with everything you do”
An everyday minor infraction can thus become part of a chain that ends in a person being packed off to a penal colony. “For those who came from a colony, that's the main fear,” Olga said. “They tell you: ‘if you don't want to work, you'll go back.’”
Who benefits from the new system
In public statements, FSIN describes correctional centers as a more humane alternative to colonies: a person is not completely isolated from society, and they can work, earn a salary, use a phone, and gradually return to normal life. In an explanatory note to the law expanding the use of forced labor, its authors wrote that such punishment allows convicts to maintain social ties, restore work skills, and compensate victims.
But this humanization also has an economic aspect. Under the Penal Enforcement Code, sections of correctional centers can be created directly at enterprises that use convict labor. The standard contract between a correctional center and a company describes the arrangement as a ready-made production scheme: the correctional center sends convicts, and the organization agrees to employ them at its site and report violations of labor discipline to the administration.
For businesses, this means access to workers whose minimal privileges depend on their successful fulfillment of assigned tasks. A convict cannot simply quit and leave for another employer, and as a FSIN representative told TASS, commercial entities are interested in creating such sections because people sentenced to forced labor are “fairly disciplined workers.”
“They are interested in doing their work well, because if they violate labor discipline or the procedure and conditions for serving their sentence, there is a risk that the punishment will be replaced with a harsher one — imprisonment,” the representative said.
The state additionally encourages businesses to take part in the scheme. Since 2026, organizations have been exempt from property tax on premises, territories, and other real estate they provide free of charge to house correctional centers.
The model is also convenient for FSIN. The agency does not need to build a traditional penal colony, as businesses provide part of the infrastructure while paying convicts enough that the state is not obliged to provide them with food, clothes, or medicine — 5% to 20% of their wages also go directly to the state.
In the end, businesses get workers whose discipline is backed by FSIN, while the agency gets infrastructure and a “contingent” — the official bureaucratic term used for prisoners and other people under state supervision — whose burden of support can largely be shifted onto the convicts themselves. At the same time, for FSIN and the state as a whole, this is a form of punishment that can be presented as humane resocialization.
A Gulag without isolation
The idea of correction through labor is not a new concept in the Russian penal system. In Soviet times, it was reflected even in the names of institutions, as camps and colonies were called “corrective labor institutions.” Soviet Russia’s Corrective Labor Code explicitly said that punishment should “correct and reeducate” convicts “in the spirit of an honest attitude toward labor.”
Under Stalin, this logic reached its extreme: the Gulag was not only a system of isolation and terror but also a vast economic mechanism. Prisoners built canals, railways, industrial facilities, and urban infrastructure. But directly comparing modern correctional centers with the Gulag would be inaccurate: the scale, conditions, and level of violence are not comparable.Today, supervision is as light as possible, as it is the system itself that stimulates the efficiency of the inmates’ labor.
The idea of correction through labor is not a new concept in the Russian penal system. In Soviet times, it was reflected even in the names of institutions, as camps and colonies were called “corrective labor institutions.” Soviet Russia’s Corrective Labor Code explicitly said that punishment should “correct and reeducate” convicts “in the spirit of an honest attitude toward labor.”
Under Stalin, this logic reached its extreme: the Gulag was not only a system of isolation and terror but also a vast economic mechanism. Prisoners built canals, railways, industrial facilities, and urban infrastructure. But directly comparing modern correctional centers with the Gulag would be inaccurate: the scale, conditions, and level of violence are not comparable.Today, supervision is as light as possible, as it is the system itself that stimulates the efficiency of the inmates’ labor.
The state does not need to fully isolate a person in order to control them. It is enough to link their place of residence, their type of work, their salary, and the threat of transfer to a penal colony into a single system. As a result, Correctional centers look like an updated version of the Soviet labor tradition — without the barracks of the Gulag, but with the same basic idea that a convict must work for the benefit of the state — and now, also, for Russia’s business sector.
Not humanization, but a pragmatic move by FSIN
Correctional centers may offer better conditions than penal colonies, but they are still a form of deprivation of liberty, no matter what the paperwork says. In the end, they create even more opportunities to exploit prisoner labor than colonies do, and FSIN directly describes people sentenced to forced labor as a convenient labor resource.
Putin’s war in Ukraine is draining prisoners from Russia’s penal colonies, and dozens of institutions have closed down due to the lack of inmates. That could have led to FSIN losing bureaucratic influence (and with it, staff and funding from the state budget). Instead, the agency’s leadership appears to have found an effective way out: it can now report growth in the number of institutions providing a more humane form of punishment, and it can do so in a way that certainly pleases Russian businesses.

Biosphere reserve management regulations under final review
