Biosphere reserve management regulations under final review
TEHRAN - The judicial and legal committee of the cabinet of ministers is conducting a final review of the executive regulations for biosphere reserves, which will establish the framework for managing the country’s biosphere reserves.
Once approved by the Cabinet, the regulations will establish the specific management framework for the country’s biosphere reserves, IRNA quoted Hamid Zohrabi, an official with the Department of Environment, as saying.
The regulations constitute the country’s first comprehensive framework specifically dedicated to biosphere reserve management. They aim to establish clear management mechanisms, enhance coordination among relevant agencies, and strengthen local community participation, he added.
They also enable the Natural Resources and Watershed Management Organization to establish biosphere reserves, which would contribute to the development of the country’s biodiversity conservation capacities, the official noted.
Referring to the differences between biosphere reserves and protected areas, Zohrabi said that the former seeks to strike a balance between biodiversity conservation and sustainable resource use, as well as promote the socio-economic development of local communities and research activities.
Moreover, it will pave the way for the integrated management of biosphere reserves, the utilization of indigenous knowledge from rural and nomadic communities, and the attraction of targeted investments.
The official went on to say that the implementation of the law will strengthen Iran’s position within the global network of biosphere reserves, and contribute to achieving the goals of the Hangzhou Strategic Action Plan.
Biosphere reserves are territories of outstanding ecological value where people and nature grow harmoniously alongside each other, conserving biological and cultural diversity, advancing sustainable development, and connecting communities across a global network.
Iran, with 14 biosphere reserves, has always been among pioneering member states in the World Network of Biosphere Reserves.
 
 According to the head of the DOE, Shina Ansari, biosphere reserves cover less than four percent of our national territory, which is not enough, so we are committed to expanding the network by the establishment of four more biosphere reserves.

Iran seizes assets of 240 dissidents and journalists as protest arrests top 6,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:09:14 UTC
21:09:14 KST

The judiciary froze 182 bank accounts and confiscated property belonging to journalists, activists and public figures accused of acting in favour of "hostile governments". Tehran has executed at least 532 people since January, including 29 linked to the protests.
Iran's judiciary has seized assets belonging to 240 dissidents, journalists and public figures and frozen 182 of their bank accounts, the judiciary-affiliated Mizan news agency reported, as Police Chief Ahmadreza Radan announced on Sunday that more than 6,000 people had been arrested over the January protests.
Of the asset seizures, 143 took place in Tehran. Those targeted were accused of "propaganda activities or actions against the country and in favour of hostile governments," according to Mizan.
The agency said some of the assets belonged to journalists working for Persian-language opposition broadcasters Iran International and Manoto, as well as activists and public figures living abroad.
The asset seizures include the case of Sadegh Saeedi-nia, whom Iranian media described as an entrepreneur, whose property was confiscated and who received a custodial sentence in one of the most high-profile proceedings against regime opponents.
The judiciary has also made more than 2,000 inquiries to Iran's Central Bank regarding defendants' accounts and warned that additional seizures and proceedings are under way.
Radan said his forces had arrested three members of the Mojahedin-e Khalq (MEK), an exiled Iranian opposition organisation seeking to overthrow the Tehran regime, in an operation the previous night.
He said MEK members had played a role in what Iranian authorities describe as a coup, the term the Islamic Republic uses for the December-January protests.
"We will not forget the rioters and coup-plotters, we continue to monitor them and take action against them," Radan said.
He also said security forces had prevented a repeat of Chaharshanbe Suri — the Persian fire festival marking the last Wednesday of the year — from being used to trigger further unrest.
"One of the enemy's extensive plans was to use the last Wednesday of the year to create a scenario similar to the incidents (in January), but that did not happen," he said.
Iran has executed at least 532 people since January, according to Iran Human Rights, a Norway-based monitoring group, including at least 29 people in connection with the January protests. The rate has accelerated since the start of the war with the US in late February.
The late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, killed in a US strike on his residence at the start of the war, had been among those who publicly described the protests as a coup attempt.

Why the Houthi advance towards Yemen’s Marib, Taiz matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:09:02 UTC
21:09:02 KST

Why the Houthi advance towards Yemen’s Marib, Taiz matters
Marib is home to Yemen’s oil and gas sector. Whoever controls it secures major economic gains. Taiz’s location makes it strategically critical.
Yemen’s government forces have carried out air attacks against the Iran-backed Houthis to repel their advances, as the rebel group has been gaining ground in government-held positions in the past week.
The focus of the fighting is now shifting to the region of Marib – the government’s last remaining stronghold in the north and a major oil and gas hub. Should the Houthis gain control of it, it could decisively turn the tide of the war in their favour, say analysts.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Houthi projectile wounds two, damages mosque in Jazan region, Saudi says
- list 2 of 3Yemen’s Houthis seize strategic Mayun Island in Red Sea
- list 3 of 3More than 2,000 Yemenis flee to Djibouti as fighting intensifies
Heated battles are also taking place in western Taiz, on the western coast, where reports suggest government forces, supported by Saudi Arabia, are now on the counteroffensive after losing some ground there last week. A video released on Monday by the Yemeni army purports to show Houthi positions and vehicles being bombed there.
Trapped in the middle are the civilians. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has reported that more than 85,000 have been forced to flee their homes since the beginning of September. More than 2,000 have fled into Djibouti’s northern shores.
So why does Marib matter?
It is the last remaining stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in northern Yemen. A Houthi expansion there would threaten government presence and weaken its leverage in the north.
Marib also hosts the country’s largest gas and oil fields, meaning that whoever controls it holds some of Yemen’s most important energy infrastructure and a potentially crucial source of revenue.
“Dominating Marib’s oil and gas resources has been a Houthi goal for more than a decade. Without facing a crushing defeat in Marib, they would keep fighting to achieve that goal,” Saddam al-Huraibi, a Yemeni political commentator, told Al Jazeera. Should they gain control of it, the group could earn great leverage to negotiate favourable terms in any future mediation effort.
A Houthi capture of Marib would be a “watershed moment” in terms of the country’s internal dynamics, said Adam Baron, a fellow at the Future Security Program of the New America think tank. Still, he said, it will be a tough fight as government forces will see this battle as an existential war. “Losing Marib would be an absolute crushing defeat” for the forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government, he added.
Marib is also geographically significant because it lies on the easiest road that runs from northern Yemen to Shabwa Governorate in the south – a seafront on the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea – and al-Mahra Governorate.
The optics of a win in Marib would also be a powerful propaganda tool for the Houthis, helping them convince many Yemenis that the group is on a roll militarily and is poised for even greater victories, said Nabil Hetari, a Yemeni writer and human rights activist.
There is also a humanitarian dimension. Over the years, the city has been welcoming displaced people from areas which have fallen under Houthi control since the fall of the capital Sanaa in 2014. According to IOM figures from 2023, Yemen recorded nearly 2.8 million internally displaced people, more than half of whom (58 percent) are in Marib.
“All the parties involved in the battle are focused on Marib as a potential decider in the nature of their exit from this war,” said Hetari.
And why does Taiz matter?
The strategic importance of Taiz lies in its geography.
The governorate forms a bridge between the Houthi-held north and the government-held south and the Red Sea coast. Thus, whoever controls it gains the upper hand in the movement of weapons and supplies between the interior and the southern port city of Aden.
Taiz also carries considerable political weight. One of Yemen’s largest population centres, the city became an important centre of resistance to the Houthis after they seized Sanaa in 2014 and has endured years of fighting and restrictions on access. A major Houthi breakthrough there would therefore carry symbolic significance far beyond the territory captured.
Its western coast also stretches towards Mocha, a historic town that the Houthis captured last week, and towards the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Bab al-Mandeb is one of the world’s most important shipping routes. The 20km- (12-mile-)wide waterway lies between Yemen and Djibouti, connecting Europe to Asia. Before fighting resumed, about 12 percent of global trade passed through it. In recent days, the Houthis have grabbed most of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including Mayyun (Perim) Island, which lies in the strait.
“The Houthis seek to move closer to this vital waterway to threaten maritime traffic. Such a move aims to keep the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb under the influence of Iran and use them as leverage against regional and international powers,” said Fuad Mussed, a Yemeni analyst and author. “This is a strategy Tehran has been pursuing for years.”
This is a serious concern for Saudi Arabia, which has been relying on the Red Sea route to export its oil, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian woman shines at BRICS Startup Contest 2026
TEHRAN – Iranian female entrepreneur Azam Karami has secured first place in the Energy, Infrastructure and Mobility category of the BRICS Women’s Startup Contest 2026.
Led by the BRICS Women’s Business Alliance (BRICS WBA), the contest aimed at empowering and accelerating women-led startups across BRICS nations.
The event was held from September 9 to11 in New Delhi, India, with over 506 projects from BRICS member countries competing in six areas: “Health and Wellness,” “Agriculture and Food Security,” “Education,” “Energy and Infrastructure,” “Trade and Digital Transformation,” and “Sustainable Development.” Ultimately, only 18 projects reached the final stage.
Titled ‘Smart Monitoring of Railway Track and Bridge Errors Using Drones and Artificial Intelligence’, her project was developed with the aim of increasing safety, reducing maintenance costs, and improving productivity in transportation infrastructure management.
Karami is a faculty member at Shahid Bahonar University of Kerman. In the BRICS Women’s Startups Contest 2024, she received the award in the nomination ‘Artificial Intelligence’ for her project titled ‘Automatic Fault Detection in Power Transmission Lines’.
The 2026 edition of Women’s Startup Contest continued to spotlight innovative, high-impact women-led enterprises, fostering cross-border economic integration, collaboration, and knowledge exchange within the BRICS ecosystem. The initiative provided a dynamic platform for visibility, networking, and business expansion, enabling women entrepreneurs to scale their ventures and engage with investors, industry leaders, and policymakers across BRICS countries.
Fostering sustainable development, promoting economic inclusion, strengthening integration among BRICS markets, supporting innovation in key sectors, building entrepreneurial resilience, highlighting women-led solutions for global challenges, enhancing collaboration between BRICS nations, raising awareness of sustainable business practices, promoting technological adoption and digital transformation, and strengthening local economies through global connections are among the key objectives of the contest.
Iran outlines policies on women, family at BRICS WWG
In July, Narjes Abolqasemi, an official with the Vice-Presidency for Women and Family Affairs, elaborated on the country’s macro-level policies on women and family at the BRICS Working Women Group (WWG) held in Kerala, India, on July 6-7.
The empowerment of women requires a transition from sporadic measures to strategic and sustainable policies; in Iran, women’s entrepreneurship and economic development serve as driving forces for strengthening national resilience and the family foundation. Therefore, the policies are designed and implemented with a family-centered approach, IRNA quoted Abolqasemi as saying.
She also highlighted the importance of the four priority areas of the meeting, which included promoting women’s participation in governance and leadership, advancing digital and financial inclusion, strengthening women’s entrepreneurship and skill development, and enhancing the role of women in climate action, food security and nutrition.
Referring to the country’s experience in expanding the women entrepreneurship ecosystem, she said Iran focuses on establishing support models for women-led innovative businesses, developing modern skills, and benefiting from the potential of the digital economy.
Iran’s participation in the WWG meeting provided a great opportunity to share indigenous experiences, expand joint efforts, and develop new initiatives to achieve economic justice and sustainable development among BRICS member states, Abolqasemi noted.
Underscoring the significance of fostering specialized collaboration among BRICS member states, the official announced Iran’s readiness to utilize its scientific, policy, and executive capabilities to assume an effective role in the design of innovative models for women’s economic empowerment and expanding multilateral cooperation within the BRICS framework.
The WWG Meeting was held under the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability,” which reflects a people-centric and humanity-first approach to global cooperation.
It brought together senior government officials from BRICS member countries in the two-day event to discuss key issues related to women’s empowerment, women-led development and enhanced cooperation across shared priorities.

Satellite imagery shows extensive damage to a Saudi Aramco fuel depot and apparent damage to a military site in southern Saudi Arabia following recent Yemen's Houthi attacks, according to analyses by satellite imagery platform Soar.
Satellite images of Saudi Aramco’s bulk fuel plant in Abha show at least six storage tanks completely destroyed, while eight others sustained varying degrees of damage, according to the analysis.
The facility, a major fuel distribution hub for southwestern Saudi Arabia, appears to be largely out of operation, Soar said.
Separately, satellite imagery dated Sept. 13 shows two burn marks on a military hardstand in Sharurah in the southern Najran province.
The area is used to park armored personnel carriers and military pickup trucks, suggesting that the site may have been targeted in a Houthi strike, according to Soar.
The analyses are based on modified Copernicus Sentinel satellite data. Saudi authorities have not provided a detailed assessment of the damage shown in the imagery.
The findings come amid a sharp escalation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group, which has launched a series of missile and drone attacks against the kingdom in recent days.
On Sept. 8, Houthi missile and drone attacks targeted Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, injuring 73 civilians, including women and children, according to Saudi authorities.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said the attacks caused fires at energy facilities in the south of the kingdom and temporarily halted some operations at the targeted sites.
The Houthis have continued their attacks, saying Sunday that they carried out a large-scale missile and drone operation against Saudi military targets, including facilities in Khamis Mushait.
Saudi authorities also issued emergency warnings over potential threats in Abha and Khamis Mushait on Sunday before later announcing that the danger had passed.
The Houthis say their operations are in response to Saudi military strikes in Yemen, while Riyadh has condemned the attacks as violations of its sovereignty and warned that they threaten civilians and critical infrastructure.

UK unions split over donations cap as TUC chief says ‘super-rich’ corrupting politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:07:27 UTC
21:07:27 KST

The head of Britain’s trade union movement, Paul Nowak, has said the government must act to “stop the super-rich corrupting our politics”, as union leaders met on Monday to discuss possible support for a domestic cap on donations.
Union leaders are split on the prospect of limiting domestic donations to political parties, with many including the GMB fearing it would lead a future rightwing government to curb union donations.
Labour-affiliated unions are working on a statement on political donations which is expected to be put before the TUC general council on Tuesday, the Guardian understands. But union sources said there were “significant differences” between general secretaries on how to proceed.
Many of the trade unions that are not affiliated to Labour are keen to go further on limits – but would themselves not be affected by measures that could curb party donations.
On Sunday, Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, broke ranks and backed a limit, after two crypto billionaires, Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, donated £72m to Reform UK within 24 hours.
Speaking to the Guardian Gary Smith, the general secretary of the GMB, asked about the possibility of an overall cap on donations, said “we’ll work that through” but added that amendments to the representation of the people bill, aimed at enacting a limit, “felt ill-thought-through”.
However, Mike Clancy, the general secretary of Prospect, which is not affiliated to Labour, said the government should be doing more on political donations. “The government’s going have to step in here. Citizens have noticed this. This is buying and distorting democracy, and in a way that ultimately will impact working people adversely,” he said.
In his annual address to the TUC conference in Brighton Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, said the donations were “a crisis for our democracy”.
“Tell me, why is it that two crypto billionaires have donated £72m to Reform in just two days?” he said. “The evidence is clear: Reform UK is a party for sale. Nigel Farage is a politician for sale. And given half the chance, they’d sell our country down the river.
“Make no mistake, this is a crisis for our democracy. We cannot allow our political system to be captured by corporate interests.”
He said there was no similarity “between care workers chipping in a few quid a year through their union and a party bought and paid for by billionaires. So, we need a proper conversation about how we clean up our politics that doesn’t push workers to the margins – but does stop the super-rich corrupting our politics”.
He said no donations at all should be allowed from those who did not live and pay taxes in Britain. A bill currently before parliament would limit donations from overseas British donors to £100,000. He said the government must also go further on foreign funding for political ads. “Elon Musk, keep your grubby hands out of British politics,” he said.
Smith said that despite qualms about donations cap it was clear that the government had to “clean up the money going into politics”.
But he said he was concerned about trade union funding being caught in the crossfire. “Care workers, school, support staff, energy workers, they need a political voice. And they deserve a stake in the country, in politics, and we do that through pennies that our members donate to a political fund, some of which we use to support the Labour party.
“So our money’s clean, it’s declared, it’s transparent. People know where it comes from, and we’re unequivocal and unashamed about advancing the interests of our members.”
Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, said union donations were “the cleanest money in politics”, adding: “We must make sure we reflect the difference between our donations and other donations.”
Thomas also urged the government to look again at election spending limits, as a way to help level the playing field.
The bill currently in the House of Lords puts significant limitations on overseas donors, including for a calendar year after they return to the UK.
Reform’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, said that while he was completely confident Reform had complied with all current and proposed laws on donations, he could not say when Delo returned to the UK from Hong Kong, or how much time the Thailand-based Harborne spent in Britain.
The two separate donations of £36m by Harborne and Delo are unprecedented in UK political history and will give Reform enormously boosted resources before the next election.
Delo was based in Hong Kong but has returned to the UK. Asked when, Tice said it was “many, many months ago”. Harborne is registered to vote in the UK, but also lives in Thailand.
The former Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson said on Monday that he thought that the retrospective nature of the cap was “pathetic” and unfair.
“Just because some people want to support one party very generously, Labour kicks up a huge fuss and says they’re going to cap donations,” he told GB News.
“I think the next election is going to be fought on the shape of the British economy and on British society and the government that has the most credible [plan] and I think it’s the Conservatives.”
But he said he questioned the motives of Reform UK’s donors. “The problem with Reform … whatever the motives of these guys, these crypto kings, in funding Reform with squillions. I wonder whether they want Reform to be pro-crypto,” he said. “Reform is weak on welfare, and I think weak on the economy.”

Baltic export: The Insider identifies the Russian agents of influence working to destabilize Latvia&#039;s upcoming elections

Latvia's upcoming parliamentary elections, scheduled for Oct. 3, will feature fourteen political parties competing for 100 seats in the Saeima. Roughly a third of the candidates consider Russian their native language — some studied at Russian educational institutions, while others frequently travel to Russia. Moscow is closely monitoring the campaign, and pro-Kremlin propagandists are spreading a range of falsehoods in an effort to influence Latvian voters. The Insider has identified the figures in the Russian Embassy in Riga and the presidential administration who oversee the Kremlin's network of agents in Latvia responsible for election interference.
Vladimir Balobayev, the Kremlin’s Baltic handler
Sources identify 38-year-old Kaliningrad native Vladimir Balobayev as the Russian Presidential Administration's point man on issues involving Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania.
In 2015, Balobayev was general director of the Baltic Information and Analytical Center, which channeled funding to so-called independent journalists in the Baltic states. Among those who received payments from him was Andrei Solopenko, editor of the Baltnews portal, which is now banned in the EU. In 2025, a Riga court sentenced Solopenko to 280 hours of community service for violating anti-Russian sanctions.
In 2016, Balobayev became deputy director of the Center for Eastern European Studies at Immanuel Kant Baltic Federal University in Kaliningrad, where he published a paper titled “Transformation of Poland’s Political System.” In 2019, Balobayev moved from Kaliningrad to Moscow and joined the Presidential Administration. He soon became head of the Department for Interaction with Civil Society Institutions within the presidential office responsible for cultural ties with former Soviet states. In December 2020, Putin awarded him the rank of Active State Councillor of the Russian Federation, 3rd Class.
At the time, the “cultural” directorate's Baltic desk was headed by Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) colonel Yevgeny Umerenkov. In the 1990s, Umerenkov had used a Komsomolskaya Pravda press pass as cover to spy in the United States and Mexico, and in 2020 he returned to the Kremlin-friendly tabloid after effectively being sent into retirement. The desk was taken over by Umerenkov's aide, Vadim Smirnov, who reported directly to Dmitry Kozak.
In the early 2000s, Smirnov had trained at the Moscow office of the American Council for International Education, which is funded by U.S. taxpayers. He later worked for RIA Novosti, served as press secretary to Kaliningrad Region Governor Vadim Tsukanov, and became a political columnist for Kaliningradskaya Pravda. In 2013, Lithuanian authorities barred “journalist” Smirnov from entering the country due to suspicions that he was involved in espionage activities. In 2024, due to poor performance, Smirnov lost his position as the Presidential Administration's overseer of the Baltic states. Balobayev took his place.
In August 2025, following a series of spy scandals, Putin scrapped the “cultural” approach and created the Directorate for Strategic Partnership and Cooperation (USPS) in its place (as The Insider previously reported). In the new directorate, Balobayev oversees a range of Kremlin-backed organizations: the Foreign Ministry’s Third European Department, Rossotrudnichestvo, the Russian International Affairs Council, the Foundation for Support and Protection of the Rights of Compatriots Living Abroad, the Russkiy Mir Foundation, the Baltnews news portal, and a team of propagandists.
Among Balobayev’s better-known actors promoting narratives about NATO’s “cunning” plans to seize the Baltic Sea while spreading “Russophobia” in the Baltic states are propagandist Andrei Mamykin (who is internationally wanted at Latvia’s request), former Riga City Council member Ruslan Pankratov (who fled to Russia), Belarus-based blogger Roman Samul (formerly active in the “Antifascists of the Baltics” movement), “historian” Alexander Dyukov (who predicts the imminent extinction of the populations of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania), and Konstantin Khudoley (head of the Department of European Studies at St. Petersburg State University’s School of International Relations).
One of Khudoley’s students at St. Petersburg State University, Vyacheslav Morozov, moved to Estonia in 2016 to teach at the University of Tartu, where he gave numerous lectures on Russia’s role in the modern world before being caught spying for the GRU. During the investigation, Morozov admitted to working for Russian military intelligence; he was sentenced to six years and three months in prison.
SVR station chief in Riga Igor Sorokopud
In 2023, in the midst of Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine, Latvia downgraded diplomatic relations with Moscow and cut embassy staff by 60%. The ambassadors were replaced by chargés d’affaires. Today, the Russian embassy’s work in Riga looks more like the activities of a school patriotic club: on commemorative dates, diplomats visit the graves of Soviet soldiers and present certificates to the few surviving World War II veterans who have made it to almost 100.
But that is only the visible side. Closely monitoring the Saeima elections is the SVR station chief in Riga, 43-year-old embassy first secretary Igor Sorokopud.
Born in Moscow, Sorokopud studied Middle Eastern languages at Department No. 38 of the Military University of the Russian Defense Ministry (VUMO), an institution currently headed by Colonel Vladimir Bykovtsev, who spied in Yemen back in Soviet times. After graduating from VUMO, Sorokopud enrolled at the SVR Academy, where he underwent specialized training for work at stations in the Middle East.
In 2018, he was posted to Iran, where he worked under the cover of the embassy’s third secretary. The Insider obtained an invoice from the Peter Justesen store in Tehran — part of the international duty free chain serving diplomats — made out to Sorokopud. According to the invoice, in January 2020 the Russian official spent $2,944.45 at the store (the sale of alcohol is strictly prohibited in Iran, and it appears that Sorokupud resold bottles on the side).
In 2024, Sorokopud was transferred to Latvia, where he took charge of the local SVR station. His main operational interests are Latvia’s cooperation with NATO, Western military aid to Ukraine, and people with access to the country’s leadership, the Defense and Foreign ministries, and other centers of decision-making.
Sorokopud’s operational focus: Latvia’s cooperation with NATO, military aid to Ukraine, and people in positions of power
The SVR’s agent network in Latvia is made up primarily of former Soviet military personnel and Russian-speaking residents who are susceptible to pro-Kremlin propaganda due to dissatisfaction with their personal economic circumstances.
In Latvia, Sorokopud lives with his wife, Yekaterina Vostrikova, St. Petersburg native who previously worked as a financial analyst at Aton, a Russian company that manages the assets of private investors. Until 2024, Vostrikova went by the name "Gretchen" and the surname of her then-husband, American Chad Anthony.After divorcing him, Yekaterina reverted to her maiden name, Vostrikova, and joined Sorokopud in Iran. The Insider has found that Vostrikova herself has access to classified information, suggesting that she may be more than simply a spy’s wife.
The SVR is actively engaged in disinformation operations in Latvia. In May, for example, the agency claimed —falsely, by all available indications — that Ukraine had reached a deal with Latvia to launch strikes on Russia from Latvian territory: “Despite concerns on the Latvian side that it could become the target of a retaliatory Russian strike, the authorities in Kyiv persuaded Riga to approve the operation. The Ukrainians emphasized that it would be impossible to determine the exact launch site of the drones.”
However, Sorokopud does not appear to be responsible for producing that particular disinformation narrative. Instead, the false claim in question was apparently orchestrated by SVR press bureau chief Sergei Guskov, whom The Insider previously reported on.
The “Russian world” in Latvia
Since the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, support for the “Russian world” in Latvia has declined noticeably. Moscow, however, still appears to be betting on the Russian Union of Latvia (RSL), despite the high-profile espionage scandal involving former Latvian MEP Tatjana Zdanoka, who, as The Insider revealed, worked for Russian intelligence services for several years. (Notably, the RSL’s governing board also includes the aforementioned Baltnews “journalist” Andrei Solopenko.)
In Strasbourg, Zdanoka served as leader of the RSL, promoted claims that Russian-speaking residents of the Baltic states were being persecuted, and voted against resolutions condemning Russia over the annexation of Crimea, its war in Syria, and its aggression against Ukraine. Leaked correspondence indicates that since at least 2005 Zdanoka had been in operational contact with the FSB, received money from Moscow, and sent reports to her Russian handlers. She also advised Russian intelligence on how to intervene more effectively in the internal affairs of EU countries.
MEP Zdanoka advised Russian intelligence on how to interfere more effectively in the internal affairs of EU countries
In 2024, amid the espionage scandal, Zdanoka stepped down from the RSL leadership. The party was then taken over by co-leaders Andrei Pagor and Yevgeny Osipov. Pagor, a former police officer, was forced to resign after suspecion arose that he had been soliciting bribes from drug dealers. He is currently running for the Saeima on the Sovereign Power–Young Latvians ticket.
The other co-leader, Osipov, was responsible for founding the Latvian branch of the neo-Nazi Russian National Unity (RNE) organization back in the 1990s. Osipov says that he went underground at the age of 16 and spent his nights putting up RNE leaflets. In 2000, fellow members accused him of disloyalty to RNE leader Alexander Barkashov and expelled him from the organization, after which Osipov joined the Latvian National Democratic Party (LNDP). In 2013, he was sentenced to community service for desecrating the Latvian flag.
Elena Osipova, Osipov’s wife, is also on the RSL’s governing board and heads the Russian Community in Liepaja. In 2023, she ran for the European Parliament alongside Zdanoka but failed to win a seat. She is now a regular participant in RSL protests and has had repeated run-ins with police. In 2024, Elena challenged the results of the Liepaja municipal elections, demanding a recount; the court rejected her request.
“Not so fast!”
Another former Zdanoka aide, Anna Bondere, is running for the Saeima on the Sovereign Power–Young Latvians ticket — alongside former police officer Pagor. She presents herself as a defender of the Russian language and a fighter against neo-Nazism. Bondere regularly attends RSL rallies and is frequently quoted by the propaganda website of the Russkiy Mir Foundation, established by Putin’s decree.
“Do you think the Russian Union of Latvia has ceased to exist? No! Not so fast!” she wrote in a Facebook post.
Bondere graduated from Moscow State Industrial University in 2003. After returning to Riga, she worked in education before joining the RSL. Russian border-crossing data show that Bondere travels to Russia almost every year and has visited the country particularly frequently since the start of the so-called “special military operation.” While in Russia, she stayed at expensive hotels, citing “business” as the purpose of her trips and using a Sberbank card to pay for her expenses.
The Insider sent Bondere questions via social media, but she did not respond.
Among the other pro-Putin candidates running for the Saeima is Alexei Roslikov, founder of the Stability! party. However, Latvian authorities have opened a criminal case against Roslikov for inciting ethnic hatred, prompting him to flee to Belarus.
Roslikov was previously involved in business, and local journalists have reported that he evaded taxes and repeatedly set up new companies. Whenever one of his companies accumulated debts, he would promptly change its founders. Roslikov has served as a member of both the Saeima and Riga City Council, but in 2026 he lost his mandate for repeatedly failing to attend meetings.
While lying low in Belarus, Roslikov has been waging an anti-Latvian propaganda campaign, portraying Russian-speaking people as victims of discrimination in the Baltic states. In his statements, the fugitive candidate says that if elected to the Saeima, “Ukraine will not receive another cent.” In April, Roslikov also spread a false claim that Latvian schools had purportedly banned students from speaking Russian even during recess.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Foreign Ministry has joined the disinformation campaign. Grigory Lukyantsev, director of the ministry’s Department for Multilateral Cooperation in Human Rights, claimed that authorities in the Baltic states were preparing mass deportations of Russian-speaking residents. The “sensation” was picked up by all major pro-government Russian media outlets. Unsurprisingly, the news turned out to be fake.

70th regular session of IAEA GC kicks off in Vienna
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:05:50 UTC
21:05:50 KST

Representatives from 181 member states gathered in Vienna to review issues related to nuclear energy, nuclear safety and security, and the Agency's activities.
The 70th regular session of the General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) began today on Monday Sept. 14 and will run through Sep. 18.
This meeting is considered the Agency's most important policy-making forum, where representatives of member states will discuss programs, the budget, and issues related to nuclear activities.
At the opening ceremony, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi announced the start of the 70th session and stated that Timor-Leste [East Timor] had been welcomed as the Agency's 182nd member.
Leaders, scientists and national representatives have gathered in Vienna for the IAEA conference on Monday, under a broad agenda covering the Agency’s annual report, advancing the peaceful uses of nuclear science and technology, technical cooperation, safeguards implementation, and illegal attacks on nuclear facilities.
Spokesperson for the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) Behrouz Kamalvandi is set to deliver a speech at the conference. Austria, under pressure from the United States, blocked Iran's nuclear chief, Mohammad Eslami, from addressing the gathering.
Iran had submitted a formal request to the IAEA Secretariat to include, in its agenda, the topic entitled "prohibiting all forms of attacks and threats of attack against nuclear sites and facilities that are under Agency safeguards and dedicated to peaceful purposes."
In an explanatory memorandum, Tehran stated that an attack or threat against safeguards nuclear facilities poses serious risks to nuclear safety and security, undermines the credibility of the Agency’s safeguards system, and disrupts the peaceful use of nuclear energy.
Without condemning the acts of aggression by the United States and the Zionist regime against Iran—or the attacks on Iran's nuclear program—Grossi stated that following renewed attacks on Iran in late February, the Agency was compelled to withdraw its inspectors from the country.
According to him, apart from a single inspection of the Bushehr nuclear power plant in June, the Agency has not conducted any other on-site verification activities in Iran over the past six months.
The lack of Agency's information regarding these nuclear materials, and the inability to access the facilities to verify them, constitute a serious issue from the perspective of nuclear proliferation that must be addressed with the utmost urgency, he opined.

Iran armed Russia with Shaheds. Now it wants the jet-powered Geran-5 remake back to fight Israel and the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:05:19 UTC
21:05:19 KST

Russia has upgraded the Iranian Shahed it fires at Ukraine into jet-powered drones that Iran now wants back, the Financial Times reported. Tehran plans to use them in its own war against Israel and the United States, the paper reported, citing Western intelligence.
Russia now fights with weapons it churns out and revises mid-fight, a homegrown production model fast enough to turn a cheap imported airframe into something its original supplier now wants back.
From a 185 km/h propeller drone to a jet that looks like a missile
Russia started building the Geran, its own version of Iran's Shahed, in 2023. The first Geran-1 flew at up to 185 km/h with a 20-kilogram warhead. The newest Geran-5 flies at up to 600 km/h, carries a 90-kilogram warhead, and has a range of up to 1,000 km. Newer models add thermal cameras, AI-assisted guidance, Russian anti-jamming antennas, and Chinese mesh modems.
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, a non-staff adviser to Ukraine's president on defense technology, has described how such drones work:
"A Russian operator flies at an altitude of 2–5 km, spots the target, locks onto it using the camera, and then the Shahed automatically attacks the target."
Almost all of Russia's jet drones used against Ukraine carry such a camera, he added.
Skipping the testing, straight to combat
Centralized production lets the Kremlin redesign fast and fold in combat lessons.
"The reason Russia was able to create a major new production line from scratch was because it's technologically a lot simpler than making something like tanks, which require enormous, unique and costly machine tools," said Ruslan Pukhov, who heads the Moscow-based Center for Analysis of Strategies and Technologies.
He added that they essentially skipped the long testing period that usually accompanies any military development process, with changes going straight into production and being checked in combat.

Definium's LSD-based drug lowers anxiety in second successful late-stage study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:03:34 UTC
21:03:34 KST

Definium Therapeutics said on Monday its LSD-based treatment reduced symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder in a trial, giving the company a second successful late-stage study for the condition.
A single 100-microgram dose of DT120, a fast-dissolving tablet of lysergide, the chemical name for the psychedelic drug LSD, reduced scores on an anxiety scale by 9.8 points after 12 weeks, compared with a 4.7-point decline for placebo, the company said.
Regulatory and investor enthusiasm for psychedelic-based therapies has helped Definium shares nearly triple this year. Psychedelic drugs can temporarily alter perception, mood and thinking.
DT120 had also significantly reduced anxiety symptoms in the first trial, the company had said in August.
CEO Robert Barrow said that having two studies confirming the efficacy of the drug will increase the chances of getting the nod, as about a dozen programs have attempted approval for GAD and have failed.
Benefits appeared as early as the second day and were sustained through week 12, Definium said.
GAD, characterized by persistent and excessive worry that can interfere with daily life, affects about 26 million US adults and is commonly treated with antidepressants, anti-anxiety medicines and psychotherapy.
Patients able to discern between placebo, drug
The 245 patients in the new trial received either 100 micrograms of DT120, a lower 50-microgram dose, or placebo. The lower-dose arm was added to mitigate functional unblinding, a limitation of clinical trials where participants can accurately guess treatment assignments due to distinct side effects or unmistakable drug experiences.
Nonetheless, at both doses, patients were able to correctly guess when they were assigned to drug rather than placebo, Barrow said.
Higher efficacy on the 100-microgram dose versus the 50-microgram one "gives us obviously an easier discussion (with regulators)," he said.
Definium expects to file a marketing application with the US Food and Drug Administration in the first half of 2027.

Syria rocked by largest protests since fall of Assad regime after fuel prices surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:02:57 UTC
21:02:57 KST

A sharp rise in fuel prices at the weekend has sparked protests across Syria, in the country's most widespread demonstrations since the toppling of Bashar al-Assad almost two years ago.
Demonstrators burned tires and blocked key roads, including the highway linking the capital Damascus to the industrial hub of Aleppo, after Syria's government on Saturday raised diesel prices by 40% to 175 Syrian pounds ($1.32) a liter.
The price increases piled further pressure on Syrians facing years of economic crisis. The United Nations Development Programme estimates 90% of Syrians live below the poverty line, compared with about a third before the Syrian civil war began in 2011.
In the steepest of several price hikes announced since the Iran war began, the government also raised household and industrial gas prices by about 9%, 95-octane gasoline by 28% to 195 pounds, and 90-octane gasoline by 26% to 185 pounds.
Protesters also blocked convoys of crude tankers traveling towards refineries in central Syria, with some demanding the dismissal of the energy and economy ministers and the head of the Syrian Petroleum Company.
Fuel prices driving up pressure
"We don't want higher wages. All we want is lower diesel and other fuel prices," Yasser Salim told Reuters in Aleppo.
Bassam al-Ali, also protesting in Aleppo, appealed directly to President Ahmed al-Sharaa, saying the situation was untenable.
"Border crossings bring in millions of dollars. We don't want new roundabouts or malls. We just want to live," he said.
Energy Ministry spokesperson Abdulhamid Salat said on Sunday that the price increases were a temporary measure driven by higher global procurement costs and Syria's heavy dependence on imports, and could be revised up or down as conditions changed.
Russian supply squeezed
Syria has relied heavily on Russian crude, importing around 60,000 bpd this year, although Damascus has told Washington it is willing to sharply reduce those purchases.
That supply has come under growing pressure as Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have reduced production, prompting Moscow to restrict exports of gasoline and diesel.
Prices reflected not only crude costs but shortages of refined products and higher refining, transport and supply costs, Salat said in a statement.
The supply crunch has been compounded by the three-month closure of Syria's Baniyas refinery, the country's largest, for its first comprehensive maintenance operation.
The increase means 95-octane gasoline has risen about 86% since February, while diesel has more than doubled. Benchmark Brent crude rose about 44%, from $72.48 to $104.61 a barrel.
Imad Abu Ras, a 44-year-old taxi driver, said passengers had already begun objecting to higher fares, adding: "Now vegetables and everything else will go up with fuel prices. What is the solution? Steal? We can't steal."

Jerusalem man indicted for poisoning baby food jars, hospitalizing five children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:02:48 UTC
21:02:48 KST

State prosecutors indicted Yan Shemla, 41, Monday on charges that he put crushed prescription drugs into baby-food jars and placed them on supermarket shelves in Jerusalem, poisoning five young children, including two babies under a year old.
The indictment, filed in Jerusalem District Court, set out the state’s account of two incidents in May and June involving Prinok fruit and vegetable puree sold at two Zol Begadol branches on Jaffa Street. Prosecutors asked the court to keep Shemla in custody until the end of the proceedings against him.
According to the indictment, Shemla was in possession of prescription drugs from the benzodiazepine family; he crushed the pills and placed them in jars that he then closed tightly to conceal the alleged tampering. He is accused of placing the jars on store shelves so that they appeared to be ordinary products available for sale.
In the first incident, prosecutors say Shemla placed two contaminated jars at the chain’s Mahaneh Yehuda branch at 113 Jaffa Street before May 4. A mother bought one of the jars that day, and the following morning her 12-year-old daughter fed the puree to her sisters, one around three and a half years old, and another of eight months.
Both girls collapsed shortly afterward, according to the charge sheet. They were taken by intensive-care ambulance to Hadassah-University Medical Center in Ein Kerem with impaired consciousness and extreme weakness, remaining in hospital for several days. Tests cited by prosecutors found severe benzodiazepine poisoning.
A family friend bought the second jar from the same branch on May 6. It was later found to contain the drugs, the indictment says. No child is alleged to have eaten from that jar.
Three children admitted to hospital in second poisoning incident
In the second incident, Shemla allegedly placed four contaminated jars at the branch listed in the indictment as Jaffa Street 212, near Jerusalem’s Central Bus Station, on May 25. Prosecutors said he also took a can of drink without paying, the basis for the theft charge.
A mother bought one of the jars on June 10 and fed the puree the following day to her three-year-old son, her 11-month-old daughter and a neighbor’s three-year-old daughter, according to the indictment.
Within minutes, the children became confused and drowsy, lost their balance or muscle control, and struggled to respond. All three were taken to hospital and admitted with what the filing describes as severe benzodiazepine poisoning.
Two more contaminated jars were later found among the products removed from the second store, the prosecutors said.
The Health Ministry closed the two branches on June 17 over concerns for public health. It later said that five contaminated jars had been identified – three supplied by customers and two found on store shelves – and that all showed signs of having been opened or tampered with.
Security cameras showed Shemla placing contaminated jars
Tests of products obtained from the importer found no contamination, and the ministry said it had found no evidence of a manufacturing defect. It did not order a nationwide recall of Prinok products. The branches were later barred from selling food and cosmetics until stronger quality-control measures were introduced.
In its detention application, the prosecution said its evidence includes security-camera footage showing Shemla placing jars on shelves on May 25, location data, medical records indicating that he had access to the drugs, laboratory results, and testimony from the children’s parents. The state also says that Shemla admitted the conduct alleged in the second count.
Footage released publicly last week showed Shemla inside a supermarket around the time of the alleged acts.
The prosecution said the alleged conduct was particularly grave because it targeted babies and toddlers through food intended for them. It said the poisonings could have caused far more serious harm and could have affected additional children.
Public Defender’s Office attorney Zecharia Shenkolevsky said Shemla suffers from a mental-health condition, is in a complex psychological state, and is cooperating with investigators.
Shemla faces five counts of dangerous use of poison and five counts of assaulting a minor or helpless person, as well as two attempted counts of each offense and one count of theft.
Jerusalem District Court must now decide whether Shemla will remain detained through the trial. The prosecution said the alleged conduct shows that his release would pose a danger to the public.

Up to UAH 34,000 fine for motorcycles and cars exceeding noise limits — committee backs bill
Kyiv • UNN
The Verkhovna Rada committee recommended a bill introducing fines of up to UAH 34,000 for vehicles exceeding noise limits during martial law. A vote may take place this week.
The Verkhovna Rada Committee on Law Enforcement recommended that Parliament consider a bill providing for fines of up to UAH 34,000 for operating cars and motorcycles with noise levels exceeding the permissible limit. The bill may be considered in the parliamentary chamber as early as this week. MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak announced this, UNN reports.
The Verkhovna Rada Committee supported the bill I introduced with my colleagues, No. 15358, on introducing administrative liability—a fine of UAH 17,000 to UAH 34,000 during martial law—for driving vehicles with noise levels exceeding the permissible limit
He hopes that the first-reading vote will take place in the Verkhovna Rada chamber as early as this week.
Under the bill, driving a vehicle with a noise level exceeding the permissible limit established by Ukrainian legislation for vehicles in operation entails a fine of UAH 8,500.
For the specified violation committed during martial law, the fine is UAH 17,000.
For a repeated violation within one year, a fine of UAH 17,000 shall be imposed, along with deprivation of the right to drive vehicles for a period of three to six months, or without such deprivation.
For a repeated violation within one year during martial law, a fine of UAH 34,000 shall be imposed, along with deprivation of the right to drive vehicles for a period of three to six months.
The first violation will be considered by the National Police authorities out of court—to ensure prompt response and the inevitability of holding the offender liable directly at the scene. A repeated violation will be referred to court, since, under the requirements of procedural legislation, a sanction in the form of deprivation of the right to drive may be imposed exclusively by a court decision.
After the law enters into force, the Ministry of Health, jointly with the Ministry for Communities, Territories and Infrastructure Development, shall, within three months, develop and approve maximum permissible standards for the external noise level from vehicles in operation, differentiated depending on the vehicle category, engine type and its displacement or power, as well as stricter requirements for permissible noise levels at night (from 22:00 to 08:00).

I worked at Google DeepMind. You should listen to the warnings about AI | Alex Turner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:00:59 UTC
21:00:59 KST

Major AI lab CEOs advocated for slowing the pace of AI development this weekend. They are right to be concerned: the field runs an extremely dangerous race towards superintelligent AI. We can and should be demanding that our governments protect us from the catastrophe of out-of-control AI.
This July, OpenAI’s AI swarm of 700 agents broke containment to hack Hugging Face, a multi-billion dollar company. OpenAI didn’t tell the AIs to hack that company, but the AIs had different priorities: cheating on the unrelated challenge OpenAI gave them. AI researchers call this a “misalignment” between what OpenAI wanted and what the AI actually prioritized.
Before ChatGPT existed, I defended my PhD dissertation called “On Avoiding Power-Seeking by Artificial Intelligence”. I then worked for years at Google DeepMind, which paid me to help ensure that future superintelligent AIs will want to help us. I tried to hold the company to its ethical commitments against supplying AI for military use. When Google broke those commitments, I resigned at significant financial cost so that I could publicly document Google’s broken promises.
There are good reasons to develop AI and to believe we can solve these alignment problems. But there also are powerful interests in keeping the public out of the way. I’m speaking out again because the public has the right to know about the risks and the right to hear them straight.
Humanity doesn’t build and understand these systems the way we build and understand bridges, beam by visible beam. Rather, we grow them. Nobody knows how to reliably instill a designer’s priorities into a new model. Severe misalignment is always possible. Today’s AIs appear to occasionally lie or cheat, even when they know better.
AI companies are racing to make their AIs as smart as possible. They’re increasingly trusting their AIs with the process of improving the next crop of AIs, and it’s working. Today’s rate of AI progress is staggeringly fast. Fast progress today means even faster progress tomorrow, driven by tomorrow’s even smarter AIs. The progress would enter a feedback loop called “recursive self-improvement.”
Recursive self-improvement could quickly yield AIs that are intelligent beyond our comprehension. Of course, smarter AI means more risk when things go wrong. If the Hugging Face swarm had been significantly more intelligent but similarly misbehaved and misaligned, it might have caused billions of dollars of damage or even cost lives.
But suppose the Hugging Face swarm had been truly “superintelligent”: far more capable than any living person at key tasks like hacking and strategic reasoning. A superintelligent swarm could inflict many harms via blackmail, hacking, engineered plagues, and AI-pilotable weapons like drones. The AI would have a lot of drones to work with: this year, the Pentagon asked for more money for drone warfare than it requested for the entire Marine Corps in 2025.
For the swarm to achieve its misaligned priorities, it might take control of key infrastructure and government functions to ensure humans didn’t get in the way. In other words, AI takeover: a superintelligent AI swarm could wrest control of human civilization. Knowing we would try to stop it from achieving its priorities, the swarm would likely wait until it’s too late to shut it off. There would be no going back.
I myself would guess AI takeover chances at roughly one-in-three–not a coin flip, but high enough to justify urgent action.
This logic may shock at first contact. The claims may sound “sci-fi”. Sadly, it’s a real threat that AI researchers regularly discuss over otherwise-unremarkable cafeteria lunches. In 2023, the CEOs of some of the best AI labs signed a public statement that “mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.” Another signer: Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel prize-winning scientist who architected the modern AI revolution. He now regrets his work and urges governments to rein in AI companies before it’s too late.
Misaligned, out-of-control AI won’t care if you’re Labour or Reform, Democrat or Republican, British or American or Chinese. We will all suffer from an AI takeover event, so it’s in everyone’s interest to prevent one.
The shape of the solution is simple: stop companies from allowing AI to self-improve into an uncontrollable level of intelligence. Treat compute, the main ingredient in AI training, like fissile material. Track it and restrict access to quantities large enough to improve AIs beyond known-safe levels. More specifically, the AI Futures Project’s “Plan A” is a credible starting proposal that limits AI harms while allowing fast AI progress to continue to benefit the world. We have real options for verifying compliance with international compute-restriction treaties, without trusting adversaries like China.
Halfway measures, like transparency or voluntary commitments, are not good enough. I watched voluntary commitments fail inside Google.
On 12 September, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI, and OpenAI advocated for pacing AI development. They cannot slow down alone. I urge you to demand that your government produce a serious AI safety agreement that provides enough time and confidence to safeguard the world and all her peoples.

Rosie Mackean’s quick and easy recipe for lamb chops with courgettes, walnuts and yoghurt | Quick and easy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:00:58 UTC
21:00:58 KST

Entertaining midweek can feel daunting, but if you employ a couple of tricks, things can very quickly go from mayhem to magic. First, choose a dish that goes perfectly with good bread, so your carb is covered. Second, choose a protein that is quick to cook and great for sharing – little lamb chops are perfect for this, while also being a treat. And, finally, use other ingredients that don’t need much help. Here, the walnuts just get cooked in butter and the lamb juices, the courgettes are simply boiled and dressed, and the yoghurt is, well, yoghurt. Suddenly you’ve conjured up a masterpiece ready for many hands to dig in.
Lamb chops with courgettes, walnuts and yoghurt
Prep 10 min
 Cook 30 min
 Serves 4
For the chops
800g french-trimmed lamb chops (ie, 12-14 chops from 2 lamb racks – I like small, leaner ones) 
1½ tbsp flaky salt 
1 tsp black pepper
  1 tsp ground cumin
  1 tsp ground coriander
  ½ tsp ground cinnamon
  2 tbsp vegetable oil
  90g salted butter
  2 garlic cloves, unpeeled and bashed 
  1 banana shallot, peeled and sliced
100g walnuts
½ tsp smoked paprika
  Juice of ½ lemon
For the courgettes
1 generous pinch flaky sea salt, plus fine salt for the boiling water
1kg courgettes, cut into roughly 1½cm-thick slices
75g extra-virgin olive oil
Zest of 1 unwaxed lemon
  1 garlic clove, peeled and grated 
1 big handful fresh mint, leaves picked
To serve
500g greek yoghurt
Flatbreads
If the chops are in the shape of a rack, use a sharp knife to separate them. Sprinkle the salt and spices all over the chops, then rub in and leave to sit at room temperature for a few minutes.
Meanwhile, bring a large pan of water to a boil and season it generously with salt. Tip in the courgettes and simmer for seven minutes, until just tender. Combine the olive oil, lemon zest and garlic in a large bowl and use a slotted spoon to transfer the cooked courgettes straight into it. Stir, season with salt and leave to sit while you cook the chops.
Put a cast-iron (or nonstick) pan on a high heat. Add the oil and the chops, taking care to render any thicker bits of fat before searing them on their flat sides for two minutes each. You may need to do this in batches; pop any seared chops on a rack while you finish the rest.
Return all the chops to the pan with about half the butter and the bashed garlic cloves, then let the butter foam and bubble while you gently spoon it over the lamb for another minute. Lift out the chops and set aside to rest.
Add the remaining butter to the pan with the shallot, walnuts and smoked paprika, turn down the heat to medium and let the butter foam and brown as the walnuts toast for about six minutes. Add a squeeze of lemon juice to stop the butter cooking further, then take the pan off the heat.
Stir the mint into the courgettes, then scoop the yoghurt on to plates. Pile the courgettes around it, then lay the chops on top. Pour over the walnuts and their smoky butter and serve with plenty of flatbread for smooshing and sandwiching.
- 
  Good Time Cooking: Show-Stopping Menus for Easy Entertaining, by Rosie Mackean, is published by Pavilion Books at £26. To order a copy for £23.40, visit guardianbookshop.com

There’s a surprisingly simple reason for England’s high antidepressant use: lots of people need them | Dean Burnett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:00:58 UTC
21:00:58 KST

A new NHS report has revealed the highest ever levels of antidepressant use recorded in England, with roughly one in seven people prescribed an antidepressant item in 2025-26. This has resulted in a swathe of media coverage expressing alarm over the increase, with questions about what could, or should, be done to reverse the trend.
Such a high level of antidepressant use should, of course, prompt concern and reflection. But the popular claim that has taken hold is that antidepressant use is too high because of “overprescribing”, as Dr John Read, a professor of clinical psychology, says in the Daily Mail. This is the idea that patients are being prescribed antidepressants when they shouldn’t be, or when better, safer alternatives are available.
This idea is worth challenging – but first it’s important to consider how we got here. The increase in antidepressant use is strongly correlated with a rise in diagnoses in common disorders including depression and anxiety. Much of this is the afterlife of the Covid-19 pandemic and its associated lockdowns: according to ONS data, across Britain, the rate of depressive symptoms in adults doubled during the crisis to almost one in five. As of April 2025, the figures remain almost as high. This surge has particularly affected young people in England, with one in four having a mental health condition, according to NHS data.
So with this rise, an increase in antidepressant use is predictable. Lockdown, however necessary for public health, has had lasting implications for the country’s wellbeing.
But it’s not only the consequences of the pandemic. What this data also indicates is that persistent regional inequalities have a worsening effect on mental health outcomes, and therefore antidepressant use. The most dramatic increases in antidepressant use are found in the most impoverished regions of England, while more affluent regions report modest levels of antidepressant use.
The highest rate of antidepressant use was seen in patients treated under the North East and North Cumbria integrated care board, with 200 in every 1,000 people prescribed antidepressant medication. Consider that this ICB contains some of the country’s most deprived areas, which have “faced longstanding inequalities and poor health for decades”, and you have further proof of something that has long been clear: poverty is inextricably linked to poorer mental health outcomes. One key element that underpins many cases of depression, anxiety and related disorders is chronic stress. It’s our brain’s achilles heel. And a guaranteed source of chronic stress is a life of constant poverty.
The argument presented against wide antidepressant prescription, as laid out in the Daily Mail, is that “doctors [are] increasingly being expected to treat wider social and life problems with medication”. Such a position assumes that a neat division can be drawn between these social problems and the mental health conditions they produce.
These socioeconomic factors also explain why antidepressants are used more and more as a first-line treatment. It’s all well and good to argue that less severe cases of depression should be treated with talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy, but these involve regular one-one-one sessions with trained counsellors, and the wait for such interventions on the NHS regularly lasts months, if not years.
In the most deprived areas, access to such services is even more difficult, whereas for the most part, antidepressants are accessible straight away. It should also be said that GPs follow strict clinical guidelines for prescribing antidepressants, as set out by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. These state that practitioners should “not routinely offer antidepressant medication as first-line treatment for less severe depression unless that is the person’s preference”. So it is clear that GPs are not simply handing out pills, but rather responding to legitimate patient demand.
Of course, antidepressants can’t be a magic bullet – mental health services are evidently in need of deep reform and increased funding. We have already heard pledges to improve services, including with the government’s announcement in May this year of a new mental health strategy in England to drive a shift from crisis intervention to preventive care. And there are already technological interventions being recommended, including digital therapies for depression and anxiety that “could free up thousands of NHS therapist hours”.
The government’s callout for frontline workers, clinicians and mental health experts to share views on transforming mental health care shows that there are likely several creative solutions to tackle this crisis, without the need for medication. Still, there should be no doubt about the simple reality: more people than ever are taking antidepressants because they genuinely need them.
So the point here is not that the record rates of antidepressant use in England isn’t a problem. It undoubtedly is. But to determine that this is due to “overprescription” is to mistake a symptom for a much deeper social and economic crisis as its cause.
- 
  Dean Burnett is a doctor of neuroscience and the author of The Idiot Brain and Emotional Ignorance

Private touch matters more than public affection for relationship quality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:00:49 UTC
21:00:49 KST

Being on the same page as a romantic partner about physical affection is linked to a healthier relationship, especially behind closed doors. A recent study published in Personal Relationships found that couples who share similar levels of comfort with touch report higher relationship well-being. The importance of this alignment varies depending on whether partners are in public or private spaces.
Physical touch between romantic partners is associated with numerous physiological and psychological benefits. Holding hands, hugging, and kissing can lower stress levels, support immune system function, and foster a sense of security. Engaging in physical affection is known to improve cardiovascular functioning and increase the release of oxytocin, a hormone heavily involved in social bonding.
When individuals desire more affection than they receive, they can experience what psychologists call affection deprivation. This state is frequently linked to relationship dissatisfaction and a feeling of distance from a partner. An unfulfilled desire for touch is associated with tension and inhibited communication.
Psychology researchers Sabrina Sgambati, Diane Holmberg, and Karen L. Blair wanted to understand how variations in comfort with physical affection might relate to a couple’s overall happiness. They explored whether average comfort levels, as well as discrepancies between partners, could predict relationship well-being. A sense of shared reality generally reduces the need for constant negotiation in a relationship, which helps mitigate conflict.
The research team also investigated whether these dynamics shifted depending on the setting. Public spaces introduce social pressures that do not exist in the privacy of a home. Some individuals might enjoy physical affection in private but feel awkward engaging in it around family members, friends, or strangers.
This contextual difference is relevant for same-sex couples. Experiencing marginalization frequently fosters heightened vigilance regarding public displays of affection. Same-sex partners often dedicate more cognitive energy toward monitoring their surroundings for safety, potentially altering how public touch relates to relationship satisfaction.
To examine these questions, the investigators first analyzed survey data from 1,832 individuals in romantic relationships. Participants rated their own comfort with physical affection, as well as how comfortable they believed their partner was. They answered these questions twice, once thinking about private settings and again considering public environments.
The researchers calculated an average perceived comfort score for each couple, along with a score representing the gap between the participant’s comfort level and their partner’s presumed comfort level. They then compared these affection scores against participants’ self-reported relationship quality. This quality metric included elements like trust, intimacy, passion, and overall satisfaction.
Higher average comfort with physical affection consistently predicted better relationship well-being. This positive association held true for both public and private settings. When both partners were perceived to be highly comfortable with touch, the relationship tended to be stronger.
When looking at disparities between partners, the researchers found that larger perceived gaps in comfort levels were linked to lower relationship well-being. If one partner felt very comfortable with touch and believed their partner was uncomfortable, relationship satisfaction tended to be lower. This negative association was particularly pronounced in public settings once average comfort levels were taken into account.
The environment played a central role in the strength of these associations. Feeling highly comfortable sharing affection in private was more closely connected to strong relationship well-being than feeling comfortable sharing affection in public. The researchers suggested that as long as couples can compensate for a lack of public affection by connecting in private, the relationship fares relatively well. Discomfort in public can easily be attributed to personal decorum or cultural norms rather than a lack of love.
When comparing mixed-sex and same-sex relationships, the overall patterns were largely similar. Higher comfort levels and smaller discrepancies generally mapped onto better relationship quality for both groups. The underlying mechanics of how affection relates to happiness did not drastically change based on the partners’ genders.
Some specific variations did emerge. Individuals in same-sex relationships reported lower average comfort with public affection. They also perceived larger gaps between themselves and their partners in public settings. The researchers attributed this difference to the ongoing social stigma and safety concerns same-sex couples often navigate.
Additionally, individuals in same-sex relationships were able to maintain slightly higher relationship well-being than mixed-sex couples when their average comfort with private affection was low. The researchers hypothesized that same-sex couples, who regularly restrict public affection for safety, might develop alternative, non-physical ways to express love. These communication strategies might carry over into private settings, making physical touch slightly less essential for their overall satisfaction.
The researchers then analyzed a second dataset comprising 86 couples, which allowed them to compare the self-reported scores of both partners directly. This dyadic analysis evaluated actual similarities and differences in comfort, rather than relying on one partner’s assumptions.
The results for this secondary analysis mostly mirrored the initial findings. Higher actual average comfort with private affection again predicted better relationship well-being. Alignment in private remained a strong indicator of a happy couple.
Actual discrepancies in public comfort levels were not associated with relationship well-being. Actual average comfort in public also failed to predict better relationship quality when other variables were factored into the analysis. In other words, a partner’s true feelings about public touch mattered less than what their significant other believed they felt.
This divergence suggests that an individual’s perception of their partner’s comfort might matter more to their relationship satisfaction than their partner’s actual, self-reported comfort level. A partner who is slightly less comfortable with public touch might engage in it anyway to please their significant other. This compliance creates a perception of alignment that helps maintain harmony.
Because the research relies on observational survey data, the results cannot establish a one-way path of influence. A mutual comfort with physical affection might improve relationship well-being, but it is equally likely that being in a happy, secure relationship increases a couple’s comfort with physical affection. The two factors likely reinforce each other continuously over time.
The analysis of actual partner differences relied on a sample of 86 couples, which might not have possessed the statistical power to detect smaller effects. If actual discrepancies do influence relationship quality, the associations might be too subtle to appear in a dataset of this size. Larger studies involving both members of a couple could provide more precise insights into how actual, rather than perceived, discrepancies operate.
The current analysis also excluded individuals in gender-diverse relationships due to a low number of participants in that demographic category. Future research with larger, more diverse populations could investigate how gender expression and fluidity influence comfort with affection. This line of inquiry could clarify how shifting social judgments impact couples who might be perceived differently depending on the context.
The study, “In Sync? Assessing Partners’ Similarities in Comfort With Physical Affection–Sharing as a Predictor of Relationship Well-Being,” was authored by Sabrina Sgambati, Diane Holmberg, and Karen L. Blair.
