Finland enters French-led European nuclear deterrence initiative
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:36:04 EEST
20:36:04 KST

Finland has joined France’s European nuclear deterrence initiative, expanding defence cooperation with Paris while ruling out the stationing of nuclear weapons on Finnish territory in peacetime.
President Alexander Stubb said on Monday that the initiative was intended to strengthen European security, increase Europe’s responsibility for its own defence and reduce the risk of escalation.
Finland and France issued a joint statement confirming the decision after confidential talks at political and official level.
The initiative, launched by French President Emmanuel Macron in March, extends the European dimension of France’s nuclear deterrence. Finland becomes the tenth country to join, alongside Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Germany, Britain, Belgium, the Netherlands, Italy and Greece.
Stubb stressed that Finland would not host nuclear weapons in peacetime.
“There would be no sense in that,” he told reporters. He declined to speculate about possible arrangements during a war.
France will retain full control over its nuclear arsenal and will continue to decide what constitutes a threat to its vital interests. The initiative does not provide participating countries with a French nuclear umbrella or collective defence guarantees.
Finland’s main nuclear deterrence remains based on NATO and the extended deterrence provided by the United States, Stubb said.
The French initiative does not replace Nato’s nuclear deterrence and is not intended to duplicate it.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said Finland’s participation would deepen bilateral defence ties with France and strengthen national security.
“The French initiative is different from Nato’s nuclear deterrence,” Häkkänen said in a ministry statement. “The participating countries will not have obligations comparable to Nato’s collective defence.”
France is also not asking participating countries to contribute to the cost of maintaining its nuclear arsenal.
A joint working group will be established to define the practical forms of cooperation. Stubb said the process could last between 10 and 15 years.
Stubb said access to information about French nuclear deterrence was one reason Finland chose to participate.
He also said the involvement of Sweden, Norway and Denmark had influenced Finland’s decision, as the Nordic countries share security interests in northern Europe.
Russia has opposed the French initiative. Asked about Moscow’s likely response to Finland’s participation, Stubb said there was no need to overstate the situation.
“Keep a cool head,” he said.
The decision received broad parliamentary backing, according to Stubb, although the Left Alliance has said it opposes Finland joining the initiative.
The announcement comes as Finland and France expand defence cooperation in other areas. Stubb said France had already committed forces to activities in Finland and that the nuclear deterrence initiative added another element to the relationship.
Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot are also due to sign a strategic partnership document in Helsinki on Monday.

Russia says Gulf instability rapidly worsening global oil market situation

Elena Teslova
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
The situation in global oil markets is rapidly deteriorating amid instability in the Persian Gulf, with major volumes of oil being removed from international supply, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday.
Speaking at a press briefing in Moscow, Peskov pointed out that "a huge amount of oil is dropping out of the market."
"Just with the disruption of the oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia, more than 4% of global supplies have been knocked out of the global market. This cannot but have the most serious consequences, and it cannot but cause concern among the world’s economies," he said.
Peskov said Russia had introduced a ban on exports of oil products in order to ensure adequate supplies for its domestic market.
"As our domestic market becomes reliably saturated, the issue of lifting such a ban will come onto the agenda, and then an additional volume [of oil products] will again be directed to global markets," he noted.
Peskov said the removal of Russian oil products from international exports was also affecting global markets.
The comments came as Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline remained shut following an attack, threatening to further reduce global supplies and push energy prices higher. The pipeline has been carrying about 4 million to 5 million barrels per day, equivalent to roughly 4%-5% of global supply.
 
Ukraine conflict, Finland, BRICS
Peskov also welcomed calls for Kyiv to stop strikes on Russian civilian economic infrastructure, including an appeal by US President Donald Trump to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt attacks on Russian diesel production amid concerns over the impact on the US economy.
"Any call to the Kyiv regime to stop strikes on civilian economic infrastructure can only be welcomed," he said.
Asked about reports in Western media saying Ukraine was losing the conflict, Peskov said he believed the course of developments on the battlefield was increasingly clear to Western analysts and professionals.
"It is becoming increasingly obvious to Western analysts and professionals that Russia, based on the dynamics on the fronts, is consistently moving toward achieving its goals," he said.
According to the official, it had previously been a "big misconception" to argue that Ukraine had the potential to withstand Russian pressure.
He added that some people still held that view, arguing that "serious analysts and professionals were increasingly drawing a different conclusion from developments on the battlefield."
"Some still retain this erroneous point of view. But professionals and truly serious analysts are increasingly realizing, based on the dynamics observed on the fronts, that Russia is indeed improving its positions day by day and consistently moving toward achieving its goals," he said.
Peskov said Russian President Vladimir Putin had positively assessed China’s and India’s readiness to contribute to efforts to settle the Ukraine conflict.
He added that any country could use its influence with Kyiv to encourage greater flexibility and contribute to bringing the conflict closer to a settlement.
"In general, any country can use its influence on the Kyiv regime to encourage it toward greater flexibility, which would be a significant contribution to the settlement," he said.
Peskov declined to comment on Finland’s decision to join a French-backed project for an advanced nuclear deterrence concept.
"I don’t quite understand what this concept is, to be honest. I still have to learn some details. Therefore, I would refrain from making any comments," he said.
Peskov said the expansion of BRICS bloc and specific candidates for membership had not been discussed at the group’s recent summit in New Delhi.
Russia, he added, supported Cuba’s desire to join the group and welcomed Havana’s intention to work within the group.

UP assembly elections and fight for Muslim votes: Decoding SP, Congress's Owaisi problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:31:36 UTC
20:31:36 KST

"I am ready to join hands. I am ready to form an alliance. Today is the time to talk. Don't cry later after the elections are over. We don't want the BJP to come to power again.”
Asaduddin Owaisi, AIMIM
That was Asaduddin Owaisi's outreach-cum-warning to Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav in July at a rally in Moradabad while he launched AIMIM’s campaign for the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections due early next year.Seeking alliance with opposition parties is now a part of Owaisi’s playbook to counter allegations of being a vote-cutter and the B-team of the BJP. We have seen AIMIM adopt similar strategy in other states like Maharashtra and Bihar. In both these states, it went all out to seek space in larger opposition alliances before deciding to contest on its own when its offer was rejected. Then the "rejection: became a part of Owaisi's campaign: we asked you to come in, you kept us out, so don't blame us for what happens next."So, when Owaisi reached out to Samajwadi Party in July, it was on expected lines and did not come as a surprise. But there is now a twist in the tale.Owaisi’s Uttar Pradesh plans suffered a jolt this month when one of his most trusted aides and the party’s national spokesperson Syed Asim Waqar dumped the party to join the Congress.Waqar, who rose to prominence defending the AIMIM and its politics, was a prominent voice for AIMIM in Uttar Pradesh and hence his crossing over to the Congress potentially impacts Owaisi's bid to make electoral inroads in UP.
But more than his exit, it was his parting remarks that will bother Owaisi. “Being in the AIMIM for so many years, I felt that we pay lip service by stating that the BJP must be removed, but on the ground, we don't fight the BJP; we fight the Congress, the SP; we are fighting every other person who wants to remove the BJP,” Waqar said when asked about his decision to leave the AIMIM.Justifying his switch, Waqar said, “If we (AIMIM) keep fighting the opposition and do not allow it to blossom, then we are helping the BJP. I have decided that if we are true nationalists and want to remove the BJP honestly, then our objective should be to fight the BJP. If we are fighting the enemies of the BJP, then we are friends of the BJP. In reality, if someone is fighting the BJP across the country, it is Congress, Rahul Gandhi and his team."Now, this is precisely the point which the opposition parties make against Owaisi and his AIMIM.
AIMIM’s UP plans
Uttar Pradesh has been a difficult story for Owaisi. His AIMIM failed to win a single seat in the 2022 assembly elections in the state. And that makes the 2027 challenge a real test of whether the Bihar formula will work or whether Akhilesh is right to believe that AIMIM is a rival he can afford to ignore.Even while offering to join hands with Akhilesh, Owaisi chose to kick off AIMIM's 2027 campaign from Matera in Bahraich, a seat held by the Samajwadi Party. He also announced AIMIM’s candidate from the seat making his intent very clear.Owaisi questioned what SP leaders had done for the area despite getting Muslim votes, while saying AIMIM was ready for an alliance only if it was treated with 'respect' and given 'equal status'.The party has dropped enough signals to suggest that it is preparing for a much bigger push in UP in 2027. The party has also divided the state into zones and appointed regional in-charges as part of its attempt to strengthen the organisation before the election.AIMIM accepted that its performance was not up to the mark in 2022 but asserted that the party has spent the last few years trying to correct that.
Bihar is AIMIM’s strongest base outside Telangana.
AIMIM's Uttar Pradesh president Shaukat Ali has said the party could contest around 200 seats if it fights alone. He has also kept the door open for a possible understanding with the BSP."Our natural alliance, if we were to forge one, would be with the BSP. Muslims and Dalits together account for nearly 40% of the vote share, enough to defeat both the SP and BJP," Ali said.The Samajwadi Party and the Congress will keep a close watch on AIMIM’s BSP outreach as it can have the potential to disrupt a lot of political calculations in the state. However, for now Mayawati has made it clear that her BSP will not forge any alliances with any party for elections.
What makes UP challenge both interesting and difficult
The 2027 assembly elections in UP is likely to see a very keen contest for Muslim votes. The switching of sides by Asim Waqar exposes the keen contest among the non-BJP parties for support of Muslims in the upcoming elections.
Non-Yadav OBCs form the biggest bloc in UP’s caste arithmetic.
The Congress, which would consider this AIMIM import as a big boost to its prospects, had contested the 2024 Lok Sabha elections in alliance with the Samajwadi Party, and, as of now, they are both part of INDIA bloc ahead of next year’s assembly elections.But this alliance has not stopped the two parties from taking measures to consolidate their individual support bases. Last month, the Samajwadi Party got a boost when the son-in-law of Congress MP from UP’s Saharanpur Imran Masood joined the party in the presence of Akhilesh Yadav. Imran Masood has been very vocal against SP and its chief Akhilesh Yadav accusing them of imposing as the ‘big-brother’ in SP-Congress alliance for the 2027 UP polls.For the SP, the Alpsankhyaks (read Muslims) form an important component of Akhilesh Yadav’s PDA outreach. In fact, his success in Uttar Pradesh till now has been largely powered by the Yadavs and the Muslims. And while, Akhilesh desperately tries to broaden his support base by reaching out to the Dalits, women and even the Pandits, he cannot make big gains without the support of Muslims.However, that does not stop the Congress from making its own outreach to the community in a bid to try and win them back. After all, for several decades the Muslims had contributed to the electoral success of the Congress. It was only with the rise of regional parties that they drifted away from the grand-old-party. So, it will naturally be happy with Asim Waqar on its side.The AIMIM, which is the third pole of Muslim politics in the state, will try to take advantage of the posturing and war of words between the two alliance partners as it tries to find its space in the state.AIMIM has shown that it can become a serious player where its support is concentrated. What it has not yet shown is that it can do the same in Uttar Pradesh, where the Samajwadi Party remains the main beneficiary of Muslim votes against the BJP.
Where AIMIM matters and where it doesn't
In the 2023 Telangana assembly election, the party contested nine seats and won seven, underlining how strong its hold remains in parts of the state.Bihar has been its most successful experiment outside Telangana till now. The party managed to win five seats in 2020 and repeated the number in 2025, mainly in the Seemanchal region.In Maharashtra, AIMIM has pockets of support but won just one assembly seat in 2024. In Uttar Pradesh, the challenge has been tougher. In the 2022 assembly election, AIMIM contested 96 seats but failed to win any. Its statewide vote share remained below 1%.
AIMIM’s Rajasthan experiment
Owaisi’s move to contest the Panchayat and Municipal body elections in Rajasthan shows the party’s intent to expand its base in states where it was not a player till now. The AIMIM chief maintains that the state needs a strong third political alternative apart from the ruling BJP and the Congress which have been the dominant players in state’s politics till now.In a bid to disturb the duoploy, Owaisi has announced that if Rashtriya Loktantrik Party chief Hanuman Beniwal emerges as a third force, the AIMIM will support him and work together to challenge both major political parties.Owaisi said, “Hanuman Beniwal and AIMIM together will make the lives of BJP and Congress leaders difficult.” He also appealed to voters to support AIMIM candidates and RLP candidates contesting elections on the party’s bottle symbol.
The BJP would be smiling either way
While the Congress and the other opposition parties keep an eye on AIMIM’s political moves, the BJP perhaps would not be worried much.When Owaisi had reached out to Akhilesh, BJP wasted no time in mocking the proposal. Former BJP spokesperson Shehzad Poonawalla had then called it a 'friend request' to Akhilesh and accused both parties of vote-bank politics.
Akhilesh Yadav and Owaisi have long competed in appeasement politics. Now they have set aside the contest over who will be the bigger 'bhaijaan' and are looking at a 'bhaijaan collaboration'. Owaisi is effectively sending Akhilesh ji a friend request. They are two sides of the same coin
Asaduddin Owaisi, AIMIM
For the BJP, Owaisi can be useful either way, more so in Uttar Pradesh.If AIMIM contests separately and takes away even a small number of votes from SP-Congress in close seats, the BJP may benefit. If AIMIM joins the alliance, the BJP can use Owaisi's presence to sharpen its attack on the opposition over minority appeasement.
Catch-22 for opposition parties
The opposition parties are reluctant to accept Owaisi’s offer to ensure that non-BJP votes, especially of the Muslims, do not split. They know that Owaisi’s offer is like a double-edged sword.Most of these opposition parties like the RJD in Bihar, Samajwadi Party in Uttar Pradesh have banked heavily on the support of Muslims for their politics. If they accept AIMIM as an ally, they fear that Muslims will back Owaisi and gradually this will weaken their own minorities’ politics.
Second, any opposition alliance with AIMIM will give the BJP a very strong weapon to engineer reverse polarisation. Since Owaisi is known for a very aggressive hardline brand of politics on issues concerning the minorities, the opposition will find it difficult to dissociate itself from the AIMIM. And this will give the BJP an opportunity to mobilise the Hindus against the opposition parties and eventually corner them.

Often juggling breaking news, long-form explainers and the everyday chaos of the newsroom, she is usually managing stress, chasing clarity and trying to log off on time (rarely successful). She also cares deeply about stories around women’s rights and social change, while two very opinionated dogs make sure she never truly switches off.

Russia Launches Kalibr Cruise Missiles Directly From Base, Ukraine Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:31:23 UTC
20:31:23 KST

Russia has been launching its naval-based Kalibr cruise missiles directly from port via its missile carriers for four months in a row, according to Ukraine.
Ukrainian Navy spokesperson Dmytro Pletenchuk noted the new trend on television, according to state media Ukrinform on Monday, Sept. 14.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Even the use of cruise missile carriers that launch Kalibrs takes place directly at the base, that is, right in the harbor. This is a trend that has been observed for the fourth month in a row,” Pletenchuk said.
The Kalibr, with a reported range of 1,500-2,500 km (932-1,553 miles), is the mainstay in the Russian Navy’s arsenal and have been frequently used against Ukrainian cities since 2022.
The missiles are typically launched at sea by Russian warships and submarines, with Ukrainian channels closely monitoring their movements ahead of potential missile strikes.
Pletenchuk noted the peculiar nature and difficulty in launching them from the harbor, before warning that the missiles’ danger should not be overlooked.
“Submarines, for example, are also not so easy to use. To do this, they need to dive. I still can’t imagine how they can use them in the mode in which they are currently launching them,” Pletenchuk continued.
“Let’s not downplay the danger: we are assuming the maximum – four carriers, but realistic figures would probably be two surface carriers,” he added.
Canada Considers Joining EU €90 Billion Ukraine Loan
Pletenchuk also estimated that Russia has four vessels capable of launching the Kalibr missiles from the Black Sea – two Buyan-M-class warships and two Varshavyanka-class submarines.
On Sept. 9, Ukraine claimed to have hit the Admiral Essen, a Russian Admiral Grigorovich-class frigate capable of launching Kalibr missiles, at Russia’s Novorossiysk.
Pletenchuk also noted the decreased frequency of Russia’s cruise missile launches, saying that two had been documented this month, compared with a summer high of three.
Based on Kyiv Post’s tallies, Russia launched at least 251 cruise missiles in July, with massive strikes documented on three days (July 2, July 6, and July 30), where 40, 55 and 65 cruise missiles were launched, respectively, based on the Ukrainian Air Force’s morning updates.
The rest of July consisted of occasional cruise missile launches of up to 16 per day.

China warns against AI ‘fear-mongering’ as US tech leaders call for slower development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:31:11 UTC
20:31:11 KST

Faisal Mahmud
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
China on Monday warned against “fear-mongering” over artificial intelligence development after prominent US technology executives backed calls to slow advances in frontier AI and introduce stronger safeguards.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said AI development concerned the “common well-being of all humanity” and urged countries to “promote its open, inclusive and universally beneficial development.”
Guo said "fear mongering," confrontation and engaging in “malicious competition” would disrupt global AI governance, which serves no one's interests.
He was responding to a question about calls by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Elon Musk and other technology executives to slow AI development, as well as Amodei’s claim that China’s advances in the technology pose a threat to US national security.
Some of the most prominent figures in the AI industry have backed Amodei after he published an essay, We Must Pace the Frontier, calling for slower development of the most advanced AI systems and stronger safeguards.
Musk said Amodei was “right,” while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said pacing frontier development had become a major subject of recent discussions at his company. 
Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis said Amodei’s proposal pointed toward the “right path forward.”
Amodei argued that rapid advances could increase risks ranging from humans losing control of increasingly capable AI systems to cyberattacks, biological threats and economic disruption, warning that commercial competition could intensify those dangers.

====================================================================================================

UK sanctions on settlements unlikely to deter Israel: Caabu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:31:07 UTC
20:31:07 KST

Breadcrumb
UK settlement sanctions a policy shift but unlikely to deter Israel, says Caabu
The Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu) has warned against excessive optimism over the sanctions regime that the UK and several other European countries plan to impose on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank and Golan Heights saying the measures are unlikely to deter Israeli aggression and settlement expansion.
Caabu Director Chris Doyle described the British government's announcement of the forthcoming sanctions as reflecting a "major reset of the UK government policy" towards Israel, but added that he did not expect the Israeli government to respond to pressure to halt either settlement expansion or deadly violence against Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
In an interview with The New Arab, Doyle said the UK's acknowledgement of acts of ethnic cleansing committed by settlers in the occupied West Bank, together with its intention to impose sanctions on settlements there, represented a "transformation, shift of policy and change in substance" that "actually puts accountability into the equation that takes action that is sanctioning these settlements because they are illegal".
'Clear determination' to go forward
On the eve of Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's appearance before Parliament to announce the sanctions regime last week, Doyle attended a meeting with Stephen Doughty, Minister for the Middle East at the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO).
He said he emerged from the meeting with "the belief that there is a clear determination to move forward" and act "without hesitation" in dealing with Israel. He added that he believed that Miliband himself "is also serious" about implementing the measures that were announced.
Doyle also attached "legal significance" to Britain's acknowledgement that the Israeli occupation and presence in Palestine are illegal.
He added, however, that the anticipated British measures do not amount to the level of punishment Israel deserves for ethnic cleansing, crimes against humanity, and the occupation.
But he said the measures showed that "the problem has at least been identified somewhat more truthfully, in the West Bank but also Gaza".
Therefore, he said, "the necessary measures to deal with this can be taken, maybe step by step", reiterating his view that the upcoming measures are "serious".
Doyle noted that the British government was "quite clear that they did not envisage a complete trade ban with Israel". Nonetheless, he asked: "who knows where things will be in six months, a year's time?"
Greater atrocities feared
Caabu considers the current British measures insufficient to punish Israel for settlement activity, even though it views them as "moving in the right direction".
"We have made our demands very clear," Doyle said. "We believe that there should be a full, complete ban on all dealings, all trade with settlements and financial services being offered to settlements".
He also argued that "the UK should not continue with business as usual in its relationship with the State of Israel" and that, "at a minimum, Britain should suspend the trade agreement with Israel, so that no Israeli products arrive (in the UK) under preferences".
"We should not be trading as usual with a state that is committing such serious violations of international law," he added.
Miliband's pledges included working to establish an operational sanctions regime within nine months. Doyle expressed optimism that the promised regime would not be weakened during the relevant ministries' review of the drafting process or because of exemptions for religious reasons mentioned in the ministerial statement.
He attributed the length of the process, as he understood it, to "ensuring that this ban cannot be challenged in the courts".
Despite Caabu's welcoming of the UK announcement, Doyle remained pessimistic about Israel's response and the likelihood of it changing its policies.
He said he was "certain this will not happen, under this government (led by Benjamin Netanyahu) or any likely government".
The Caabu director added that pressuring Israel enough to change its policies would necessitate "additional measures to prove that this (Israel's stance) cannot pass". He said that "when the (British) government is ready to implement the measures it announced, who knows what it might be prepared (to do) if Israel, for example, goes ahead with E1, conducts even greater atrocities in the West Bank?"
However, whatever Britain's capacity to act and influence, Doyle stressed that it would not be enough to "stop and deter Israel from continuing" its settlement programme, which he linked to the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. He added that "further international action, including by Britain, will almost certainly be required".
No to 'business as usual'
Doyle also hoped that the upcoming British measures would be a step towards reassessing overall relations with Israel, saying relations "should not continue as usual" following "Israel's serious violations of international law, including the genocide in Gaza".
He also hoped that Andy Burnham's government's towards the Middle East in general would be influenced by his experience of visiting the West Bank, which Caabu co-organised with the Labour Friends of Palestine group for Burnham and several MPs in September 2012.
Doyle said Caabu's activities had helped in "building a much better understanding of certain (Middle Eastern) issues within the British Parliament", including Syria and Lebanon, as well as raising debates over the US war on Iran and ways to address issues such as Islamophobia.
A parliamentary bloc against Israel
Caabu has sought over the past 59 years to "stimulate a debate on the Middle East and its issues based on accurate knowledge".
Its work has included hosting speakers from across the Middle East to address British politicians and providing opportunities for them to connect with influential British media outlets.
Doyle said this was "one of the reasons why you see, for example, a very strong parliamentary bloc demanding action against Israel regarding the atrocities it commits in Gaza, as well as in the West Bank, Lebanon, and its role in the war against Iran".
Caabu also continues to build relations with British MPs. At its most recent meeting with MPs in June, Doyle used maps and data to explain the dangerous consequences of Israel's new E1 settlement project in the occupied West Bank. Extremist Israeli minister Bezalel Smotrich has previously boasted that the project makes a Palestinian state impossible.
'Dehumanised' peoples
Despite its efforts, Caabu believes Britain's policy towards the Middle East, regardless of which party is in power, does not contribute sufficiently to conflict-resolution efforts or support for human rights and civil society in the region.
Doyle attributed this to a lack of "informed debate and rational policymaking" based on accurate information about countries in the region and developments there.
He cited the US-Israeli war on Iran, which began last February, as a clear example. Doyle said British officials "believed absolute nonsense" that prevailed within the administration of US President Donald Trump regarding the war, the fragility of Iran's ruling regime and the disposition of its people.
He said "there are many people in the British political system who shared these views, who genuinely believed, somehow, that the regime would be easily toppled", adding that they "still believe that some outfit had been toppled (and) there would have been some very pro-Western, reasonable government to take its place".
Doyle said very few people in Britain and the West "were certainly aware before the war, and perhaps still are now, of the type of state Iran represents, with all its different identity groups".
He attributed this to "a great deal (among the British and the West) of dehumanising the peoples of the region", which he said had led to "the widespread presuming that the people in Iran would not be able to put up a fight against the United States and Israel, and that Iran would not possess a reasonable, effective strategy to counter".
However, he said the Iranian leadership "proved that wrong, whether we like it or not".
Doyle said this reflected "a lot of very naive assumptions about the Middle East, [and] a lack of understanding of that, the differences between communities, the huge variety in terms of life, ways of life, different sects, ethnicities, and the like".
Caabu believes Arab countries themselves bear some responsibility for the lack of understanding of their positions in Britain, despite longstanding historical ties between the two sides.
'Honest and genuine' dialogue
Doyle said Arabs "can play a more effective role in trying to build an understanding of the region" in the West.
However, he said "in the Arab world, there needs to be more united positions on certain issues, and sometimes there needs to be a greater clarity to some of their positions on what is going on".
He also criticised the lack of Arab consensus, which he attributed partly to the absence of "a very honest dialogue, genuine dialogue, between Arab states".
He said there should be such dialogue "between Arab states and their partners, to build, construct, and develop more sophisticated and effective policy approaches".
At the same time, Doyle said the Arab world needed "a better understanding of both Europe and the United States".
He stressed that responsibility did not lie with governments alone, saying "there should be a collective effort" by civil society organisations and government institutions "to have an informed debate on all of these issues on the way forward, on many challenges".

Germany to expand intelligence-gathering fleet, defense minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Ayhan Simsek
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Germany will order a fourth new reconnaissance ship for its navy, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said on Monday at a keel-laying ceremony for the third vessel of the same class in the Baltic port of Wolgast.
A draft budget for the additional ship has been submitted to parliament for approval, he said at the Rheinmetall yard, according to German media reports.
Pistorius said the ships can pick up signals and sounds that other vessels cannot. He described them as vital tools for building a clearer picture at sea, adding that they collect and evaluate a wide range of maritime signals.
German officials have long argued that the navy needs better tools to monitor the Baltic Sea, where undersea cables and energy links have been damaged and Russian military activity has risen since the Ukraine war began in 2022.

Kharkiv Holds First Pride March Since Russia’s Full-Scale Invasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:29:47 UTC
20:29:47 KST

About 200 people joined KharkivPride’s first march on foot since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, walking through underground metro stations, before holding a protest near the regional administration building.
The 500-meter (550-yard) march took place on Saturday, along a route designed for safety in the northeastern city, which remains close to the front line. Participants included civil society activists, LGBTQ+ allies, active-duty service members, and veterans.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The procession began on the platform of the Derzhprom metro station, continued through an underground passage to the Universytet station, and ended near an exit from the subway system.
Participants then staged a stationary protest outside the Kharkiv regional administration building, a location that organizers described as symbolic for public demonstrations in the city during the full-scale war.
The march was closed to the general public. Participants registered in advance and underwent security checks. Organizers said they worked with regional police to prepare several possible scenarios and planned the route around wartime security risks.
KharkivPride said it remains Ukraine’s only Pride event held in a front-line city.
Organizational demands
The event highlighted four demands through separate performances.
In the first, participants displayed a 28-meter (92-foot) scroll containing proposed amendments to Ukraine’s draft Civil Code. KharkivPride argues that the current proposal contains discriminatory provisions and should be withdrawn.
Canada Considers Joining EU €90 Billion Ukraine Loan
“More than four months have passed since the first reading of the draft new Civil Code,” KharkivPride co-organizer Yakiv Lavrynetz said. “We prepared 95 pages of amendments and personally met with Ruslan Stefanchuk [Chairman of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine], but we still have neither specifics nor clear decisions – only promises.”
Lavrynetz said organizers would continue calling for the draft to be withdrawn while it remained in its current form.
                                                                                                                                                                         
A second performance focused on hate crimes. Participants listed reported attacks against LGBTQ+ people, their allies, and previous KharkivPride events. Items used in past attacks, including antiseptic dye and pepper spray, served as props.
The organization called for changes to Ukraine’s criminal law to ensure that alleged homophobic and transphobic motives are considered during investigations and court proceedings.
The third performance addressed the policies of the Kharkiv city government. Participants displayed an oversized mock “Kharkiv resident card” divided into two columns.
One listed what organizers said the city guaranteed, including benches, trash cans, fountains, decorative plastic tulips, corruption, and populism. The other listed what they said was being ignored: shelters, funding for Ukraine’s armed forces, respect, accessibility, equality, and honesty.
KharkivPride called on the city government to prioritize accessible shelters, civil protection, inclusive infrastructure, and equal rights.
“I understand what Pride means for Kharkiv. Despite threats from bigots and the city authorities’ silent acceptance of violence, we held KharkivPride today,” co-organizer Anna Sharyhina said.
Sharyhina, who also heads the Kharkiv Women’s Association Sphere, said the movement would continue demanding greater inclusion and equality from the state.
“Because this is about freedom, diversity, and human rights. It is about us, our city, and our Ukraine in the greater European family.”
The final performance honored LGBTQ+ Ukrainian service members killed in the war. Participants held their portraits and read several of their stories.
Organizers said the partners of fallen LGBTQ+ troops lack many of the rights granted to legally recognized family members, including the ability to carry out a partner’s final wishes or receive certain state benefits.
Ukraine does not provide nationwide legal recognition for same-sex partnerships. In 2023, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Ukraine’s failure to provide legal recognition and protection to a same-sex couple violated the European Convention on Human Rights. The judgment did not require Ukraine to introduce same-sex marriage but found that the couple had been treated differently without sufficient justification.
KharkivPride described legal recognition of civil partnerships as an initial step toward marriage equality.
During September, the organization was working with the Shields charity foundation to raise Hr.500,000 ($11,230) for a pickup truck for Ukraine’s 160th Separate Mechanized Brigade.

====================================================================================================

During attacks, crossing operations are suspended — Demchenko spoke about security measures at border crossing points
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:29:16 EEST
20:29:16 KST

During attacks, crossing operations are suspended — Demchenko spoke about security measures at border crossing points
Kyiv • UNN
Demchenko said that during attacks, the operation of border crossing points is suspended and people are dispersed. Resumption may take anywhere from hours to days.
In the event of a threat of enemy strikes, the operation of border crossing points is temporarily suspended, and people are dispersed throughout the area to protect their lives and health. Andrii Demchenko, spokesperson for the State Border Guard Service, said this on a televised national marathon, as reported by UNN.
If we look at the past few weeks, five crossing points in Odesa region came under attack, with strikes hitting both the premises of the crossing points and the service areas. These were four crossing points on the border with Moldova and one on the border with Romania. But, as we can see, as the enemy expands its attack zones, particularly to the western regions—and we have emphasized this—the threat may also affect other sections of the border
He noted that recently, near the border with Poland, reactive "Shaheds" also struck in the direction of the Yahodyn crossing point.
Fortunately, the crossing point itself was not damaged, but there were strikes both on the highway leading to the border and on the railway infrastructure in that direction, destroying infrastructure and hitting a locomotive as well. This is, in fact, a major risk to people's lives and health posed by Russia. The enemy frankly does not care about people's lives and health in general
According to him, during attacks, crossing operations in various sections are suspended in order to protect people's lives and health and prevent crowds from forming.
The situation is monitored, including what weapons the enemy is using and in which direction they are moving, and based on this, a decision is also made to suspend crossing operations in various directions, at each crossing point
He emphasized that the resumption of crossing point operations depends on the extent of the damage and destruction, which may take anywhere from several hours to several days.
Demchenko separately noted that border guards observe that Belarus continues to support Russia, as air attacks on Rivne and Volyn regions were carried out from Belarusian territory via retransmitters located on Belarusian territory.
We remind you
In August, a crossing point in Odesa region was damaged by a Russian attack, which led to its temporary closure. After restoration work, crossing operations resumed.
In September, Russia attacked the Orlivka crossing point in Izmail district.

Chinese-made ballistic missile debris found in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:28:33 UTC
20:28:33 KST

- Open-source analysts say missile debris found in Marib Governorate, Yemen, came from a Chinese-made DF-15A, possibly fired by Saudi Arabia for the first time.
- Saudi Arabia has previously acquired medium-range DF-3A and DF-21 missiles from China, but no confirmed history of the shorter-range DF-15.
Open-source analysts say wreckage from a short-range ballistic missile turned up in northern Yemen this week, and they believe it points to a weapon type Saudi Arabia has never been confirmed to use before.
The debris, identified as the booster stage of a Chinese-made DF-15A, was found in the Raghwan district of Marib Governorate, according to social media accounts that track weapons in the region.
The find comes amid a sharp escalation in fighting around Marib. Houthi forces and Yemen’s internationally recognized government have traded strikes across multiple provinces since early September, and Saudi Arabia has continued carrying out airstrikes in support of government forces there.
OSINT analyst MenchOsint wrote online that “Saudi Arabia fired Chinese-made DF-15A Ballistic Missiles at Yemen last night, likely for the first time.” A second account, OSINTWarfare, described the debris more specifically, saying the booster stage came from “a Chinese-made DF-15A (Dong Feng-15A) ballistic missile operated by Saudi Arabia” that fell in Raghwan district.
The DF-15A is a short-range ballistic missile, with a range generally estimated at around 600 kilometers (370 miles), well short of the medium-range systems Saudi Arabia is known to have acquired from China in the past. Riyadh purchased roughly 60 DF-3A missiles from China in the late 1980s, and a U.S. congressional commission later confirmed reports that Saudi Arabia bought DF-21 medium-range missiles from China around 2007, with the U.S. having reportedly required the DF-21s be modified so they could not carry nuclear warheads. Neither country has publicly confirmed Saudi Arabia holds any short-range DF-15 variant.
That gap in the public record is why some analysts online have floated an alternative explanation: that the debris could belong to a Pakistani-operated missile rather than a Saudi one. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a mutual defense pact in September 2025, declaring that an attack on either country would be treated as an attack on both, and the two militaries have a long history of cooperation, including Pakistani troops training in the kingdom for decades. Whether that relationship extends to Pakistani missile crews or hardware operating from Saudi territory has not been established, and no source has offered evidence tying Pakistan directly to the Marib debris.
For now, the origin of the missile wreckage in Raghwan rests on the assessments of open-source researchers rather than any government statement. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Defense has not commented on the reported strike, and it remains unconfirmed whether the DF-15A theory, the Pakistani-missile theory, or another explanation will hold up as more information becomes available.

Lithuania police open hate-incitement probe after pig’s head displayed at Kaunas mosque

Lithuanian police have opened a criminal investigation into possible incitement against a group of people and interference with religious rites after a group of bikers displayed a pig’s head outside a mosque in Kaunas last week.
Kaunas County Police said Monday that the decision to launch the pretrial investigation was made after officers reviewed video footage and assessed reports received about the incident.
The bikers gathered Friday in Kaunas’ Ramybės Park while Muslims were praying at the mosque. They played loud music, revved their motorcycles, chanted nationalist slogans and displayed a pig’s head they had brought with them.
Police had already opened administrative proceedings on September 11 over possible violations of rules governing assemblies and other events. They were also reviewing the circumstances surrounding possible incitement to hatred.
Odeta Vaitkevičienė, a spokeswoman for Kaunas County Police, told BNS on Monday that no one has been formally suspected in the criminal investigation so far.
“The identity of the person holding the pig’s head is clear, and the identities of other people have also been established, but everything is still part of the investigation,” she said. “There was no physical contact and, according to the information we have, no one was injured and no medical assistance was required.”
Vaitkevičienė did not rule out the possibility that victims could be identified as the investigation proceeds. The prosecutor’s office is expected to provide information about any victims, she said.
Police said their officers deliberately avoided intervening physically during the incident.
“It was a tactical decision to document [the incident] and, in the absence of a need – that is, in the absence of physical contact – to avoid intervention because of the possibility of escalating tensions,” Vaitkevičienė told BNS.
The incident has drawn criticism from Lithuanian political leaders and calls for greater protection of the country’s Muslim community.
Parliament speaker Juozas Olekas said the right to express an opinion must not become an excuse for humiliating other people.
Mufti Aleksandras Beganskas has said he wants to meet with government officials to discuss additional security measures for Muslims. He has raised the possibility of putting a fence around the Kaunas mosque and called for new legislation aimed at preventing people from inciting hatred on the basis of race, nationality or religion.
Beganskas has also called for an internal police investigation into officers’ conduct during the incident, saying some Muslim women who were present felt unsafe and that public safety may not have been adequately ensured.

Moving stories, worrying numbers: Behind the wave of immigration from North America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:27:32 UTC
20:27:32 KST

They are leaving comfortable lives, careers, and personal security for a reality of war, high costs, and uncertainty. Yet despite rising antisemitism, only a small fraction of Jews in the US and Canada are choosing to make aliyah.
Walla joined a flight from New York to Tel Aviv and met those who refuse to remain on the sidelines.
They are coming from the US and Canada not because life there has collapsed, but despite the fact that it remains comfortable, orderly, and familiar. That is precisely what makes their decision so striking: leaving behind security, language, careers, and community to make aliyah to an Israel facing prolonged war, high costs, division, and uncertainty. It is not an escape from something bad, but a conscious move toward a more demanding place because it is theirs.
Israeli stand-up comedian Yohay Sponder, who performs in English for Jewish and Israeli audiences, has captured this paradox in recent years with both humor and sharpness. In a clip that went viral, he offers a simple test of who qualifies as a Zionist: "Zionism is only if you came from somewhere better than Israel. It is not Zionism if you upgraded your life; Zionism is when you downgraded your life to help us reach the level of the country you came from. Very simple."
Last week, Walla joined several dozen Zionists of this elite variety as they traveled from New York to Tel Aviv in the middle of the seasonal peak for aliyah, just before the beginning of the school and university year.
They were not being pushed onto the plane by immediate circumstances. On the contrary, many were leaving behind full and established lives, driven by a sense of belonging that had grown stronger after the massacre and the war, as well as by antisemitism that has become increasingly visible on the streets, on campuses, and online.
"This is the last exile," 28-year-old Aaron Dahan, owner of Cafe Aharon on Manhattan's Upper East Side, told Walla two days earlier. His antisemitic employees abandoned him after October 7. "There are almost no Jews left in Europe. All the Jews left their homes and moved to Israel, except in the United States in general and New York in particular."
Dahan insisted that Walla take a copy of Jewish historian Prof. Pamela Nadell's book, Antisemitism, an American Tradition, which he prominently displays on the counter of his coffee shop.
Referring to Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whom he views as notorious, he remarked: "Thank God he was elected. If it takes this garbage antisemitic mayor to get us moving, then it is a blessing. Even my wife, who does not speak a word of
Hebrew and who, when we got married, agreed we would make aliyah only after celebrating our 75th birthdays, is already ready to leave tomorrow."
Ilana and Steven
Among the new immigrants were Ilana and Steven Snyder, both 67 and from New York State, who stood excitedly at John F. Kennedy International Airport last Wednesday, moments before boarding El Al Flight 010.
They were leaving the US, where they were born and raised and where, by their own account, life is comfortable and easy, for an apartment they had rented in Jerusalem's Arnona neighborhood.
"America is beautiful, welcoming, and comfortable, but if you are Jewish, you are still an outsider," Steven explained. "The more observant you are, the slightly harder it becomes. In Israel, religious or not religious, you are no longer a stranger. It is your country. That is something I always felt I was missing, and it is time to come home."
Ilana said a similar feeling had grown stronger for her since October 7, as it had for many other immigrants.
"We became more aware that if you wear or carry something that identifies you as Jewish, maybe you should hide it. That is a terrible feeling, and we do not want to live in an environment where you have to hide who you are," she said.
Two of their three daughters have already made aliyah, one 12 years ago and the other exactly a year ago, while their third daughter may join them next year. Their daughters were also the ones who selected their Jerusalem apartment after giving them a video tour.
Steven, an accountant, and Ilana, a baker and personal chef, hope to quickly integrate into their new lives.
"We want to integrate, to be Israelis," they said. "We do not want to be Americans living in Israel."
The flight carrying the Snyders landed Thursday morning and was one of six flights that brought about 150 immigrants from North America to Israel that day. Their flight alone carried about 40 new immigrants.
Behind those numbers was an entire system of guidance and assistance provided by Nefesh B'Nefesh, which works in partnership with the Aliyah and Integration Ministry, the Jewish Agency, KKL, and JNF-USA. Since its founding in 2002, the organization says it has helped more than 100,000 Jews from North America make aliyah.
According to Nefesh B'Nefesh, more than 2,200 new immigrants arrived from North America this summer. They included about 480 families, nearly 100 group flights from the US and Canada, and additional immigrants who obtained citizenship while already in Israel.
More than 1,100 made aliyah in August alone, a month the organization describes as one of its strongest for immigration since it was founded.
The organization sees the figures as a sign of an especially strong year. Since the beginning of 2026, about 2,700 new immigrants from North America have moved to Israel, while the forecast for the full year stands at more than 4,000. If that projection is realized, the organization says, it will be one of the strongest years for North American aliyah since its establishment.
According to Nefesh B'Nefesh, the numbers also reveal a relatively young wave of immigrants whose scale has been almost unexpected. The average age is 29.
They include about 1,100 single men and women, roughly 250 retirees, and around 700 children and teenagers who began the school year in Israel this week, including approximately 80 first graders. Another 300 young men and women are expected to join the IDF or National Service.
Among the immigrants are professionals from a wide range of fields, including doctors, nurses, teachers, lawyers, accountants, and technology workers.
Their places of origin stretch from New York, New Jersey, Florida, and California to Maryland, Illinois, Ontario, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Georgia. In Israel, they are expected to settle in Jerusalem, Beit Shemesh, Ra'anana, Modi'in Maccabim Reut, Tel Aviv, and Haifa.
About 650 are also expected to make their homes in communities in the Negev and Galilee under the Zinuk Ba'Aliyah program, a joint initiative by Nefesh B'Nefesh and KKL that encourages settlement in national priority areas.
Eleanor
Beyond the statistics, however, the real story begins when the numbers are given faces. It lies in the gap between the lives left behind and the lives these immigrants hope to build in Israel.
Eleanor Kotler, 43, from Minneapolis, is one of them. She left what she described as a dream job in design, sustainability, and inclusion at the headquarters of retail chain Target.
Kotler first came to Israel in December 2023 to volunteer and has returned repeatedly since then, as though something in the course of her life had permanently shifted.
Her moment of disillusionment came just days after the massacre, during a professional conference in California focused on equality and social justice.
"It was like an indoctrination camp for the pro-Palestinian movement," she said. "I felt like I was the only Jewish person there." A non-Jewish colleague who attended the conference with her even urged her to leave. "She said it was not safe for me as a Jewish woman."
Kotler stayed, documented what was happening, and sent the videos to Jewish organizations and the conference's sponsors. "I was completely shocked. It was my big wake-up moment."
The personal cost came quickly, too. Her public support for Israel distanced her from close friends, including some she described as being close to her "like sisters." She also came to understand that the views she had begun expressing could narrow her employment prospects.
"I knew that could happen, but ultimately I do not want to work for an organization that would be like that," she said.
Then came the love story.
During a visit to Israel last December, Kotler met Moti, 47, at the beach. Within a few months, they were engaged. She is now leaving her job, plans to live with him in Ramat Hasharon, and is preparing for a wedding at Midburn.
"Before that, I was thinking about making aliyah because I did not feel at home there," she said. "But once I met him, everything became simple, and I will always prefer a happy love story."
Nefesh B'Nefesh also became her gateway into the aliyah process. "Everyone I spoke with who had made aliyah recommended Nefesh B'Nefesh. I did not even consider any other way," she said.
For Kotler, the main advantage was knowing that someone would guide her through the bureaucracy.
"I love the idea that you have a resource you can turn to with questions throughout the process, and it simply felt very safe and very supportive," she said.
She began the process through the organization's website and had already completed her first interview by January. After Moti proposed, she accelerated her preparations and moved up the aliyah date she had initially planned for the end of the year.
Roni
Roni, a pseudonym, with her full name withheld by the editorial staff, is 18 and from Manhattan's Upper East Side. She also made aliyah alone, though under different circumstances.
She grew up in an Israeli household; her father is Israeli, and she attended the private Jewish Abraham Joshua Heschel School. Israel had always been part of her life, but she said the October 7 attack profoundly changed the way she saw it.
"Before that, Israel was the place where my father grew up and a fun place to go on vacation. After October 7, I realized these are my people, and that they are not safe now."
In the months after the attack, Roni began following events in Israel closely, attending rallies and demonstrations of support, and deepening her connection to Judaism.
A two-month stay in Israel last summer further strengthened her sense that she needed to act.
"I kept asking myself how I could help and do my part. I realized that the best way I could contribute would be to make aliyah to Israel and enlist in the army."
Her decision to leave Manhattan also stemmed from a growing feeling that New York, the city where she was born and raised, was no longer home.
She had grown tired of graffiti and stickers carrying harsh anti-Israel messages and calling for a free Palestine, which appeared repeatedly on bus seats, traffic light poles, and road signs across the city.
At a pro-Palestinian demonstration, Roni and a friend stood holding an Israeli flag. The two were surrounded and shouted at.
"I saw how much hatred there is there," she said. "It made New York feel even less like my home. I felt hated by many of the people around me."
The contrast between New York and Israel became even clearer during her visit to the country. Against the alienation she felt in her hometown, she found a sense of belonging, warmth, and community in Israel.
"In Israel, I felt love from everyone, something I can no longer say about New York."
The anti-Israel hostility, she said, did not weaken her Zionist feelings. It had the opposite effect, prompting her to learn more about Israel and deepening her connection to the country.
Roni will begin a six-month pre-military preparatory program through Kol Ami in Kiryat Ye'arim. She is then expected to enlist through Garin Tzabar, hoping to serve in a combat position.
She said her family "completely" supports her decision to make aliyah and enlist.
As an American football player, she has already contacted the coach of Israel's national team and hopes to train with the team and perhaps eventually join it.
Her main concern is being far from her family, particularly her younger sister.
"I know it will be difficult and there will be days when I ask myself why I did this. But I believe the purpose and the fulfillment I will feel will make it all worthwhile," she said firmly.
Chava and Akiva
For Chava and Akiva Lessin, the decision followed a different path. It was less about romantic love and more about a family and religious commitment.
The couple, aged 46 and 47, are moving from Virginia to Modi'in with their three children, aged 12, 10, and two.
For Akiva, aliyah is explicitly a religious and ideological decision. In his view, Judaism and Zionism cannot be separated.
"Anyone who studies Torah understands that a Jew should make aliyah to the Land of Israel. And yes, not everyone can, there are obstacles."
Those obstacles delayed their plans for years.
Akiva fell in love with Israel at 18, when he arrived at the Ohr Somayach yeshiva after becoming religious. Chava developed her connection to the country in her 20s while studying at Neve Yerushalayim.
Their aspiration to make aliyah was repeatedly postponed, however, because of the demands of careers and family. Akiva believed he first needed to establish himself financially. He built a successful technology company and eventually sold it to an international firm.
The move also presented a delicate challenge for the family. Their children had never visited Israel and did not know what to expect, so the parents chose Modi'in in part because its English-speaking community could ease their transition.
"October 7 shattered the bubble of inner calm in which I had lived when it came to being Jewish and the world's acceptance of Jews," Chava said.
"I found myself repeatedly defending Israel on social media, to friends and family. It was difficult, but at the same time my love for Israel and my determination to defend it also became stronger. I realized that for me, being Jewish means that I must live in Israel."
For Akiva, Judaism is not simply a religion that his family practices, but an entire life they build. In the Land of Israel, he said, faith, family, community, language, history, and Jewish responsibility come together.
The family is deeply grateful for the life they had in the US and for the values it gave them, including freedom, self-determination, and personal responsibility.
Akiva stressed that Jews had been welcomed in America from its earliest days in an unprecedented way. The family is now choosing, "with courage and hope," to join the next chapter of the Jewish people in Israel.
Akiva describes aliyah as a "sacred adventure" and an act of faith and hope.
"We are choosing not to make comfort the only measure of a good life," he said.
Their children are also central to the decision. Chava and Akiva want them to grow up somewhere Judaism is not merely a private belief, but something lived through language, the calendar, culture, and the shared responsibility of the Jewish people.
Akiva praised the assistance provided by Nefesh B'Nefesh, saying that without it the family would not have seriously considered making aliyah. Chava has followed the organization's work for years and becomes emotional whenever she sees immigrant families arriving at their new homes.
They are well aware of the cost of the move: helping three children adjust to new schools, the Hebrew language, and a different culture; rebuilding their professional and community lives; and facing the economic uncertainty that comes with starting over.
They are also saying goodbye to a beloved community in Richmond, Virginia, where they lived for years.
"We have concerns, but we have no doubts," Akiva concluded. "We are not making aliyah because we think life in Israel will be easier, but because we believe this is where God wants us to live and grow."
Leah
Also on the flight was Leah Shusterman, 27, from Indianapolis, who made aliyah alone.
She, too, says without hesitation that October 7 was the turning point. The rise in antisemitism in the US since then has only strengthened her Jewish identity, and she is no longer willing to hide it.
"On the contrary," she said, pointing to the pendants with Jewish motifs she wears around her neck.
Shusterman is the daughter of Freidel and Mendel Shusterman, Chabad emissaries in Indianapolis, Indiana. She knows her parents will miss her, but during earlier visits to Israel, she came to understand that "Israel is home."
Zionism 2026
"The historic wave of aliyah we are experiencing this summer is the most moving testament to the resilience of the Jewish people and to the deep connection between North American Jewry and the State of Israel," said Rabbi Yehoshua Fass, co-founder and CEO of Nefesh B'Nefesh.
The organization has made changing the rules of the game its mission and, according to Fass, has helped about 100,000 immigrants from North America and the UK move to Israel since its establishment in 2002 by removing professional, logistical, bureaucratic, and financial obstacles.
It has also maintained a retention rate of more than 90%, compared with approximately 50% to 60% before the organization was founded.
"The fact that thousands of families and young people are choosing to relocate their lives and build their futures here, precisely at this time, is a Zionist shot of energy and an enormous engine of growth for Israeli society and the economy."
Yet it is here, alongside these personal stories, that the harder question emerges.
Despite the moving stories and the work of organizations driven by a deep sense of mission, the broader demographic picture of aliyah to Israel remains troubling.
Much of the hope rests on the roughly seven million Jews living in the US and Canada. Yet total aliyah to Israel fell from a peak of about 75,000 immigrants in 2022 to only around 22,000 in 2025. At the same time, more than 150,000 Israelis left the country between October 7, 2023, and the end of 2025.
In other words, aliyah from North America is providing Israel with remarkable stories of belonging and love, but it has yet to alter the larger picture. Israel's migration balance remains worryingly negative.
Compared with the years before October 7, the number of immigrants arriving from North America has remained stable at best, rising only from about 3,700 in 2002 to roughly 3,920 in 2025.
Their share of total aliyah has increased because immigration from other parts of the world has fallen significantly. In absolute terms, however, the numbers remain far below the hoped-for potential.
Even Nefesh B'Nefesh's forecast of more than 4,000 immigrants in 2026 represents only a tiny fraction of the total Jewish population of North America, roughly one immigrant for every 1,750 Jews, or just 0.057%.
At that rate, it would take 2,000 years to bring them all back.
Israel, of course, hopes that more Jews will be willing to leave America for Israel, and to do so in significant numbers. But despite rising antisemitism, high costs, and the need for heavy security to maintain communal Jewish life in America, for now, that is not happening.

Animal rights group calls on Israeli municipalities to bar chicken for kapparot ahead of Yom Kippur
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:27:21 UTC
20:27:21 KST

Six Israeli local authorities have said they will not permit the use of live chickens for the traditional kapparot ceremony ahead of Yom Kippur, following an appeal by animal rights organization Let the Animals Live to dozens of municipal leaders across the country.
Tel Mond, Yeruham, Mevaseret Zion, and Yavne joined the initiative this year, while Kiryat Bialik and Rishon Lezion, which responded to the organization's appeal last year, renewed their commitments.
They join Kfar Saba, Ra'anana, Tel Aviv-Jaffa, Beersheba, Ashkelon, Ramle, and Petah Tikva, which the organization said have prohibited the practice within their jurisdictions for several years.
The campaign marks the second consecutive year Let the Animals Live has approached heads of local authorities about the practice.
According to the organization, Veterinary Services procedures governing kapparot allow a local authority to prohibit ceremonies using live chickens within its jurisdiction. In any case, organizers must obtain authorization from the municipality's veterinary department, whether or not slaughter takes place at the site.
The use of live chickens in kapparot has long prompted animal welfare objections. In 2019, the Environmental Protection Ministry similarly urged the public to use alternatives, including donating money to charity rather than performing the ceremony with a chicken.
Let the Animals Live said chickens used in the ceremony can undergo severe distress beginning with their transport to the site. According to the organization, the birds are packed into small cages, sometimes without food or water, and subjected to movement, noise, and overcrowding.
What does the ceremony entail?
During the ceremony, the chickens are held and raised into the air, which the organization said can cause extreme fear, injuries, and broken bones. Most are subsequently sent for slaughter, while in some cases they are slaughtered at the ceremony site.
The organization stressed that kapparot can also be observed without harming animals, primarily by giving money to charity or donating to charitable institutions.
"Yom Kippur represents introspection, compassion, and mercy, and there is no justification for marking it through a custom that involves fear and severe suffering for animals," Let the Animals Live CEO Yael Arkin said.
"The kapparot custom can be observed in a way that respects tradition while at the same time helping people in need, through a donation to charity. We welcome the authorities that have already made a clear decision and call on additional heads of local authorities to join them: Do not grant permits for the chicken kapparot custom, and ensure that the public space under their responsibility is not used to harm animals," she added.

Music festival survivors, victim's relatives discuss PTSD, substance abuse, mental health effects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:27:19 UTC
20:27:19 KST

Survivors and relatives of those murdered at the Nova, Mushroom, Psyduck, and Midburn music festivals during the October 7 massacre met during a conference in Tel Aviv Port on September 8 to discuss connections between trauma, substance abuse, and other mental health ramifications of the terror attack.
The conference, titled "Maintaining the Balance," was organized by the Nova Tribe Community Association and the Israeli Center for Addiction and Mental Health (ICA), with the support of the Welfare and Social Equality Ministries, as well as the Mifal Hapayis national lottery.
Over 500 people attended the conference, which organizers described as the first event of its kind to bring the connection between trauma, substance use, and mental health into open, non-judgemental discussion within society.
The event was hosted by Daniela Dor Levin, the sister of Idan Dor, who was murdered at the Nova festival, and Doron Mizrahi, a Nova festival survivor.
During the massacre, Mizrahi helped evacuate wounded people and later served in the IDF reserves during the Israel-Hamas War. Today, he supports other survivors through the association’s mentoring program.
"We chose to hold this evening because we understand that there is a real need within our community to talk about substance use openly, responsibly, and without judgment," Rif Peretz, CEO of the Nova Tribe Community Association, said.
The event featured a lecture by ICA co-founder and academic director, Prof. Shauli Lev-Ran, followed by a panel of festival survivors and members of bereaved families who discussed coping methods and ways to maintain balance within their lives.
Need for an open, non-judgemental space, linking trauma, substance use, mental health, keeping balance
Lev-Ran's research data, presented at the conference, reflected the understanding that coping with the aftermath of the massacre continues to affect survivors, their families, and the bereaved families of the murdered victims.
This creates "a need for an open, non-judgemental space that places the connection between trauma, substance use, mental health, and the ability to maintain balance within a complex reality at the center of the conversation," according to conference organizers.
"We believe that building a support community can heal the community members, and that open conversation, mutual support, and knowing that help is available without shame can make an enormous difference," Peretz said.
Trauma, substance use are interconnected, Lev-Ran's research data shows
Lev-Ran cited data during his address at the conference, which showed that 54% of Israelis who present with post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms have reported problematic substance use.
During his lecture, he discussed how PTSD can reshape patterns of substance use and blur a person's ability to recognize when it stops serving them and starts becoming a potentially harmful pattern.
"The substances may provide relief in the short term, but over time, they can interfere with the recovery process. Therefore, it is impossible to treat trauma without also addressing substance abuse," Len-Ran said.
"Any mental health treatment needs to see the person and the full picture," he added.
"The unique conference we are holding is an important opportunity to connect these worlds, reduce shame and stigma, and allow festival survivors and those around them to talk about substance use, trauma, and ways of maintaining balance," he told the conference.
"Since October 7, for some members of the community, substance use has become a way to fall asleep, relax, disconnect, or silence the pain," Peretz said.
"We are not here to preach or tell people how to live but rather to provide knowledge and tools that will allow each person to stop and ask themselves: 'Am I managing my substance use, or is it beginning to manage me?' Our responsibility as a community is to look out for one another, recognize distress, and reach out in time," Peretz added.
The conference concluded with a stand-up comedy performance by comedian Israel Katorza.

Roads closed, death toll may rise
RTMC added that the N1 is closed in both directions and urged drivers to avoid the area, expect significant delays, and follow instructions given by authorities operating at the scene.
The RTMC added that the death toll “may change as emergency services and authorities in the Western Cape continue their assessment of the scene.”

Jewish joy, not fear, is the strongest weapon against hate - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:27:04 UTC
20:27:04 KST

There are pro-Israel voices, and then there are the ones you actually believe.
After two years in this fight, I can usually hear the difference within a sentence or two – the talking points clicking into place, the rehearsed outrage. So when I sat down with Yuval David, the Emmy Award-winning actor and filmmaker who has become one of our community’s most visible advocates, and he grinned and told me, “I’m glad you can sense the BS – I can as well; in fact, I now call it out professionally,” I knew we were going to get somewhere honest.
I run IMPACT, an organization built on one conviction: fear is loud, but joy is louder. For a long time that sounded, even to me, like a line to put on a sticker. I no longer think it’s a slogan. I think it’s a strategy – and quite possibly the only one that has ever kept the Jewish people alive.
Here is what the last two years have taught me: you cannot out-shout hatred. The coordinated networks Yuval told me he’s been alerted to – Islamist, Russian, Chinese, Qatari and Turkish operations that target Jewish public figures – will always have more rage than we have hours in the day. If the plan is to match them post for post, insult for insult, we lose. We burn out, and they don’t.
But there is something they cannot manufacture, and it’s the thing Yuval kept returning to: joy. Simchat Chayim, he called it – the joy of life. “As long as we have life, we must find our joy,” he said.
“We’ve been occupied, exiled, dispersed. There have been real genocides against us. Yet that is not what defines us. What defines the Jewish people is our joy, our faith, our peoplehood.” He’s right, and it isn’t sentimental – it’s tactical. A people that celebrates cannot be demoralized, and demoralizing us is the entire objective of the campaign against us.
This is why I’ve stopped telling young people to simply “fight back.” Yuval put it better than I could: the tradition, he said, is “not fighting back, but fighting forward.” Fighting back is defensive; it cedes the terms to whoever swung first. Fighting forward means building – coalitions, culture, joy, institutions – so that we are not merely surviving the next news cycle but outlasting it.
Take the algorithm, the battlefield where most of this actually happens. We treat it as weather, something that happens to us. Yuval’s reframe, which he traced to a briefing from the FBI, changed how I see it: get friendly accounts to follow, engage, and amplify, because that is how you shift what the machine decides to show.
'Movement-building 101'
“We too are the algorithm,” he said. When our enemies boost hateful content, their networks assume anyone adjacent is an ally and pile on, building the wrong audience by sheer engagement. The counter is not to argue harder. It’s to show up for each other – which, as he put it, is “movement-building 101.” Every share is a vote for which reality the machine treats as real.
And it cannot only be Jews doing the sharing. The most hopeful part of our conversation was about allyship – real allyship, not the transactional kind. Yuval co-founded the Jewish and Indian Alliance, linking two ancient, indigenous peoples; he noted that one of the oldest Hebrew words for another nation, Hodu, is simply the name for India.
We are building the same bridges to Christian, Hindu and Muslim partners. “We don’t only join in allyship because we have a shared enemy,” Yuval said. “We join because we have shared promise, shared hopefulness and optimism.” A coalition held together only by fear dissolves the moment the threat recedes. One held together by shared joy endures.
I think about the teenagers most of all – the ones telling us they feel outnumbered and exhausted in the endless scroll. We keep calling them the leaders of tomorrow. Yuval refuses to. “You are not the leaders of tomorrow,” he said. “You’re the leaders of today. What you do today, facing the hardship and moving forward, is going to change all of our worlds.” I want every Jewish kid who has been made to feel small in a comment section to hear that and believe it.
None of this means pretending the danger isn’t real. It is. But we get to decide what we lead with, and that choice has consequences. If we lead with fear, we hand our opponents the only victory they can actually win – a Jewish community too anxious to be visible, too tired to be proud. If we lead with joy, we become the one thing hatred has never, in three thousand years, figured out how to defeat.
Yuval said one more thing I haven’t been able to shake. At the end, he waved off any thanks for the work he does. “Don’t ever thank me for what I do,” he said. “Join me.”
Consider this my acceptance – and my invitation to you.
