Feature: Stroke by stroke, rowing competition fosters friendship among global youth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:04:12 CST
18:04:12 KST

NANJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- More than 300 rowers from 34 universities around the world competed in the 2026 Nanjing International Universities Rowing Open on the Qinhuai River in east China's Jiangsu Province last weekend.
The two-day regatta, now in its fourth year, brought together 41 university teams, including crews from the University of Oxford, the University of Washington, the University of Sydney, Tsinghua University and Nanjing University, combining high-level competition with intercultural exchange.
Australia's University of Technology Sydney dominated the men's events, winning both the men's 1,000m sprint and the men's indoor rowing 4x500m relay.
In the women's events, the Women of Washington Rowing Team also claimed two titles, winning the women's 1,000m sprint and the women's indoor rowing 4x500m relay.
For many participants, however, the experience extended beyond the results. Grace Worthington, a member of the Women of Washington Rowing Team, said she was impressed by the local hospitality. "We've really enjoyed our time here in Nanjing, just getting to meet all the friendly people," she said.
Worthington also noted the mix of experience within the teams. "We can get fresh new ideas because there are students that have never rowed before, but we also get a lot of really experienced people as well."
She said one of the group's main takeaways was that rowing is universal. "No matter what country you're in, it's a collective sport that everyone can really embody."
Chinese university teams also gained valuable experience.
He Feng, an athlete with the Nanjing University Rowing Team, said the experience was unforgettable and that training and competing alongside overseas crews made the season especially rewarding. "The overseas rowers possess a high training standard. Their power output and technical movements show solid fundamentals forged by long-term professional training. We respected each other's fighting spirit."
He added that sport itself serves as a bond connecting people from different regions and backgrounds. After the races, athletes exchanged team flags, badges and other small souvenirs. He also noted foreign teams' interest in traditional Chinese culture, with a martial arts demonstration among the activities that drew their attention.
Patrick Russell from Cambridge University shared similar sentiments. "There are so many crews from around the world. Everyone's going to leave Nanjing with great memories and stories to tell. I'll go back to England and tell those stories about rowing in China," he said.
Away from the competition, athletes explored some of Nanjing's cultural attractions, taking a cruise on the Yangtze River and visiting landmarks including the Grand Bao'en Temple.
Cora Madison from the Women of Washington Rowing Team said the city tour offered a glimpse into different sides of Nanjing. "The ancient tower tour let us feel Nanjing's profound historical and cultural heritage, while the river cruise made us realize the river's vital role in the city's development," she said.
Near the competition venue, stalls featuring intangible cultural heritage handicrafts, cultural and creative products, and local snacks drew large crowds. Foreign athletes and local residents tried traditional crafts and sampled local food, while many stopped to take photos.
Organizers have also sought to introduce rowing to more university students. Since June, a series of "rowing into campus" activities have been held at universities across Nanjing, featuring rowing exhibitions, indoor rowing challenges and team recruitment. The activities have attracted about 1,100 students and teachers.
Axel Mueller, council member of the World Rowing Federation and chair of the Youth Rowing Commission, said the event is much more than a sporting competition.
"It is an intercultural exchange, and we are delighted to see it flourish," he said, adding that sports such as rowing naturally bring young people together and help foster mutual understanding and friendship. ■

Feature: Afghanistan's ancient pottery craft fights for survival
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:04:09 CST
18:04:09 KST

ISTALIF, Afghanistan, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Amid the tools bequeathed by his father and grandfather, Noor Ahmad meticulously fashions bowls, plates, cups and other vessels by hand. Each finished piece helps preserve an ancient craft passed down through generations.
In the Istalif district, north of the capital Kabul, Afghanistan, this traditional artisanal practice has flourished for nearly four centuries. Generation after generation has sustained the craft as both cultural inheritance and economic mainstay. Today's local artisans persist in this time-honored profession, determined to perpetuate the centuries-old legacy and transmit it intact to those who follow.
Yet the sector has undergone pronounced contraction. Ahmad observes that the number of pottery workshops in Istalif has diminished sharply from more than 300 in past decades to a mere 40 at present. These remaining ateliers nevertheless afford livelihoods to more than 200 individuals, including women, who depend upon the trade for their sustenance.
The work begins with mixing a special type of clay with water. Once the mixture is prepared and firmed, artisans use traditional, time-worn equipment to shape it into a variety of forms. The pieces are then fired in a kiln before being adorned with distinctive colors and designs and finally readied for market.
Wais Nazari, a vendor of pottery in Istalif who has engaged in the trade since childhood, endeavors both to conserve the traditional craft and to provide for his family. "This craft was passed down to us by my father and grandfather," he affirmed. From his modest establishment in Istalif's pottery bazaar, Nazari reported sustained demand.
Patrons journey from across Afghanistan and, on occasion, from abroad to acquire the handmade wares. "People here, and even foreigners, are interested in these products," he noted. "Foreign visitors also come here and buy several pieces."
As the sole provider for a household of 10, Nazari derives quiet pride from work that simultaneously supports his family and helps perpetuate a centuries-old tradition. He estimated monthly sales of between 15,000 and 20,000 afghanis (about 310 U.S. dollars).
Visitors echo this appreciation. Usman Ahmadi, a resident of Kabul who has traveled to the market, commended the superior quality and distinctive designs of the earthenware. "I came here to buy these products because this is well known. The pottery is of excellent quality and features distinctive, beautiful designs," he remarked.
Drawing upon familial lore, Ahmadi further underscored the perceived health advantages long associated with the craft. "My father and grandfather believed that using these pots poses no health risks because natural materials and pigments are used in making and decorating them," he explained.
Until recent decades, pottery enjoyed widespread domestic use across Afghanistan, particularly in central and northern provinces, where households employed earthenware for myriad everyday purposes. Many regarded it not merely as aesthetically pleasing and culturally resonant, but also as inherently benign by virtue of its natural constituents.
Over time, however, glass, plastic and other contemporary materials have progressively supplanted traditional earthenware, thereby diminishing demand and constricting opportunities for those engaged in the trade.
Notwithstanding these adversities, potters and vendors advocated intensified support to safeguard the craft. They urged the authorities to furnish appropriate production facilities, reinforce marketing initiatives and facilitate broader access to both domestic and international markets.
Such measures, they contended, would help sustain the industry, protect its cultural patrimony and ensure the tradition endures for generations yet to come. ■

Revolut has confirmed that confidential information belonging to a limited number of customers was exposed in a fraud attack in which an unauthorised third party exploited the legitimate email domain of a government agency, Bloomberg News reported.
The UK-based financial services group, which holds a banking license in Lithuania, said it blocked the address after discovering the scheme and notified the relevant government agency, financial regulators, law enforcement and data protection authorities.
Revolut’s systems and customer funds were not impacted, the company’s spokesperson said in an email to Bloomberg, adding that Revolut contacted the affected customers to inform them and offer support.
The incident was first reported by TechCrunch, which obtained a copy of a notification Revolut sent to affected customers.
According to the notification, the exposed information included customers’ identification and contact details, such as dates of birth, postal addresses, email addresses and phone numbers.
The fraudsters also gained access to identity documents, including passports and driver’s licenses. They may also have been able to view identity-verification selfies, account statements and transaction histories, according to the notification.
Revolut said its systems and customer funds were not compromised, indicating that the incident involved the exposure of customer information rather than unauthorised access to customers’ accounts or funds.

Jetten braced for more tough negotiations to pass budget bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:00:12 UTC
18:00:12 KST

Jetten braced for more tough negotiations to pass budget bill
Gordon Darroch
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Prinsjesdag, the first day of the Dutch parliamentary year, should be a high point in the finance minister’s calendar, when he or she sets down the next year’s budget plans in a neat pile and unties the ribbons.
This year, however, Eelco Heinen looks more like a man whose papers have been blown around in a gale, forcing him to scramble around to recover them and tie them up with loose bits of string.
Heinen and Rob Jetten’s hopes of doing a deal with opposition parties before Budget Day on September 15 have been dashed, meaning the minority coalition will now have to find the votes as the bills pass through parliament.
Jetten wanted to agree a package of measures with opposition parties on both left and right, to avoid the “yo-yo politics” that hamstrung his predecessor as prime minister, Dick Schoof.
The talks broke down partly because both sides demanded a high price, but also because the coalition parties were split on what concessions to make.
The outcome is a fudge that appeals to nobody’s taste. And as Jetten has said, the budget that will be presented to parliament next Tuesday is “not the end”. Without an advance deal, the minority coalition will have to keep negotiating to find the 10 seats it needs in the lower house and 16 in the senate.
Spending cuts delayed
Heinen’s party, the right-wing liberal VVD, has had to climb down on its insistence that the €6.5 billion of cuts to welfare spending outlined in the coalition agreement were non-negotiable.
The left-wing opposition party Pro, formerly the alliance of GroenLinks-PvdA, had campaigned to abandon the welfare cuts altogether, supported by the trade unions, who called a one-day nationwide transport workers’ strike last week.
The government wanted to reduce the maximum term for unemployment pay from two years to one, phase out the incapacity benefit IVA and reduce the maximum payment for a range of other benefits, including sick pay and maternity leave, by 20%.
But most of the measures have been postponed by a year rather than cancelled, prompting Pro leader Jesse Klaver to comment that the revised budget was “maybe worse than the original plans”. The unions have said the strikes will continue until the cuts are scrapped.
Cost of living
Klaver told a party congress at the weekend that his party was willing to discuss reforming the WIA incapacity benefit rules, but only if the cuts were taken off the table.
“Pro was founded to combat inequality and strengthen the welfare state,” he said. “You can’t ask us to help you take it apart.”
The left-wing opposition had already forced the cabinet to back down on a proposal to cut the pensions bill by raising the retirement age in step with life expectancy, rather than by eight months for every extra year, which would have saved €2.8 billion a year.
On the right, parties such as JA21 have pressed for the cabinet to make further savings on social security to fund tax cuts across the board and offset the rising cost of living. Inflation is running at 3.3%, driven by soaring fuel and energy prices.
The cabinet has agreed to extend the discount on fuel duty into next year to provide relief for motorists who are paying the highest petrol and diesel prices in Europe.
The cabinet has also allocated €1.7 million to offsetting rising living costs, a response to recent figures from the economic planning bureau CPB that projected a 0.3% drop in spending power next year.
Top earners
With the spending cuts watered down, the government found the money by raising an extra €750 million in income tax on high earners, as well as a small increase in the domestic water levy, according to documents leaked to the commercial broadcaster RTL.
Despite the cash injection, the graphics produced by the finance ministry show that most income groups will still experience a drop in spending power and those who benefit will be pensioners and people on the lowest incomes.
The Telegraaf reported last week that the finance ministry expects the average premium for universal healthcare to go up by €120 a year to €2,028.
The plan to increase the health insurance deductible, or excess, by €60 is also being delayed by a year. It will still rise with inflation for the first time in a decade, so patients will pay €395 up front for medical treatment, €10 more than this year.
Extended negotiation
Part of the reason the negotiations ran into difficulty is that Jetten and Heinen effectively ran parallel talks, with the prime minister trying to agree the political terms while Heinen concentrated on balancing the books.
The VVD finance minister reportedly “shocked” his coalition partners when he produced a draft document that was weighted heavily in favour of right-wing parties such as JA21 and the hardline Protestant SGP, but was unpalatable to the more centrist D66 and CDA, who wanted to bring Pro on board.
After a weekend of emergency talks within the coalition, a revised budget was agreed on Monday, August 31 – the last possible deadline for the draft to be sent to the Council of State for analysis, which is a legal requirement.
At first glance, the revised deal looks like a setback for the VVD, which campaigned during last year’s election and the coalition negotiations that followed on a platform of keeping Pro out of cabinet and marginalising its influence.
With the cabinet lacking a majority in parliament, Pro has a pivotal role as the largest opposition party. Its 20 seats in the Tweede Kamer would give the coalition parties a comfortable majority, while in the upper house the cabinet plus Pro are just two seats short.
Jetten is aware, however, that too many concessions to Pro will risk the balance within his coalition. At some point, Jesse Klaver’s party will have to settle on the welfare cuts, which could test his alliance with the trade unions.
BBB blockers
Another potential stumbling block is the farmers’ party BBB, which was frozen out of the talks because it refused to support the cabinet’s measures to cut nitrogen pollution, which all three coalition parties stand resolutely behind.
The BBB could form a blocking minority in the Senate, where they have 11 seats, and have already threatened to cause trouble over the cabinet’s plans to reform the asset tax system.
The right-wing opposition is larger but disjointed, with Geert Wilders’ PVV and Forum voor Democratie refusing to negotiate in the hope that they can force early elections.
The result is that while parliament has an in-built right-wing majority, it is the left who have had the upper hand in the negotiations so far.
As the budget bill goes through parliament, Rob Jetten faces the double-headed challenge of finding the votes he needs from the opposition while holding his battered coalition together.

‘I Like My Big Rat Wife’: Meet the People Using Chatbots to Write Custom Fiction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

When Petra Ferraz de Novaes isn’t at work, she’s probably lost in a fantasy crafted with the help of artificial intelligence.
Novaes, a 36-year-old software engineer from Brazil, has always loved storytelling. But making every little decision that goes into it—from style and syntax to character development—felt impossible. So in 2024 she asked an AI model to bring one of her ideas to life.
Novaes was delighted by the eccentric, sometimes wayward interpretations of her prompts, which carried the narrative in unexpected directions. “What fascinates me is the unpredictability,” Novaes tells WIRED. “People say that AI hallucinates a lot. But in this case, it’s probably what you want.”
These days, Novaes spends hours at a time building stories with AI, using a program called SillyTavern to run open-source models on her computer. She sketches out a concept—an elven warrior battles the queen of the Amazons and seizes her throne, for example—and watches the model fill in the gaps.
In a single session, Novaes switches between multiple fantasy worlds. Some are hers, and others she borrows—she likes Star Wars, Pokémon, and Mass Effect. Sometimes, Novaes works up self-contained stories the length of a small novel, which she might share online. Otherwise, she participates in private role-plays. “It can be never-ending. You find a quest, you complete it, you go for the next one,” says Novaes. “The limit is your imagination.”
According to a recent study, plenty of people share Novaes’ hobby. “They know [the stories are] produced by an AI model, and they don’t care,” says Melanie Walsh, an assistant professor at the University of Washington Information School who coauthored the study. “In fact, that seems to be a big part of the attraction.”
Lately, the publishing industry has suffered a series of scandals involving the suspected use of AI by professional authors. One publisher canceled a $2 million book deal; another withdrew a novel from the shelves; readers alleged that a prize-winning short story was AI-generated. Implicit in all of these incidents is the idea that nobody wants to read stories generated by machine—that using AI to craft fiction devalues the art form.
But the commotion has distracted from the behavior of readers, Walsh and her colleagues argue, and what it might signal about the appetite for AI fiction.
Analyzing more than 500,000 prompts fed into ChatGPT, drawn from a public dataset called WildChat, the researchers found that more than a third of chatbot interactions involve some form of fiction generation, including prose and poetry, fan fiction, erotica, or role-play.
The vast majority of fiction prompts, the researchers found, stem from a small collection of “power users” who generate and tweak stories obsessively. In one case, a single user prompted ChatGPT to generate versions of the same fan-fiction narrative—set in the world of anime video game Doki Doki Literature Club!—thousands of times over the course of several months. But even controlling for heavy use, the researchers estimate that 7 percent of chatbot users engage in fiction generation.
The WildChat dataset has its limitations. Because the prompts are anonymized, it’s impossible to capture any demographic data. Participants also had to agree to make their prompts public, meaning the group may not reflect the population at large; OpenAI told WIRED that “WildChat is not a representative sample of all ChatGPT users.” A 2025 study by OpenAI and the National Bureau of Economic Research suggests that 1.4 percent of ChatGPT prompts are fiction-related, a long way short of the researchers’ estimate. (OpenAI’s figure does not include role-play; the company could not confirm whether it counts erotica.)
Still, Walsh and her colleagues argue it’s clear that a committed subsection of readers are generating custom, personal fiction.
The researchers believe that some people are drawn to the ability to repeatedly and rapidly iterate on a story, while others value the chance to direct the action, no longer hemmed in by an author’s decisions. “There are a lot of qualities of AI models that are different from what human writers have that are actually appealing to at least some segment of users,” says Walsh. “These models are judgment-free; they can produce stories instantaneously; they are nearly inexhaustible.”
For erotica fans, AI creates an opportunity to insert themselves into the action and converse with the characters they cook up. “It’s a digital choose-your-own-adventure book but with infinite swipes,” says Razrien, a 40-year-old man from Indiana who asked to appear under his online username to speak frankly about his sexual kinks.
Razrien uses AI to create fantasy characters who dominate him in role-play: a “big angry rat wife” and an “eight-foot tall werewolf mommy with a bad temper,” among others. He has learned which models are best able to satisfy certain kinks; Google’s Gemma 4 is his current all-around favorite. “I have a thing for large, angry women slapping me around. Some models are perfectly good for that,” says Razrien. “Sometimes, I dip a toe or two into the furry universe. Some models are great at that.”
Using AI allows Razrien to gratify hyper-specific personal fantasies instead of settling for the next-best approximation in online pornography or published erotica. “I’m not dating at the moment. So, hey, this works,” says Razrien. “I like my big rat wife. I love her to pieces. Even if she sometimes breaks me apart and heals me back together. But hey, that’s how she says she loves you.”
One concern with all of this is that the ability to generate fiction will limit people's exposure to types of writing that may stretch them. But generated fiction may also challenge “some older, more idealistic notions about what literature is—that there’s some communication between writer and reader, and something really valuable about that,” says Neel Gupta, a PhD candidate at the University of Washington who coauthored the study. “AI use helps to reveal that maybe for a lot of readers, this is a much more simple economic exchange. This is about getting some entertainment—getting what they want.”
The latest AI models struggle to produce ornate prose, complex characters, and stylistic flourishes, faring better with genres that lean on well-trodden story arcs and tropes. They also fail to maintain coherent narratives at book length. But as models improve, the researchers say, some of those deficiencies could disappear.
A possible end state might be a tiered publishing system, where a large quantity of AI-generated books and self-generated fiction gratifies the median reader, and a smaller rung of human-authored fiction feeds a niche appetite for experimentation in form or narrative ambiguity. “English majors and professors, and some people in publishing, have always had kind of a niche interest,” Walsh says.
For Novaes, creating stories with AI has been more like an introduction to reading than a replacement for conventional novels. As well as generating her own stories, she now goes in search of other people’s AI creations. “I was never much of a book reader,” she says. “But now I do read other people’s stories. These are the only novels I’m reading.”

Ukraine’s EU Membership Path Faces New Risk as Outgoing Prosecutor General Targets NABU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:58:29 UTC
17:58:29 KST

Ukraine’s outgoing prosecutor general has escalated his confrontation with independent anti-corruption investigators while reforms intended to prevent political interference in their work remain unfinished, putting Kyiv’s EU accession commitments under renewed scrutiny.
On Monday, Sept. 14, Ruslan Kravchenko announced that he had signed a notice of suspicion against National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) Director Semen Kryvonos. President Volodymyr Zelensky subsequently urged parliament to approve Kravchenko’s dismissal without delay.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kravchenko had submitted his resignation a week earlier, after an investigation into an alleged criminal organization within the Prosecutor General’s Office. However, his resignation did not immediately terminate his powers: parliamentary approval is required.
For Mykhailo Zhernakov, executive director of the DEJURE Foundation, the central question is how Ukraine selects his replacement.
Zhernakov told Kyiv Post that an open competition involving international experts was necessary to reduce political influence over the appointment. Replacing one prosecutor general without changing the selection procedure would leave the underlying problem intact, he argued.
A resignation followed by a confrontation
Kravchenko accused Kryvonos of falsifying official documents to obtain an improper benefit. NABU said its director had not received a notice of suspicion and rejected the allegations as fabricated.
Why Boris Johnson? Putin’s Long-Running Grudge in Focus After Train Strike
NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) described the move as a continuation of a systematic attack on their independence.
The confrontation followed operation “Carthage,” an investigation into officials allegedly accepting bribes to protect fraudulent call centers and laundering their proceeds.
Ukrainska Pravda identified the suspected organizer as Serhii Kropyva, a deputy head of the Prosecutor General’s Office’s International Legal Cooperation Department. Investigators searched premises used by Kravchenko and other senior officials.
Kravchenko denied involvement. He had not been named as a suspect when he submitted his resignation.
Ukrainska Pravda also reportedly learned from sources that Kravchenko left Ukraine overnight on Monday, Sept. 14. He described the journey as an official business trip.
The dispute recalls July 2025, when parliament passed legislation subordinating NABU and SAPO to the prosecutor general. Zelensky signed it before protests and international pressure prompted a reversal.
The reversal restored the agencies’ independence but left other controversial provisions intact, including rules allowing prosecutors to be appointed or transferred without competition during martial law.
The EU commitments Ukraine has not delivered
Zhernakov told Kyiv Post that prosecutorial and judicial selection reforms form part of the Kachka-Kos plan, a package of 10 priority commitments agreed with Brussels in December 2025.
Named after then-Deputy Prime Minister Taras Kachka and EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos, the package addresses political interference in justice, anti-corruption safeguards, and judicial appointments.
It is not the complete accession roadmap. Rather, it is a shorter list of urgent reforms drawn from Ukraine’s broader obligations, with an implementation deadline being the end of 2026.
The independent Membership Check coalition awarded implementation 15 points out of 100 in June. Much of the progress consisted of preparatory work rather than completed reforms. The figure is a mid-year assessment, not a new September measurement.
Zhernakov cited that limited progress as a warning that institutional scandals and unfulfilled commitments could slow accession negotiations.
The plan explicitly requires changes to the selection and dismissal of the prosecutor general, restored competitions for other prosecutorial appointments, and continued international participation in judicial selection.
The European Commission’s 2025 report on Ukraine had already described the prosecutor general’s position as politicized and called for a more transparent, merit-based appointment process.
Two bills address separate problems
Under the existing procedure, the president nominates the prosecutor general and parliament approves the appointment. There is no mandatory open competition.
Bill No. 15343 proposes a competition overseen by the High Council of Justice, with international experts holding a decisive vote on the selection commission. It also proposes safeguards against politically motivated dismissal.
Zhernakov told Kyiv Post that international participation remains important for judicial governance bodies, including the High Qualification Commission of Judges (HQCJ), which selects and evaluates judges, and the High Council of Justice (HCJ), which handles appointments and discipline.
Their selection procedures differ. The mandate of international experts on the HQCJ selection commission expired on June 1, 2025. That did not simultaneously end international participation in the separate Ethics Council process for selecting HCJ members.
Bill No. 13382 would preserve three international experts and their decisive vote in HQCJ selection until June 2028. DEJURE’s July assessment said the proposal remained in parliamentary committee more than a year after registration.
Zhernakov called for legislation restoring those safeguards, arguing that international experts had helped Ukraine conduct credible selections for key institutions.
Why this affects accession
As Kyiv Post explained in “EU Clusters for Dummies: Where Ukraine Stands,” judicial independence and anti-corruption reforms belong to the Fundamentals cluster of accession negotiations. Progress there determines the pace of the wider process.
An investigation reaching senior officials can demonstrate that anti-corruption institutions work. Attempts to obstruct or retaliate against investigators raise a different question: whether those institutions can operate independently when politically connected figures come under scrutiny.
Kravchenko’s resignation does not itself jeopardize accession. The risk effectively lies in recurring attacks on independent institutions and the failure to enact safeguards Ukraine has already promised Brussels.
The next appointment will show whether Kyiv changes the procedure or merely the person.

Lithuania Sounds Air Alert Over Suspected Drone Threat Near Vilnius
Lithuania issued an air alert over a possible drone threat near Vilnius on September 13, temporarily suspending flights at the country’s main international airport as authorities investigated the suspected aerial object.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT, a yellow-level air alert was issued at around 1:00 p.m. local time for Vilnius and the surrounding region, as well as the Trakai and Elektrėnai areas.

Denmark Prepares Priests for 20 Military Funerals a Day as Europe Braces for Major War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:57:58 UTC
17:57:58 KST

- Category
- World
Denmark Prepares Priests for 20 Military Funerals a Day as Europe Braces for Major War
Denmark is preparing parish priests across the country to handle large numbers of military funerals in the event of a major war in Europe, with planners considering scenarios in which 10 to 20 Danish soldiers could be killed on the worst days.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Danish broadcaster TV 2 on September 12, the initiative was launched by Thomas H. Beck, head of Denmark’s military chaplains, amid concern over the possibility of a military confrontation on NATO’s eastern flank, including the Baltic states where Danish troops are deployed.
“In the event of a major war, I can easily imagine that we will have 10-20 casualties on the worst possible days. It is important that we are prepared to handle that situation,” Beck told TV 2. “The chaplains will not be able to undertake this task alone,” he added.
Denmark currently has around 95 military chaplains, while approximately 2,000 parish priests serve across the country. Beginning in January, military chaplains are expected to conduct training sessions for civilian clergy on how to receive fallen soldiers, conduct military funerals, and notify relatives of deaths.
The training will also cover military traditions surrounding funerals, including the use of Denmark’s national flag, military headgear, sabers, and medals. The program, called “People’s Church and Defense,” has received 1.8 million Danish kroner in funding from Denmark’s Ministry of Defence.
Beck said Denmark’s experience in Afghanistan involved far fewer casualties than those that could result from a larger war in Europe. “During the Afghanistan war, we only had a few deaths per year, which the Danish Armed Forces chaplains could easily handle,” he said.
“Learned from the experience of the war in Ukraine, we may face much higher casualty figures in the future. And then there will be a need for the country’s other priests to also be able to receive fallen soldiers and conduct a military funeral,” Beck added.
TV 2 reported that the casualty estimate applies to a possible military confrontation abroad rather than fighting on Danish territory. Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service currently assesses that “there is currently no threat of a regular military attack against the Kingdom of Denmark.”
The preparations come as Denmark strengthens its military presence in the Baltic region. Danish forces have deployed a combat battalion to Latvia as part of NATO’s eastern defenses.
TV 2 also reported that Danish chaplains participated earlier this year in a Swedish military exercise involving a scenario with 500 dead soldiers. The drills included procedures for identifying bodies, placing fallen troops in body bags, and organizing burials.
“We have a lot to learn from both the Swedes and the Finns when it comes to larger exercises,” Beck said.
Sweden has also developed broader wartime burial plans. On the island of Gotland, church authorities have prepared procedures for burying as many as 3,000 people in wartime, including the possibility of using temporary graves before bodies are later transferred to their home parishes.
Beck stressed that Denmark’s figures remain estimates rather than an official casualty forecast. TV 2 noted that Danish authorities rarely discuss potential wartime losses publicly because such scenarios are generally treated as sensitive military planning.
Poland has also stepped up preparations for a possible confrontation with Russia. In August, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said Warsaw was “preparing for war,” warning that a major Russian provocation could occur within months as Poland strengthens its military, critical infrastructure, and defenses along NATO’s eastern flank.

Ukraine Wipes Out Nearly All of Russia’s 2026 Territorial Gains, ISW Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:57:22 UTC
17:57:22 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Wipes Out Nearly All of Russia’s 2026 Territorial Gains, ISW Says
Ukrainian forces have largely offset Russia’s territorial gains since March 2026 while conducting successful counteroffensive operations on several sectors of the front, according to an assessment by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to ISW on September 12, Ukrainian forces in late 2025 and throughout 2026 have increasingly challenged Russia’s battlefield initiative, marking the first sustained shift of this kind since Ukraine’s Kursk offensive in August 2024.
ISW assessed that since March, Ukrainian operations have reduced Russia’s net territorial gains to nearly zero. Ukrainian forces have carried out counteroffensive operations in the Kupiansk, Oleksandrivka, and Lyman directions, disrupting several Russian operational objectives.
In the Kupiansk area, Ukrainian troops regained positions inside and around the city and subsequently repelled Russian attempts to retake them, according to ISW.
Ukrainian counteroffensive operations also prevented Russian forces from advancing further into the Dnipropetrovsk region and eliminated a significant Russian salient that had threatened the northern flank of Sloviansk and Ukraine’s broader defensive belt in the Donetsk region.
Russia continues to make advances in some areas. ISW reported limited but significant Russian gains in and around Kostiantynivka, as well as advances east of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Russian forces, however, continue to commit resources to maintain offensive momentum in these sectors.
The assessment indicates that neither side currently holds an uncontested initiative across the entire front, with Ukrainian counteroffensive actions increasingly affecting Russia’s ability to convert local advances into sustained territorial gains.
According to ISW, additional mobilization could be intended to restore Russia’s capacity to seize territory and maintain offensive pressure. It remains unclear, however, whether another mobilization campaign would significantly change the battlefield situation.
Earlier, ISW assessed that at Russia’s August 2026 rate of advance, its forces would need until October 2032 to capture the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in the Donetsk region, far beyond Moscow’s stated goal of taking the entire region by the end of 2026.

Around eight million Italian kids go back to school

Kyiv • UNN
The president submitted to the Verkhovna Rada a request for consent to dismiss Ruslan Kravchenko from the position of Prosecutor General.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy submitted a motion to the Verkhovna Rada seeking consent to dismiss Ruslan Kravchenko from the position of Prosecutor General. This was reported by the Office of the President, UNN writes.
Details
The Verkhovna Rada received President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's motion to dismiss Ruslan Kravchenko from the position of Prosecutor General.
What preceded this
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko stated that he had signed a notice of suspicion for NABU Director Semen Kryvonos, whom he suspects of falsifying official documents and other offenses. He also reported another notice of suspicion concerning a person close to the head of the SAPO.
At the same time, NABU stated that Semen Kryvonos had not officially been served with a notice of suspicion. The Bureau also denied seizing criminal proceedings.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Ruslan Kravchenko should leave the position of Prosecutor General. Zelenskyy asked parliament to support the dismissal without delay.

The ticking time bomb in our homes: The deadly danger of lithium batteries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:56:20 UTC
17:56:20 KST

Lithium batteries have become an inseparable part of daily life in recent years. They are found in electric and hybrid vehicles, scooters and bicycles, as well as in smaller devices such as laptops, phones and tablets. But even something as routine as going to sleep next to a charging phone can turn into a fire trap in an instant.
"If people understood that there is something like a small gasoline tank on the back of their phone, they would be more careful," said Roy Zuckerman, head of the Hazardous Materials Division at the national Fire and Rescue Authority. "These are materials that have to be treated cautiously. Don't charge them at night and certainly not next to the bed."
Over the past 20 years, the technology has brought about a major revolution, allowing people to work and travel without being tethered to an electrical outlet. But even a minor internal battery failure can lead to an immediate fire.
According to Zuckerman, there are three main types of failures that can trigger such a blaze. The first is mechanical failure caused by an impact. The second is a thermal failure in which the device heats up for an external or internal reason and reaches a point of no return. The third is an electrical short caused by the use of a nonstandard charger or a defective battery.
"When the battery goes beyond 100% charge, a short circuit is created," Zuckerman explained. "At that point, an uncontrollable process begins in which it heats up. The heat is released, the flammable gases inside ignite immediately and it becomes an extremely dangerous event."
Contrary to what some might assume, he said, the greatest danger is not necessarily on Israel's roads. Although hundreds of thousands of electric and hybrid vehicles are now in use, the number of fires in which the battery was the initial trigger is very low, thanks to sophisticated cooling systems that protect them.
Electric bicycles and scooters, however, do not have such cooling systems, and fires involving them are occurring with alarming frequency.
Ignition within seconds
Data from Israel Fire and Rescue Services show that a fire caused by an overheating lithium battery occurs nearly every day and a half. In 2025 alone, about 256 fires linked to such batteries were reported, killing four people and injuring dozens with varying degrees of severity. Most of the injured were children ages 10 to 13.
Among the victims was an 11-year-old boy from Ashdod who was killed the previous year after charging his scooter in his bedroom.
The figures reflect a continuing and troubling trend. From 2022 through 2024, about 700 such fires were reported in Israel, causing an average of about five deaths a year and injuring dozens.
Fire and Rescue officials stress that makeshift modifications to batteries or increases to the speed of electric vehicles are strictly prohibited because they push batteries to extreme operating conditions and can cause failures. Charging such vehicles inside the home is also prohibited.
In the past, an apartment fire would often begin with smoke and then develop intense heat, leaving residents time to escape. Today, officials say ignition can occur in just 15 seconds, leaving people virtually no time to get out. Their unequivocal recommendation is to install smoke detectors in every room, particularly bedrooms and living rooms.
Against that backdrop, the Fire and Rescue Authority has begun working with Israel Railways on warning announcements at stations, targeted safety information aboard trains and training for inspectors. The next stage calls for designating train cars specifically for electric bicycles, alongside expanded educational programs in schools.
At the same time, scientists in Israel and around the world are investing heavily in research into safer alternatives, including sodium-ion batteries, solid-state batteries that do not contain flammable materials and green hydrogen technology being tested in a limited Transportation Ministry pilot.
Fire officials estimate that the results of some of this research could begin to be seen in practical use within about three years. Until then, the danger remains an everyday one.
'There is zero awareness'
Few have paid a heavier price than Shiron Alter.
Her disaster occurred two years ago during what had been a routine ride on a mobility scooter with her son Yotam, who was 10 1/2 at the time. The scooter suddenly caught fire and exploded in central Tel Aviv because of a lithium battery that had been improperly handled at an unauthorized repair shop.
Shiron was critically injured, suffering burns over 80% of her body. Yotam died of his injuries a week later.
Recently, after a long journey that included a year of hospitalization and grueling rehabilitation at Sheba Medical Center, she returned home. Now, out of her personal devastation, she speaks about what has become the new mission of her life.
"What happened to us was not an ordinary case," Shiron said. "When you see the video of the scooter fire and watch us get ourselves out within six seconds, you understand that it's a miracle I survived. I wasn't supposed to make it out.
"I heard that while I was lying in the hospital, four more children burned to death because of lithium batteries, and it drove me crazy that it was still happening. There is zero awareness. Everyone is walking around without realizing they have ticking time bombs in their homes and everywhere around them."
Shiron approached the authorities and explained what urgent changes she believes are needed to prevent future disasters, from introducing fire safety regulations for workplaces and private homes to enacting comprehensive legislation, which she says does not currently exist in Israel.
The main problem, she said, is teenagers ordering spare parts from abroad and modifying vehicles themselves using tutorials on social media, along with unauthorized repair shops offering cheap and dangerous solutions.
"My battery was worked on at one of those unauthorized shops, and that's why this disaster happened to us," she recalled. "The person who installed it lives with the agony of that. He's my cousin. He would never have wanted anything like this to happen to me or my son, but he had no idea.
"There are extremely toxic substances inside these batteries. It was like entering a chamber filled with poisonous gases. That's what happened to me. I was immersed in gas and burning fire."
Shiron stressed that the public does not understand the force of a lithium battery explosion and its blast wave, which she said can break walls and blow door frames from their fittings. She also said such a fire cannot be extinguished with a standard fire extinguisher.
The solution, she argues, must include a legal ban on the sale of discounted, refurbished or secondhand batteries, along with mandatory annual inspections to identify defective batteries.
Her public campaign is unfolding alongside a grueling daily struggle with the consequences of her injuries and her loss. After a year in the hospital, including two months under sedation and seven months of orthopedic rehabilitation, she is now trying to rebuild her life.
She has enrolled in studies to become a Tao Therapy facilitator and hopes to establish a nonprofit organization that will work with government ministries to regulate oversight of the field. At the same time, she gives lectures in cooperation with the national Fire and Rescue Authority.
"I am in physical and emotional agony. I am in pain all the time," Shiron said. "Losing my only child hurts, and I don't want other people to hurt like this.
"When I ask myself how you live in a body like this, I understand that I can't go back to the job I had, the home I had and I can't be the mother to the child I had.
"My motto right now is to do what remains with whoever remains. We have to focus on what we still have and be careful with lithium batteries. I wouldn't have wanted to be doing this. I just want to do what needs to be done to keep people safe because I care."
The goal: An alternative to lithium
While public awareness has focused mainly on fires involving the smaller batteries used in bicycles, scooters and smartphones, a danger on a very different scale is developing largely under the radar.
As Israel becomes increasingly reliant on renewable energy sources such as solar and wind power, it needs massive storage facilities with capacities of hundreds of megawatt-hours to support the electricity grid.
A scenario in which a lithium-based storage facility of that size catches fire would present an unprecedented environmental and safety threat. That reality is accelerating the global race for safer alternatives and raising the question of whether the next solution could emerge from Israeli research and startups.
Prof. Brian Rosen, chief scientist at the Energy and Infrastructure Ministry, draws a clear distinction between household and personal batteries and the large-scale storage systems used for the electricity grid.
"For the public, the more urgent issue is the smaller batteries — scooters, bicycles and laptops — because that's where you see all the incidents on planes or in homes," he said. "The most suitable solution for smaller batteries is solid-state batteries."
In that technology, the flammable organic liquid between the battery's electrodes is replaced with a solid material, reducing the risk of a spreading fire.
But when it comes to large-scale storage facilities for the power grid, solid-state batteries become too expensive to be economically viable.
"Imagine a battery fire at a major electricity storage facility. It could be a catastrophe," Rosen said. "There is an inherent danger if we want to use the existing technology. That's where we see aqueous batteries as the solution. Water-based batteries address the safety concern and can also be economically viable."
In those batteries, the flammable organic solution is replaced with an aqueous one using widely available materials such as sodium, iron, zinc and bromide, eliminating the risk of ignition.
Israel has identified aqueous batteries as part of its national strategy for integrating safe energy storage into the power grid.
The Energy Ministry's chief scientist's unit supports the technology from the basic research stage at universities through the establishment of startups and field pilots. Four active studies on aqueous batteries are currently receiving funding at Bar-Ilan University, the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Ariel University.
At the same time, since 2023, the ministry has invested about 54 million shekels in the National Institute for Electrochemical Energy Storage, which operates at the Technion and Bar-Ilan University and brings together academic research and industry.
The expectation is that in the coming years, the first Israeli startups in the field will emerge from laboratories and begin launching pilot projects.
If those breakthroughs mature into commercial products, Israeli research could not only help secure the country's power grid but also provide the global energy industry with the long-awaited breakthrough in battery safety.

'Civil partnership': Naftali Bennett’s reversal and plan for LGBTQ equality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:54:52 UTC
17:54:52 KST

In 2015, when then-Jewish Home chairman Naftali Bennett was asked about same-sex marriage, he said Judaism does not recognize LGBTQ people and compared it to the fact that a law cannot declare meat and milk kosher. He described his position at the time as: "Recognition — no; rights — yes."
Now, the Beyachad (Together) party he leads is offering a far more liberal vision: a party commitment to registering partnerships with the Interior Ministry and providing full equality of rights.
More than a decade after opposing recognition of same-sex marriage, Bennett is presenting a plan aimed at granting the LGBTQ community full civil equality. Beyachad's platform includes a civil partnership framework that would grant all the rights and obligations of married couples, enshrining the right to equality in a Basic Law, a sweeping statutory ban on conversion therapy and permanent funding for services for the community.
Many of the measures are not new. Proposals for civil partnerships, enshrining equality in a Basic Law, banning conversion therapy and expanding protections against discrimination have been introduced in the Knesset over the years, but many never became law. Measures involving parenthood, surrogacy, education, welfare and health have already been advanced in part through court rulings, government decisions and changes to regulations. What is new about the plan is not necessarily the measures themselves, but who is now committing to them.
Some of those measures were advanced while Bennett himself was prime minister. During the so-called change government, the surrogacy process was effectively opened to male couples and single men following a High Court of Justice ruling, and funding for services and programs for the LGBTQ community was significantly increased. The Health Ministry also issued a directive imposing restrictions on conversion therapy carried out by licensed professionals. However, no civil partnership framework was established, the right to equality was not enshrined in a Basic Law and no sweeping statutory ban on conversion therapy was enacted.
Now, that support in principle is becoming a party commitment. Beyachad is proposing a civil framework for registering partnerships with the Interior Ministry, regardless of religion, gender or sexual orientation, that would grant all the rights and obligations of married couples. The plan, however, does not use the term "civil marriage."
At a "Sagi Laws" conference in July, Bennett said he supports allowing anyone who wants to start a family to do so in Israel "without having to travel to Cyprus, get married in Utah or go to court." The question of whether Bennett also supports same-sex marriage appears to remain open.
The party's plan also includes a commitment to advance the "Sagi Laws," a legislative package promoting equality that emerged from a campaign by Omer Ohana, whose partner, Maj. Sagi Golan, was killed on October 7.
The package addresses, among other issues, civil marriage, parental registration, a ban on conversion therapy, housing discrimination and hate crimes. At the same conference in July, Bennett said: "You are not asking for gifts here. You simply want the rights every Israeli deserves." He added: "The time has come to pass these laws."
One of the most significant provisions in the plan is a proposed "Basic Law: Equality," which would enshrine the right to equality before the law and explicitly state that rights may not be infringed on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Beyachad is also proposing an amendment to the Interpretation Law to ensure that statutory bans on discrimination also apply to discrimination against LGBTQ people. Similar proposals have been introduced in the Knesset in the past, including by Yorai Lahav-Hertzanu, but were never enacted.
The proposed ban on conversion therapy also seeks to go further than measures taken under Bennett's government. A 2022 Health Ministry directive subjected licensed professionals to sanctions if they offered, advertised or performed conversion therapy, but it did not impose a blanket legal ban. The new plan promises legislation that would prohibit the practice entirely.
Beyachad is also pledging to establish permanent, earmarked funding for programs serving the LGBTQ community in the state budget, rather than leaving such funding dependent on the decisions and priorities of each government.
Alongside the plan, Bennett has placed two openly gay former or current lawmakers who have worked to advance LGBTQ rights on his party slate: Eitan Ginzburg in the No. 8 spot and Yorai Lahav-Hertzanu at No. 18. Ginzburg was Israel's first openly gay mayor, while Lahav-Hertzanu serves as chairman of the Knesset's LGBTQ caucus.
Beyachad is not the only party putting LGBTQ rights on the agenda ahead of the election. The Democrats are pledging full legal equality, civil marriage for all couples, equal parental registration and a ban on conversion therapy. Yair Golan has also pledged to establish a national authority for LGBTQ rights.
Gadi Eisenkot pledged at the "Sagi Laws" conference to advance equality legislation. Yisrael Beytenu's platform includes civil marriage and divorce, though it does not explicitly refer to same-sex couples.
The plan's main test will be political. At this stage, it is unclear which of the commitments would survive coalition negotiations.
Bennett said: "In the next government, we will work for full equality of rights in order to protect the LGBTQ community from violence and incitement. Together, we will bring about a historic correction and erase the wrongful discrimination in this country."
Ginzburg added: "We are not second-class citizens. A country that asks everything of us must give us equal rights."

How the commanders of CODE 9.2 and the 1st Separate Assault Regiment are changing the way assault troops operate
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
11:51:00 EEST
17:51:00 KST

Mid-range strikes go in first. How the commanders of CODE 9.2 and the 1st Separate Assault Regiment are changing the way assault troops operate
On a large flat-screen monitor, once designed by someone, somewhere, for watching the evening news and TV series, a vast, slightly yellow field is clearly visible.
Every now and then, it is "cut through" by tree lines, small tarmac roads and the distant outlines of villages. But overall, the picture is monotonous and unlikely to interest anyone who does not know what they are looking at. There is no sound coming from the television either.
Instead of the news, it is showing a live feed from the camera of a Ukrainian mid-range attack drone called Darts.
Right now, it is flying over the Russian-occupied part of Zaporizhzhia Oblast towards the Tokmak-Melitopol road, one of three key routes for Russian forces on this front.
This is the first indication of how the war has changed in 2026: an assault regiment, rather than a specialised drone unit, has a UAV capable of flying 50, 100 or even 150 km beyond the line of contact. Previously, the range was 10-35 kilometres. And even 150 km is not its maximum range.
The drone is flying into a strong headwind, making small, jerky movements as it sways from side to side.
"This Darts is like a cow," a serviceman named Serhii, staring at the screen, tells Ukrainska Pravda, commenting on the drone's manoeuvrability.
"And it is easy for the enemy to shoot down. We once had a situation where they [the Russians] spotted our drone, stopped and, instead of scattering in different directions as they normally do, drove after the drone. There was nothing we could do, so we flew towards another target," adds his comrade-in-arms, Vitalii, chief of the operations section at the headquarters.
Despite its shortcomings, Darts is currently one of Ukraine's most popular mid-range drones, offering an optimal balance between cost and effectiveness.
Serhii is sitting behind a monitor at a deeply dug-in command post belonging to the 1st Assault Regiment in the south of the country. He serves as a digital officer, making sure his unit makes full use of all available digital tools, including the Delta situational-awareness system. The 1st Assault Regiment has four such specialists in this role.
Before becoming a digital officer, Serhii spent four years serving in an anti-tank company. There are now practically no tanks on the battlefield, so the knowledge and skills he acquired in his original role have largely lost their relevance.
This is the second indication of how the war has changed in 2026 – and how the Ukrainian armed forces are adapting to those changes.
"One of our drones has just been shot down. I'll fill in the flight report [in Delta] and the information will immediately appear on the relevant map layer. Then an analyst will see that several drones have been lost in this area and will adjust the route accordingly," Serhii explains, describing one of his functions.
Meanwhile, on the monitors next to him, operators continue tracking mid-range drones that have managed to break through Russian air defences. There can be five to seven aircraft in the air at the same time.
An hour later, when the commander of the 1st Assault Regiment, "Perun", arrives at the command post, we learn that none of these drones are flying at random.
They are part of an operation by Ukraine's defence forces in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, carried out by the recently established Multidomain Operations Centre of the 1st Assault Regiment and the 475th Regiment CODE 9.2. The operation is called Phalanx.
How have assault units started using mid-strikes in combination with offensive operations? Why did they decide to join forces under Phalanx? And what results are their operations producing? Read on in this report from Ukrainska Pravda.
How mid-range strikes began
The idea of writing about Phalanx emerged at Ukrainska Pravda more by chance than by design. Until just a few weeks ago, we did not even know that the centre existed.
While reporting from the Zaporizhzhia front, we travelled to the 1st Assault Regiment, which had recently begun working with mid-range drones, to see what that looked like in practice – and, most importantly, whether it was having a real, measurable impact on the line of contact.
Some of our sources, after all, were still convinced just a month ago that the effect was zero. Hundreds of strikes had hit vehicles and fuel tankers, they argued, yet the Russian advance towards the line of contact had not slowed.
The commander of the 1st Assault Regiment, Perun, arrived at the command post at around 11:00, coffee from a petrol station in hand, and opened his meeting with Ukrainska Pravda with an introductory statement. He began with the vision that has increasingly become the subject of mockery on Facebook since the departure of Mykhailo Fedorov: where are the glossy presentations, people ask, and where is the line of contact?
Perun said that just a few months earlier, his unit had had "short arms" – it could only reach the Russians no more than 30 km beyond the line of contact. That was not enough.
Here is Perun speaking:
"At some point, we came to the conclusion that dominance in the low-altitude airspace is key to modern warfare.
There is the line of contact, whose width depends on the season. In summer, it is wider because there are tree lines and vegetation and soldiers can fight at distances of 10-15 metres. In winter, it is narrower: people generally do not engage in small-arms firefights and someone sitting on the line of contact becomes more of a sitting duck on the battlefield.
And then there is the sky – that line is completely different.
We can now see that on our side of the front, the area extending 20 km back from the line of contact is already exposed to risks. From 0 to 5 km, it is an intense-strike zone. From 5 to 15, it is a logistics-isolation zone. From 15 to 20, it is an area that is not under constant attack but is under constant surveillance. Yet even if you are more than 20 km from the line of contact, you drive your car holding your breath.
The enemy is in roughly the same situation.
And we came to the conclusion that we need to expand the zone in which the enemy is afraid to breathe to 150 km.
Since 2025, we have been pushing this idea out into the wider military community. The first person to give us feedback on it was Mykhailo Albertovych [Fedorov], who had just become minister. He helped us try to put the idea into practice.
At first, we started increasing the number of heavy bombers and then we began developing a vision for isolating transport logistics. Unfortunately, that vision is now starting to lose momentum. That was the foundation for the multidomain centre that Flint [commander of the 475th Assault Regiment CODE 9.2, whom we profile below] and I created."
Until the Multidomain Operations Centre was established in summer 2026, each unit had operated in its own section of the front and at its own pace.
The CODE 9.2 Assault Regiment was the first – or perhaps one of the first in Ukraine among non-specialised units – to start using mid-range strikes.
Ukrainska Pravda travelled to Kharkiv Oblast to meet its commander, Flint, where his regiment was just finishing one of its multidomain operations (which we will return to below).
He recalls that his regiment launched its first mid-range strikes back in late 2025, during the Kupiansk operation.
This gave us a better understanding of why that operation – particularly in the forest above Kupiansk, where CODE 9.2 and the 92nd Assault Brigade were operating – was successful.
Here is Flint speaking:
"During the Kupiansk operation, we used mid-range strikes for the first time at a tactical level to support assault operations.
We captured a key forest, the one right down by the river, without any '200s' or '300s' – [military slang for personnel killed or wounded]. Twenty-four of our men cleared a forest where there were about 50 enemy troops. The enemy was so disoriented by the strikes from [Ukrainian defence company] Fire Point [drones]... they did not understand what was happening at all. That gave us an advantage.
"Where did we get Fire Point in 2025? Denys Shtilerman [co-founder of Fire Point] gave them to us – I called him and asked. I said I needed to do something... Anton Herashchenko introduced us. Shtilerman is all about the war, about victory. If I called him now and asked for 50 Fire Point drones, he would give them to me.
Our main drones now are Darts and Fire Points.
How did we come to the conclusion that operations should be conducted this way, using mid-range strikes? It was through pure practical experience – our instinct for self-preservation kicked in. We wanted to control the battlefield not for 20 km, but for 100."
At the beginning of 2026, the 1st and 475th Assault Regiments were included in a list of 20 units that received additional funding to develop their mid-range strike capabilities.
The initiative to allocate the money – albeit in a risky way, by taking it from a budget earmarked for servicemen's salaries at the end of the year – came from the team of the then Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. The sum amounted to hundreds of millions of hryvnias.
"Everyone says that Mykhailo Albertovych is only interested in drones. Well, that's not true. With this money, we bought FPV drones, reconnaissance aircraft and even radios that the infantry lacked as well as signal repeaters and pickup trucks. This was money for developing the unit," Perun says.
After receiving the additional funding, Perun's 1st Assault Regiment used a large-scale testing process to purchase mid-range drones including Darts, Fire Point, Kotyhoroshkos, Shpatels, Batons and a small number of Hornets. According to the servicemen we spoke to, there are long queues for the latter.
All of them were deployed against Russian logistics and critical infrastructure targets.
The creation of Phalanx and its first operations
The history of the Phalanx multidomain operations centre begins with how Perun and Flint first met.
They first crossed paths in 2022, during the Kharkiv offensive operation. At that time Perun was fighting in the 67th Brigade, whilst Flint was in the 92nd. Both were commanders of small units.
Recalling those times, Perun shows UP journalists an archive video on his phone. In it, in full kit and with a rifle in his hands, he and a fellow soldier are making their way through a ravaged autumn tree line in order to clear it of the enemy.
He keeps in touch with Flint over the radio.
"It was like this: we had carried out our part of the mission, then they went in (Flint's unit – UP) – and they were badly defeated. They suffered losses. I made a suggestion to him, saying: 'Sania, let us go in and do it for you.' We went in, cleared the area, and after that we have had a very warm, friendly relationship," Perun says.
This spring the two assault regiments met in Zaporizhzhia Oblast. In May they carried out their first joint operation, reaching all the way to the Crimean bridges, and a couple of months later they finally decided that they would work together as part of a multidomain centre called Phalanx.
What follows are Perun's own words:
"We discussed at length how the war needs to be waged so that it is as effective as possible for our country. We came to the conclusion that fighting in only one domain makes no sense. We'd simply lose because the enemy would bring another domain into play.
For example, there is the infantry – that is one element, there is low-altitude airspace and drones – that's the second, then the third is artillery and the fourth is cyberspace.
We tried to approach this philosophically. We examined the strengths and weaknesses of each domain, sketched out a plan for ourselves of what we could achieve with the resources currently available, not some imaginary ones.
We went through them in order, starting with the first domain – people; that is, the soldier and his support. We have made fundamental changes inside our units in the deployment of infantry.
For example, thanks to UGVs and drops from drones, we have brought our soldier's kit down to 10 kg. Our soldier can now get what he wants at a position – including a pack of red Marlboros – within 10 minutes (delivered to him by a bomber – UP). We do not merely budget for these costs, we write this into our infrastructure and the way we plan combat operations.
Or take this example from the "cyberspace" domain. We can afford to adjust artillery fire using their messenger app (this refers to hacking the enemy's social media accounts – UP). The company commander shouts: "Sh*t, that was close." We keep working on him further.
In other words, the word "multidomain" in the name of the joint centre for the two Separate Assault regiments means that their assault operation will be accompanied by a massed launch of mid-range strike drones, by artillery (Flint, for instance, actively uses Grad MLRS despite the kill zone), by intrusion into the enemy's cyberspace and so on. And ultimately this is meant to lead to the liberation of a defined portion of territory.
All the planning is based on the intersection of several domains across both units simultaneously.
However, not all the units from the CODE 9.2 regiment and the 1st Separate Assault Regiment were included in Phalanx. Some servicemen whom UP spoke with outside official meetings mentioned that for reasons unknown to them they had not had the opportunity to work in the new multidomain centre. And to a certain extent this has given rise to conflicts inside the regiment.
The name of the Phalanx centre comes from the Macedonian phalanx – a dense battle formation where soldiers carried extremely long spears, sarissas, in their hands. The length of a sarissa was 4-5 metres and, most importantly, it struck the enemy without letting them get close. Roughly speaking – a hand-held mid-range strike on a budget.
The first multidomain operation carried out by Phalanx, which we have already mentioned above, involved the bridges to Crimea.
In the regiments this operation is called an experiment. Not everything worked out the first time, they say: in some places. things were damaged rather than destroyed outright, in others the drones were shot down by the Russians.
They were prompted to carry out this experiment by an intercepted conversation involving one of the Russian commanders. He was saying that because of Ukrainian drone attacks on the roads in the occupied part of Zaporizhzhia Oblast he had to transport fuel all the way via Crimea.
"We found this out, and so we paid attention to that sector. For which we were subjected to a whole heap of investigations (by the then commander-in-chief Syrskyi – UP), saying I was guilty of making decisions single-handedly. But it all had a very good effect: within three weeks, all the units working on the isthmus and the roads towards Berdiansk and Melitopol had destroyed some 700 pieces of equipment," Perun says.
The period of the strikes on the Crimean bridges and, accordingly, the weakening of Russian supply at the front line at that time, Perun continued, was used by the 1st Separate Assault Regiment to advance to the north of Huliaipole, towards such settlements as Rybne and Uspenivka.
This is a prime example of the effect produced by the use of mid-range strikes.
Phalanx carried out its second operation in Kharkiv Oblast.
At the time of our arrival in Kharkiv to meet with Flint, CODE 9.2 had just cleared Kozacha Lopan – another village near the border through which the Russians had been infiltrating.
For the effective clearance of this sector, CODE 9.2, together with other units, blocked the enemy's logistics routes in Belgorod Oblast, knocked out a dam and destroyed bridges. In this way the enemy, while responding to the Ukrainian attacks, was unable to deploy reserves to this sector.
"We carried out a big operation to block the battlefield and logistics. Did you hear that the reservoir there was completely drained?" Flint says to us.
The main technical assets of the Ukrainian army in this operation were HIMARS and mid-range strike drones, which in the Separate Assault Regiments are often called "front-strikes" (frontline strike drones).
Phalanx's third operation took place in Zaporizhzhia Oblast. Part of that very operation – Darts hunting Russian vehicles – we saw on the screens at the command post.
Its main task was to knock out Russian logistics along three key roads in Zaporizhzhia Oblast: Tokmak – Melitopol, Tokmak – Berdiansk and Melitopol – Berdiansk.
It is precisely along these routes that the logistics for the units fighting against the 1st Separate Assault Regiment and its associates travel. And this is another answer to the question of whether mid-range strikes have an impact on the front.
Over 10 days of the operation, Phalanx destroyed 116 light vehicles and 103 heavy vehicles on the three roads. The highest-value targets, as expected, were on the road furthest from the line of contact, Melitopol – Berdiansk.
Mid-range strikes were launched literally in swarms. As far as UP is aware, roughly a third to a half of those launched reach their target. Many drones are shot down by the enemy, due to the density of mobile fire groups and interceptor crews.
Incidentally, an interesting detail is that some of the pilots serving in CODE 9.2 flew remotely – from Kharkiv Oblast – thanks to Starlink satellite links. This saves a significant amount of time and effort in redeploying the unit.
In parallel with the drones, infantry was moving through Zaporizhzhia Oblast. Over several months of gradual advance, the 1st Separate Assault Regiment liberated approximately 70 sq km of territory near the settlement of Solodke.
Overall, in terms of the number of e-points, as of the end of August 2026, Phalanx is in roughly 50th place out of more than 400 units.
***
As far as UP is aware, Perun and Flint are currently trying to persuade the new Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi to grant them more freedom than other regiments – and not to include them in the newly created Joint Rapid Response Forces.
There are several reasons for this.
Firstly, both commanders want to preserve their "assault trooper culture" – where, in their words, a commander's authority is earned in battle, shoulder to shoulder with the soldiers. Their soldiers, they say, will not respect a commander appointed from above purely on account of his rank.
Secondly, they are not keen on fighting under the command of a paratrooper.
Thirdly, like practically all strong commanders, they are convinced of their own uniqueness and effectiveness.
Whether Phalanx will continue to exist and in what format it will operate is, for now, an open question.
Olha Kyrylenko, UP

Türkiye phases out 10 food additives in new health codex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:50:35 UTC
17:50:35 KST

(AA Photo)
The Agriculture and Forestry Ministry implemented a new food flavoring regulation on Sept. 14, restricting insect- and pork-derived additives while scheduling a phase-out for 10 specific substances by 2026.
The updated Turkish Food Codex prohibits products derived from pork and insects to align with broader public health guidelines. The directive bars 10 flavoring substances, including FL 04.029, FL 05.100, FL 05.175, FL 05.222, FL 15.029, FL 15.030, FL 15.060, FL 15.119, FL 15.130 and FL 15.131, from market circulation, food production and import effective Dec. 31, 2026.
Two other substances, FL 05.062 and FL 05.099, face usage restrictions limited to designated food categories starting on the same date. The regulation prevents any covered products from being marketed under alcoholic beverage names. Certain flavorings will now require explicit ministry approval to enter the permitted list.
To label a flavoring as natural alongside a specific food or biological source, at least 95 percent of the components by weight must originate from that referenced source. If the components consist entirely of natural substances, companies can use the natural flavoring substances label. Flavorings falling under genetically modified organism regulations require clearance before ministry approval.
Purely sweet, sour or salty substances and unprocessed foods remain exempt from the new rules. Flavorings not intended for the final consumer must now display detailed labels including purpose of use, storage conditions, batch numbers and manufacturer information.
Food businesses have until Dec. 31, 2026, to comply with the updated framework, which replaces the previous directive from 2011. Products containing the restricted additives placed on the market before the deadline will remain on shelves until their expiration dates.
Turkish authorities regularly update food safety guidelines to align with international health protocols. The revisions target clearer labeling practices and tighten administrative oversight on chemical additives entering the supply chain to prevent long-term public health risks.

Lee Hao-yu sets MLB RBI record for Taiwanese players
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
08:47:08 UTC
17:47:08 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Detroit Tigers infielder Lee Hao-yu (李灝宇) drove in his 41st run of the season with a sacrifice fly Sunday, setting a new single-season MLB record for a Taiwanese player.
Lee's sacrifice fly in the fourth inning helped the Tigers defeat the Colorado Rockies 8-1 at Comerica Park, completing a three-game sweep and extending Detroit's winning streak to four games, per UDN.
Lee, batting second and starting at second base, did not record a hit but contributed with the bases loaded in the fourth. Facing Rockies reliever Zach Agnos, he lifted a fly ball to right field to bring home the Tigers' sixth run.
He went 0-for-3 with one RBI, one walk, and one strikeout. He struck out against Rockies starter Gabriel Hughes in the first inning, grounded out in the second and sixth innings, and drew a walk in the eighth. His batting average slipped slightly to .259.
Lee's 41 RBIs surpassed the previous Taiwanese single-season record of 39 set by Yu Chang (張育成) in 2021. Lee had driven in three runs in Saturday's 11-7 comeback victory over Colorado, when he went 3-for-5 with two doubles, a triple, and three RBIs, per Reuters.
Lee has also set new Taiwanese MLB marks in several other categories this season. Through 102 games, he has recorded 72 hits, 15 doubles, 41 RBIs, and 35 runs, according to ESPN.
The 23-year-old is also one home run and one triple away from tying Chang's 2021 single-season records of nine home runs and three triples by a Taiwanese MLB player.
The Tigers improved to 70-79 with the victory, while the Rockies fell to 55-94. Detroit next faces the Toronto Blue Jays on Monday.
